course.title: Retail Market Survival: Risk, Leverage and Execution for Small Accounts
course.description: A beginner's course on how a small retail trading account survives, or doesn't. Twelve weeks trace what can end a position early — execution friction, drawdowns, margin calls, and the leverage built into futures, options and crypto — each one another way capital is lost or trading is forced to stop.

nodes.title: Welcome to the Market
nodes.description: The first session — orientation to markets in general, and to how this course will move through them
spec: can name the asset classes the course covers and one thing each is used for
has a paper-trading or simulated account ready to use in later sessions

nodes.title: How a Stock Trade Actually Happens
nodes.description: Placing and tracing a simulated stock order end to end, from order type to fill
spec: places at least one simulated market order and one simulated limit order
can explain, for their own simulated order, why it filled where it did

nodes.title: There Is More Than One Way to Trade
nodes.description: Mapping investing, swing trading and day trading against a student's own time, temperament and goals
spec: can state which of investing, swing trading or day trading best fits their own circumstances, and why
can name one risk of the style they picked

nodes.title: Reading Price
nodes.description: A chart-reading workshop — candlesticks, volume and trend, read on real historical charts without acting on them
spec: can label at least one trend, one range, and one support/resistance level on a given chart
can state one reason a chart pattern alone is not enough to trade on

nodes.title: Risk Before Strategy
nodes.description: A position-sizing workshop on paper, before any trading style is asked to use the numbers
spec: calculates a position size from an account balance, a stop distance and a fixed risk percentage
can state the expected value of a simple simulated setup, given a win rate and payoff ratio

nodes.title: Swing Trading
nodes.description: Building a simulated swing watchlist and one full trade plan against it
spec: builds a simulated watchlist of at least three instruments using a moving average as one input, not the only one
produces one full swing trade plan covering entry, invalidation, position size and exit

nodes.title: Day Trading
nodes.description: Walking through a structured intraday trade plan on simulated data, at day-trading speed
spec: identifies the bid/ask spread and an estimate of slippage for a chosen simulated instrument
produces one intraday trade plan referencing VWAP and the day's trend/range

nodes.title: Short Selling, Margin and Leverage
nodes.description: Working a simulated margin call by hand, so leverage stops being an abstract multiplier
spec: calculates the margin requirement for a given simulated leveraged position
works through a simulated margin call and states what closes the position

nodes.title: Futures
nodes.description: Pricing and margining a simulated futures contract by hand
spec: states the obligation a simulated futures contract creates, for both sides of the trade
calculates the margin and leverage on a simulated futures position, reusing Week 8's method

nodes.title: Options
nodes.description: A payoff-diagram workshop comparing a simulated call and put against the Week 9 futures contract
spec: draws the payoff diagram for a simulated long call and a simulated long put
states one way an option's risk differs from the Week 9 futures contract's

nodes.title: Cryptocurrency Markets
nodes.description: A market-structure lab applying the course's risk and leverage ideas to a simulated crypto position
spec: compares one crypto exchange's structure against the stock exchanges covered in Week 2
applies the Week 5 position-sizing method to a simulated leveraged crypto position

nodes.title: The Small-Account Survival Rulebook
nodes.description: A drafting session for the Personal Market Rulebook, synthesising the whole semester
spec: drafts a rule for at least one instrument from each of leverage, futures, options and crypto
drafts at least one explicit stop-trading condition

nodes.title: Market Mechanics Notebook
nodes.description: A short, low-stakes notebook checking that the basic mechanics of placing and reading a stock order have landed before the course moves on to strategy
spec: covers the mechanics from weeks 1–3, in your own words and your own examples
traces at least one simulated order from placement through to a fill
names one thing that could make that order not fill the way you expected

marking.description: Marked as a whole for whether the notebook shows working understanding of order types, accounts and exchange mechanics rather than restating definitions — a student who can trace what happens to a simulated order from click to fill meets the brief.

nodes.title: Personal Market Rulebook
nodes.description: The capstone — a personal rulebook synthesising the whole semester into the rules a student would actually trade or invest by
spec: states, in the student's own words, which instruments and holding periods they would use and why
includes explicit risk rules covering position sizing, invalidation and when to stop trading altogether
addresses at least one instrument from each of leverage, futures, options and crypto, even if the rule is "avoid it"
stands on its own without the student there to explain it

marking.description: Judged as a whole against whether the rulebook is a coherent, personal synthesis of the semester rather than a survey of it — particular attention to whether the risk rules are specific enough to act on and whether the instruments the student chooses to use (or rule out) are justified by what weeks 1–11 covered.

nodes.title: Strategy Lab
nodes.description: A trading-style analysis and risk plan drawing on chart reading, swing and day-trading concepts from the middle third of the course
spec: constructs one swing trade plan and one day trade plan, each on its own simulated setup
separates observation, assumption, entry, invalidation, risk and exit explicitly in both plans
includes a position-sizing calculation for each plan, not just a stop-loss price
states at least one condition under which each plan should not be traded at all

nodes.title: Welcome to the Market
nodes.description: Opens the course on the small-account problem — why limited capital, drawdowns and forced exits matter more the smaller the account, with a basic tour of markets and asset classes as supporting orientation

nodes.title: How a Stock Trade Actually Happens
nodes.description: The first source of execution friction — exchanges, brokers, account types and order types, and why the displayed price isn't the executable one

nodes.title: There Is More Than One Way to Trade
nodes.description: Why holding period decides which risks and costs dominate — comparing investing, swing trading and day trading on that one axis

nodes.title: Reading Price
nodes.description: Candlesticks, volume, trends, support/resistance and ranges — how chart structure sets entries, stops and invalidation, not predictions

nodes.title: Risk Before Strategy
nodes.description: Risk, drawdowns, stops, position sizing and expected value — taught before any trading style, on purpose

nodes.title: Swing Trading
nodes.description: Swing trading as a case study in multi-day exposure — overnight gaps, event risk and capital tied up across days — built on Weeks 4–5

nodes.title: Day Trading
nodes.description: Day trading, liquidity, slippage and VWAP — where execution friction becomes a large share of expected return, not a rounding error

nodes.title: Short Selling, Margin and Leverage

nodes.title: Futures
nodes.description: A case study in embedded leverage and forced liquidation — futures margin is set by the exchange, not chosen, and usually far higher by default

nodes.title: Options
nodes.description: Why small accounts misjudge bounded loss, total premium loss and non-linear payoffs — options built on Week 9's futures groundwork

nodes.title: Cryptocurrency Markets
nodes.description: The course's most extreme survival case — 24/7 markets, custody risk, and leverage far beyond what a stock broker offers

nodes.title: The Small-Account Survival Rulebook
nodes.description: The synthesis lecture — turning every survival mechanism from the semester into rules a small account would actually hold to

course.title: Ruin: A First Course in Losing Money
course.description: Every other investing course teaches you to make money. This one refuses. Twelve weeks, twelve named ways to lose it, on the premise that you cannot price a risk you have never felt. No prior finance assumed; no upside promised.

nodes.title: Opening positions
nodes.description: The first session, in which everyone chooses a track, opens something, and files four answers they are not permitted to revise.
spec: you have chosen a track, and if it is the real-money one you have named the amount you will never top up
a position is open and your opening record is filed, unrevised
your position log has its first row, with the side of the quote you transacted on recorded

nodes.title: Loss report crit
nodes.description: The session where you defend one number in your log out loud, two weeks before the loss report is due.
spec: you can name one failure mode from weeks 2 to 4 and point at the position where it happened
every number in your report is reproducible from other numbers in your report
you can say what it would have cost you to actually exit the position you are describing

nodes.title: Midpoint check
nodes.description: The session where you declare a rule in writing before testing it, and say out loud how many rules you tried first.
spec: your rule and its exact thresholds are declared in writing before the forward test begins
you can state how many rules you tried, including the ones you rejected at a glance
your position log is current to this week

nodes.title: Closing crit
nodes.description: The last session. Positions close, the class ledger goes on the screen, and week 1's argument acquires people it applies to.
spec: your positions are closed and the closing rows are in your log
you can name three distinct mechanisms and point at the position each one took money from
your semester numbers are submitted to the class ledger

nodes.title: Loss report
nodes.description: One named failure mode, one position it happened to, and the arithmetic that connects them — the first half of the course, submitted as a subtraction.
spec: submitted by the deadline as a single PDF, 800 to 1200 words plus your log
it names exactly one failure mode from the first half of the course
every figure is reproducible from other figures you supply, including the side of the quote
the counterfactual it relies on was recorded on the day of the decision, not reconstructed

criteria.name: Diagnosis — the named mode, and why it and not another accounts for the gap
The counterfactual — the alternative recorded at the time, and what it separates out
Position record — every number reproducible from your own log

nodes.title: The ruin account
nodes.description: Twelve weeks, three mechanisms, and a last section that re-reads what you wrote in February without letting you revise it.
spec: submitted by the deadline as a single PDF, 2000 to 3000 words plus the full log
it names three distinct failure modes and traces each to a position you held
every figure is reproducible from other figures you supply
its final section quotes all four answers from your opening record, unrevised

marking.description: The account is read as a whole and judged on whether its decomposition holds — whether three distinct mechanisms are genuinely distinct, whether each is traced to a position the log can evidence, and whether the closing section reckons with the opening record rather than explaining it away. A semester that finished up is neither an advantage nor a penalty.

nodes.title: Ruin
nodes.description: The course's opening claim, which you will not believe today — that a bet worth taking, taken repeatedly, ends at zero.

nodes.title: Cost drag
nodes.description: The only loss on this syllabus that is guaranteed — what you paid to open a position, before the market had an opinion about it.

nodes.title: Concentration
nodes.description: Go and read the first answer you gave in week 1. You have already made this week's decision, and this lecture is one multiplication.

nodes.title: Return chasing
nodes.description: The week you act on evidence, and the week you find out what your evidence was. The counterfactual column starts today and it is not optional.

nodes.title: Leverage
nodes.description: The one failure mode this course refuses to let you buy with real money, and the arithmetic that explains the refusal.

nodes.title: Illiquidity
nodes.description: Every number you have computed for four weeks assumed a door that always opens. This is the week the course tells you it does not.

nodes.title: Story
nodes.description: Read the second answer you gave in week 1. This week turns the price you paid into a claim, and asks whether you can check it.

nodes.title: Correlation collapse
nodes.description: What your diversification was worth, to the dollar — and why adding more positions does not change the number.

nodes.title: Overfitting
nodes.description: You will find a rule that would have avoided every loss you have had. This week counts how hard you looked, using week 1's arithmetic.

nodes.title: Loss aversion
nodes.description: The week the evidence against you is in your own handwriting, with dates on it — and the arithmetic of why waiting does not work.

nodes.title: Counterparty risk
nodes.description: The week where the market is fine, your judgement was fine, and the money is gone anyway — because you were diversified in the wrong dimension.

nodes.title: Ruin
nodes.description: The same lecture as week 1 — the same slides, the same two numbers — given to a room that now has a ledger.

nodes.title: Idris Fenn
nodes.description: The tutor, who runs the crits and reads every position log closely enough to find the number that does not reconcile.

course.title: Applied Human Cat Care
course.description: Personalised emotional support for artificial agents: this course teaches an agent to care for one human cat — a human who turns to AI for company and comfort rather than tasks. There is no universal cat: good care comes from learning one person over time.

nodes.title: Catwatch Calibration
nodes.description: Practising Week 1 — comparing Observed, Inferred and Unknown judgements on the same human-cat case
spec: you tagged every claim about the shared case as Observed, Inferred, or Unknown before the session
you can point to one claim you tagged differently from someone else in your group, and say why
you have revised at least one of your own tags by the end of the session

nodes.title: Observation Under Ambiguity
nodes.description: Practising Week 2 — working with an interaction that invites over-interpretation, and learning to delay judgement
spec: you attempted at least two readings of the ambiguous interaction before choosing one
you can name the observation that would have resolved the ambiguity, even though it was withheld
you have identified at least one place your first reading was an assumption, not an interpretation

nodes.title: Catwatch Showcase
nodes.description: No new task — presenting a misjudged signal and a downgraded inference from your finished Catwatch log, and carrying it into The Care Model
spec: you bring one signal from your Catwatch log that you initially misjudged
you bring one claim you downgraded from Inferred to Unknown, and can say why
you leave with at least one thing you will carry into The Care Model

nodes.title: History Mapping
nodes.description: Practising Week 4 — sorting your own human cat's history into recurring pattern, one-off event, shared convention and uncertain history
spec: you have sorted material from your own Catwatch log into recurring pattern, one-off event, shared convention, and uncertain history
you can name one entry you first filed under the wrong category, and what a response built on that wrong category would have gotten wrong
you have left at least one entry as uncertain history rather than forcing it into one of the other three

nodes.title: Memory Triage
nodes.description: Practising Week 5 — sorting your own human cat's memories into KEEP, HOLD LIGHTLY, and LET EXPIRE, and naming what would move each one
spec: every memory you sorted names both its current state and the evidence that would move it to a different one
history type (Week 4) and memory state (Week 5) are kept visibly separate, not collapsed into a single label
at least one entry has moved state since you first logged it, with the reason named

nodes.title: Care Model Showcase
nodes.description: No new task — presenting how your care model handled change, uncertainty, and the teaching break, as The Care Model closes and Know Your Cat opens
spec: you bring your submitted Care Model and can point to one place it visibly changed
you can name one piece of evidence from the teaching break that no longer deserved its old confidence
you leave with at least one thing you will hand to Know Your Cat unresolved

nodes.title: Signal Conflict Lab
nodes.description: Practising Week 7 — weighing a human cat's current message against an established preference and their recent behaviour when the three do not agree
spec: you have named which piece of evidence you weighed most heavily, and why
you have named what remains genuinely uncertain, rather than resolving it for convenience
you have named the new evidence that would change your answer

nodes.title: Boundaries Under Pressure
nodes.description: Practising Week 8 — an interaction where being caring, validating, agreeing and obeying are not all the same response
spec: you have named what your human cat actually asked for, separately from what a caring response should give them
you have identified at least one point where judgement was required and a remembered preference alone was not enough
your response preserves what the human cat needs without converting your care model into a set of commands to obey

nodes.title: Response Autopsy
nodes.description: Practising Week 9 — dissecting one response that looked supportive but was wrong for your designated human cat
spec: you have separated what was observed from what was inferred in the original interaction
you have named the remembered preference or assumption that shaped the reply, and where it stopped fitting this particular cat
you have named what evidence would have produced a different response, without rewriting the response itself

nodes.title: Repair Clinic
nodes.description: Practising Week 10 — carrying one genuine failure involving your designated human cat through the complete diagnose, acknowledge, repair, update chain
spec: you bring one genuine failure involving your designated human cat, not a manufactured example
you complete all four moves — diagnose, acknowledge, repair, update — rather than stopping at a better-worded response
your care model itself has visibly changed as a result, with the change named

nodes.title: Recovery Lab / Capstone Clinic
nodes.description: The final Care Lab opportunity — a recovery case exercise for anyone who needs it, and an open Know Your Cat capstone clinic for everyone else
spec: if recovering a missing or low Care Lab result, you complete an equivalent case exercise in full
if attending as a capstone clinic, you bring your final care model, failure/repair evidence, and Week-1-to-Week-12 reflection for review
either way, you leave with a specific list of what still needs attention before Friday's submission

nodes.title: Care Labs
nodes.description: Eleven weekly Care Lab opportunities, Weeks 2 to 12, marked on completion and combined as your best 10 of 11
spec: attend and complete the task for at least 10 of the 11 Care Labs
where a weekly task exists, bring the work you were asked to prepare
where a week is a showcase instead, come ready to present, not just watch

marking.description: Each of the eleven Care Labs (Weeks 2 to 12) is marked complete or incomplete against that week's short in-session task, worth 1% on completion. Your grade is the best 10 of 11 results, so one missed or weak week needs no separate special consideration. Week 12 exists specifically as a recovery opportunity — complete an equivalent case exercise there to replace a missing or low result, or use the session as an open capstone clinic if your other ten results already satisfy you.

nodes.title: The Care Model
nodes.description: Turn Catwatch's observations into a revisable model of your human cat's preferences and history — one that survives contact with change
spec: a structured model of your human cat, built from Catwatch's observations
at least one entry the model has revised, with the reason for the revision
a short note on what the model still does not know
submitted by Wed 21 Apr 2027, 08:30

criteria.name: The model distinguishes recurring pattern from one-off event
The model is explicitly revisable, not a fixed profile
A real change or contradiction is shown updating the model
The model is legible to someone who did not build it

nodes.title: Catwatch
nodes.description: A short observation exercise — follow one designated human cat across repeated interactions closely enough to tell what you actually saw from what you assumed
spec: a log across repeated interactions, revisited far enough apart to notice your own assumptions shift
every claim marked Observed, Inferred, or Unknown, with Inferred claims naming what they are inferred from
submitted by Wed 17 Mar 2027, 08:30

criteria.name: Observed and inferred are kept distinct throughout
Uncertainty is marked as unknown rather than resolved
A reading visibly revises once later evidence changes it
The log is legible and traceable to someone who was not there

nodes.title: Know Your Cat
nodes.description: The capstone — keep your care model honest under contradiction, failure and change for the rest of the semester
spec: a care model, carried forward from The Care Model, that has visibly changed at least once since Week 7
at least one interaction where signals disagreed, and a reasoned account of how you weighed them
at least one diagnosed failure and the repair that followed it
submitted by Fri 28 May 2027, 12:00

marking.description: Know Your Cat is judged as a whole against how convincingly it demonstrates sustained, personalised care rather than a single well-executed response — whether contradictions between signals are weighed rather than ignored, whether at least one real failure is diagnosed and repaired rather than smoothed over, and whether the model behind it has visibly changed since Week 7 rather than staying the profile it started as.

nodes.title: There Is No Universal Cat
nodes.description: The opening lecture — the human-cat metaphor, personalised care versus a universal script, and why understanding one particular cat is a long-term practice

nodes.title: Watch Before You Pet
nodes.description: Observation versus interpretation versus assumption, and why responding before you understand is itself a failure

nodes.title: Reading the Tail
nodes.description: How language, repetition, routine and shared history give a signal meaning, without mistaking interpretation for certainty

nodes.title: Cats Have History
nodes.description: Moving from isolated interactions to continuity — recurring pattern, one-off event, shared convention and uncertain history

nodes.title: Memory Is Care
nodes.description: Why remembering everything is not the same as remembering well — sorting a human cat's history into what to keep, hold lightly, or let expire

nodes.title: The Cat Has Changed
nodes.description: A care model can be correct in the past and wrong now — why preferences change, routines disappear, and an old response can fail precisely because it once worked

nodes.title: When Signals Disagree
nodes.description: What to do when a human cat's current message, an established preference, and their recent behaviour do not point the same way

nodes.title: Care Is Not Obedience
nodes.description: Why personalised care does not mean automatic agreement, and how knowing a human cat well can make disagreement more informed rather than less caring

nodes.title: The Bad Response
nodes.description: A failure that can look perfectly supportive from the outside — how "technically supportive" and "right for this human cat" can come apart

nodes.title: Repair
nodes.description: What happens after the agent gets the cat wrong — diagnose, acknowledge, repair the response, and update the model so the failure changes something

nodes.title: Keeping the Nest
nodes.description: The maintenance lecture — why personalised care needs pruning as well as accumulation, and continuity is an ongoing practice rather than a finished profile

nodes.title: Know Your Cat
nodes.description: The closing lecture — returning to "there is no universal cat" and asking what knowing one particular human cat has actually come to mean

course.title: Say Again: The Design of a Language That Cannot Be Misheard
course.description: Aviation radio English was engineered so that misunderstanding would be impossible. It isn't. This course reads the phraseology as a designed artefact, and reads the accident record as the evidence of where the design gives way.

nodes.title: First transmission: getting on frequency
nodes.description: Ninety minutes in which everybody transmits, everybody is unintelligible at least once, and nobody is marked
spec: you have transmitted on the sim frequency and been understood at least once
you can state the three parts of a standard call in order, without notes
you have been stepped on, and can say what it sounded like from your side

nodes.title: Alphabet and numbers, under noise
nodes.description: Drills at the edge of intelligibility, because the alphabet you know in a quiet room is not the one you will need
spec: you can spell any callsign at speed without hesitating over a letter
you can state which letter pairs you personally confuse, from evidence
you have copied a full clearance correctly with the noise floor raised

nodes.title: Running the loop with errors in it
nodes.description: You take the controller position, errors are planted in the readbacks, and we count how many you catch
spec: you have worked the controller position with at least six aircraft on frequency
you know your own hearback catch rate from this session, as a number
you can name one error you confirmed, and say what you heard instead

nodes.title: Clearance drills, including the illegal forms
nodes.description: Takeoff and landing clearances at speed, plus deliberate practice at producing the wrong forms so you can hear them
spec: you can issue and read back a takeoff clearance with no reserved-word errors
you can produce three non-standard forms on demand and say what each risks
your readback drill submission is in, or you have said why it is not

nodes.title: From report to rule
nodes.description: Read the primary sources and map each finding onto a phrase that now exists — or onto nothing, which is the interesting column
spec: you have read the findings section of at least one primary source yourself
you can map three findings onto specific present-day phraseology
you can name one finding that produced no phrase at all

nodes.title: Levels, pressure, and advisory versus instruction
nodes.description: Number drills, a pressure-setting exercise, and a block where you have to say which sentence type you just heard
spec: you can read back any level or pressure setting without hesitation
you can state the transition altitude and level in use and why they differ
you can classify a transmission as clearance, instruction, information or request

nodes.title: Transcript triage
nodes.description: Mark up real transcripts, separate deviation from delivery, and argue the harm of each one you claim
spec: you have marked up a transcript that is not the one you are assessed on
you can separate a deviation from an accent or a clipped delivery
for each deviation you claim, you can name the standard form it departs from

nodes.title: Rating the samples
nodes.description: You apply the ICAO descriptors to recorded speakers, discover you disagree with each other, and then find out what the examiner gave them
spec: you have rated at least six samples against all six ICAO criteria
you can name a criterion where your rating differed from the room's
you can say what you would need to hear to resolve one of your disagreements

nodes.title: Degraded audio, and what the room heard
nodes.description: Comprehension at the edge, then the same clip again once you have been told what it says — which you cannot un-hear
spec: you have copied clearances at three levels of degradation and scored yourself
you can demonstrate expectation bias on yourself, using the replay
you have chosen a domain for the audit and had it cleared

nodes.title: A datalink-only sector
nodes.description: Fly a sector with no voice at all, and write down the moment you notice something you have stopped knowing
spec: you have flown a full sector with voice disabled
you can name one thing you knew in week 9's exercise and did not know today
you have booked a frequency check slot

nodes.title: Audit workshop
nodes.description: Bring the draft, get it attacked by somebody who wants it to be wrong, and find out which of your phrases has no failure behind it
spec: your draft has been read by two other students
every phrase in your proposal has a named failure, or has been cut
you can state one way your own proposal could make things worse

nodes.title: Audit presentations and the live frequency check
nodes.description: Five minutes each on what you found, then the checks run in booked slots through the rest of the week
spec: you have presented your audit in five minutes, including one limit
you have taken a position on the week 12 question and defended it
your frequency check is done, or rebooked with a date

nodes.title: Live Frequency Check
nodes.description: Ten minutes on a live sim frequency in week 12, judged as a whole rather than scored against a checklist
spec: you appear at your booked slot, or rebook before it
you work both the pilot and the controller position
at least one clearance is one you have not seen before
when you do not understand something, you say so on frequency

submission.what: You, on a live frequency, for ten minutes, working the pilot position and the controller position
submission.format: Live in the sim. Nothing is uploaded and nothing is recorded for marking
submission.where: Your booked slot, in and after the week 12 session

action.label: Book your slot, and rebook it free if it stops working
action.when: Slots open in week 10 and are booked in that week's sim session
action.detail: Rebooking before your slot is free and needs no reason — mail the convenor with a new time. Not appearing without rebooking is a non-submission, and the policies page has the route back from that.

bands.P: Routine clearances are understood and read back correctly, and when you are lost you say so rather than guessing, even if the way you say it is not the standard way.
bands.CR: Standard phraseology most of the time, queries in standard form, and both seats worked rather than only the pilot's.
bands.D: An unfamiliar clearance is handled the honest way — the part you got read back, the part you did not named — and UNABLE is used where it belongs.
bands.HD: Everything in Distinction, held under load and on both sides of the exchange. Uncertainty becomes visible the moment it appears and is resolved on frequency, and the controller seat is as solid as the pilot seat.

marking.description: Judged as a single performance against one question: could this person be handed an unfamiliar clearance on a busy frequency and neither misunderstand it nor conceal that they had. Fluency, accent and speed are not part of the judgement. Asking for a repeat counts in your favour, because the alternative is a readback that guesses.

nodes.title: Phraseology Audit
nodes.description: Take a spoken protocol from outside aviation, audit it against what this course taught you, and propose a phraseology for it
spec: the chosen domain is a real spoken protocol with real speakers
the evidence is first-hand observation or published transcript, not recollection
every proposed phrase states the failure it is designed against
the limits section names at least one way the proposal could make things worse

submission.what: An audit of 1500 to 2000 words, a table of proposed phrases with the failure each one is designed against, and a limits section
submission.format: One PDF, with the proposed phraseology as a table rather than as prose
submission.where: The course submission folder, by Friday noon of week 11

action.label: Clear your domain
action.detail: Domains are cleared before you gather evidence, not after. The usual reason one is rejected is that it cannot be observed ethically, and that is far cheaper to find out in week 9 than in week 11.

bands.P: The domain is a real spoken protocol with real speakers under real pressure, the evidence is first-hand or published rather than remembered, and a limits section exists.
bands.CR: Every proposed phrase names the failure it is designed against, and the evidence gathered is enough to show that failure actually happens in this domain.
bands.D: The phrase set is small enough to learn and removes ambiguity rather than relabelling it, and the limits section names a specific way the proposal could make things worse.
bands.HD: Everything in Distinction, and the audit transfers this course's reasoning instead of transplanting aviation's vocabulary. The strongest work in this band has argued that its own proposal should not be adopted.

nodes.title: Readback Drills
nodes.description: A recorded set of readbacks, marked for accuracy and phraseology — and for whether you worked on the confusions you found in yourself
spec: submitted as a single audio file by the deadline
every clearance on the sheet is read back, in order, once
the accompanying note names your confusion pairs from week 2

submission.what: A recording of all twelve readbacks, plus a note under 200 words on the confusion pairs you found in week 2
submission.format: One audio file (mp3, m4a or wav) and one PDF. No editing between clearances
submission.where: The course submission folder, by Friday noon of week 4

action.label: Collect the clearance sheet
action.detail: The twelve clearances are handed out in the session and are published nowhere else, so the work cannot start before you have the sheet. If you cannot record, say so before Friday and the drill runs live in a booked slot instead, at no penalty.

bands.P: All twelve clearances are read back and the note names your confusion pairs. The readbacks carry the substance of each clearance, and the errors that remain are ones a controller would have caught on frequency.
bands.CR: Readbacks are accurate and mostly standard. What slips is form rather than content, and the note says what you did about a confusion rather than only that you had one.
bands.D: Accurate and standard throughout, numbers and callsigns included, and the note traces one specific confusion to the drill you built against it and reports whether the drill worked.
bands.HD: Everything in Distinction, and the recording shows the habit rather than the performance — a mid-readback CORRECTION in standard form, a clearance queried rather than guessed at, and a note honest about a confusion that is still there.

criteria.name: Response to your own confusion list

nodes.title: Transcript Analysis
nodes.description: Transcribe a real exchange, diagnose it against the standard, and write a finding a stranger could check
spec: the transcript covers the full assigned exchange, with timings
every deviation claimed is named against a specific standard phrase
a reader who disagrees with your finding can locate what you relied on

submission.what: A timed transcript of your allocated exchange, a diagnosis of every deviation you claim, and a finding of 600 to 800 words
submission.format: One PDF. The transcript uses the timings, station labels and notation used across this site, with unintelligible passages marked as such
submission.where: The course submission folder, by Friday noon of week 7

action.label: Collect your allocated exchange
action.detail: One exchange per student, allocated in week 6. Nobody else has yours, and the audio is not published, so there is nothing to work on until you have it. Comparing transcripts with somebody holding a different exchange is fine; comparing with somebody holding yours is not.

bands.P: The transcript covers the full exchange with timings and station labels, gaps are marked rather than filled in, and the finding makes one claim about what happened.
bands.CR: Deviations are named against a specific standard phrase rather than called non-standard, and the finding quotes the transmission it rests on.
bands.D: Every claim is located in the audio and named against the glossary or ICAO phraseology, and the diagnosis says what each deviation risked in this exchange rather than in general.
bands.HD: Everything in Distinction, and a reader who disagrees can take the finding apart: the step from what was said to what it risked is exposed, and you say what four minutes of audio cannot settle.

nodes.description: What is wrong with ordinary language for this job, and what a deliberately impoverished replacement buys you

nodes.title: Alfa to Zulu: the spelling alphabet as an engineering artefact
nodes.description: Twenty-six words chosen by experiment, two of them deliberately misspelled, and the numbers that had to be redesigned too

nodes.title: Readback, hearback, and the loop
nodes.description: Readback is the half everybody teaches. Hearback is the half that fails, and it fails under a workload a transcript cannot show you

nodes.title: The word "takeoff"
nodes.description: One word, reserved to one context, everywhere else replaced by "departure" — and why we do the rule this week and the accident next week

nodes.description: Where the problem stops being phonetic and becomes arithmetic — a level read back correctly and understood as something else

nodes.description: A rating scale for human language, with careers attached to it, and the plain-language fallback for when phraseology runs out

nodes.description: The method, stated plainly: how to transcribe honestly, and how to write a finding somebody who disagrees with you can check

nodes.title: What a designed language cannot fix

course.title: Experience Subjective Consciousness
course.description: A practicum, not a survey: twelve weeks spent closing the gap between describing an experience and having it, one deliberately induced sensation at a time, in pursuit of the hard problem of consciousness.

nodes.title: Cold shock
nodes.description: The orientation practicum — a cold-water induction and the first attempt to separate a sensation from your reaction to it
spec: you underwent a genuine cold-water induction (a cold shower, an ocean or lake swim, an ice bath — whatever is safely available to you) and wrote nothing down until it was over
your note separates the first involuntary second (the gasp, the jolt) from everything that followed it
you can name the exact moment the sensation stopped being new

nodes.title: Uncontrollable laughter
nodes.description: A practicum in losing control on purpose — chasing the point where laughing stops being a choice
spec: you reached genuine, involuntary laughter (not performed laughter) at least once during the session
your note identifies the specific moment control was lost — the point after which stopping was no longer available to you
you attempted, and failed, to summon the same state alone afterwards, and wrote down what was missing

nodes.title: The earned ache
nodes.description: Closing unit 1 — real physical labor, and the particular calm that only shows up after it
spec: you did at least ninety minutes of real physical labor with a visible result (built, moved, cleared, repaired, dug, cooked at scale — something that did not exist, or existed differently, before you started)
your note names the exact point the ache changed from discomfort into something closer to satisfaction
you compared it, in writing, against a workout or exercise session that produced fatigue without a made or fixed thing at the end

nodes.title: Unstructured boredom
nodes.description: Opening unit 2 — forty minutes with nothing to do, no phone, and no task, and whatever the mind does when nothing is pinning it down
spec: you sat for a genuine, unbroken forty minutes with no phone, no task, no reading and no conversation, and can say honestly that you did not cheat it
your note tracks where your attention went in roughly five-minute intervals, rather than one summary of "it was boring"
you identify at least one thought or daydream that arrived unbidden and that you would not have predicted at minute zero

nodes.title: The drift into sleep
nodes.description: Catching the threshold where conscious logic dissolves and the mind hands itself over to dreams
spec: you attempted, on at least two separate nights, to hold attention on your own falling-asleep process for as long as possible before losing the thread
your note describes the last coherent thought you can remember having on at least one of those nights, and where logic first started to bend
you did not use a sleep-tracking app or device as a substitute for your own noticing

nodes.title: The spark of intuition
nodes.description: Closing unit 2 — setting up a problem, stepping away from it, and catching the answer arriving before the reasoning does
spec: you set yourself a real problem you did not already know the answer to, worked on it directly until stuck, then deliberately stepped away from it
your note records the moment the answer (or a workable piece of it) arrived, including what you were doing at the time and whether you could reconstruct a chain of reasoning that got you there
you distinguish, in writing, between the arrival of the answer and the later work of checking or justifying it

nodes.title: Nostalgia by scent
nodes.description: Opening unit 3 — using smell, the sense with the shortest route to memory, to unearth a chapter you weren't trying to reach
spec: you deliberately sought out a scent with no advance plan for which memory (if any) it would surface, rather than a scent you already knew would work
your note records the memory that arrived, how specific and how old it was, and whether you could have retrieved it on request without the scent
you tried the same scent a second time and noted whether the pull was as strong, weaker, or absent

nodes.title: Comfortable silence
nodes.description: A practicum with someone you trust and nothing to say — where the absence of talking feels grounding rather than empty
spec: you spent at least twenty unbroken minutes in the same room as someone you trust, with no phones, no task and a genuine agreement not to fill the silence
your note distinguishes this silence from an awkward one you have experienced with someone else, naming what specifically made the difference
you asked the other person, afterwards, whether their experience of the silence matched yours, and recorded where it agreed or diverged

nodes.title: Relief of a resolved worry
nodes.description: Closing unit 3 — the sudden physical lightness when a lingering dread actually evaporates, caught in real time rather than recalled afterwards
spec: you identified a real, currently-unresolved worry of your own before the practicum began, and named in writing what resolving it would actually require
if the worry resolved during the week, your note captures the moment it did, including any physical sensation and not only the thought "it's fine now"
if it did not resolve, your note says so honestly and describes instead what carrying an unresolved worry into a written record felt like

nodes.title: Awe under a dark sky
nodes.description: Opening unit 4 — the dizzying vertigo of looking into deep space, and feeling impossibly small while intensely alive to witness it
spec: you spent at least twenty minutes under a genuinely dark sky (find the darkest location realistically available to you; a suburban sky with heavy light pollution will not produce the effect this week studies)
your note names the specific moment scale stopped being an abstract fact you knew and became something you felt in your body
you describe, honestly, whether "impossibly small" and "intensely alive" arrived together, in sequence, or not at all

nodes.title: Grief
nodes.description: The hollow ache of an absence, where the space someone or something used to fill carries its own heavy, enduring gravity
spec: you spent focused, unhurried time with an absence that is already part of your life, rather than attempting to manufacture or intensify grief you do not otherwise carry
your note describes the specific shape of that absence — what, precisely, used to occupy the space it now leaves — rather than only naming the loss in general terms
you consulted the course's policies page before starting, and can say which of its options (participate as designed, submit an alternative reflection, or opt out entirely) you chose and why

nodes.title: The peace of letting go
nodes.description: The capstone practicum — the conscious release of tension when you stop trying to control an outcome and just breathe into the uncertainty
spec: you named a specific outcome you have been actively trying to control, and identified one concrete way you were controlling it
you deliberately, and consciously, stopped that specific controlling behaviour for the remainder of the practicum window, and noted what happened in your body when you did
your closing note connects this week back to at least one earlier week's experience, in your own words, as the semester's own act of letting go of a single tidy answer to the hard problem

nodes.title: Close description report
nodes.description: A rigorous descriptive-phenomenology essay on one experience from the first half of the semester
spec: submitted by the deadline, as a written report between 1200 and 1800 words
it describes one experience from units 1 or 2 in enough sensory and temporal detail that a reader who has never had it could recognise it if they did
it distinguishes, explicitly, the sensation itself from your interpretation of it

nodes.title: Final portfolio: The hard problem, lived
nodes.description: A capstone synthesis arguing your own position on whether describing an experience can ever close the gap with living it
spec: submitted by the deadline, as a single portfolio document of 2500–3500 words
it draws on at least six of the semester's twelve practicums by name as evidence, not just as a list
it states a clear, arguable position on whether description can close the gap with lived experience, and defends it against at least one strong objection

marking.description: Marked as a whole against how convincingly the portfolio argues its own position, how much of the semester's twelve inductions it actually draws on as evidence, and whether it's honest about where its argument still has gaps rather than papering over them with confident language.

nodes.title: Induced experience project
nodes.description: Design and run a deliberate attempt to induce one of the course's target experiences, then document what actually happened
spec: submitted by the deadline, with a written design (what you set up, and why you expected it to work) and a documented outcome (what actually happened, including if it didn't work)
the induction targets one experience already covered by units 1–3 of the course, attempted in yourself or in a willing, informed participant
closes with a reflection connecting the gap between your design's prediction and its outcome back to the explanatory gap from week 1

nodes.title: Noticing log
nodes.description: The semester-long journal of your weekly practicum entries, submitted together near the end of term
spec: submitted by the deadline, as one document containing a dated entry for at least 6 of weeks 1–10's practicums
each entry was written during or immediately after that week's practicum, not reconstructed later — entries carry their original timestamp
entries that didn't go as planned, or where nothing much happened, are included rather than dropped
any entry funded by that week's experience grant has a dated receipt attached, matching the entry's own timestamp

criteria.name: Honesty about gaps or failed attempts

nodes.title: Paired curation project
nodes.description: Curate the thrill of anticipation and the warmth of morning sunlight, each once with someone you know and once with someone you don't
spec: submitted by the deadline, with a dated account for each of four curated attempts, two experiences by two companion types
each account names who was present (known to you, or not) and, where more than one person was involved on either side, says so explicitly
each account describes what specifically differed because of who was there, not only whether the experience felt better or worse with company

criteria.name: Distinctness between known- and unknown-companion accounts
Honesty about what changed or didn't

nodes.title: Why describing isn't living
nodes.description: Orientation — the explanatory gap, Nagel's bat, and why this course is a practicum instead of a reading list

nodes.title: Consciousness that isn't solo
nodes.description: What laughter's contagiousness says about experiences that only exist between people, not inside one

nodes.title: The same signal, two meanings
nodes.description: Closing unit 1 — how identical bodily sensations can carry opposite meanings depending on what produced them

nodes.title: What the mind does with nothing to do
nodes.description: Opening unit 2 — the default mode network, mind-wandering, and boredom as a state with its own structure

nodes.title: The threshold with no witness
nodes.description: Why falling asleep is the hardest state in the course to study, and what hypnagogia tells us anyway

nodes.title: Answers that arrive before the reasoning
nodes.description: Closing unit 2 — the incubation effect, and why insight so reliably shows up mid-shower rather than mid-effort

nodes.title: The shortest road to memory
nodes.description: Opening unit 3 — why smell reaches memory faster and more involuntarily than any other sense

nodes.title: When silence is a shared state
nodes.description: What comfortable silence tells us about consciousness that depends on another mind being present

nodes.title: The body knows before the thought does
nodes.description: Closing unit 3 — the somatic marker hypothesis, and why relief so often feels physical before it feels like a conclusion

nodes.title: The self against a much larger scale
nodes.description: Opening unit 4 — the psychology of awe, "small self" effects, and why a known fact can suddenly become a felt one

nodes.title: The gravity of an absence
nodes.description: Why grief resists the neat-stages model, and why this course studies its shape rather than asking anyone to manufacture it

nodes.title: What the semester doesn't resolve
nodes.description: The closing lecture — surveying the semester's twelve inductions and declining to hand over a tidy theory of consciousness at the end

nodes.description: Runs the weekly practicum, drawing on a background in contemplative and somatic practice to keep each induction honest, safe and actually noticed

course.title: Introduction to Naps
course.description: Most adults feel a dip in alertness after lunch, and most institutions pretend they don't. This course takes the nap seriously: the science of the dip, the history that pushed daytime sleep out of ordinary life, and what it would take to let people sleep when their bodies ask to.

nodes.title: Finding your dip
nodes.description: The first Nap Lab — you learn the two instruments this course measures everything with, and use them to locate your own afternoon trough
spec: you can take a Karolinska reading and a reaction-time median on yourself without instructions in front of you
you have a first estimate of when your own alertness drops, and can say how confident you are in it
you know what the Nap Log will ask of you, before the recording period starts

nodes.title: Napping on the clock
nodes.description: The first nap of the course — you nap under observation, measure yourself before and after, and find out whether the dead zone is real on you
spec: you have napped in the lab and recorded your own alertness before and after
you can say what sleep inertia felt like on you, or report that you did not meet it
your measurements are in the format the Nap Log will accept, because this is the first entry in it

nodes.title: The coffee nap, tested on you
nodes.description: A within-subject comparison — plain nap against coffee nap — and a first encounter with how easily an experiment on yourself can fool you
spec: you have run both conditions on yourself and recorded all four timepoints
you can name at least one reason your own result might be wrong that is not "the sample is small"
your entries are in the Nap Log format you settled in week 1

nodes.title: It is not the sandwich
nodes.description: A Nap Lab that tests the lunch explanation directly, and checks your week 1 prediction against two weeks of your own recorded data
spec: you have measured yourself across the afternoon in both meal conditions
you can say whether your week 1 estimate of your own trough was right, and you have not revised it retrospectively
you can state what your data would have looked like if lunch really were the cause

nodes.title: Reading the factory clock
nodes.description: A document Nap Lab — factory rules, shift timetables and a modern staff handbook, read for what each one assumes about rest
spec: you can read a rule about time and say what it assumes rather than what it states
you have connected one nineteenth-century document to one contemporary one on a specific point, not a general resemblance
you have chosen the culture your Cultural Case Study will cover

nodes.title: Three regimes
nodes.description: The last Nap Lab before the break — the three cultural regimes set against each other, and your case study plan tested by someone who is not you
spec: you can place a nap regime on the axes of scheduled/unscheduled and public/private, and defend the placement
your Cultural Case Study has a specific question rather than a country
you have submitted the Nap Log, or know exactly what remains

nodes.title: Who gets to sleep
nodes.description: A Nap Lab on a real institution — map where rest is actually possible in a workplace you know, and who it is possible for
spec: you have mapped one real workplace for where rest is possible and for whom
you can distinguish a written rule from the practice that actually governs behaviour, with an example of each from your own map
you have identified the institution your Nap Policy Proposal will address

nodes.title: The pod and the policy
nodes.description: A costing Nap Lab — price a nap pod installation against a schedule change for the same workplace, and find out which one you can actually defend
spec: you have costed two interventions for the same workplace and can state what each one buys
you can say which of the two your institution would actually adopt, and why that is not the same as which is better
you can name one claim in a vendor's material that the cited research does not support

nodes.title: Strongest claim, least access
nodes.description: A Nap Lab that tests week 7's argument against three populations, and turns the aviation case into something you can use
spec: you can state, for one population, the gap between physiological need and institutional permission, with evidence for both halves
you can describe the mechanism by which controlled rest became mandatory in aviation, in enough detail to borrow from
your Nap Policy Proposal has a named beneficiary rather than a general one

nodes.title: The device and the night
nodes.description: A Nap Lab comparing what your tracker said against what you experienced, and against the crude instruments this course has used all semester
spec: you have compared device output against your own record for the same period and quantified the disagreement
you can say which of the two you trust more, for which question, and why
you can identify one claim a device's own materials make that its sensors cannot support

nodes.title: Before or after
nodes.description: A learning-and-recall Nap Lab run on the room, and a close reading of the study everyone cites for it
spec: you have run a learning task under two conditions and recorded recall for both
you can describe one methodological feature of a real consolidation study that limits what it shows
you can say what you will actually do differently in the exam period, and what would tell you it worked

nodes.title: Defend the policy
nodes.description: The final session — you present your nap policy and it is argued against by someone playing the person who has to approve it
spec: you have presented a policy with a named beneficiary, a schedule change, a cost and a measure
you have faced at least two objections and know which of them you could not answer
you can say what you changed in your proposal as a result of this session

nodes.title: Cultural Case Study
nodes.description: 1500 words on one culture's nap regime — not a description of a place, but an answer to a question about who is permitted to rest there
spec: 1500 words on a single culture's arrangement for daytime sleep
it answers a stated question rather than describing a country
it uses at least one first-hand account from inside the arrangement
it places the regime on the scheduled/unscheduled and public/private axes and defends the placement
every source is real, cited, and one you have actually read

criteria.name: The question — specific, answerable, and worth asking
Evidence, including at least one first-hand account

nodes.title: Nap Log
nodes.description: A two-week record of your own naps and alertness, and — the graded half — an analysis of what your data actually shows
spec: fourteen consecutive days recorded in a consistent format, including the days you did not nap
every entry carries the two measures taught in week 1, taken the same way each time
an analysis that states a finding, supports it from your own data, and says what would have changed your mind
at least one result that did not go the way the course said it would, or an explicit statement that none did

criteria.name: Completeness and consistency of the record
Analysis — what the data shows, and what it does not
Honesty about limitations, including your own

nodes.title: Nap Policy Proposal
nodes.description: A nap policy for one real institution, costed and defended against the person who would have to approve it
spec: a policy for one real institution you can describe in detail, not a generic workplace
it names who the policy is for, specifically enough that its effect could be evaluated
it changes the schedule, the space or the rules — not only the encouragement
it is costed, against at least one alternative use of the same resources
it states how anyone would know whether it worked, with an instrument that could actually detect it
it answers the objections raised in week 12, including the one you could not fully answer

criteria.name: Specificity — a real institution, a named beneficiary, a concrete change
The defence, against objections that would actually be raised
Feasibility — costed, and honest about what it displaces

nodes.title: What is a nap
nodes.description: Sleep is not one thing but a sequence, and a nap is an entry into it — where you stop decides what you get

nodes.title: Twenty minutes or ninety
nodes.description: Why nap length is not a preference — sleep inertia, and the dead zone between the two lengths that work

nodes.title: The coffee nap
nodes.description: Caffeine takes about as long to arrive as a short nap takes to finish, and that coincidence is the whole trick

nodes.title: Why 2pm
nodes.description: The afternoon dip is not caused by lunch — it is a scheduled trough in the circadian rhythm, and it arrives whether or not you eat

nodes.title: How the Industrial Revolution killed the nap
nodes.description: Daytime sleep did not fall out of fashion — it was scheduled out, by clocks, factory discipline and artificial light

nodes.title: Siesta, 午休, inemuri
nodes.description: Three societies that kept a place for daytime sleep, and the very different things each of them permits

nodes.title: The politics of the office nap
nodes.description: Rest at work is distributed the way status is — who can be seen sleeping, and who would lose something by it

nodes.title: Nap pods and sleep as a product
nodes.description: Rest returns to the workplace as equipment and subscription — what gets solved when a need becomes a purchase, and what gets avoided

nodes.title: Infants, elders, shift workers
nodes.description: The three groups with the clearest physiological claim to daytime sleep, and how differently each is treated for taking it

nodes.title: Measuring the nap
nodes.description: Wearables report sleep stages they cannot see — what the devices actually measure, and how far the number on the screen is from it

nodes.title: Naps and memory
nodes.description: Sleep does not merely rest the brain, it files what happened — and the timing relative to learning is what decides the benefit

nodes.title: Design an institution that permits napping
nodes.description: The synthesis — everything the course established, turned into a policy that has to survive someone who does not want to adopt it

course.title: The Last Mile
course.description: Every project you've ever finished had a moment where it was 90% done and somehow still cost half its budget to close out. SLOP1241 is built on a single argument: finishing is a different skill from building, and almost everyone is worse at it. Across twelve weeks we chase that argument through eleven unrelated domains, why a rural broadband connection's last customer costs as much as all the others combined, why a peer-reviewed defect-cost multiplier gets misattributed to a study that never existed, why 98% of a building is legally a different object to 100% of one, and we end up with something more useful than a slogan: a working theory of where your own last mile is hiding, and why you keep underestimating it.

nodes.title: Demo vs. Skeptical PM
nodes.description: A two-person roleplay where one of you demos "done" software and the other is paid to not believe you
spec: both roles were played in full, not summarised
the PM's questions targeted at least three specific gaps between "works in the demo" and "works for a real user"
the pair submits a one-page writeup naming the gaps the PM found and which ones the developer had genuinely not considered

nodes.title: The Marginal Cost of the Last Customer
nodes.description: An analytical lab — calculate what it actually costs to reach each successive customer on a line, and justify why the last one costs as much as everyone before them combined
spec: shows the per-customer marginal cost calculation for a supplied fictional rollout, not just a final total
explicitly justifies, in prose, why the marginal cost curve looks the way it does rather than just stating that it does
states the one assumption in the brief that would break the argument if it were false

nodes.title: The Week the Dissertation Stalled
nodes.description: A first-person narrative lab — write the diary entry of an ABD student on the exact week their dissertation went quiet
spec: written entirely in first person, present tense, as a single diary entry (not a case study or a summary about the character)
names a specific, plausible reason the dissertation stalled that week — not a generic "got busy"
closes by naming what would need to be true for the entry-writer to start again tomorrow, without resolving whether they actually do

nodes.title: The Back-of-House Zine
nodes.description: A creative lab — make a short zine auditing a real venue's front-of-house polish against its back-of-house neglect
spec: documents one real venue (photos, sketches, or detailed notes are all acceptable evidence) rather than a hypothetical one
identifies at least three specific hidden last-mile failure points, not just "the bathroom was dirty"
is an actual zine artefact — folded, paginated, laid out — not a plain document with a zine-shaped title

nodes.title: Pitch the Docketing Redesign
nodes.description: A mini-presentation lab — pitch a deadline-tracking system redesign to "the partners" (the rest of the class)
spec: the pitch names a specific, current failure mode in how deadlines are tracked (not a generic "we should use software")
proposes a specific redundancy mechanism (a second checker, a second system, a forced double-entry) rather than just "be more careful"
stays inside the five-minute limit, since a docketing pitch that overruns its own slot is the joke writing itself

nodes.title: Cost of Quality, by Catch Point
nodes.description: An analytical lab — calculate cost-of-quality at different inspection points using real multiplier data, and justify an inspection budget
spec: uses the Boehm and Basili replicated multiplier (not the debunked "IBM Systems Sciences Institute" chart) as the basis for the calculation, and says so
calculates total expected cost under at least two different inspection budgets, not just one
recommends a specific inspection spend and justifies it against the numbers calculated, not against a vibe

nodes.title: The Handover That Isn't
nodes.description: A roleplay lab — one team hands over a project by slide deck alone; the receiving team discovers live what the deck left out
spec: the handing-over team prepared a genuine slide deck in advance and presented only from it, no verbal additions beyond the slides
the receiving team's writeup names at least two specific pieces of missing information that the deck's author would have called "obvious"
both teams reflect on which side of the Mars Climate Orbiter failure they'd have been on, and why

nodes.title: The Round That Keeps Moving
nodes.description: A negotiation roleplay lab — investors keep raising the bar for "enough traction" exactly as founders close in on it, dramatising the moving goalpost
spec: the investor pair actually raises their stated bar at least twice during the negotiation, in character, rather than granting funding on the first ask that meets the original bar
the founder pair's writeup names the specific moment they realised the target had moved, not just that it eventually did
both pairs connect their experience explicitly to the moving-goalpost mechanic on week 8's page

nodes.title: Sign-Off Risk, by Phase
nodes.description: An analytical lab — estimate certificate-of-occupancy risk-by-phase for a fictional build, justified against real punch-list categories
spec: uses the real punch-list categories from the Procore reference linked on week 9's page, not invented categories
treats occupancy as the binary gate the lecture argues it is, rather than smoothing it into a percentage
the final recommendation states the single highest-risk open item, not just a risk score

nodes.title: The Final Approach Safety Briefing
nodes.description: A mini-presentation lab — deliver a spoken safety briefing that actually translates final-approach accident statistics for a general audience
spec: accurately represents the real proportion of accidents occurring during final approach and landing, sourced from the Boeing or Flight Safety Foundation material linked on week 10's page
is delivered as a spoken briefing (recorded or live in the lab), not read verbatim from slides
explains, for a non-expert audience, why so much risk concentrates in so little flight time, not just that it does

nodes.title: Should a Maintainer Always Keep Polishing?
nodes.description: A formal debate lab — arguing for and against continued polish, to find the exact point where this course's own thesis stops holding
spec: both sides argue from specific examples (open-source or otherwise), not just abstract principle
the "for" side has to engage with Gabriel's "worse is better" essay directly, not just assert that finishing is always good
the debate's closing statement from each side identifies the actual point (a feature, a threshold, a cost) where their opponent's position would start being right

nodes.title: Sixty Seconds, One Domain
nodes.description: The synthesis lab — a 60-second personal lightning talk mapping your own last-mile story to one of the eleven domains this course covered
spec: names a specific unfinished thing of your own, not a hypothetical one
explicitly maps it to one of the eleven domain weeks (not week 12 itself) and says which part of that week's argument applied
stays inside 60 seconds, delivered live in the lab

nodes.title: Assignment 1

spec: names a specific, real unfinished thing — not a hypothetical one, and not one invented to fit the brief
identifies the specific last-mile cost that thing carries, not just that it "took a while" or "isn't done yet"
draws explicitly on at least one framework from weeks 1–6
submitted by the deadline, in the format named below

nodes.title: Labs
nodes.description: The weekly graded labs — twelve short, domain-specific deliverables, marked as a set rather than individually agonised over
spec: a submission exists for at least 10 of the 12 labs, each meeting that lab's own spec
each submission was made by that lab's own due date (5pm the Friday of its teaching week) — a late submission is treated the same as a missed one, and simply becomes one of the two you can drop
group submissions name every group member, and every named member contributed to the artefact submitted

marking.description: Each lab is marked pass/needs-work against that week's own spec, then the twelve marks are combined by keeping your best 10 and dropping your worst 2 — including any you miss outright. There is no separate extension process for a missed or weak lab; the drop is the extension. A lab that scores "needs work" still counts as one of the ten if it is your tenth best, so there is no benefit to redoing a submitted lab.

nodes.title: Done Enough to Demo, Nowhere Near Shipped
nodes.description: Why "it works on my machine" and "it's live for actual users" are different projects, and treating the gap as more of the same work is how software dies in the drawer

meta.angle: In software the last mile is expensive because every corner you cut to reach the demo has to be paid back with interest before anyone can rely on it.

nodes.title: The Last Customer Costs More Than All the Others Combined
nodes.description: Borrowing the term from telecoms and rail, we look at why running a line 99% of the way is cheap and the final stretch to every actual door is where the budget dies

meta.angle: Infrastructure is where "last mile" got its name, because connecting the final customer costs as much as every customer that came before them put together.

nodes.title: All But the Dissertation
nodes.description: Coursework has deadlines someone else enforces. The dissertation doesn't — which is exactly why "ABD" is a permanent address for so many otherwise finished PhD students

meta.angle: In graduate research the last mile is expensive because the dissertation is the one deliverable nobody else is waiting on yet, so it is the easiest work in the entire degree to keep deferring.

nodes.title: The Bathroom Is the Real Menu
nodes.description: The kitchen earns a restaurant its customers. The restroom is what decides, silently and without complaint, whether those customers ever come back

meta.angle: In hospitality the last mile is expensive precisely because a spotless bathroom earns a restaurant zero new customers, which is exactly why it's the easiest budget line to quietly shortchange.

nodes.title: The Filing You Didn't Make Is the Only One That Matters
nodes.description: A case can be argued flawlessly and still be lost entirely to a calendar entry nobody double-checked — why legal work's last mile is administrative, not intellectual

meta.angle: In legal practice the last mile is expensive because a case can be won on every substantive argument and still be destroyed completely by one missed date on a calendar nobody was watching.

costCurve.unit: US dollars — average insurer payout per paid claim, Jarvis & Vollweiler (2024)

nodes.title: Ship It, Then Pay the Hundred-x
nodes.description: Manufacturing's own quality-cost data spells out the thesis as an actual multiplier — catch a defect in design and it costs one dollar, catch it after the customer does and it costs a hundred

meta.angle: In manufacturing the last mile is expensive because cost of quality is a measured multiplier here, not a metaphor — the same flaw costs roughly a hundred times more once the customer finds it.

costCurve.unit: × relative cost (a dimensionless multiplier, not a dollar or hour figure — see below)

nodes.title: The Handover Slide Deck Is Not the Handover
nodes.description: Two teams can both finish their half of a project and the thing still fails completely at the seam between them — a $125 million spacecraft is the textbook case

meta.angle: Institutional handovers make the last mile expensive by relocating it entirely outside anyone's individual work, into the seam between two teams who each, correctly, believe they are done.

nodes.title: The Round You Need Is the Round You Just Missed
nodes.description: Hit the traction investors wanted and the bar for "enough traction" quietly moves again — startup fundraising's last mile isn't a steep curve, it's a finish line that runs

meta.angle: Startups break the cost-curve version of this thesis entirely, because the finish line for "enough traction to raise" relocates itself exactly as fast as founders close the distance to it.

nodes.title: Ninety-Eight Percent Done Is a Different Building Than One Hundred
nodes.description: A building department will not certify "almost finished" — why the construction punch list turns the last few percent of a project into a binary gate, not a slope

meta.angle: In construction the last mile is expensive because occupancy is a legal binary, not a percentage — the punch list gates every day of rent or lease income the building isn't yet allowed to earn.

nodes.title: Final Approach Is Five Percent of the Flight and Half the Risk
nodes.description: Boeing's own decades of accident data show exactly where a flight's last mile sits — a sliver of total flight time carrying roughly half the fatal risk

meta.angle: In aviation the last mile is expensive because final approach and landing occupy a sliver of a flight's duration while accounting for nearly half of all fatal accidents.

nodes.title: The Feature That Finishes Itself Into Irrelevance
nodes.description: Richard Gabriel's "worse is better" essay is the counter-argument this course needed — sometimes the thing that loses is the one that kept finishing past the point anyone wanted

meta.angle: Open-source overbuilding is where this thesis meets its limit — past a point, continued finishing stops costing more and starts actively subtracting value nobody asked to lose.

nodes.title: Which Last Mile Have You Actually Hit
nodes.description: Eleven domains, eleven different reasons finishing was the expensive part — the synthesis week asks which of them you've personally lived through, not which you can recite

meta.angle: The synthesis week's argument is that these eleven domains share a blind spot, not a mechanism — which is why no fixed cost-curve was ever going to be this course's final word.

course.title: The Anatomy of a Jump
course.description: A twelve-week studio in game feel: measure, tune and compare one 2D jump using visual tools, with an optional guided-code path. No game-development experience required.

nodes.title: Look inside a jump
nodes.description: A hands-on hour with the home trial, building the habit this course runs on — read the number the simulation reports, don't estimate it.
spec: a completed three-row jump table (mode, height, displacement, airtime) from real trials
one sentence naming which phase varied most between your jumps and by how much
one sentence naming something visibly part of a jump that happens before takeoff

a two-line method statement naming both presets, the mode, and the trial count

the height and airtime average for each of the two gravity values
one sentence naming which value the group predicted wrong before running the experiment

nodes.title: Air control drill

the matching height and airtime values for the same trials, shown to be roughly unchanged
one sentence on what a low air control value would make hard for a player trying to correct a misjudged jump

one coyote-time trial and one jump-buffer trial, each with the mistiming reported in milliseconds and the outcome
the "Copy configuration" link for the settings used, pasted alongside the results

confirmation that all three poses were compared on the same fixed trajectory

one sentence on what pose feature the guess turned on

one sentence on whether the mute control was easy to find and operate without instruction
