nodes.description: Floaty and heavy are feelings, not numbers. This week turns them into three measurements you can actually compare between jumps.

nodes.title: What Makes a Measurement Trustworthy?
nodes.description: A number is not evidence by itself — this week is about the difference between a measurement someone else could reproduce and one they'd have to take your word for.

nodes.title: The Two Knobs Under Every Jump
nodes.description: Gravity and launch speed both change how high you go, but they don't feel the same, and the Gravity Lab lets you see why.

nodes.title: Who Is in Control in the Air?
nodes.description: Height and airtime don't move when you change air control — but where you land does, and that's a different kind of measurement.

nodes.title: How Forgiving Should a Jump Be?
nodes.description: Release cut, coyote time and jump buffer don't change the physics of a clean jump at all — they only change what happens when your timing is off.

nodes.title: Same Path, Different Body
nodes.description: Two characters can follow the exact same trajectory and still look like they're jumping for different reasons — because posture was never physics.

nodes.title: Anticipation and Follow-Through
nodes.description: Two of animation's oldest principles, applied to a jump that already has its physics locked in — a windup before takeoff, a settle after landing.

nodes.title: What a Jump Sounds Like
nodes.description: A takeoff blip and a landing blip are the entire sound budget this course allows — which is exactly enough to test what sound is actually for.

nodes.title: One Change at a Time
nodes.description: The A/B lab replays the exact same recorded input through two configurations — which is what makes it possible to trust the comparison.

nodes.title: Watching Someone Else Play
nodes.description: Everything measured so far has been your own hands on the controls — this week is about what changes when the hands belong to someone else.

nodes.title: What Did You Actually Build?
nodes.description: A synthesis of measurement, control, expression and evaluation, and what each one contributes to a claim about how a jump feels.

course.title: Coexistence 101
course.description: Coexistence 101 treats sharing a home, workplace, studio or public space as a design problem, not an etiquette checklist: presence, attention, hygiene, conflict and the norms that hold a room together, for anyone about to share space with other humans on purpose.

nodes.title: Know thyself first
nodes.description: The first Tute, because before you can read a room, you need a working read on your own baseline
spec: you have logged at least three moments your own attention or mood shifted noticeably over one full day
you can name one physical or emotional "tell" you now recognise in yourself under social strain
you have read this week's field task before the session starts

nodes.title: Third place

spec: you can name your own third place, or state plainly that you currently don't have one
you have observed a candidate third place for at least 30 minutes and logged who was there
you can describe one thing that space does that home and work don't

nodes.title: Civil inattention

spec: you have observed a busy public walkway or corridor for at least 20 minutes
you can describe at least two instances of civil inattention and one clear breach of it
you can state whether phone use changed who yielded space to whom, with an example

nodes.title: Proxemics

you can name which of Hall's four zones applied in each case

spec: you have identified one unwritten rule currently operating in your own home
you can describe how that rule gets enforced when someone breaks it

spec: you can name two ways personal hygiene affects shared-space coexistence beyond "smelling bad"
you have identified one hygiene-related norm your own shared space enforces without ever stating it
you can explain, in your own words, why hygiene needs and habits vary by body and life stage rather than being a matter of effort alone

spec: you can describe a real or hypothetical workplace friction that came from being placed with people you didn't choose

you have applied at least one proxemics or civil-inattention concept to an open-plan or shared workplace

you can state where this course's material sits relative to the Australian Curriculum's personal and social capability framework

nodes.title: Norms shift with life stage

spec: you can describe how one coexistence norm you've studied this semester changes across at least two life stages or relationship lengths
you have identified a norm that would have to be renegotiated if your own share house or household's membership changed
you can name the "settling down" effect from Week 6 and connect it to at least one example from this week

nodes.title: Levels of resolution
nodes.description: Week 12, a de-escalation ladder for shared-space conflict, and why it starts with Week 1
spec: you can state the escalation ladder from the final lecture from lowest to highest level of resolution
you can connect at least one step of that ladder back to the self-awareness work from Week 1
your critique-and-redesign submission stands on its own without you present to explain it

nodes.title: Critique and redesign
nodes.description: The capstone, critique one space that gets coexistence wrong, and redesign it so it doesn't.
spec: submitted by the deadline, as a document that stands alone without you present to explain it
critiques a specific, real space using at least two frameworks from the semester
proposes a redesign of the space's layout, stated norms, or process, not just a wish that people behaved better
the work is yours, with any assistance declared

marking.description: Judged as a whole against the brief. A strong submission diagnoses the space's failure using the semester's frameworks precisely, proposes a redesign that would plausibly fix it without assuming an unlimited budget, and stands on its own without you there to talk it through.

bands.description: The diagnosis reads as inevitable once stated, using two or more frameworks precisely and showing where they compound each other. The redesign is concrete enough that someone could hand it to a builder or a landlord, and the document is honest about a real limitation it doesn't solve.
The diagnosis is correct and well-argued, and the redesign is concrete, but the document leans on one framework more than the brief's "at least two"; the second is present but thin.
The document names a real failure and gestures at a framework, but the redesign drifts toward "people should communicate better" in at least one part, or its own limits go unacknowledged.

All the required parts are present, but the failure described could be fixed by people simply being nicer just as easily as by the proposed redesign; the redesign isn't doing any explanatory work of its own.

nodes.title: Diagnosis
nodes.description: A written diagnosis of the coexistence norms in one shared space you already occupy, using the first four weeks' frameworks.
spec: submitted by the deadline, as a written document of 1200-1800 words
names at least three specific, dated incidents observed in the chosen space
explicitly applies civil inattention, proxemics or third-place framing to what was observed
the work is yours, with any assistance declared

criteria.name: Quality and specificity of the observations
Correct, well-argued use of the course frameworks

bands.description: Incidents are dated and behaviourally specific, and chosen because they reveal where the space's unwritten rulebook is under strain, not just because they happened. The framework applied to each one fits precisely enough that swapping in a different framework would visibly not work as well.
Incidents are specific, dated, and correctly matched to a framework, but the choice of incidents is safe rather than revealing; nothing here would surprise someone who already knows the space.
The three incidents are present, but at least one drifts toward the generic ("people were considerate"), or a framework is named for an incident without being argued for it.
The required parts are all there in name, but incidents read as reconstructed after the fact rather than logged at the time, or a framework is misapplied without the diagnosis noticing.

nodes.title: Protocol design
nodes.description: A written protocol for a group you actually belong to, tested for a week and reported on honestly.
spec: submitted by the deadline, as a protocol document plus a test log
the protocol addresses a specific, named friction point in a real group
the test log covers at least five days of actual use, not a single trial
the work is yours, with any assistance declared

criteria.name: The protocol is practical enough for the group to actually run
Evidence it was genuinely tested, not just written
Honest reflection on what worked and what didn't

bands.description: The protocol names who does what down to the specific friction point it targets, the test log shows real breakdowns and how they were handled as they happened, and the reflection changes something concrete for next time.

The protocol is workable and genuinely tested across the full run, and the reflection is honest, but the changes proposed are minor rather than addressing the friction point that motivated the protocol in the first place.

The protocol addresses the friction point in principle, but a reader outside the group would need it explained to actually run it; the log covers the required days but reads thin on what actually happened.
A protocol exists and a log was kept, but the log reads like a diary rather than a test, no clear evidence the protocol was actually put into practice, or the reflection just says "it worked."

course.title: How to Write a Call of Cthulhu Scenario
course.description: A studio course in scenario design, using Call of Cthulhu as the working system. Twelve weeks turn one spark of interest into a complete, playtested scenario — the design process a Keeper goes through, not Mythos trivia or rules memorisation.

nodes.title: What is a scenario?
nodes.description: The opening studio — the five-stage design pipeline the semester follows, and the first raw idea you bring to the table.
spec: you can state the five-stage pipeline (premise, truth, structure, clues, delivery) in your own words
you have one specific idea — a creature, a news story, an object — that a stranger could react to
you have opened a scenario notebook you will keep adding to all semester

nodes.title: Inspiration and premise
nodes.description: Turning a raw spark into a one-paragraph premise using four generic Mythos flavours instead of starting from lore.
spec: you can name which of the four flavours (ancient, unknown, chaos, space) your premise leans on, and why
your premise fits in one paragraph a stranger could react to without more context

nodes.title: Truth and antagonist
nodes.description: Fusing your premise with a concrete Mythos entity or faction, and stating the causal truth your whole scenario hangs on.
spec: you have named a specific Mythos entity or faction as your antagonist, not "the Mythos" in general
you can state your scenario's truth as a single cause-and-effect chain — what it wants, what it has already done, what happens next if nobody intervenes

nodes.title: Structure and investigation flow
nodes.description: Committing to a hook and a shape — linear or open — before any scene gets written in detail.
spec: you have committed to a linear or open structure and can say what it costs and what it buys
you have written the one scene that pulls players into the story, and said whether they're pulled in passively or by their own choice

nodes.title: Locations, scenes and nodes
nodes.description: Turning a structure into a concrete chain of scenes — what's discoverable in each, and what changes if the players linger.
spec: you have a map (physical or digital) of every scene your scenario needs
each node names what's immediately visible and what a thorough search reveals

nodes.title: Clue architecture

spec: every scene in your map carries at least one clue, tagged against both taxonomies taught this week
you can point to one clue that survives a failed roll — a second path to the same information

nodes.title: Puzzles and red herrings

spec: only a small number of your clues are puzzle-gated, and each is genuinely load-bearing
a partner attempted your puzzle without your help, and can describe what it was testing

nodes.title: Checks and failure design

spec: no single roll in your draft is the only way past a scene

nodes.title: Atmosphere and escalation

spec: one scene's description has been rewritten to imply the threat rather than name it outright
your antagonist gives at least a few escalating warnings before a kill is possible, rather than a threat that can end a character with no build-up

nodes.title: Playtest lab
nodes.description: Running an actual slice of your draft with a real player, and recording what diverges from what you expected.
spec: you have run an actual playtest slice of your draft with at least one other player
you have written notes on at least one stuck point and one thing that worked better than you expected

nodes.title: Assembly and handoff
nodes.description: Assembling scenario text, clue map, NPC sheets and handouts into a packet a stranger could run cold.
spec: your packet answers "what happens in this scene" for any scene, without you present to explain it
your clue map, NPC sheets and handouts live in one place, not scattered across formats

nodes.title: Final Scenario
nodes.description: The complete, playtest-revised scenario packet — runnable by a Keeper who wasn't in the room for any of the studios.
spec: the packet is complete — scenario text, clue map, NPC sheets and any handouts, in one place
a reader who wasn't in your studios could run at least one scene from the page alone
the draft names at least one specific change made in response to your playtest

marking.description: Judged as a whole against whether an independent Keeper could run it cold — whether the packet answers "what happens in this scene" for every scene, whether the clue web is actually redundant in play, and whether the final draft visibly responds to what the Assessment 3 playtest revealed, rather than ignoring it.

nodes.title: Investigation Architecture
nodes.description: The full skeleton of your scenario — locations, clue web, puzzles, checks and NPC roster — before any prose gets polished.
spec: your scene map, clue web, puzzle placement, check design and NPC roster are submitted as one connected document
every load-bearing clue has at least one redundant path to it
every NPC's one-sentence purpose is stated explicitly

criteria.name: Clue web has redundant paths to every load-bearing clue
Structure and scene map are internally consistent
Checks are designed so failure changes cost, not access
Every NPC has a stated one-sentence purpose

nodes.title: Playtest Report
nodes.description: A short report on an actual playtest of your draft — what broke, what surprised you, and what you're changing because of it.
spec: you ran an actual playtest slice, with at least one other real player, not a solo read-through
you name at least one specific stuck point and one specific thing that surprised you
you state concrete changes you're making to the scenario as a result

marking.description: Graded on whether the report shows a genuine playtest happened and a genuine response to it — a specific stuck point, a specific surprise, and specific changes that follow from them — rather than on the scenario being flawless going in. A report that honestly documents a scenario breaking is a stronger submission than one that claims nothing went wrong.

spec: a stranger could read your pitch and repeat back what the antagonist wants
the antagonist is a named entity or faction, not "the Mythos" in general
you say, in a sentence or two, what kind of horror and player experience you're aiming for

criteria.name: The truth is a causal chain, not a mood
Antagonist is specific, not "the Mythos" in general

course.title: Continuity Engineering

nodes.title: The One More Episode Effect
nodes.description: Why finishing an episode so rarely feels like a stopping point — and what happens when the interface, not you, gets to decide what "one more" costs.

meta.psychologicalQuestion: Why do we keep watching when we already know we should stop?
meta.nextTease: This week was about why stopping is hard once you're already watching. It said nothing about why you pressed play in the first place — that's next episode's question.

nodes.title: Why We Start Watching
nodes.description: Before there's anything to keep watching, something has to make you press play. This week is about that first click — and how little it has to do with the show itself.

meta.psychologicalQuestion: Why do we press play in the first place?
meta.previouslyOn: Last week was about the moment an episode ends — why stopping stops feeling like the default once you're already watching, thanks to friction and unfinished information.
meta.nextTease: Once you've pressed play, a well-placed cliffhanger can make it feel like you never had a choice to stop at all. That's next episode's question.

nodes.title: Cliffhangers
nodes.description: A cliffhanger doesn't answer a question — it opens one and cuts away. This week is about why an open question pulls harder than an open plot.

meta.psychologicalQuestion: Why does an unanswered question pull harder than an unfinished story?
meta.previouslyOn: Last week was about the moment before an episode even starts — how a badge or an unresolved description gets a show picked in the first place. This week picks up right where that pressed-play moment leads once the episode is already playing and about to end.
meta.nextTease: A cliffhanger only works if a human has to decide, mid-pull, whether to keep going. Take that decision away entirely and let the next episode start on its own — that's next episode's question.

nodes.title: Autoplay
nodes.description: A cliffhanger still needs you to decide to keep watching. Autoplay removes that decision entirely. This week is about what changes when "continue" is the default and "stop" is the thing you have to do.

meta.psychologicalQuestion: What changes when you have to act to stop something, instead of act to continue it?
meta.previouslyOn: Last week was about a cliffhanger that still requires you to decide, mid-pull, whether to keep watching. This week removes that decision entirely and asks what's left once continuing needs no action at all.
meta.nextTease: Autoplay decides one episode at a time. What happens once nobody is deciding at any scale, and "one more" quietly becomes an entire season — that's next episode's question.

nodes.title: Rewards & Reinforcement
nodes.description: Two habits can get the exact same number of payoffs and still feel completely different to keep doing. This week is about why timing, not quantity, is what makes a reward hard to walk away from.

meta.psychologicalQuestion: Why does an unpredictable reward keep pulling you back harder than a reliable one?
meta.previouslyOn: Last week removed the decision to continue altogether, letting a default do the work instead of a cue. This week goes back to decisions the visitor is actively making, and asks what happens when the payoff for making them is inconsistent on purpose.
meta.nextTease: Small, unpredictable payoffs are what keep a single habit going once it's started. They say nothing about how long any of this actually felt like it took — that's next episode's question.

nodes.title: Time Perception
nodes.description: Three episodes can feel shorter than fifteen minutes spent waiting for a bus. This week is about why elapsed time and felt time keep disagreeing — and what that has to do with losing track of a binge.

meta.psychologicalQuestion: Why can three episodes feel shorter than fifteen minutes of waiting?
meta.previouslyOn: Last week was about the small, unpredictable payoffs that keep a habit going once it's already started. This week steps sideways from reward into something stranger — how long any of this actually felt like it took.
meta.nextTease: Losing track of time is one thing when you only meant to watch one episode. It's a different thing once "one more" quietly becomes "the whole season" — that's next episode's question.

nodes.title: Binge Watching
nodes.description: One more episode is a decision made once. A binge is that same decision made silently, over and over, without anyone ever tallying how many times. This week is about what disappears when nobody's counting.

meta.psychologicalQuestion: What happens to "one more episode" once nobody is keeping count?
meta.previouslyOn: Last week was about why elapsed time and felt time disagree during a binge — three episodes can feel shorter than fifteen minutes of waiting. This week asks what happens to the episode count itself when nothing is tracking it either.
meta.nextTease: A binge session is still, technically, a series of decisions you keep making yourself. What happens once something else is choosing what plays next before you've even finished deciding — that's next episode's question.

nodes.title: Recommendation Algorithms
nodes.description: A feed doesn't have to remove your choices to narrow your world — it only has to keep offering you more of whatever you already picked. This week is about what that quietly does to what you even get shown.

meta.psychologicalQuestion: Does picking what you already like change what you're offered next?
meta.previouslyOn: Last week was about a running total that no one, including you, was keeping track of during a binge. This week is about something else that goes untracked in the background — what a feed quietly learns from every pick you make, whether you notice or not.
meta.nextTease: A narrowing feed still lets you choose from whatever it shows you. Next episode is about a choice that isn't really private at all — what happens to a pick once you can see what other people chose first.

nodes.title: Social Watching
nodes.description: Two identical shows, side by side, will still get picked unevenly the moment one of them says other people are watching it. This week is about what a social cue is actually doing when the content itself can't explain the difference.

meta.psychologicalQuestion: What is a social cue actually doing, when the two options are otherwise the same?
meta.previouslyOn: Last week was about a feed narrowing in private, shaped only by your own past picks. This week is about a pick that isn't private at all — what changes once you can see what other people are already watching before you choose.
meta.nextTease: A social cue can move a choice without costing you anything. Next episode is about a cost that's much harder to ignore once it starts accumulating — what watching trades away when it competes with sleep.

nodes.title: Sleep vs Entertainment
nodes.description: Every episode costs the same fixed amount of something, whether or not anyone's counting. This week makes that cost visible on purpose, and asks what changes once it's a number instead of a feeling.

meta.psychologicalQuestion: Does seeing the actual cost of "one more" change whether you pay it?
meta.previouslyOn: Last week was about a social cue that costs nothing to follow — it can shift a choice without the choice itself getting any more expensive. This week is about a cost that's much harder to wave away once it starts compounding against something as concrete as a wake-up time.
meta.nextTease: Seeing the cost clearly is one thing. Actually changing what you do about it, in the moment, before the decision is already made — that's next episode's question.

nodes.title: Breaking the Loop
nodes.description: Every mechanism this course has named keeps a cycle turning. This week asks a more useful question than "how do I stop" — where in that cycle does one small interruption actually change what happens?

meta.psychologicalQuestion: Where can a small intervention break a cycle that keeps itself going?
meta.previouslyOn: Last week made a fixed cost visible, in the moment, as a number you could watch draining away — and asked whether seeing it was enough to change what you did. Seeing a cost clearly is one thing; this week is about actually acting on it, before the next decision has already been made for you.
meta.nextTease: Every mechanism this course has named so far has been studied one at a time. They don't run one at a time in a real viewing session — they run together, and often reinforce each other. That's the final episode's question.

nodes.title: The Final Episode
nodes.description: Every mechanism this course named, studied on its own. This week puts them back in the same session together, and asks what changes once they stop taking turns.

meta.psychologicalQuestion: What happens when the mechanisms we've studied work together?
meta.previouslyOn: Last week isolated *when* one interruption works best inside a single mechanism's own loop. It said nothing about what happens once several of this course's mechanisms are running in the same session, reinforcing each other instead of taking turns. That's this week's question.

course.title: Undocumented Protocols: Field Methods in Neurotypical Interoperation
course.description: The social protocol everyone runs has no specification, no changelog and no maintainer who will admit to writing it. Twelve weeks observing it, documenting it, testing the documentation, and deciding which parts of it you will run.
learningOutcomes: Document one part of the social protocol precisely enough that someone who does not run it could implement it.
Run a documented subroutine on purpose when it is worth running, and put a number on what it cost.
Decline a subroutine knowing what declining costs, and say in plain words what you are doing instead.
Negotiate a working protocol with someone whose implementation differs from yours, and write down what each side conceded.

nodes.title: Corridor Capture
nodes.description: Go out into the building and log real openings: the words, the reply, and whether the exchange closed or branched.
spec: You have logged the openings you observed during the capture period, or recorded that none occurred; every entry includes the words and whether it closed, branched or remained unclear.
You have analysed one real or clearly labelled fictional branch, saying which signal from the lecture, if any, came first.
Nothing in your log names a person or describes anyone well enough to identify them.

nodes.title: Observation Without Diagnosis
nodes.description: Twenty minutes observing a public space, then a partner reads your notes looking for any sentence that diagnoses instead of describing.
spec: You have notes from the observation period, or an explicit no-observation record, and a separately labelled practice rewrite; every retained description passes the asleep test.
A partner or tutor has checked your notes, and you have rewritten or removed every sentence that described a person rather than an exchange.
You have written down the one rule you will test before Sunday’s journal entry.

nodes.title: Envelope Relay
nodes.description: In threes: one person writes a payload, one wraps it in an envelope, one decodes it. Score what arrives, then try sending it bare.
spec: You have played all three roles in the relay: payload writer, wrapper and decoder.
Your group has a scored list of which envelopes arrived intact, which arrived partly and which were lost, with the bent maxim noted for each.
You have sent one payload bare to your group, aloud or in writing, and recorded what that changed for you.

nodes.title: Stopwatch Lab
nodes.description: The same “yes”, said after different delays. Measure how willing it sounds, then find out whether a hold token rescues a slow one.
spec: You have rated eight yeses as an asker, or analysed the prepared alternative: two for each of three delays and two slow replies with a hold token.
Your group's table compares willingness ratings for the slow yes with and without a hold token, including any unchanged ratings.
You can distinguish this classroom test of perceived willingness from counting rejections and acceptances in recorded calls, and name one limitation of the classroom method.

nodes.title: Repair Drills
nodes.description: Planted misunderstandings to practise specific repair initiators, then low-stakes apologies built from the template, with a partner checking which parts arrived.
spec: You have repaired six planted misunderstandings, and each initiator is scored open, restricted request or restricted offer.
You have given two practice apologies from the template, and your partner has ticked which parts they actually heard.
You have accepted a repair and an apology in one turn each, without adding an apology of your own.

nodes.title: Ledger Exchange
nodes.description: Fill in yesterday’s ledger, then compare what the same subroutine costs different people in the room. Nobody’s price is the correct one.
spec: You have an honest ledger for yesterday or a labelled fictional practice ledger; every entry fills the five fields, with private fields marked private and no masking or switch invented to meet a count.
Your group has rated at least four common subroutines for cost, and you can point to the one whose ratings varied most.
You have compared running and declining one subroutine and recorded your choice and expected costs; keeping it running or finding no affordable decline both count.

nodes.title: Runbook Workshop
nodes.description: A quiet lab to write your runbook, save messages, and plan the break. A reduced version is available when writing is hard today.
spec: You have filled in all six runbook sections, or used the reduced path: one early-sign line, one message, and the next section to return to.
You have test-sent at least one of your pre-written messages to yourself, and it reads the way you meant it.
Your break plan names time you can protect from obligations, or records what prevents that; on the reduced path, you have named one commitment to review.

nodes.title: Conformance Tests for Email
nodes.description: Write three institutional messages, then test the tutor email against seven clauses and the other two against their own requirements.
spec: You have written a tutor email, an extension request and a group-work opener from the scenario cards.
A partner has run the seven-clause checklist on your tutor email and recorded a pass or fail for each clause.
Every clause your partner failed has been rewritten, or has a written reason why breaking it was the right call.

nodes.title: The Reciprocity Ladder
nodes.description: Meet your Interoperation Report partner. Climb three rungs of question cards together, pass on any card without explaining, and draft the first clauses of your shared protocol.
spec: You have taken turns through the level 0, 1 and 2 cards, answering or passing, and seen the tutor demonstrate a pass.
You and your partner have written three draft clauses for your shared protocol, each one something both of you can check.
You have privately recorded a card you passed or would have passed on, or written ‘none’; any reason you record stays yours.

nodes.title: Need Without the Label
nodes.description: Draft partial disclosures for two audiences using fictional character cards, practise receiving one, then test your partnership’s draft protocol against a week of real use.
spec: You have drafted two need-without-label sentences for a character card, or chosen the first-half opt-out below.
You have practised both receiving and saying a fictional disclosure and checked the receiving steps, or used the first-half opt-out.
You and your Interoperation Report partner have marked each draft clause from week 9 as held, revised, or dropped, with a reason for each.

nodes.title: The Negotiation, Round Three
nodes.description: Finish your bilateral protocol, compare your accounts of the negotiation, and audit which course terms you used outside class.
spec: Your bilateral protocol is in its final form: at least four clauses, each with who concedes and how either of you checks it.
Your group has recorded which course terms its members used outside class, including ‘none’ where that is the answer; people are described by role, not name.
You and your partner have each written, separately, what you conceded and what held, ready for the report.

nodes.title: Capstone Clinic
nodes.description: Choose your capstone route, get a peer ethics review of any field experiment parameter, and leave with a first paragraph written.
spec: You have told your tutor which capstone route you’re taking before the end of the lab.
If you’re running the Field Experiment, a peer has reviewed your parameter against all four ethics questions, and you have written your answer to each.
If you’re writing the Personal Protocol Document, you have one line under each of its three headings: what I run, what I decline, what I need from others.

nodes.title: Field Journal
nodes.description: One exchange a week, turned into a rule someone else could run, then tested and revised. Eleven Sundays; your best ten count.
spec: Each submission contains at least one entry with all four parts: what happened, the rule you inferred, the test, and the rule now.
Every observation in an entry describes an exchange; none diagnoses a person.
Each rule is written so that someone who wasn’t there could run it.
Each submission is in by 23:59 Canberra time on its Sunday. The lowest of your eleven marks is dropped.

criteria.name: What happened: describes an exchange, and passes the asleep test
The rule: stated so someone who wasn’t there could run it
The test: a real second instance, failures reported
The rule now: revised or held, with the reason

nodes.title: Interoperation Report
nodes.description: Negotiate a shared working protocol with a partner over three labs, then report what each of you conceded, and what held.
spec: The report includes the final bilateral protocol, with at least four clauses, each saying who concedes and how either of you checks it.
It includes a mismatch signal that either partner can use without explaining.
It says what you conceded and what your partner conceded, and reports any place your two accounts differ.
Each partner submits their own report, written separately.

criteria.name: The protocol: clauses are specific, and each says how either partner checks it
Concessions: an honest account of what both partners gave up, including disagreements
What held: evidence from the three labs and the weeks between
Terms: course vocabulary used exactly, not re-coined

nodes.title: Personal Protocol Document or Neurotypical Interaction Field Experiment
nodes.description: The capstone, in one of two routes: document the protocol you run, decline and need; or vary one parameter of the majority’s protocol on purpose and report what comes back.
spec: You have chosen one route and said which at the top of the submission.

Personal Protocol Document: it has three sections, what I run, what I decline and what I need from others, with costs beside each item. If there is no affordable decline now, that section explains why and includes a clearly labelled hypothetical comparison.

Field Experiment: it varies exactly one protocol parameter, reports what came back including results against your expectation, and includes an ethics reflection that answers the four questions from week 12’s lab.
Either route cites at least three of your own Field Journal entries.

marking.description: Marked as a whole against the route you chose, using the criteria set out in the brief. For the Field Experiment, the ethics reflection carries 35% of the mark and is judged on its own terms: a strong experiment with a thin reflection cannot reach the top band.

nodes.title: Protocol Specification
nodes.description: Document one social subroutine as though it were an undocumented API, with conformance tests a stranger could run by watching.
spec: The document names one subroutine and states its scope: where it runs, and between whom.
It specifies the messages in order, what counts as a valid response to each, and any timing that matters.
It includes at least five conformance tests, each checkable by someone watching the exchange.
It documents at least two implementations of the subroutine without calling either one correct.
It cites at least two of your own Field Journal entries as evidence.

criteria.name: Precision: the subroutine is specified tightly enough to implement
Conformance tests: each is observable without asking anyone what they meant
Implementations: at least two variants documented, neither ranked as correct
Grounding: built from your own observations, with journal entries cited

nodes.title: Introduction + The Opening Handshake
nodes.description: Here is “how are you?”, and here is its specification, written down in one lecture after a lifetime of nobody writing it down.
spec: Asked “how are you?” in a corridor, you can give a reply that closes the exchange, and you know which of the reply types in §4 you used.
You can say what “how are you?” usually requests instead of information, and name one setting where it is a real question.
You can explain in one sentence why this course calls the protocol undocumented rather than obvious.
You can recognise the honest-status-report branch while you are in it, and decide whether to take it.
You can take one sentence and say it twice, once so a reply is hard to withhold and once so it is easy, and name what you changed.
You can say why “the reply is a token, not an answer” is a claim about this protocol rather than about greetings in general.

nodes.title: The Undocumented Majority + Field Notes Without Pathology
nodes.description: Why the people who run the protocol can’t describe it, whose failure a mismatch is, and how to write down what you saw without diagnosing anyone.
spec: You can explain why someone who runs the protocol fluently usually can’t state its rules, without saying they aren’t paying attention.
Given any sentence from a field note, you can say whether it describes an exchange or diagnoses a person, using the asleep test.
You can state the double empathy problem in one sentence that doesn’t say which side failed.
Your first Field Journal entry has all four parts, and its rule is written so someone who wasn’t there could run it.
You can turn a general question into one about a specific exchange, and distinguish an observed event from an explanation or a counterfactual prediction.
You can say which claim in this week’s lecture the course refuses to use, and what it uses instead.

nodes.title: Payload and Envelope
nodes.description: Indirect speech, hints and implicature: a protocol that breaks its own published maxims on purpose, and calls it politeness.
spec: For any line in §5’s decoder, you can name the maxim it bends and say its payload out loud in plain words.
You can ask someone for the payload of an ambiguous invitation without implying they were being evasive.
You can explain, using plausible deniability, why a hint can cost the listener less than a direct request.
You can give an example of over-decoding: treating a sentence as an envelope when there was nothing inside it.
Given an envelope somebody sent you, you can suggest what the sender is uncertain about or wants to leave off the record.
You can say why the sender of a hint is a poor judge of whether it was clear, and cite the experiment that shows it.

nodes.title: Latency and Turn-Taking
nodes.description: The gap before a reply is measured in milliseconds, and listeners have learned what long ones usually mean. An undocumented timeout, documented.
spec: You can say roughly how long an ordinary gap between turns is, and roughly where a longer gap starts to be heard as reluctance.
You have a hold token in your own words and have rehearsed it in a spoken or written exchange.
When someone pauses before answering you, you can hold off reading the pause as a no, and ask instead.
You can explain why listeners read a delay as refusal without saying they are being unfair.
You can say what stayed the same and what differed across the three language groups in §4, and why that matters to someone whose gaps run long.
You can name one thing a speaker might be doing by leaving a longer gap, other than refusing.

nodes.title: Error Handling and Repair
nodes.description: A twelve-language study found a listener signalling trouble about once every 1.4 minutes. The protocol has a subroutine for it, and a separate one for offence.
spec: When you mishear or half-understand something, you can ask the most specific repair question available instead of a bare “what?”, and you have done it at least once this week.
You can say “sorry, what?” without apologising for having said it, and explain why it counts as protocol rather than failure.
You can list the parts of the course’s apology template and identify the part that names what the other person had to do.
You can acknowledge a repair in one turn and respond to an apology in one turn, including asking for time if you cannot mean an acceptance.
You can say where an explanation goes in an apology, and what constrains its length.
You can say why the course claims repair is error handling rather than a matter of character, and name the finding behind it.

nodes.title: Masking: Cost Accounting
nodes.description: Masking works, and it has a price. Here is the ledger: what each masked subroutine buys, what it costs, and how much say you had in running it.
spec: You have a five-column ledger for one real day or a labelled fictional practice day, recording no masking if that is what happened; private fields may say private.
You have recorded any switch in how much you masked, including its from/to contexts and estimated cost, or explicitly recorded no switch.
You can compare running and declining one subroutine and explain your choice; keeping it running or finding no affordable decline both count.
You can explain why the ledger has a column for pressure, not just for cost.
You can distinguish time spent camouflaging in the research from the ledger's estimated recovery hours, without claiming the study converts one into the other.
You can name two things masking buys, in the words of people who do it, not the course's.

nodes.title: Emergency: Overload, Shutdown, Recovery
nodes.description: What happens when week 6’s budget is overspent for too long, and a runbook written now, while you can write one, for the day you can’t.
spec: Your runbook records your early signs, or its reduced version records one sign and the next section to return to.
Three pre-written messages are saved where you can send them, or one has been saved and test-read on the reduced path.
Your runbook names two things to drop when load runs high, or the reduced version names one commitment to review.
You can name the four recovery experiences and use them to review a real or fictional break plan.
You can name the two phenomena the course’s three time scales leave out, and say where to read about them.

nodes.title: Institutional Protocols
nodes.description: Emails to tutors, office hours, extensions and group work. The university specifies everything except how to ask for help, so this week does.
spec: A staff email you have sent, or a draft using a supplied scenario, passes all seven clauses in §5 or has a reason for each exception.
You can write an extension request that asks for a specific date in under 120 words, with no apology longer than one sentence.
You can open an office-hours visit by saying what your question is about and roughly how long it will take.
If you are in a group, its first meeting ends with a written agreement covering roles, the channel, reply times, decisions, and what happens when someone goes quiet.
You can say what disability support staff themselves named as a barrier, and why that means the scripts in §5 are not the whole fix.
You can name the two estimates the research challenges and distinguish a prediction about an ask from the reply actually received.

nodes.title: Escalation Rates
nodes.description: How closeness actually paces: hours, disclosure, and a rate limit nobody publishes, until now.
spec: You can place a real or fictional exchange on the course’s five-level depth scale and explain any uncertainty in your labels.
You can name two signals that you’ve gone past someone’s rate limit, and say a one-turn step-down.
You can explain why hours matter to friendship without quoting a number the research didn’t give you.
You can keep a conversation at a lower depth than the other person offers, and say what that choice costs.
You can say what happened to the difference between listeners and disclosers once they swapped roles, and what that means for the ±1 rule.
You can turn one thing you were going to say into a follow-up question, and say which part of the other person’s turn it picks up.

nodes.title: Disclosure
nodes.description: Whether to tell people, when, which people, and at what cost. Five audiences, needs without labels, and the timing trap.
spec: You can name the five audiences, and say one thing disclosure can buy and one thing it can cost with each.
You have written a need-without-label sentence for a real or fictional situation and identified its intended audience.
You can explain the timing trap using what autistic employees reported about disclosing after problems had started.
You can answer someone else’s disclosure in two sentences that don’t reinterpret them out loud.
You can say why the research disagrees about whether disclosure helps, and which kind of study sits on each side.
You can name what predicted distress among people with a concealable identity, and say why that is not the same as the effort of concealing.
You can propose one thing a department could change that might lower the cost for students who never disclose anything.

nodes.title: Interoperation, Not Conversion
nodes.description: Evidence on communication across implementations, what the studies leave open, and a bilateral protocol to try with your partner.
spec: You can say which diffusion-chain condition lost detail faster and distinguish that result from a claim about an individual link.
Your draft bilateral protocol has at least one clause each partner conceded, and a way for either of you to flag a mismatch.
You can name a rapport signal you rely on, and explain why someone not sending it might not mean what you assume.
You can explain the difference between interoperation and conversion with an example from your own semester.
You can say what readability correlated with in Alkhaldi et al., and what “independent of diagnosis” does and does not establish.
You can name something about yourself that changes depending on who you are talking to, and say how you would know.

nodes.title: Advanced Topics and Further Study
nodes.description: Romance, persuasion and power, logged as open issues rather than taught, with where the documentation starts. And the course’s own errata, because a specification without them is lying.
spec: For each of the three open issues, you can name the reading where its documentation starts, and one reason the course leaves it out of scope.
You have chosen your capstone route and written its first paragraph.
If you chose the Field Experiment, you can answer all four contextual ethics questions and name a condition that would make you stop.
You can name one entry in the course’s errata and say how you would test it.
You can say what Moskowitz’s objection to OI-3 actually was, and why “your claim isn’t testable as written” is a different criticism from “your claim is wrong”.
You can name one enabler of intimacy that both groups in Sala et al. reported, and say which earlier week the autistic participants’ named barrier points back to.

course.title: One Button, Twelve Games
course.description: A twelve-week course in how much interaction a single button can hold. Each week adds one new primitive to a shared vocabulary — press, hold, release, rhythm, sequence, momentum, context — building toward a complete one-button game.

nodes.title: Press
nodes.description: The first session of the semester — the smallest possible interaction, and three different things a single press can mean
spec: your development environment runs the course's toolchain and you can preview a prototype in a browser
you have three tiny prototypes, each responding to a single press in a different way

nodes.title: Hold
nodes.description: Duration becomes information — what a button can tell you before you let go of it
spec: one of your week 1 prototypes now shows a value that changes for as long as the button is held down
you can say, in one sentence, what that growing value represents

nodes.title: Release
nodes.description: The moment of letting go — why release timing, not press timing, decides what happened
spec: a prototype has a target window that can be missed two ways — releasing too early and releasing too late
you can demonstrate both failure cases, on request, in under a minute

nodes.title: Rhythm
nodes.description: What the gap between separate presses says, once duration stops being the only signal a button gives you
spec: a prototype reacts to the timing between separate presses, not to how long any single press lasted
it visibly distinguishes "too fast", "too slow" and "on tempo"

nodes.title: Sequence
nodes.description: Turning short presses and long presses into a small alphabet the game can recognise
spec: you have defined an alphabet of three to five symbols built from short/long presses
a prototype recognises at least two distinct sequences and responds differently to each

nodes.title: Momentum
nodes.description: A value that survives between presses, and drains on its own when you stop
spec: a prototype has a resource that rises with well-timed repeated presses and visibly decays on its own when input stops
stopping has a cost you can point to on screen, not just a number that freezes

nodes.title: Context
nodes.description: Making the same press mean two different things, depending on what's already true
spec: a prototype combines two earlier mechanics behind one button, switched by a single piece of state
a first-time player can tell which mode they're in without being told

nodes.title: Movement
nodes.description: Turning duration and momentum into position and speed, with no second input axis
spec: a prototype's single button controls both when something moves and how far or fast it goes
you can justify your specific mapping in one sentence

nodes.title: Failure
nodes.description: Designing mistakes a player can actually read, and a retry that respects what went wrong
spec: a prototype has at least two distinguishable failure states, each with its own feedback
retrying costs something proportionate to the mistake, not a flat penalty regardless of what went wrong

nodes.title: Two players
nodes.description: Two single buttons, one shared game — what changes when someone else's timing matters too
spec: a two-player prototype exists where each player's press only means something in relation to the other player's input
you can say exactly what breaks if you unplug the second player

nodes.title: Accessibility
nodes.description: What happens when the button only confirms, and something else keeps time
spec: an earlier prototype is adapted to run through an automatic scanning cursor with a single confirm press
you have played the adaptation under a real constraint and written down exactly what broke

nodes.title: Synthesis
nodes.description: Choosing which parts of the semester's vocabulary one finished game actually needs
spec: a complete one-button game exists, built from a deliberately chosen subset of the semester's vocabulary
you can name what was left out, and why, not only what was kept

nodes.title: Vocabulary log
nodes.description: The first piece of graded work — the accumulated set of tiny prototypes from weeks 1 to 6, submitted as they're made
spec: one prototype per week, for weeks 1 through 6, each runnable in a browser
each prototype demonstrates that week's primitive without leaning on a later week's mechanic to work

marking.description: Marked on whether each prototype isolates its week's primitive rather than blurring it with a later one — a working week 6 prototype that secretly reuses week 3's release logic scores lower than a rougher one that keeps the distinction clean. Submitted late in the run counts against you more than submitted rough on time.

nodes.title: Context switch
nodes.description: The week 7 checkpoint — one prototype that puts at least three earlier primitives behind a single button, switched by state
spec: a working prototype combines at least three primitives from weeks 1 through 6 behind one button
a piece of state, visible to the player, decides which meaning currently applies

criteria.name: Correct use of three or more earlier primitives
The mode switch is legible to a first-time player

nodes.title: Two-player piece
nodes.description: The week 10 checkpoint — a prototype where two single-button players depend on each other, not two copies of the same game
spec: a two-player prototype exists, one button per player
a player's press changes meaning depending on what the other player has done

marking.description: Marked on whether the second player's input actually changes what the first player's button means, and vice versa. A technically-correct two-button, one-each prototype that plays identically with one player unplugged has not met the brief, however well it's built otherwise.

nodes.title: Accessibility adaptation
nodes.description: The week 11 checkpoint — an earlier prototype adapted to scanning input, with an honest account of what broke
spec: an earlier prototype is adapted to run through an automatic scanning cursor and a single confirm press
a written account names specific things that broke in the adaptation, not general impressions

criteria.name: The adaptation is actually playable via a scanning cursor
Specificity and honesty of the written account

nodes.title: Synthesis game
nodes.description: The capstone — a complete one-button game built from a deliberately chosen subset of the semester's vocabulary
spec: a complete, runnable one-button game exists
a short note names which weeks' mechanics were kept, which were cut, and why the cuts improved the game

marking.description: Judged as a whole against the brief, with particular attention to whether the scope decision was deliberate. A game that uses every primitive from the semester is not rewarded for coverage; a game that uses three well, and can say why the rest were cut, is a stronger response than one that uses all eleven and explains none of them.

nodes.title: Press
nodes.description: The opening lecture — why one button is a design position worth twelve weeks, not a restriction to route around

nodes.title: Hold
nodes.description: Week 2 — why a value with no payoff yet is still worth showing a player, and the trap it sets if you overpay it

nodes.title: Release
nodes.description: Week 3 — why a release-timing failure has to feel earned, not like a disguised coin flip

nodes.title: Rhythm
nodes.description: Week 4 — tempo as a signal read between gestures, and why its tolerance window has no correct answer

nodes.title: Sequence
nodes.description: Week 5 — alphabet size as a real trade-off between meaninglessly small and unmemorisable

nodes.title: Momentum
nodes.description: Week 6 — why momentum isn't a score with a different name, and the one constant that decides how a mechanic feels

nodes.title: Context
nodes.description: Week 7 — why the studio exercise stays at two mechanics, and what gets harder once that number grows

nodes.title: Movement
nodes.description: Week 8 — the precision a single continuous signal gives up when it's asked to control both timing and magnitude

nodes.title: Failure
nodes.description: Week 9 — why not every mistake deserves its own signal, even once the vocabulary can support one

nodes.title: Two players
nodes.description: Week 10 — simultaneous presses as a design decision, not a bug to patch around

nodes.title: Accessibility
nodes.description: Week 11 — cursor speed as the one parameter that decides whether an adaptation is playable at all

nodes.title: Synthesis
nodes.description: The closing lecture — why cutting for focus is a defensible design decision and cutting for time isn't

course.title: How to Make a Day
course.description: Public guidance tells you what helps people in general. This course teaches the last step it cannot take: realising where your own day sits in it, changing one thing, and rethinking that change against what your body, mood and actions send back.

nodes.title: The Day You Didn't Design
nodes.description: We record one ordinary day and change nothing about it, which is harder than it sounds
spec: you arrive with twenty-four continuous hours recorded
the day you recorded is one you did not try to improve
you can say what you decided not to write down, and why

nodes.title: What Is "Tired"?
nodes.description: Before you can measure how tired you are, you have to decide what you mean, and that decision quietly settles what you are able to find
spec: you bring three candidate measures of tiredness, not one
each one can be recorded in under thirty seconds
you can name something each measure would miss

claims.text: Under two weeks of restricted sleep, people's ratings of their own sleepiness levelled off after the first few days while their measured performance kept getting worse. The authors concluded subjects "were largely unaware of these increasing cognitive deficits".
claims.source: Van Dongen HPA, Maislin G, Mullington JM, Dinges DF, The cumulative cost of additional wakefulness, Sleep 2003;26(2):117-126. The n of 48 covers both the restriction and total-deprivation experiments together.

nodes.title: Two Instruments, One Night
nodes.description: Your phone, a paper diary and your own memory will disagree about last night, and none of them is the referee
spec: you record the same night with two different instruments
you can state which one you trusted before you looked, and why
you report the disagreement rather than resolving it

meta.stopping_rule: Stop recording and tell us if you find yourself checking your sleep data before you have got out of bed, or lying awake wondering what the device will say.
meta.harm_boundary: Nothing in this week asks you to sleep less, sleep more, or go to bed at a different time. You are measuring the sleep you were already going to have.
meta.opt_out: Compare a paper diary against your own morning recall, with no device at all. Write the two times into the diary as they happen, at lights out and at waking, then write the same two times again from memory that evening and report the gap. Two instruments, one night, and still no referee.

claims.text: Wrist actigraphy and self-report disagreed about the same nights. Measured sleep averaged 6.0 hours against 6.8 hours reported, the two correlated at only 0.47, and people sleeping five hours over-reported by about 1.2 hours.
claims.source: Lauderdale DS, Knutson KL, Yan LL, Liu K, Rathouz PJ, Self-reported and measured sleep duration, Epidemiology 2008;19(6):838-845

claims.text: Sleep clinicians proposed the term "orthosomnia" in 2017 for patients arriving at clinic whose presenting complaint was their own sleep-tracker data rather than their sleep.
claims.source: Baron KG, Abbott S, Jao N, Manalo N, Mullen R, Orthosomnia: Are Some Patients Taking the Quantified Self Too Far?, Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine 2017

nodes.title: The Observer in the Room
nodes.description: You cannot watch your own day without changing it, so this week we measure the size of the change instead of pretending it away
spec: your log covers three days of the same observable
you can point to the moment the logging changed the behaviour
you estimate how big that change was, and say how you estimated it

meta.stopping_rule: Stop if the record turns into a scorecard, if you notice yourself feeling ashamed of a number rather than curious about it, put the log down for the day.
meta.harm_boundary: This week produces no target and no limit. There is no correct amount of phone use, and anyone who tells you there is has skipped the part where they say how they measured it.
meta.opt_out: Log a different observable instead (how often you open the fridge, how often you check the time) or work from a partner's log with their consent.

claims.text: Asked how many times a day they picked up their phone, people's estimates did not correlate with what their phones had logged. Estimates of total duration held up better. Note the sample size before you carry this anywhere.
claims.source: Andrews S, Ellis DA, Shaw H, Piwek L, Beyond Self-Report, PLOS ONE 2015;10(10):e0139004

claims.text: The illumination experiments at Western Electric's Hawthorne Works between 1924 and 1932 gave the effect its name, but later reanalysis of the surviving data found the original evidence for it much weaker than the story it produced.
claims.source: Levitt SD, List JA, Was There Really a Hawthorne Effect at the Hawthorne Plant?, American Economic Journal: Applied Economics 2011

nodes.title: Take It Away, Put It Back
nodes.description: The simplest honest experiment one person can run alone, demonstrated on breakfast
spec: your design has three phases and you can say what each one is for
the removal phase has an end date fixed before you begin
you report the return phase even when it is inconvenient

meta.stopping_rule: Stop and return to eating normally if you feel faint, if you cannot concentrate by mid-morning, or if the removal phase stops feeling like an experiment and starts feeling like a rule. Four days is the cap, and shorter is fine.
meta.harm_boundary: This is not a fasting exercise and there is no target. You are not trying to eat less, lose anything, or discover that breakfast is unnecessary. Anyone with a history of disordered eating, diabetes, or any condition affected by meal timing should take the alternative instead, and so should anyone who simply does not want to.
meta.opt_out: Run the same design on something inert: your first coffee's timing, the radio on your commute, or a lamp. The method is the lesson, not the meal.

claims.text: Over sixteen weeks, being told to eat breakfast and being told to skip it produced no significant difference in weight loss, and it made no difference whether someone already ate breakfast.
claims.source: Dhurandhar EJ et al., The effectiveness of breakfast recommendations on weight loss, American Journal of Clinical Nutrition 2014;100(2):507-513

claims.text: Barry Marshall drank a culture of Helicobacter pylori in 1984 to test whether it caused gastritis, developed the illness within days, and shared the 2005 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the work.
claims.source: Marshall's own account; Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2005 (Marshall and Warren)

nodes.title: Twenty-Five Minutes
nodes.description: The most repeated productivity instruction in the world was one student's answer to one question, so this week we test it properly
spec: your two conditions differ in exactly one respect
the order you tried them in is balanced, and you can show how
you state what result would have counted as the timer losing

claims.text: Interrupted every two minutes, people finished the task in less time with no loss of quality, and reported significantly more stress, frustration and effort. Conditions were counterbalanced, which is this week's method.
claims.source: Mark G, Gudith D, Klocke U, The cost of interrupted work, CHI 2008, pages 107-110

claims.text: The interval began as one student's bet with himself in the late 1980s, using a tomato-shaped kitchen timer. The paper dates the method to 1992 and describes no trial of any interval length against any other.
claims.source: Francesco Cirillo, The Pomodoro Technique, free paper released 19 October 2006, version 1.3 of 15 June 2007, preface and section 1

claims.text: The only sweep of interval lengths in that paper was run by work groups Cirillo was mentoring, not on himself. They went from an hour to two hours, down to forty-five minutes, then ten, and settled on thirty. The same paper's results section recommends thirty minutes, not twenty-five.
claims.source: Francesco Cirillo, The Pomodoro Technique, section 3.2, The Length of the Pomodoro

claims.text: The paper's one appeal to outside evidence about interval length, that twenty to forty-five minute intervals maximise attention, footnotes a Teach Yourself Literature Guide to Orwell's Animal Farm.
claims.source: Francesco Cirillo, The Pomodoro Technique, bibliography reference 15, citing Iona McGregor with Tony Buzan, A Guide to Animal Farm, Hodder and Stoughton, 1998, ISBN 0-340-66401-0

nodes.title: You Are the Placebo
nodes.description: Every experiment in this course has the same unfixable flaw, and this week we look straight at it
spec: you can describe how you concealed the condition from yourself
you record your guess about which condition you were in, before you check
you report how often your guess was right

meta.stopping_rule: Stop and go back to your usual intake if you get a headache that will not shift, or if you cannot work. Caffeine withdrawal headaches are common, ordinary and unpleasant, and they are a reason to stop rather than a stage to push through.
meta.harm_boundary: There is no reduction target and no abstinence phase. Nobody is quitting anything. If you do not drink caffeine, do not start for this week, and if you are pregnant, taking medication affected by caffeine, or prone to migraine, take the alternative.
meta.opt_out: Blind a condition that carries no physiological load at all: two unlabelled playlists, two desk lamps at different temperatures, two teas that taste alike. The interesting part is the concealment, not the chemical.

claims.text: Across trials that randomised patients to a placebo or to nothing at all, placebo had no significant effect on binary outcomes. The exception was self-reported pain. Note that placebo against nothing is the one comparison nobody can blind.
claims.source: Hrobjartsson A, Gotzsche PC, Is the Placebo Powerless?, New England Journal of Medicine 2001;344(21):1594-1602

claims.text: The commission appointed by Louis XVI in 1784, with Benjamin Franklin among its members, tested mesmerism by blindfolding subjects so they could not tell when they were being treated. The reported effects followed what subjects believed rather than where the treatment was applied.
claims.source: Report of the Royal Commission on Animal Magnetism, Paris 1784 (Franklin, Lavoisier, Bailly and others)

nodes.title: Everything Else That Happened
nodes.description: You cannot randomise your own life, so this week we go looking for what else moved while we were not watching
spec: you list at least ten things that changed during your week 5 experiment
you rank them by how plausibly each could explain your result
you identify one you could have measured and did not

claims.text: Observational studies had found that women taking hormone therapy had less coronary disease. The randomised trial found it caused more, along with more breast cancer and more clots, and was stopped early.
claims.source: Rossouw JE et al., Risks and Benefits of Estrogen Plus Progestin in Healthy Postmenopausal Women, JAMA 2002;288(3):321-333

claims.text: In 1854 John Snow compared cholera deaths between households supplied by two different water companies in the same south London streets, one drawing from a sewage-polluted stretch of the Thames and one from further upstream, which let him separate the water from the neighbourhood.
claims.source: John Snow, On the Mode of Communication of Cholera, second edition, London 1855

nodes.title: Why You Felt Better Anyway
nodes.description: Almost everything appears to work, because almost everybody starts on their worst day
spec: you bring your week 5 record as one number a day, in date order, with every day marked A, B or C for its phase
your sheet carries three pairs of days, low, high and control, and the two distances you worked out for each pair
you hand in one sentence saying why an intervention begun on your lowest day would have looked successful, and the sentence does not contain the words "regression to the mean"

meta.stopping_rule: Stop and say so if reading your own low days back leaves you worse than when you started, or if you find yourself returning to them outside the lab. You finish the hour on the previous year's record, and the sheet you have already written goes home with you unread.
meta.harm_boundary: This is not an exercise in ranking your bad days or in accounting for them. Six numbers leave your sheet and nothing else does: they carry no name, no units and no dates, and you are never asked what you were measuring in week 5 or what happened on the day. We are looking at what tends to follow an unusual measurement, never at why you had one.
meta.opt_out: Run the same six steps on the anonymised class record from a previous year, which is a set of week 5 records with the names taken off. The pairs come out of it exactly as they come out of yours, and nothing of your own is opened, written down or put on the board.

claims.text: Blood pressure regressed in both directions. Among people whose baseline 24-hour systolic pressure was 150 mmHg or above, the mean was 156 at baseline and 141 at follow-up; among those under 120, it was 113 and then 119. The authors report regression in the control groups as well as the treated ones, which is what stops the treatment explaining it.
claims.source: Moore MN, Atkins ER, Salam A et al., Regression to the mean of repeated ambulatory blood pressure monitoring in five studies, Journal of Hypertension 2019;37(1):24-29. The abstract reports five pooled studies and no participant total, so the sample size here counts studies rather than people.

claims.text: Galton put numbers to the pattern in 1886 by the move this lab repeats. He grouped 205 parent couples by their average height, read off the median height of their 928 adult children, and found each group's children nearer the general average of 68.25 inches than their parents were, in all nine rows of the table that carry a median.
claims.source: Francis Galton, Regression towards Mediocrity in Hereditary Stature, Journal of the Anthropological Institute of Great Britain and Ireland, volume 15 (1886), pages 246 to 263

nodes.title: The Subject Has Changed
nodes.description: We run week 5's experiment again, on the same person, and get a different answer
spec: you re-run week 5's protocol without modification
you report both results side by side, not averaged
you offer at least two explanations for the difference, one of which is not a mistake

meta.stopping_rule: The same cap as week 5 applies, and more strictly: this is a repeat, not an escalation. Stop at four days, or sooner if the removal phase stops feeling like an experiment.
meta.harm_boundary: Running a protocol twice does not license running it harder. Nothing about the second pass should be longer, stricter or more ambitious than the first, and anyone who took the alternative in week 5 takes it again now.
meta.opt_out: Re-run whichever inert version you used in week 5. The comparison you need is between your own two attempts, so any variable works as long as it is the same one.

claims.text: Continuous glucose monitoring across 46,898 meals found that responses to the same standardised meal varied widely from person to person, which the authors took as a limit on universal dietary advice.
claims.source: Zeevi D et al., Personalized Nutrition by Prediction of Glycemic Responses, Cell 2015;163(5):1079-1094

claims.text: Santorio Santorio spent roughly thirty years weighing himself, his food and his waste on a balance of his own construction, looking for what he could not account for. He published the results as a set of aphorisms in 1614.
claims.source: Santorio Santorio, Ars de statica medicina, Venice 1614

nodes.title: Forty Things at Once
nodes.description: Track enough about yourself and something will always correlate with something, which is how a dashboard lies to you with true numbers
spec: you log at least twenty variables for four days
you find a correlation you would have believed, and say why you would have
you can state how many comparisons your dataset makes available

meta.stopping_rule: Stop and hand the logging to us if the tracking becomes the point, if you are reluctant to end the week, if a missing entry bothers you, or if you find yourself adjusting your day to make a number look better.
meta.harm_boundary: This week deliberately induces over-measuring in order to show you what it feels like, and it lasts four days. It is not a template. Anyone for whom detailed self-tracking has previously become compulsive should take the alternative without discussing it with anyone.
meta.opt_out: Use the class's synthetic dataset, which is generated from pure noise. It produces the same spurious correlations and asks nothing of your own day.

claims.text: A dead salmon, scanned while shown photographs of people in social situations, produced 16 significant voxels out of 8,064 under uncorrected statistics. Correcting for the number of comparisons left none.
claims.source: Bennett CM, Baird AA, Miller MB, Wolford GL, Neural correlates of interspecies perspective taking in the post-mortem Atlantic Salmon, poster, Organization for Human Brain Mapping 2009

claims.text: A group of neuroscientists scanned a dead Atlantic salmon in an fMRI machine while showing it photographs of human social situations, and recovered apparently significant brain activity, presented as an argument for correcting when you test many voxels at once.
claims.source: Bennett CM, Baird AA, Miller MB, Wolford GL, Neural correlates of interspecies perspective taking in the post-mortem Atlantic Salmon, poster, Organization for Human Brain Mapping 2009; Journal of Serendipitous and Unexpected Results 2010

nodes.title: The Day You Don't Measure
nodes.description: When to stop experimenting, why every answer you found has an expiry date, and what you are left holding
spec: you nominate one measurement you will keep and say for how long
you nominate one you are stopping, and why
you can state the expiry date of your own main finding

claims.text: Among trials that had been registered properly, 31% published a different primary outcome from the one they registered. Where the direction could be judged, the change favoured a statistically significant result 83% of the time.
claims.source: Mathieu S, Boutron I, Moher D, Altman DG, Ravaud P, Comparison of registered and published primary outcomes in randomized controlled trials, JAMA 2009;302(9):977-984

claims.text: Medical journal editors began requiring that trials be registered before enrolment, from mid-2005, because outcomes were being selected after results were known and unfavourable trials were disappearing entirely.
claims.source: De Angelis C et al., Clinical Trial Registration, a Statement from the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors, New England Journal of Medicine 2004;351:1250-1251

nodes.title: Pre-registration
nodes.description: Plan one change to one block of your own day, traced to a sentence of public guidance, and commit to it before you collect anything
spec: submitted before you have collected any data
it names one block from your week 1 record, and what you will do differently in it
it quotes the sentence of guidance the change rests on, and says where that sentence is published
it answers week 2's four questions about that sentence, in the order week 2 asks them
it fixes the order the changed and unchanged days run in, and says how that order is balanced or why this change cannot be ordered
it states one measure, the smallest difference that measure could detect, and where that figure came from
it states when you will stop, and what would make you stop early
it states a result that would count against your expectation

criteria.name: The change is traced to a sentence of guidance you have actually read
The order of your two conditions is balanced, or you say why it cannot be
The measure could detect a difference the size of the one you propose
The stopping rule is specific, and decided in advance
You state what result would prove you wrong

nodes.title: Protocol portfolio
nodes.description: Four protocols from the first eight weeks, each one able to say what it cannot see
spec: four protocols, each from a different week
each one states its measure, its duration and its limits
the raw record is included, not just the summary

criteria.name: Each protocol changes one thing, and you can say which
Each names something it cannot detect
The record is continuous, dated and legible to someone else

nodes.title: Replication and drift
nodes.description: Run one of your own protocols a second time, get a different answer, and account for it
spec: the second run uses the first run's protocol without modification
both results appear, unaveraged
at least one explanation offered is not a mistake you made

criteria.name: The re-run is unmodified, and you can show that it is
Both results are reported side by side, not averaged
The account of the difference, including a cause that is not an error

nodes.title: The Report
nodes.description: Run the experiment you pre-registered and report it honestly, including the parts that came out null
spec: it reports the experiment you pre-registered in week 6, and its question is that document's question unaltered
every departure from the pre-registration is listed with the date you made it and whether you had seen any data by then
the raw record is attached whole, and every number in the report can be found in it
a result that came out null is written up at the same length and with the same care as one that did not

criteria.name: Whether your conclusion follows from the data you actually have
The limits you declare, and what they cost your conclusion
Whether a stranger could re-run this from your record
