course.title: Introduction to Preparing Meal
course.description: A meal is decided before it is cooked. Ten weeks on choosing, storing, portioning and cutting what you will eat, then two at the stove to measure what the preparation already settled. No experience assumed.

nodes.title: Why prepare at all
nodes.description: Why week 1 carries no tutorial exercise: establishing the case for preparation is not itself a preparation decision, and the exercises begin once one exists to practise.
spec: you can state the course thesis in one sentence, unprompted
you can say why week 1 carries no tutorial exercise while weeks 2 through 10 each carry one

nodes.title: Vegetables
nodes.description: A hands-on exercise reading a vegetable's fat, protein and calorie content off the same USDA database this week's lecture cites, in grams rather than impressions.
spec: you can compute the fat, protein and calorie content of a stated quantity of at least one vegetable using this week's calculator
you can name the USDA FoodData Central entry a chosen vegetable's figures come from
you can compare two vegetables' calorie density and say, in one sentence, what the difference tracks (starch and water content, not fat or protein)

nodes.title: Animal protein I: poultry and fish
nodes.description: A hands-on exercise computing fat, protein and calorie content across four items this week's lecture covers by anatomy, to see what that anatomy means in grams.
spec: you can compute the fat, protein and calorie content of a stated quantity of at least one poultry or fish item using this week's calculator
you can rank this week's four items by fat content and connect the order to the anatomy the lecture described
you can name the FoodData Central source a chosen item's figures come from

nodes.title: Animal protein II: red meat
nodes.description: A hands-on exercise comparing two ground-beef blends against lamb and goat, to see what a stated fat percentage actually means in grams.
spec: you can compute the fat, protein and calorie content of a stated quantity of at least one red-meat item using this week's calculator
you can compare 85%-lean and 93%-lean ground beef at the same quantity and state the difference in fat content
you can name which of this week's four items is leanest and connect that to the anatomy the lecture described

nodes.title: Spices, aromatics and oil
nodes.description: A hands-on exercise computing how long a cut allium or a prepared leaf herb can wait before it must be refrigerated or discarded.
spec: you can compute a safe-until time for a cut allium or a prepared leaf herb using this week's calculator, given a preparation time
you can state how much longer a refrigerated item's safe window is than the same item held at room temperature
you can say why this week's refrigerated allium and herb items apply a general storage window rather than an allium-specific one

nodes.title: The kitchen: tools and surfaces
nodes.description: Chopping boards, choppers, strainers and containers, and their maintenance — including an honest look at what board material actually does to hygiene, knife wear and particle shedding.
spec: you can name one advantage and one disadvantage of each of wood, plastic and marble as a cutting-board material
you can summarise the Yadav et al. (2023) finding accurately, including what it did not find
you can describe a maintenance routine for a wooden board and say why each step is there

nodes.title: Cuts, under supervision
nodes.description: This week's lecture describes the knife; this session is where the grip and the standard cuts are practised at the bench and checked against the deck's own figures for length, weight, hardness and edge angle.
spec: you can state the edge angle and Rockwell hardness typically claimed for a Western-style kitchen knife, and where the bench knife you used sits against those figures
you can hold pinch grip on the knife hand and claw grip on the guiding hand without being reminded partway through a cut
you can state the difference between honing and sharpening in terms of whether metal is removed, and say which one was due on your knife today

nodes.title: Timed mise en place
nodes.description: A hands-on exercise computing how long a held item — a portioned vegetable, a stock, a sauce — can safely wait before it must be served or refrigerated again.
spec: you can compute a safe-until time for a held item using this week's calculator, given a preparation time
you can state why a held item's safe window differs by a factor of dozens depending on whether it is kept at room temperature or refrigerated
you can connect the "held" category from the guest lecture to a specific, sourced cold-chain figure

nodes.title: Fruit
nodes.description: A hands-on exercise comparing calorie density across this week's fruits, and checking whether ripening behaviour tracks nutritional composition or is unrelated to it.
spec: you can compute the fat, protein and calorie content of a stated quantity of at least one fruit using this week's calculator
you can state, from the calculator's own figures, that calorie content across this week's fruits tracks sugar content more than fat or protein
you can name the FoodData Central source a chosen fruit's figures come from

nodes.title: Food safety and the cold chain
nodes.description: A hands-on exercise computing a safe-until time for the raw materials and the already-prepared leftovers this course has handled since week 2, using the same cold-chain rule throughout.
spec: you can compute a safe-until time for at least one raw material and one already-prepared leftover using this week's calculator
you can state which of this week's items carries the shortest safe window and why (danger-zone exposure, not anatomy)
you can name the source the calculator's durations are drawn from

nodes.title: First heat
nodes.description: The same dish, cooked twice from batches of material prepared two different ways, so that any difference in the result can be attributed to the preparation rather than to what happened at the stove.
spec: you can state which single preparation variable your pair is testing, and what was held identical between the two batches so that variable is the only difference
you can check doneness with a thermometer against the correct minimum internal temperature for your material, rather than by colour or time
you can describe one difference in the finished result and trace it back to a specific preparation decision from an earlier week, not to the cooking method

nodes.title: The live test
nodes.description: The teaching session built around week 12's assessed practical — what is watched before the heat is applied, and whether the semester's preparation decisions hold up in front of an audience under a clock.
spec: before you begin, you can state which single preparation decision from your invent-a-recipe account you are least confident in, and why
your dish is completed inside the stated time allowance, or you can say exactly where the run departed from the plan and what you changed to recover
you can point to one specific decision made before the heat was applied — a selection, a storage choice, a cut — and show where it shows up in the finished plate

nodes.title: Assignment — invent a recipe
nodes.description: A written account of an invented dish, argued before it is cooked — preparation process, nutritional composition and sensory prediction.
spec: the dish has not been cooked; the account reasons about a result rather than reporting one
the preparation process is given as an ordered sequence of steps, each stating what is done to the ingredient and why
every nutritional figure is attributed to a named entry in a stated food-composition database, with enough detail (food code or item name) that a marker could look it up
the sensory description addresses colour, aroma, flavour and texture as four distinct claims, not one paragraph of general approval
submitted by the deadline, in the format named below

nodes.title: Final — the public kitchen
nodes.description: The week 12 practical, assessed live — preparation decisions, execution under time constraint, whether the result matches what was predicted, and how the student handles an independent taster's report of it.
spec: the dish prepared and cooked matches the recipe described in the invent-a-recipe assignment, or the departure is stated and explained
preparation work (selection, storage handling, cuts, mise en place) is completed before cooking begins and is visible to the examiner as such
the dish is completed within the time allowance stated for the session
the student can account for any difference between the predicted sensory description and the finished dish
the student presents a sensory report of the finished dish from a taster other than themselves, on the same four terms as the week 6 prediction, and states where the two accounts agree or diverge

nodes.title: Why prepare at all
nodes.description: The case for preparation, made with time-use figures rather than assertion, and the thesis the semester is built to test.

course.title: Three Shots Ahead: Pool, Physics & Strategic Thinking
course.description: A 12-week beginner pool course built on one idea: every shot should prepare the next. Complete beginners and casual players progress from aiming and cue-ball contact through spin and positional control to full three-shot planning, safety and table strategy.

nodes.title: Know the Game
nodes.description: An orientation to the table, the equipment and the basic rules — everything a complete beginner needs before technical stroke instruction begins.

objectives: Identify the cue ball, object balls, rails, cushions, pockets and basic table areas.
Understand the basic purpose of pool.
Understand basic turn-taking and common fouls.
Recognise simple legal and illegal situations.
Handle the cue and table safely and respectfully.
meta.learn: This week is an orientation to the table and the game, not a rulebook. You'll meet the cue ball and the object balls, the pockets and cushions, and the basic parts of the cue, then learn the basic objective of pool, how turns pass between players, the most common beginner fouls, and simple etiquette and safety around the table and other players.
meta.see: Simple table diagrams point out the cue ball, the object ball you're aiming at, the pocket you're aiming for, and the rail — the four things you'll be asked to identify before every shot from here on.
meta.think: Beginner situations to reason through: which pocket is the most natural target for a given ball? Which shot is obviously legal, and which is obviously illegal? What should you check before taking any shot at all?
meta.play: A light, low-pressure session at the table: walk around and identify the parts described above, place balls where asked, and try a few simple straight shots. The aim is comfort holding the cue and moving around the table, not potting percentage.
meta.tableCheck: A short knowledge check on table anatomy, the basic rules, and simple legal/illegal decisions.

nodes.title: Build Your Stance
nodes.description: The complete pre-shot setup, taught in order — the routine every later week's stroke depends on. "A good shot starts before you bend down."

objectives: Stand behind the cue ball and read the shot line before entering the stance.
Set the feet and cueing arm in line with the shot before lowering.
Use a relaxed grip and a stable, guiding bridge.
Lower into a stable stance with the head and chin aligned to the cue.
Repeat the full setup sequence, in order, on demand.
meta.learn: This week is entirely about the pre-shot setup: how to stand, find the line, grip the cue, and settle into a stable stance and bridge before ever committing to a stroke. Each part of the setup is explained on its own below, in the order it happens.
meta.see: A numbered sequence walks through the setup from standing to warm-up strokes, so the order is as clear as the individual steps.
meta.think: Examples of poor setup are shown so you can name what's wrong — entering the stance before finding the line, a tight grip, an unstable bridge, a cueing arm outside the shot line, or the body moving during delivery.
meta.play: This week is mainly setup practice. Students repeatedly enter and leave the stance without worrying heavily about potting percentage.
meta.tableCheck: Tutor or self-check: can the student repeat the setup in the correct sequence, in order, without skipping a step?

nodes.title: The Straight Shot
nodes.description: A practical continuation of Week 2 — turning the stance and cue action into a repeatable straight stroke.

objectives: Repeat the observe-enter-set-aim sequence from Week 2 without skipping steps.
Deliver the cue in a smooth backswing and forearm-driven stroke.
Follow through and stay down after impact instead of standing up immediately.
Diagnose a likely technical cause behind a repeated miss.
Use a cue-line test to check delivery consistency.
meta.learn: This week reinforces a stable upper body, a relaxed grip, a smooth backswing, a stable upper arm, forearm-driven delivery, a full follow-through, and staying down after impact rather than standing up immediately. The common errors below are worth checking against your own stroke.
meta.see: Before/after diagrams show the cue travelling straight through the cue ball against the cue deviating left or right, and how body movement during the stroke causes cue-line errors.
meta.think: Given a pattern of repeated misses, work out the likely technical cause from the setup and stroke covered this week and last.
meta.play: Repeated straight-shot practice: fixed-position straight shots and gradual consistency drills, including a cue-line test and a simple practice log.
meta.tableCheck: Complete a short straight-shot consistency drill and identify one technical issue to improve.

nodes.title: Finding the Angle
nodes.description: Moving from straight shots to angled shots, by understanding the relationship between the cue ball, the contact point, the object-ball path and the pocket.

objectives: Visualise the object-ball path from the pocket back through the object ball.
Locate the contact point on the object ball using the ghost-ball reference.
Tell apart the object-ball path, the cue-ball aiming line, the contact point and the ghost-ball position.
Apply the same pre-shot routine from Week 2 to an angled shot, unchanged.
Judge whether an aim looks too thick or too thin.
meta.learn: The core idea this week is a chain: cue ball, contact point, object-ball path, pocket — and you work it out starting from the pocket, not the cue ball. Because both balls have physical size, you cannot aim the centre of the cue ball at the centre of the object ball for an angled shot; you aim at the contact point that sends the object ball where you need it to go. The pre-shot routine from Week 2 and the stroke from Week 3 don't change just because the shot is angled.
meta.see: Visual examples progress from a straight shot through small, medium and larger-angle cuts, so the object-ball path and the cue-ball aiming line are visibly different from one shot to the next.
meta.think: Given a cut shot, work out which pocket line is correct, where the contact point is, which ghost-ball position is correct, and whether the aim looks too thick or too thin.
meta.play: Progress gradually through straight, slight-angle, medium-angle and larger-angle shots, using the same pre-shot routine each time.
meta.tableCheck: Given several illustrated cut shots, identify the correct contact point or aiming option before playing the shot.

nodes.title: Cue Ball Direction & the Tangent Line
nodes.description: A new question after potting: where will the cue ball go after contact? This week introduces contact thickness and the tangent line.

objectives: Distinguish full, thick, half-ball and thin contact.
Predict the approximate first direction of the cue ball after contact.
Understand the tangent line as a reference for cue-ball separation.
Recognise that cue-ball path depends on the state of the cue ball at impact.
Make a prediction before playing a shot.
meta.learn: Potting the object ball is only half the shot — the cue ball has to go somewhere too. This week introduces contact thickness (full, thick, half-ball, thin) and the tangent line: a useful 90-degree reference for where a sliding cue ball separates from the object ball, not a fixed law.
meta.see: A diagram compares the separation angle produced by centre-ball, high-ball and low-ball contact after collision.
meta.think: Prediction questions: which direction will the cue ball initially leave? Is this hit thick or thin? Which path best matches a stun shot?
meta.play: Predict the cue-ball direction out loud or by pointing, before playing — using repeated fixed ball positions with different contact thicknesses.
meta.tableCheck: Given several simple layouts, predict the approximate first cue-ball direction before playing each one.

nodes.title: Stop, Follow & Draw
nodes.description: Using vertical spin on purpose — stop, follow and draw shots, built on last week's tangent-line reference.

objectives: Identify stop, follow and draw shots.
Understand how cue-ball contact height affects spin.
Select stop, follow or draw for a simple position problem.
Recognise the difference between initial tangent-line movement and the later effect of spin.
Execute basic versions of each shot.
meta.learn: Week 5 established a natural reference — the tangent line. This week is about intentionally changing that natural outcome using vertical spin: stop (near-centre contact), follow (above centre) and draw (below centre). Speed and spin interact, so avoid treating "hit higher" or "hit lower" as a guaranteed distance.
meta.see: A diagram compares the stun/90-degree reference against a follow path bending forward and a draw path bending backward.
meta.think: Given a desired cue-ball finishing area, decide: stop, follow or draw? Given a path, ask which cue action most likely produced it.
meta.play: A three-shot control drill on the same or a similar simple layout: one stop, one follow, one draw — so the outcomes can be compared directly.
meta.tableCheck: Complete one basic stop, one follow and one draw task.

nodes.title: Side Spin & Cushion Reactions
nodes.description: Left and right side spin, and how they can change the cue ball's reaction off a cushion. "Spin is a tool, not a shortcut."

objectives: Identify left and right side spin.
Understand that side spin changes cue-ball behaviour at cushions.
Compare no-spin and side-spin cushion reactions.
Use side spin only when it has a clear positional purpose.
Recognise that adding spin increases difficulty.
meta.learn: Contact to the left or right of centre — side spin, sometimes called English — can change how the cue ball leaves a cushion. This week keeps the idea at a conceptual level: a simple no-spin reference, then how left and right spin can alter the exit angle. Side spin also makes aiming and delivery harder, so it's a deliberate choice, not a default.
meta.see: A cue-ball contact map and three cushion-reaction diagrams (centre, high and low ball with side spin) are shown.
meta.think: Given a cue-ball path after hitting a rail, which spin was most likely used?
meta.play: A fixed cushion experiment: same starting position, same rail, tried with centre, left and right contact — observe the exit differences.
meta.tableCheck: Predict, then test, one side-spin cushion reaction.

nodes.title: Point Positioning
nodes.description: The first formal positioning method, Point Positioning: can I make the cue ball finish at a specific location?

objectives: Select a specific cue-ball finishing point.
Combine speed with simple stop/follow/draw control.
Understand when precise point positioning is useful.
Recognise that high precision creates a smaller margin for error.
Use point positioning mainly for simple or short-range position play.
meta.learn: Point Positioning asks a precise question: can I make the cue ball finish at a specific location? It combines speed with the stop, follow and draw control from Week 6 to aim at one target point. It works best for simple, short-range position, because it demands accurate cueing and speed control — a small error can send the cue ball too far, too short, or onto the wrong angle for the next shot.
meta.see: Diagrams show one exact target point, a small error short, and a small error long.
meta.think: Is point positioning appropriate for this simple position problem, or is the target too demanding?
meta.play: Short-range position drills, aiming for a visible target marker.
meta.tableCheck: Pot the object ball and finish the cue ball inside or close to a small target area.

nodes.title: Zone Positioning
nodes.description: Zone Positioning — a more forgiving alternative to an exact point: aim for a workable area, not a single spot.

objectives: Identify a workable zone rather than a single target point.
Understand why a zone is more forgiving than an exact point.
Judge which side of the next object ball the cue ball needs to be on.
Recognise the angle a zone needs to leave for the following shot.
Choose zone positioning for less demanding position problems.
meta.learn: Zone Positioning relaxes the target from a single point to a workable area. Instead of asking "can I stop exactly here?", it asks "can I finish anywhere in this region and still have a workable next shot?" This is more forgiving of small speed or angle errors, and it starts from a simple three-ball question: which side of the next object ball should the cue ball end up on?
meta.see: A diagram shows a target zone (rather than a single point) and the side of the next object ball the cue ball should finish on.
meta.think: Given the cue ball, an object ball and a following ball, which side should the cue ball finish on to keep a workable angle for the next shot?
meta.play: Practise landing inside a marked zone rather than on an exact spot, across a range of simple three-ball layouts.
meta.tableCheck: Pot the object ball and finish the cue ball inside an acceptable zone for the next shot, not on one exact point.

nodes.title: Route Positioning & Three Shots Ahead
nodes.description: Route Positioning — reading the cue ball's whole travel path, planning a three-shot sequence rather than treating each shot in isolation.

objectives: Read the cue ball's whole travel path, not just its finishing point.
Recognise how a chosen route affects the shot two positions ahead.
Combine point, zone and route thinking on the same layout.
Plan a shot as part of a three-shot sequence, not in isolation.
Understand the course theme "three shots ahead" in concrete terms.
meta.learn: Route Positioning is the third and most demanding layer, after Point (Week 8) and Zone (Week 9). It looks at the cue ball's entire travel path across the table, not only where it stops — because the path itself can open or block a route to the shot after next. This is where the course's own theme, planning a three-shot sequence rather than treating each shot in isolation, becomes a concrete table skill rather than a slogan.
meta.see: A diagram shows a three-ball layout with a chosen cue-ball route connecting the current shot to a workable position two shots ahead, followed by two worked route examples on a real table.
meta.think: Given three balls, which route keeps the third ball workable, not just the second?
meta.play: Simple three-ball layouts, planning and executing a route that keeps the next two shots open rather than just the next one.
meta.tableCheck: Complete a three-ball sequence, explaining beforehand which route the cue ball will take and why.

nodes.title: Safety, Attack & Recovery
nodes.description: Not every shot has to be a pot attempt — recognising when to play safe, when to attack, and how to recover from a poor position.

objectives: Recognise when a pot attempt is not the best available option.
Understand the basic purpose of a safety shot.
Distinguish attacking decisions from safety decisions.
Choose a sensible recovery option from an awkward position.
Weigh risk against reward before committing to a shot.
meta.learn: Good pool is not always about potting a ball. This week introduces safety play as a deliberate decision, not a failure to attack — sometimes the correct choice is to leave the opponent (or yourself, in practice) with a difficult next shot instead of taking a low-percentage pot. It also covers recovery: what to do when position play hasn't gone to plan and you're left with an awkward shot.
meta.see: A diagram shows one example safety route.
meta.think: Given a layout, is this shot worth attacking, or does a safety option give a better outcome overall?
meta.play: Practise recognising and playing a basic safety shot, and recovering sensibly from a deliberately awkward starting position.
meta.tableCheck: Given a difficult layout, explain your decision — attack or play safe — before playing it.

nodes.title: Play the Table
nodes.description: Bringing the course together — reading a full layout and playing it with point, zone and route thinking, attack and safety, all in view.

objectives: Read a full table layout rather than one shot in isolation.
Apply point, zone and route positioning as appropriate within one run.
Decide between attacking and playing safe throughout a run.
Plan more than one shot ahead consistently, not only when reminded to.
Reassess and update the plan after every shot, not just at the start.
meta.learn: This final week doesn't introduce new technique. It brings the course together into one repeatable sequence: read the layout, plan a shot order, aim, set up, execute, control the cue ball, position for what comes next, and reassess. The aim is to practise thinking three shots ahead across a whole run, not just on a single shot when asked to.
meta.see: Reading a full layout means visually scanning which balls are available, where the difficult balls sit relative to the easier ones, and how a chosen shot order affects position for what comes next.
meta.think: Given a full layout, what shot order makes sense, and why — considering position, not just which balls are easiest to pot?
meta.play: Full-layout practice runs, narrating position and risk decisions while playing.
meta.tableCheck: Play a full layout, explaining your shot order and at least one position or safety decision along the way.

nodes.title: Final: Three Shots Ahead Challenge
nodes.description: The capstone: plan and play a short sequence of shots where each one sets up the position for the next, under the same conditions as a real game.

course.title: Partner Photography
course.description: Partner Photography is a twelve-week, in-person course with one central aim: helping students make photographs their girlfriends will genuinely love. It teaches the complete process before, during and after taking the photos.

nodes.title: The First Photo Conversation
nodes.description: Compare technical quality with personal preference, then identify the small decisions that make a photograph easier to like and the outing easier to enjoy.
spec: you can separate technical quality from the subject's personal preference
you can explain why photographer and subject may select different frames
you can identify one visual change and one process change for the next outing

nodes.title: Build the Date and Shoot Plan
nodes.description: Turn seasonal research, a location scout, preparation time and two short photo windows into a realistic outing that protects both light and energy.
spec: your plan uses current seasonal and location research
it protects preparation, travel, food and rest time
it identifies no more than two short photo windows and a stopping condition
every prop or extra item has a reason connected to weather, comfort or the visual idea
it includes an easier fallback for crowds, weather or fatigue

nodes.title: Choose the Camera and Portrait View
nodes.description: Compare available devices and 35mm-, 50mm- and 85mm-equivalent views, then justify the smallest kit that suits a real partner portrait plan.
spec: you compare how at least two available devices or camera modes affect the experience
you make portraits with three noticeably different equivalent focal-length views
you connect aperture or subject separation to the purpose of the frame
your final kit choice includes only equipment with a stated reason

nodes.title: Distance, Height and Framing Lab
nodes.description: Compare camera distance, height and crop on the same person, then identify which combination looks most natural to the subject.
spec: the comparison keeps subject, location and expression as consistent as possible
it includes near and far camera positions plus high, eye-level and lower viewpoints
it tests full-body, half-body and close-up framing without accidental joint crops
the subject chooses the frame that feels most recognisable and explains why

nodes.title: Find the Light Walk
nodes.description: Move one subject through difficult, front, back, side-back and artificial light, then compare what changed before any editing.
spec: you identify light direction and shadow pattern before each frame
the sequence includes open shade plus front, back and side-back light
you use an environmental artificial source or a small continuous light
the subject selects the light in which they prefer their face

nodes.title: Background Rescue Lab
nodes.description: Turn one ordinary location into clean centre, thirds, negative-space and layered portraits by moving the photographer rather than replacing the place.
spec: you photograph one subject in four clearly different composition structures
each version removes or deliberately controls visible background distractions
one frame uses foreground and one preserves recognisable environmental context
the final selection explains why the person remains visually clear

nodes.title: Freeze It or Let It Move
nodes.description: Use aperture, shutter speed, bursts and exposure compensation to produce a sharp action portrait, an intentional blur and two different exposure moods.
spec: you make one sharp walking or turning sequence using a deliberate shutter speed
you create one intentional motion-blur portrait after recording a sharp safety frame
you compare two aperture or depth-of-field decisions
you make brighter and darker exposure versions without losing the intended face

nodes.title: Find, Analyse, Recreate
nodes.description: Break one reference portrait into visible decisions, recreate its style with available conditions and then make one intentional variation.
spec: the reference is analysed through light, camera position, space, exposure, colour and moment
the recreation prioritises decisions that can be made before editing
the subject confirms which parts of the reference they want or do not want copied
one final variation changes a single major decision for a stated reason

nodes.title: Translate the Picture Into Direction
nodes.description: Convert a visual reference into short instructions for place, body, action, gaze and timing, then improve them through subject feedback.
spec: the shoot begins with an agreed purpose, feeling and boundary
each direction changes only one or two observable actions at a time
vague phrases are rewritten as place, action, gaze or timing cues
the subject evaluates clarity and comfort before the photographer evaluates the frame

nodes.title: Movement and Encouragement Lab
nodes.description: Replace fixed poses and critical language with simple actions, specific encouragement and short sequences that help the subject relax.
spec: you direct walking, turning, sitting or leaning as actions rather than fixed poses
each hand and gaze instruction has a clear purpose
feedback names what worked before asking for another change
the subject identifies which action and encouragement felt most natural

nodes.title: Two Shortlists, One Story
nodes.description: Compare independent selections, remove repeated frames and agree on a varied sequence of environment, portrait, movement and detail.
spec: photographer and subject shortlist independently before discussion
duplicate groups are reduced through visible expression and gesture differences
the final set contains purposeful variation in framing, action and context
every delivered image has subject approval and a clear role in the sequence

nodes.title: Finish, Approve and Reflect
nodes.description: Complete a consistent edit, agree on retouching and sharing boundaries, collect partner feedback and compare the final series with Week 1.
spec: the final sequence receives a consistent exposure, colour and crop pass
retouching preserves recognition and follows the subject's agreed boundaries
the subject approves the delivered sequence and its permitted uses
partner feedback and self-reflection use specific evidence from the finished work

nodes.title: Assessment 01: Critical Analysis
nodes.description: Analyse a supplied photo set and its date and shoot plan, then use course theory to explain what works, what does not, and how it could be improved.
spec: one analysis report is submitted by the deadline
the report evaluates both the supplied photographs and their date and shoot plan
judgements are supported with relevant ideas and terminology from the course
weaknesses are diagnosed clearly and paired with practical improvements
the work is your own, with sources and assistance acknowledged

marking.description: The teaching team marks the report as a whole, considering its use of course theory, quality of critical judgement, evidence from the supplied material, and the practicality of its proposed improvements.

nodes.title: Assessment 02: Unedited Partner Shoot
nodes.description: Plan and photograph one session with your partner, submit the original unedited images, and explain the plan and photographic thinking in a report.
spec: one partner portrait session is planned and completed
the selected photographs are submitted as original unedited captures
the report explains the complete plan and the thinking behind the photographic decisions
the photographs and report are each worth half of the assessment mark
the work is your own, with sources and assistance acknowledged

nodes.title: Assessment 03: Final Partner Portrait Series
nodes.description: Design, photograph and finish your strongest partner portrait series, then submit the final images with partner feedback and your own reflection.
spec: the project demonstrates the complete process from design through capture and post-production
the final edited portrait series represents your highest level of work in the course
partner feedback is collected in an interview after the photographs are finished
the submission includes the final photographs, partner feedback and self-reflection
no separate process statement is required

nodes.title: Tutorial Participation
nodes.description: Ten marked tutorials run from Week 2 to Week 11. Each contributes one mark for participation and one mark for a photograph submitted in the tutorial.
spec: ten tutorials are marked from Week 2 through Week 11
each tutorial awards one mark for attendance and participation
each tutorial awards one mark for a photograph submitted during that tutorial
each tutorial contributes two marks and the ten tutorials contribute twenty marks in total

criteria.name: Attendance and participation across ten tutorials

nodes.title: Learn Which Photos She Likes
nodes.description: Start with the question that matters in everyday partner photography: not whether a portrait is technically correct, but whether your girlfriend likes it, wants to share it, and enjoyed making it with you.

nodes.title: Plan a Date She Can Enjoy
nodes.description: Research the season, scout the location, protect time for getting ready and build soft-light photo windows into a day that both people can still enjoy.

nodes.title: Choose the Camera You Will Carry With Her
nodes.description: Choose between a phone, compact or interchangeable-lens camera, understand portrait focal lengths and build the smallest kit that suits the photograph.

nodes.title: First, Make Her Look Like Herself
nodes.description: Learn how distance, camera height, angle and framing change a face and body, then use those choices to make portraits that feel natural and recognisable.

nodes.title: Put Her in Beautiful Light
nodes.description: Learn to recognise difficult overhead light, use front, back and side-back light, and find simple artificial light for portraits after dark.

nodes.title: Find a Beautiful Frame for Her
nodes.description: Use simple composition, clean backgrounds and spatial separation to make the person clear—even in an ordinary street, park or tourist location.

nodes.title: Photograph Her the Way You Intend
nodes.description: Use aperture, shutter speed and exposure decisions to control depth, movement and mood instead of accepting the camera's automatic result.

nodes.title: Bring Your Own Feeling to Her Portraits
nodes.description: Analyse how light, composition, perspective, exposure, colour and timing produce a style, then recreate a reference without reducing it to a filter.

nodes.title: Tell Her How You Want to Photograph Her
nodes.description: Turn the picture in your head into simple, shared and actionable direction before and during the shoot.

nodes.title: Help Her Feel Natural in Front of the Camera
nodes.description: Use simple actions, movement, attention and specific encouragement to help an ordinary person look comfortable without training her to perform like a model.

nodes.title: Choose the Photos You Both Truly Love
nodes.description: Compare photographer and subject selections, remove repetition and build a varied series that remembers the whole experience rather than one repeated pose.

nodes.title: Edit Her Portraits, but Keep Her Looking Like Herself
nodes.description: Refine exposure, colour, skin, crop and distractions without replacing the person, then finish the sequence, delivery, partner feedback and reflection.

course.title: The Universe Gets Stranger
course.description: Begin with a dark night sky and follow the questions it refuses to settle. This course traces one chain of explanation through cosmology, heat, entropy, life, stars, quantum mechanics and matter, ending where our best physical theories stop agreeing.

nodes.title: The CMB spectrum, from real data
nodes.description: Real COBE/FIRAS measurements, plotted against a blackbody curve you compute yourself, so "the early universe looks thermal" stops being something you were told.
spec: you have downloaded and plotted the actual FIRAS monopole spectrum, not values copied from a textbook
your plot compares the measured spectrum against a 2.725 K blackbody curve you compute yourself
you can say how large the measured departure from that curve is, in the data's own units

nodes.title: Counting microstates by hand
nodes.description: A system small enough to list completely, until the statistical argument for entropy is something you counted rather than something you read.
spec: you have enumerated, by hand, every microstate of a system small enough to list completely
you can say which macrostate has the most microstates, and why that makes it the one you would actually find the system in
you can explain entropy's statistical basis using only the counts you produced, without using "disorder" as the explanation

nodes.title: The Sun's lifetime, calculated
nodes.description: The estimates that rule out chemical burning and gravitational contraction, redone by hand instead of read off the lecture.
spec: you have redone, on paper, the chemical-burning and gravitational-contraction lifetime estimates for the Sun
your answers land in the same range the lecture reported, and you can say why rough inputs were enough to get there
you can state which number ruled out each explanation, not just which argument sounded weaker

nodes.title: What degeneracy pressure can and cannot hold up
nodes.description: Reasoning quantitatively about why squeezed electrons push back harder, and why that pushback runs into a ceiling gravity does not share.
spec: you can estimate, quantitatively, why compressing a white dwarf raises the pressure resisting the compression
you can say, in your own reasoning, why that pressure eventually stops keeping up with gravity as mass increases
you have not attempted a derivation from Fermi-Dirac statistics, only reasoning at the level the lecture established

nodes.title: Let the numbers decide
nodes.description: Two explanations can both sound plausible. Only a calculation tells you which one the evidence actually supports.
spec: submitted by the deadline, in the format named below
states two genuinely competing explanations for the same physical situation
shows a calculation or estimate for what each explanation predicts
reaches a judgement the numbers themselves force, not one assumed in advance
does not reuse the Sun's lifetime calculation from Week 7 as the assignment itself

criteria.name: Correctness of the estimates or calculation
Whether the numbers actually decide between the explanations
Clarity of the reasoning connecting numbers to judgement

nodes.title: What the explanation leaves out
nodes.description: Pick one explanation everyone already believes, and find the exact edge where it stops being enough.
spec: submitted by the deadline, in the format named below
names one specific, familiar explanation rather than a vague topic
states plainly what the explanation gets right before criticising it
identifies precisely what is left out, oversimplified, or conditional
names the extra physics actually required to close that gap

criteria.name: Precision about where it stops being sufficient
The physics that closes the gap

nodes.title: Where explanation breaks
nodes.description: Locate an open question the course leads to, and map exactly where present physics stops being enough to answer it.
spec: submitted by the deadline, in the format named below
names one open question connected to material from the course
distinguishes what is established, what is inferred, and what remains uncertain
identifies exactly where or why the current explanation stops being sufficient
does not attempt to solve or resolve the open question

criteria.name: Accuracy separating the established, the inferred, and the uncertain
Precision locating where or why explanation currently stops
Scope discipline — mapping the edge rather than surveying the field

nodes.title: Why is the night sky dark?
nodes.description: The darkness between the stars looks empty. It is not. A dark night sky already tells us that the universe has a history.

meta.question: Why is the night sky dark?
meta.leftover: What is the oldest light we can see?

nodes.title: What is the oldest light we can see?
nodes.description: The dark sky is not really dark. Point the right instrument upward and the whole sky glows in microwaves — with a spectrum that looks exactly like something at a temperature.

meta.question: What is the oldest light we can see?

nodes.title: What is a temperature?
nodes.description: One molecule in an empty box has a speed and an energy. It does not have a temperature. Add an enormous number of them and temperature becomes one of the most reliable things you can measure.

meta.question: What is a temperature?
meta.leftover: How does a crowd have properties its members don't?

nodes.title: How does a crowd have properties its members don't?
nodes.description: You cannot predict where one gas molecule will be a second from now. Give a physicist a litre of the gas and they will tell you its pressure to several decimal places.

meta.question: How does a crowd have properties its members don't?
meta.leftover: Why does time run one way?

nodes.title: Why does time run one way?
nodes.description: Run the film of a gas filling a room backwards and it looks obviously wrong, even though every collision in it still obeys ordinary mechanics. The arrow of time is not written into the laws. It has to come from somewhere else.

meta.question: Why does time run one way?
meta.leftover: How do organised structures persist at all?

nodes.title: How do organised structures persist at all?
nodes.description: The second law says disorder tends to grow. A whirlpool, a flame, and a living body all keep their shape anyway. None of them are cheating. All of them are open.

meta.question: How do organised structures persist at all?
meta.leftover: Why hasn't the Sun burned out?

nodes.title: Why hasn't the Sun burned out?
nodes.description: Chemical burning gives the Sun a few thousand years. Gravity gives it tens of millions. The rocks say billions. This is the week where arguing stops working and you have to calculate.

meta.question: Why hasn't the Sun burned out?
meta.leftover: How do two nuclei that can't touch, touch?

nodes.title: How do two nuclei that can't touch, touch?
nodes.description: The Sun's core is hot, but not remotely hot enough to force two protons past their mutual repulsion. Quantum mechanics does not get them there by giving them more energy. It gets them there by not requiring a sharp edge at the wall.

meta.question: How do two nuclei that can't touch, touch?

nodes.title: What is a particle?
nodes.description: Fire particles through two slits one at a time, and each one lands as a single point. Do it enough times and the points draw stripes only a wave could make. No single old picture explains both facts.

meta.question: What is a particle?

nodes.title: What happens when you look?
nodes.description: A measurement is not a human blinking at reality. It is a physical interaction that spreads a quantum system's alternatives across an enormous environment until they can no longer interfere. That explains a great deal. It does not explain everything.

meta.question: What happens when you look?
meta.leftover: Why does matter behave like matter?

nodes.title: Why does matter behave like matter?
nodes.description: A table feels solid. Push on it and it pushes back. The honest explanation for that push is not one tidy principle — it is atomic structure, electric repulsion, and quantum exclusion, all doing work at once.

meta.question: Why does matter behave like matter?

nodes.title: Where does explanation break?
nodes.description: Push a dead star's mass past its limit and gravity wins outright — that part we understand. Push relativity and quantum mechanics into the same extreme regime and neither is enough alone. Zoom out and most of the universe's contents have never been identified. Those are three different kinds of not-knowing.

meta.question: Where does explanation break?
meta.leftover: Why does the universe have the history, contents and laws that made the dark sky of Week 1 possible?

course.title: Welcome to Dota. You Will Lose.
course.description: Dota 2 for people who have never played it, taught one decision at a time: which creep to hit, when to leave the lane, who to pick, what to buy, when not to fight. Mechanics are the tools that answer each decision.

nodes.title: Finish a whole game
nodes.description: Five-person bot match, nobody looks at the scoreboard, and everybody leaves with a client that works
spec: you arrive with a Dota 2 client that runs and a headset with a working mic
you finish a whole game without leaving
you can say what was destroyed at the moment the game ended

meta.needs_others: Week one's real failure is a client that will not install or a student who does not know where to click, and nobody solves that alone in their room — or admits to it.

nodes.title: Count the last hits
nodes.description: In pairs, one player takes last hits while the other counts out loud — the baseline Assignment 1 measures you against
spec: your partner counted your last hits over a fixed stretch and you wrote the number down
you denied at least once and your partner confirmed it
you can say whether the creeps you missed were hit early or late

meta.needs_others: Counting your own last hits flatters you, because you remember the ones you got; somebody else counting is the only way to get a number you did not choose.

nodes.title: Hold the line
nodes.description: A one-versus-one solo lane where the win condition is not kills but which side of the lane the wave ends up on
spec: you played both sides of the lane
you deliberately let a last hit go in one round, and can say why
you can name the moment the wave got away from you

meta.needs_others: Holding a lane is adversarial: you need an opponent who is also trying to hold it before the wave moves at all, and bots will not contest it.

nodes.title: Stack against the clock
nodes.description: The whole class stacking camps to a called clock, then doing it while keeping a lane off its own tower
spec: you stacked at least one camp and can say at what point you pulled
in the second round you managed both tasks, or can say which you dropped and why
you can predict the next camp spawn before it happens

meta.needs_others: Stacking is pure timing, and timing is learned when somebody is calling the clock and the person beside you is stacking more than you are — alone, "close enough" always feels fine.

nodes.title: Three heroes, one item
nodes.description: Buy the same item on a strength, an agility and an intelligence hero, then pool the class's results into one table
spec: you tried the same item on three heroes of different primary attributes
you can say which hero it was worth most on, and point to the exchange rate that made it so
you can look at an untried hero and infer from its attribute roughly how it plays

meta.needs_others: One student gets three data points and the class gets thirty, and "the same item is worth different amounts" only holds up with a sample — the session's product is one shared table nobody could have built alone.

nodes.title: Watch one player
nodes.description: The class watches one replay together, each student following a single position start to finish, then reassembles the game from five accounts
spec: you followed one position for the whole game and can retell their timeline
you named their power spike and how you spotted it
you named one decision they made well or badly — a decision, not a piece of execution

meta.needs_others: Five positions need five people watching at once to reassemble one game; one person watching five times is a worse exercise, because every pass after the first already knows the answer.

nodes.title: Build along
nodes.description: One bot match following a recommended build exactly, with the build order written down and marked up as you buy
spec: you followed one build guide for a whole game without changing it
every item on your written order carries a word for what it does
you marked at least one place you wanted to deviate, and what you would have bought instead

meta.needs_others: A build order you wrote alone is a build order you already agree with; handing it to somebody who has played the hero is the only way to find out which of your reasons were wrong.

nodes.title: Hold the stun
nodes.description: A five-versus-five where every control spell must be called out loud before it is used — and once called, used
spec: you called your intent before every control spell
at least once you called it, saw the timing was wrong, and can say what was wrong
you can describe one time you held it and were right to

meta.needs_others: The mechanism of this drill is being heard: calling your intent only means something with teammates present and an opponent who will punish the timing you chose.

nodes.title: Cross the map unseen
nodes.description: One group wards a route, the other tries to walk it without being seen, then they swap and review the vision together
spec: you played both attack and defence
on defence, you can say what each ward was for — not "this is where people put them"
on attack, you can say how you went around a ward or walked into one

meta.needs_others: A ward's value only shows when somebody is actively trying to avoid it; warding for yourself, you never find out whether it worked.

nodes.title: Call the objective
nodes.description: A custom match where somebody must call the next objective aloud after every won fight, then the game is retold without mentioning kills
spec: your team called an objective after every won fight and executed it
you called at least once and can say why that objective and not another
your team can retell the game from its objective timeline without mentioning kills

meta.needs_others: A call needs four people to hear it and follow it, and the habit this drill breaks — everyone drifting home to shop after a won fight — only breaks when somebody calls you back.

nodes.title: Draft, don't play
nodes.description: A full Captains Mode draft against a real opposing team, justified aloud pick by pick, and then not played
spec: your team completed a full Captains Mode draft
your team could name, for every ban, the specific matchup or plan it closed off
you can say at which stage of the game your lineup intends to win

meta.needs_others: Drafting needs a real opponent, because a draft is a conversation — drafting against yourself teaches nothing, since nobody on the other side is answering you.

nodes.title: Match day
nodes.description: The Assignment 4 best-of-three, played with a tutor as coach, ending with each team writing down three decision points before they leave
spec: your team played the games the series required
you wrote down at least three decision points before leaving the room
you know who is writing which part of your team's review, and when it is due

meta.needs_others: This week is the match: ten people, two captains and a coach are the exercise, and there is no version of it that one person does at home.

course.title: Wait: The Design of Delay
course.description: Every system you use has decided how long you will wait and what you will be told while you do. This course treats that decision as design work: the thresholds, the progress indicators, the hold scripts, the queues, and the politics of who is asked to wait.

nodes.title: The Clock and the Feeling
nodes.description: Week 1. Measured duration and felt duration are two different quantities, and the gap between them is what this course studies.
spec: you can state the difference between a measured duration and a perceived one
you have timed and rated at least six of your own waits
you can name a wait where the two numbers moved in opposite directions

readings.cite: Maister, D. H. (1985). The Psychology of Waiting Lines. In J. A. Czepiel, M. R. Solomon and C. F. Surprenant (eds), The Service Encounter, 113-123. Lexington Books.
Block, R. A. and Zakay, D. (1997). Prospective and retrospective duration judgments: a meta-analytic review. Psychonomic Bulletin and Review 4(2), 184-197.

nodes.title: Three Thresholds
nodes.description: Week 2. The perception gap becomes engineering. Three numbers decide which affordance a delay is given.
spec: you can state the three response time limits and what each one governs
you can find the threshold a given interface is designed against
you can say what a threshold assumes about the person waiting

readings.cite: Miller, R. B. (1968). Response time in man-computer conversational transactions. AFIPS Fall Joint Computer Conference, vol. 33, 267-277.
Nielsen, J. (1993). Response times: the three important limits. In Usability Engineering. Morgan Kaufmann.

claims.text: Nielsen's three response time limits are 0.1 seconds, 1 second and 10 seconds
claims.source: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/response-times-3-important-limits/
claims.measures: three design limits stated in Usability Engineering as durations of system response after a user action, argued from perceptual and attentional grounds rather than measured as population means

nodes.title: The Throbber
nodes.description: Week 3. The indeterminate spinner communicates only that something is happening. This week asks what the silence around that is for.
spec: you can say what an indeterminate indicator does and does not communicate
you can find a delay whose duration is known and shown as indeterminate anyway
you can argue for a spinner over a progress bar in a specific case

readings.cite: Myers, B. A. (1985). The importance of percent-done progress indicators for computer-human interfaces. CHI 85, 11-17.
Bouch, A., Kuchinsky, A. and Bhatti, N. (2000). Quality is in the eye of the beholder: meeting user requirements for Internet quality of service. CHI 2000, 297-304.

nodes.title: Ninety-Nine Percent
nodes.description: Week 4. Determinate progress, where the system tells you something and the something is false.
spec: you can explain why a progress bar estimate is usually wrong
you can name two animation properties that change perceived duration without changing real duration
you can say who benefits from a bar that pauses near the end

readings.cite: Harrison, C., Amento, B., Kuznetsov, S. and Bell, R. (2007). Rethinking the progress bar. UIST 2007, 115-118.
Harrison, C., Yeo, Z. and Hudson, S. E. (2010). Faster progress bars: manipulating perceived duration with visual augmentations. CHI 2010, 1545-1548.

claims.text: the strongest augmentation cut perceived duration by 11%
claims.measures: reduction in perceived duration of a progress bar with backwards moving decelerating ribbing, against a plain solid bar of identical real duration in paired comparison tests, as reported by the authors

nodes.title: The Labour Illusion

readings.cite: Buell, R. W. and Norton, M. I. (2011). The labor illusion: how operational transparency increases perceived value. Management Science 57(9), 1564-1579.

nodes.title: Occupied Time

meta.extra: barrier that folds a queue back

nodes.title: Fairness Before Speed

nodes.title: Who Waits

course.title: Every Battle Is a Spreadsheet
course.description: A semester spent reading the arithmetic under Japanese RPG combat: turn order, initiative counters, damage formulas and the rolls around them. You measure real fights, rebuild their systems in a spreadsheet, and design one of your own.

nodes.title: A Round Is a Decision the Game Made For You
nodes.description: The round as a container — what a battle loop has to decide before it can ask you anything, and how Pokémon and Dragon Quest answer it differently
spec: you have a spreadsheet open and can enter a formula into it
you have watched the recorded fight all the way through once
you can name one battle system you find annoying, and why

meta.serves: Before you can read a single number, you have to know when the game stops and asks you something.
meta.capability: After this week you can diagram who acts, in what order, in a round-based battle, and name what the game had to decide to make that happen.

nodes.title: Speed Is a Reset, Not a Rate
nodes.description: The initiative counter — why Final Fantasy X's Agility doesn't make anybody faster, and what that buys a designer that an ATB gauge can't
spec: week 1's turn table is finished, even if parts of it are guesses
your spreadsheet can do a lookup and a floor
you can say, in one sentence, what surprised you about turn order last week

meta.serves: This is the clearest case in the course of a number doing something other than what its name says it does.
meta.capability: After this week you can predict the next five turns from a speed table and say exactly where the prediction breaks.

nodes.title: The Animation Is Not the Attack
nodes.description: The damage equation — reading a formula's shape off its curve, and why a cubic and a quadratic in the same game make two different economies
spec: your week 2 counter model runs and roughly agrees with the recording
you can plot a column of numbers as a scatter chart
you have ten logged hits from the same attacker and target

meta.serves: This is the week the costume comes off — the number floating up the screen is the output of an equation you can write down.
meta.capability: After this week you can reverse-engineer a damage formula from ten logged hits.

nodes.title: Most Randomness Is There to Be Removed
nodes.description: The roll — variance, critical hits and hit chance, and how to tell a random element that is doing work from one that is only adding noise
spec: your week 3 fit predicts a hit you had not logged, within a stated tolerance
you can compute a weighted average in a spreadsheet
you have picked one boss fight to work on

meta.serves: Once the formula is written down, the rolls around it stop being atmosphere and become a design choice you can price.
meta.capability: After this week you can say which random elements a fight needs, which it should remove, and defend it with expected values.

nodes.title: A Status Effect Is a Rule Change, Not a Debuff
nodes.description: The status effect sorted by which rule it edits — rate, cost, order or outcome — and the ones that refuse to go in any of the four boxes
spec: you have played, or watched, a fight where a status effect decided it
two games picked, with wikis you can actually read

meta.serves: A status effect is the game editing its own rules mid-fight, so the numbers you learned to read in weeks 1 to 4 stop holding still.
meta.capability: After this week you can classify any status effect by what it rewrites — rate, cost, order or outcome.

nodes.title: Every Turn Has a Price Tag
nodes.description: The cost of a turn, worked through a PP budget — why the price of an action shows up two fights later, and where a boss gets solved by spending
spec: week 5's twelve effects are sorted, misfit included
one boss fight chosen, with a recording or a save you can replay

meta.serves: Reading the numbers is half of it; the other half is what each one costs to produce, and the answer is always turns.
meta.capability: After this week you can model a fight as a budget and find where it's solved by spending.

nodes.title: The Extra Turn Is the Whole Game
nodes.description: The action economy — Press Turn written out in six lines, what falls out of it, and the strategy that empties it of decisions
spec: week 6's budget model runs to the end of a fight
you have watched at least one Press Turn or One More fight, start to finish

meta.serves: An action economy is the purest form of this course's claim — a handful of rules, no hidden numbers, and a fight that is entirely arithmetic.
meta.capability: After this week you can write the rules of an action-economy system in one page and show its degenerate strategy.

nodes.title: A Stagger Bar Is a Second Fight Hidden in the First
nodes.description: The pressure gauge — why the stagger threshold rather than the multiplier is the design, and what moving it by fifty points does to a fight
spec: your one-page Press Turn rules are written
a break system picked, with its numbers findable

meta.serves: A break gauge is a threshold, and a threshold is the cheapest way to put two fights inside one, which makes it the easiest thing here to tune badly.
meta.capability: After this week you can tune a stagger threshold so a fight has a second phase, and show the tuning in numbers.

nodes.title: A Role Is a Constraint Someone Else Doesn't Carry
nodes.description: The party role defined by what it removes rather than what it does, tested by taking a member out and seeing which other role stops working
spec: week 8's three numbers, for both threshold settings
a game in mind whose party you know well enough to argue about

meta.serves: Roles are where a fight's numbers stop being one character's problem and become the party's, which is the last thing to get straight before the boss.
meta.capability: After this week you can define a party role by the constraint it removes from another role.

nodes.title: The Grind Is a Curve Someone Drew
nodes.description: The level curve against the encounter table — six experience groups, the ratio that defines grind, and the level where fights-per-level doubles
spec: your week 9 party is defined in four sentences
a game chosen whose experience table and encounter yields are published

meta.serves: Difficulty in a JRPG is mostly a question of when you fight something, and when is set by two curves the game never shows you.
meta.object: the level curve against the encounter table
meta.capability: After this week you can plot an experience curve against an encounter table and find where the grind starts.

nodes.title: A Boss Is a Puzzle With a Health Bar
nodes.description: The boss script as a decision tree — state, telegraphs and thresholds, read off one Final Fantasy X fight and its two solutions
spec: your week 10 plot exists and its spike is marked
one boss chosen, with a recording long enough to see the pattern twice

meta.serves: A boss is where every week so far gets pointed at one encounter, and the script is the document doing the aiming.
meta.capability: After this week you can write a boss's script as a decision tree and identify the intended solution and the unintended one.

nodes.title: If a Stranger Can Implement It, You Designed It
nodes.description: The design document tested by handing it to somebody else and watching them build it — where every question they ask you is a defect you wrote
spec: a draft design document, however rough, that somebody else can open
your week 11 decision tree, since one enemy script goes in the document

meta.serves: The semester was reading other people's systems off their numbers; the last week is writing one that can be read the same way.
meta.capability: After this week you can specify a combat system in numbers a stranger could implement without asking you a question.

nodes.title: Combat system design
nodes.description: A combat system specified in numbers plus a spreadsheet prototype, marked by whether a stranger can implement it without asking you a question
spec: a design document specifying the system entirely in numbers
a spreadsheet prototype that evaluates one complete fight
one worked example fight, with the arithmetic shown at every step

meta.capability: After this week you can specify a combat system in numbers a stranger could implement without asking you a question.

marking.description: Judged as one artefact against a single question — could a competent stranger implement this fight from the document alone? Every question they would have to ask is a defect, and the count and severity of those defects is the mark.

nodes.title: Damage-formula teardown
nodes.description: Ten logged hits, the formula fitted to them, the predicted eleventh, and one page of method — marked on the method more than the fit
spec: ten logged hits with every constant held constant, and the constants named
a fitted formula, with the shape you assumed stated before the fit
a predicted eleventh hit with a tolerance, and the actual value

meta.capability: After this week you can reverse-engineer a damage formula from ten logged hits.

nodes.title: Fight logs
nodes.description: Twelve recorded fights reconstructed as turn tables across the semester, marked on whether a reader can replay the fight from the table alone
spec: twelve tables, one per week, each from a recorded fight
a reader can replay the fight from the table without the recording
every row where the turn order surprised you is marked and explained

meta.capability: After this week you can diagram who acts, in what order, in a round-based battle, and name what the game had to decide to make that happen.

it runs against a fight it has not been tuned on
you have written down where it breaks before anyone tells you
