course.title: Factorio: Engineering Addiction
course.description: A production-engineering studio taught entirely inside Factorio: throughput analysis, logistics design, and the discipline of building systems that don't jam, from the first furnace to an orbiting megabase.

nodes.title: Automate the Basics
nodes.description: Research Automation using only hand mining, a manual smelting line and starter power — no belts or assemblers beyond what it unlocks.
spec: Automation research is complete by the end of the tutorial
the smelting line feeding it was never left idle waiting on ore
no belts or assemblers were used ahead of what Automation unlocks

meta.practical: Complete the research required to unlock Automation, using only what's covered this week — hand mining, a manual smelting line, and starter power — with no belts or assemblers beyond what Automation itself unlocks.
meta.goal: Establish efficient early-game resource, smelting and power fundamentals before any automation exists to lean on.

nodes.title: Two Bases, One Verdict
nodes.description: Compare a spaghetti base against a bus base on throughput, maintainability and how easily each expands.
spec: the comparison names specific throughput differences, not just impressions
it addresses maintainability — could a third person trace a fault in each base
it states which base would cost less to expand, and why

meta.practical: Compare two working bases — one built spaghetti-style, one built around a bus — and produce a short written comparison of their throughput, maintainability, and how easily each could be expanded.
meta.goal: Learn to design a base with future expansion in mind, not just present output.

nodes.title: Build a Balancer
nodes.description: Design a 5-belt-to-4-belt balancer from splitters and underground belts, then prove it holds under an uneven input.
spec: the balancer accepts 5 input belts and produces 4 evenly loaded output belts
output stays even when any single input lane is starved, demonstrated live
only splitters and underground belts were used

meta.practical: Design a working 5-belt-to-4-belt balancer using only splitters and underground belts, and verify it distributes load evenly regardless of which input lane is starved.
meta.goal: Develop logistics problem-solving skills — reasoning about flow through a network rather than just placing entities down.

nodes.title: Automate Science Packs
nodes.description: Fully automate red or green science packs end to end, from raw ore to a working lab feed, without starving or overflowing.
spec: the line runs unattended from raw ore to lab feed for a sustained period
no assembler in the chain sits starved or backed up under steady supply
the ratios used are stated, not just arrived at by trial and error

meta.practical: Fully automate red science packs (or green science packs), end to end, from raw ore to a working science lab feed.
meta.goal: Build production systems that don't bottleneck under constant input and output — no starved machines, no overflowing buffers.

nodes.title: Clear a Biter Nest
nodes.description: Destroy a biter nest using this week's transport, defence and terrain tools, opening up access around the base.
spec: the targeted nest is destroyed, not just suppressed
at least one non-turret tool (vehicle, capsule, or terrain change) is used as part of the approach
the base's pollution and evolution state at the time is noted

meta.practical: Destroy a biter nest, using the transport, defence and terrain tools covered this week.
meta.goal: Improve access and travel time around the base by clearing the threats and obstacles that were limiting them.

nodes.title: Bidirectional Rail Line
nodes.description: Design a three-lane rail line with a bidirectional middle lane, and verify it under simulated traffic from both directions.
spec: the middle lane carries trains in both directions without a deadlock
signalling is demonstrated holding under simultaneous opposing traffic
the design is explained in terms of signal blocks, not trial and error

meta.practical: Design a three-lane rail line where the middle lane runs bi-directionally, and verify it under simulated traffic from both directions.
meta.goal: Learn to design train networks that scale without deadlocking.

nodes.title: Form Your Crew
nodes.description: Form the group project teams and agree on a role split and shared conventions before anyone touches the shared save.
spec: a group is formed and recorded before the tutorial ends
each member has an assigned zone or subsystem, agreed by the group
a shared convention (belt colour, stop naming, or bus contents) is written down, not left implicit

meta.practical: Form the groups for the Group Project, and agree as a group on the role split and shared conventions the project will use.
meta.goal: Understand how to collaborate effectively and the concrete methods — role allocation, shared conventions — that make collaboration work in a shared factory.

nodes.title: Diagnose the Factory
nodes.description: Diagnose a supplied base exhibiting a brownout and an unrelated bottleneck, and fix both root causes. Assignment 1 is due this week.
spec: the brownout's root cause is identified, not just the symptom
the unrelated bottleneck is correctly separated from the power issue
both are fixed, and the fix for one didn't mask or worsen the other

meta.practical: Diagnose a supplied base exhibiting a brownout and an unrelated bottleneck, identify both root causes, and fix them.
meta.goal: Solve common production and power issues using the diagnostic method covered this week, not trial and error.

nodes.title: Tileable Blueprint
nodes.description: Design a tileable green science pack blueprint, and confirm two copies placed side by side connect cleanly.
spec: the blueprint converts iron and copper plate to green science packs at a stated ratio
two copies placed edge to edge connect belts, pipes and power without manual patching
the blueprint is captured with bots, not placed by hand

meta.practical: Design a tileable blueprint that turns iron and copper plates into green science packs, and confirm that two copies placed side by side connect cleanly.
meta.goal: Learn the late-game tools and design habits — bots, blueprints, tiling — that make repeatable expansion possible.

nodes.title: Jam-Free Uranium
nodes.description: Design a circuit-controlled uranium processing setup that runs continuously without jamming or starving under normal supply variation.
spec: the setup runs unattended through a supply-rate change without jamming
at least one circuit condition (not a fixed timer) governs part of the process
the failure mode the circuit logic is guarding against is stated

meta.practical: Design a uranium processing setup, controlled with circuit logic, that runs continuously without jamming or starving under normal supply variation.
meta.goal: Apply advanced circuit-network optimisation to a system where a jam has real consequences.

nodes.title: Compare Two Designs
nodes.description: Given two base designs aimed at different goals, explain the purpose of their differences.
spec: each design's actual optimisation target is correctly identified
at least three specific design choices are tied back to that target
the comparison doesn't just declare one design "better" overall

meta.practical: Given two base designs aimed at different goals, explain the purpose of their differences — which one is optimising for what, and why that shows up in the specific design choices each one makes.
meta.goal: Learn to optimise for different metrics, not just raw output.

nodes.title: TPS Audit
nodes.description: Given a supplied base, explain how it has been TPS-optimised and identify what, if anything, is still costing it performance.
spec: existing TPS optimisations in the supplied base are correctly identified
any remaining performance cost is correctly attributed to entity count, entity type, or pollution/biter activity
the audit distinguishes a TPS problem from a production-ratio problem

meta.practical: Given a supplied base, explain how it has been TPS-optimised and identify what, if anything, is still costing it performance.
meta.goal: Leave the course able to grow a base without the game itself becoming the bottleneck.

nodes.title: Assignment 1
nodes.description: A bottleneck-diagnosis report on a supplied mid-game save, covering everything from balancer theory to rail intersections.
spec: submitted by the deadline, as a save file plus a written report
the report correctly identifies the save's actual bottleneck, not a plausible-sounding but wrong one
any proposed fix is justified with ratios or measurements, not vibes
the work is yours, with any assistance declared

nodes.title: Final Exam
nodes.description: A closed-book puzzle set covering balancer design, rail intersections, bottleneck identification and TPS diagnosis.
spec: answered individually, without external references, in the exam window
each answer shows working, not just a final figure or diagram
covers the full syllabus, not only the weeks nearest the exam

marking.description: Judged on whether each puzzle's answer is correct and whether the working shows real understanding of the ratios or mechanics involved, not a memorised pattern that happens to fit.

nodes.title: Group Project
nodes.description: A team-built Space Science production line, taken from a shared starting save through to a self-sufficient rocket launch.
spec: a shared save file that reaches a sustained Space Science output, or launches a rocket, without manual intervention
a design report explaining the base's key structural decisions and how they were reached
evidence that the work was actually shared across the group, not produced by one member alone

nodes.title: Weekly Practicals
nodes.description: Participation and submission across all twelve tutorials, from the Week 1 automation practical to the Week 12 TPS audit.
spec: a submission for each tutorial, meeting that week's stated practical
submissions reflect the student's own save at the time, not one built afterwards to match the brief

marking.description: Judged on the completeness and quality of the twelve weekly submissions as a set, not on any single week in isolation — a strong run of ten weeks with two missed still scores far better than none.

nodes.title: Early-Game Foundations
nodes.description: Reading the map, hand-fed smelting and power ratios, and the first automation research — the fundamentals everything later depends on.

nodes.title: Base Design Philosophy
nodes.description: Furnace stacks and footprint trade-offs, then the named layout styles — spaghetti, bus, bot base, tileable base, train base — and what each buys and costs.

nodes.title: Logistics I
nodes.description: Splitters, T-junctions, inserters, underground belts and buffers as the components of belt logistics, building up to balancer theory.

nodes.title: Ratios and Bottlenecks
nodes.description: Reading recipes as rate problems, an introduction to fluids and oil refining, and how module and beacon choices change a line's ratios.

nodes.title: Transport and Defence
nodes.description: Cars, tanks, trains and terrain tools, then biters, worms and nests, and the firepower and wall placement that manage them.

nodes.title: Rail Engineering
nodes.description: Fluid wagons, train fundamentals, deadlock-free intersection design, and automating a rail network end to end.

nodes.title: Coordinating at Scale
nodes.description: Why independently-designed subsystems clash, and the role allocation and shared conventions that make a team's factory coherent.

nodes.title: Diagnosing the Factory
nodes.description: Brownouts and solar sizing, a real method for finding bottlenecks, and a case study in the everlasting chip shortage.

nodes.title: Blueprints at Scale
nodes.description: Construction bots, capturing a working design as a blueprint, and designing blueprint edges so copies tile cleanly.

nodes.title: Advanced Optimisation
nodes.description: Circuit-network logic gates, nuclear power layout, and dispatching trains only when the network actually needs them.

nodes.title: Megabase Economics
nodes.description: Travel time and TPS as real design costs, expansion versus productivity growth, and speedrunning as a different optimisation target entirely.

nodes.title: The Factory Must Grow
nodes.description: What actually costs simulation time at scale, pollution's own TPS cost, and a checklist for what causes a slow base.

course.title: The Science of Guitar Tone
course.description: How a vibrating guitar string becomes the sound recognised as electric guitar tone, followed as one engineering system: string, pickup, circuit, gain stage, filter, amplifier, speaker and the ear, each week tracing what changed physically into what changed audibly.

nodes.title: Getting started
nodes.description: Setting up a listening environment and the toolchain the rest of the course's demonstrations run on
spec: you can build and preview the course site locally
you have working headphones or monitors and have checked levels before Week 1's lab bench plays anything

nodes.title: First review
nodes.description: A first look at spectral analysis on a real recorded sound, ahead of Tone Autopsy
spec: you can point to a specific feature of a waveform or spectrum plot and state what it shows
you can name one claim you are not confident enough to call an observation

nodes.title: Engineer a Guitar Tone
nodes.description: Design and justify a complete guitar-tone signal chain for a stated target sound, using the course's principles rather than "it sounds better".
spec: a target tonal description is stated before any signal-chain decision is justified
every stage of the chosen chain, from source assumptions through to cabinet, has a stated setting and a reason tied to a specific course principle
at least one trade-off accepted by the design is named explicitly, not just the benefit chosen

marking.description: Assessed as one integrated piece of work rather than a checklist of separate marks: does the chosen signal chain plausibly achieve the stated target, does every major decision carry a justification grounded in a course principle rather than taste, does the response show it understands how stages interact (not just what each stage does alone), and does it name at least one real trade-off the design accepts. A chain with a weaker overall design but stronger, more specific justification at every stage will mark higher than a plausible-sounding chain justified only by assertion.

nodes.title: Pedal Laboratory
nodes.description: Change one or more variables in a simplified nonlinear pedal model, and trace the full chain from parameter change to audible consequence.
spec: at least one pedal parameter is changed and its new setting is stated explicitly
the causal chain from parameter change through to audible consequence is written out step by step, not asserted in one line
waveform or spectrum evidence from the lab bench supports the predicted electrical or mathematical effect

criteria.name: Predicted causal chain is correct end-to-end
Linking the technical change to what is actually audible

nodes.title: Tone Autopsy
nodes.description: Analyse an existing guitar sound using only what the first four weeks have covered — and say which of your claims are evidence and which are guesses.
spec: the sound sample under analysis is named and reproducible by the marker
every claim is labelled as an observation, a supported interpretation, or an assumption
the analysis draws only on Weeks 1-4 ideas — fundamental frequency, harmonic spectrum, transient shape, pickup position, basic filtering — not distortion or amplifier behaviour taught later

nodes.title: What Is Guitar Tone?
nodes.description: Pitch, loudness, and timbre — and why two guitars can share a note but never sound the same

nodes.title: The Vibrating String
nodes.description: Standing waves, harmonics, and how picking position becomes an early kind of tone shaping

nodes.title: From Vibration to Voltage
nodes.description: How a magnetic pickup turns string motion into the electrical signal the rest of the chain works with

nodes.title: The Guitar Is a Circuit
nodes.description: Why passive resistors, potentiometers, and capacitors inside the guitar already start shaping tone before any pedal

nodes.title: Gain, Headroom and Clipping
nodes.description: What actually happens, mathematically, when an amplified signal stops behaving linearly

nodes.title: Inside overdrive, distortion and fuzz
nodes.description: Why circuits that all clip the same input waveform can still sound distinct from one another

nodes.title: Filters, EQ and Tone Stacks
nodes.description: Once a signal contains many frequencies, how a circuit reshapes its tonal balance

nodes.title: Modulation: Phase, Pitch and Motion
nodes.description: How continuously changing delay, phase, pitch, or amplitude creates the sensation of movement

nodes.title: Delay, Reverb and Space
nodes.description: How a single feedback loop produces echoes, and how the same idea scales up into the simulation of physical space

nodes.title: Inside the Guitar Amplifier
nodes.description: Why an amplifier is a small signal chain of its own — gain, filtering, and nonlinearity, repeated and rearranged

nodes.title: Speaker, Cabinet and Air
nodes.description: Why the same amplifier can sound dramatically different through different speakers and cabinets — the last physical stage before sound reaches the air

nodes.title: Engineering the Complete Tone
nodes.description: Integrating the whole semester — reasoning backwards from a target sound to a deliberately engineered signal chain

course.title: Psychogeography of the Supermarket
course.description: The supermarket is a designed terrain, not a shop. Twelve weeks of structured drift, exhaustive observation, and critical mapping turn its aisles, queues and loyalty schemes into a site to read, and to resist.

nodes.title: The Threshold
nodes.description: The automatic door doesn't open for you. It opens because a sensor decided you were a body worth processing — and that's the whole argument for the semester, delivered before you've bought anything
spec: you can name the sensor that triggers the door before it triggers for you
you can time the gap between the door's motion and the greeting that follows it
you can say, in one sentence, what "welcome" is doing instead of being friendly

nodes.title: The Route
nodes.description: Milk is at the back. Bread is at the back. Everything you came for is at the back — and the forty metres between the door and the fridge aisle is not an accident, it is the store's whole argument
spec: you can draw the shortest path from the door to the three things you actually needed
you can name at least four products that path forces you past
you can say whose interest the detour serves, and whose it doesn't

nodes.title: The Trolley
nodes.description: The wheel that pulls left is not broken. A trolley that tracked straight would let you leave in a straight line — this one keeps you circling, and calls the circling browsing
spec: you can describe the trolley's default drift, left or right, without pushing one
you can say what a trolley that tracked perfectly straight would cost the store per aisle
you can name one way your body already compensates for the drift without deciding to

nodes.title: Eye Level
nodes.description: The shelf at a child's eye height is not for adults, and it is not an accident either — it is the store's smallest, most patient argument, repeated one metre off the ground
spec: you can name one product placed at a height that isn't yours to reach
you can list, Perec-style, everything at your own eye level in a single aisle without looking twice
you can say who decided your eye level was worth more shelf space than someone else's

nodes.title: The Endcap
nodes.description: The endcap isn't a display. It's a détournement of your own attention, staged at the end of an aisle you were already walking down
spec: you can name the last endcap you passed and what it was selling
you can say what made it feel urgent, and whether the urgency was true
you can describe one way an endcap could be turned against its own message

nodes.title: The Fresh Wall
nodes.description: Fresh food runs around the outside wall of every supermarket you've ever been in. Walk the whole perimeter and you've already walked the whole store — that's not a coincidence, it's the layout's real argument
spec: you can trace the perimeter of a real store from memory, aloud
you can name what sits at the four points where the perimeter meets an aisle
you can say how many aisles you'd cross if you only wanted the perimeter

nodes.title: The Queue
nodes.description: The queue is the one part of the store nobody designed. Everything up to here was routed for you — this is where the routing runs out
spec: you can time your own queue, start to end, without exaggerating it
you can name what you were made to look at while you waited
you can describe one thing another person in the queue did that the store didn't plan for

nodes.title: Self-Checkout
nodes.description: Self-checkout didn't remove a job. It handed the job to you, unpaid, and called the demotion a convenience
spec: you can name the exact phrase the machine uses to accuse you of a mistake
you can say what task you now perform that a cashier used to be paid for
you can describe the one moment the machine asks a human to intervene, and why

nodes.title: The Sonic Floor
nodes.description: The music in a supermarket was never for you to enjoy. Its only job is your walking speed, and it has been doing that job the whole time you thought you were browsing in silence
spec: you can name the tempo of the music playing the last time you noticed it
you can say whether it sped you up or slowed you down, and where in the store
you can describe a store with no ambient music at all, and what that absence would do instead

nodes.title: The Loyalty Card
nodes.description: The loyalty card isn't a discount. It's a toll booth, and the currency it collects is a complete record of everything you have ever wanted enough to buy twice
spec: you can say what data field the card actually needs, versus what it collects
you can name one discount you've received and what it cost you in information
you can describe who else the store's data could plausibly be sold to

nodes.title: The Car Park
nodes.description: The car park isn't part of the supermarket, and it isn't part of anywhere else either. It's the exact non-place Marc Augé was describing — before you've even reached the automatic door
spec: you can name one feature of a car park that exists in every car park you've been in
you can say how long you spent in it and what you remember about that time
you can describe why nobody photographs a car park unless something is wrong

nodes.title: The Exit
nodes.description: The receipt is the only document the store ever gives you back. Twelve weeks of argument end here, in a strip of paper that itemises everything except what just happened to you
spec: you can read your own last receipt and say what it doesn't itemise
you can state the semester's argument in one sentence, without hedging
you can say what a supermarket would have to change to no longer earn this course

nodes.title: The Dérive Report
nodes.description: A documented drift through a real or invented supermarket, read against at least three of the semester's mechanisms
spec: a single drift through one store, documented as you go, not reconstructed from memory afterwards
at least three of weeks one to six's mechanisms named and located in that specific store
a reader who has never been to the store can follow the route from the report alone

nodes.title: Counter-Mapping the Supermarket
nodes.description: A détournement of a real or invented store's layout, built from the semester's twelve mechanisms rather than restating them
spec: A counter-map of a single store. It actively reroutes, relabels or détournes a physical layout — a standard, descriptive floor plan fails.
Integrates a minimum of four mechanisms from the twelve teaching weeks, explicitly named and deployed as evidence.
Total standalone legibility. A marker who has not read your previous dérive report must be able to follow the map's argument completely cold.

marking.description: Judged as a whole against the brief — whether the counter-map stands on its own without the semester there to explain it, whether it integrates at least four of the twelve mechanisms as structural evidence, and whether its scope fits a project built in the closing weeks of a twelve-week semester rather than a full year of fieldwork.

nodes.title: Nothing Welcomes You
nodes.description: What the automatic door is actually doing, and why the semester starts here instead of at the shelves

nodes.title: The Store's Real Floor Plan
nodes.description: Why the shortest path to what you need is never the path the aisles give you

nodes.title: A Wheel That Fails on Purpose
nodes.description: Trolley geometry as a designed failure, and what a leash looks like when it has four wheels

nodes.title: Shelf Space Is Rented
nodes.description: Perec's inventory method turned on a single aisle, and what eye level turns out to cost

nodes.title: The Aisle's Momentum, Spent for You
nodes.description: Détournement as a way of reading — and eventually rewriting — the endcap's manufactured urgency

nodes.title: One Lap Is the Whole Store
nodes.description: The fresh wall's perimeter loop, and the fieldwork brief that turns it into evidence

nodes.title: The Last Unscripted Minute
nodes.description: Why the queue is the one part of the building nobody designed, and what that makes it worth

nodes.title: The Job the Machine Didn't Keep
nodes.description: Self-checkout as de-skilling in reverse, and the surveillance apparatus hiding inside a convenience

nodes.title: A Tempo You Didn't Choose
nodes.description: Retail sound design as pacing, zone by zone, and why the silence you thought you shopped in was never silent

nodes.title: The Toll Disguised as a Reward
nodes.description: The loyalty card read through Baudrillard's simulacrum, as a fee paid in data rather than currency

nodes.title: Nowhere, Exactly Repeated
nodes.description: Augé's non-place, found in the car park before you've even reached the automatic door

nodes.title: What the Receipt Leaves Out
nodes.description: Closing the argument the door opened in week one, and setting the counter-mapping brief

course.title: Picture Books That Misbehave
course.description: Picture Books That Misbehave is a studio course about what happens when picture books break their usual rules. Students explore visual, textual, spatial, and narrative conventions, then break them with purpose through prototypes, reader testing, and revision. No polished drawing skills required.

nodes.title: How Should a Picture Book Behave?
nodes.description: What a picture book seems to do without trying — and what happens once you go looking for the rules underneath it.
spec: you bring one familiar picture book to pull apart
you have found five implicit rules shaping how it is read
you have one rough alternative spread breaking one of those rules
you have completed this week's Misbehaviour, Find a Rule

nodes.title: The Picture Isn’t What You Think
nodes.description: One source image, four different framings — and what each one quietly tells the reader to assume.
spec: you bring one source image you can reframe four different ways
you have four framings that each suggest something different from one source
you can say what changed and what stayed the same across them
you have completed this week's Misbehaviour, Crop It Wrong

nodes.title: Words and Pictures Disagree
nodes.description: One fixed sentence, three pictures — and three different things a reader has to do with them.
spec: you have one fixed sentence used across three visual versions
you have an Agree, a Contradict, and a Reveal version of that sentence
you can say what meaning exists only when the words and image are read together
you have completed this week's Misbehaviour, Make the Caption Lie

nodes.title: The Story Is Lying
nodes.description: A four-page story that means one thing on the first read and something else on the second — if the clue was really there all along.
spec: you have a four-page micro-story that supports two different interpretations
you can point to at least one clue that was available before the reveal
rereading the earlier pages still makes sense under the second interpretation
you have completed this week's Misbehaviour, Fool Someone

nodes.title: The Story Behind the Story
nodes.description: A short sequence where one story is obvious and a second one is quietly happening behind it.
spec: you have a short sequence, about four spreads or page-like units, carrying two stories at once
Story A stays readable on its own even if Story B is missed
Story B changes meaningfully across the sequence rather than repeating once
you have completed this week's Misbehaviour, Background Business

nodes.title: The Page Is a Place
nodes.description: A short sequence where something establishes a spatial rule about the page — then breaks it, and something changes because it did.
spec: you have a short sequence, about three or four page-like units, built around one primary page boundary
the sequence establishes a spatial rule and then deliberately breaks it
you can name a consequence of breaking the rule, not just the break itself
you have completed this week's Misbehaviour, Use the Edge

nodes.title: Don’t Turn the Page
nodes.description: One page-turn pair, designed so the reader has to turn the page to find out what changes.
spec: you have one before/after page-turn pair built around a single effect
you can name exactly what information the turn withholds
the effect would not work the same way if both pages were visible at once
you have completed this week's Misbehaviour, also called Before / After, testing turn timing rather than a second pair

nodes.title: Read It the Wrong Way
nodes.description: Six fixed cards, two different orders, two meaningfully different stories — and a way for a reader to find both.
spec: you have six cards used, unchanged, in two different orders
Story A and Story B are meaningfully different, not the same story told awkwardly
you have designed a simple way for a reader to discover another order is possible
you have completed this week's Misbehaviour, Wrong Order

nodes.title: The Reader Did It
nodes.description: A short prototype where one story event cannot happen until the reader actually does something.
spec: you have a short sequence where one important event requires a reader action
you can name the one primary action, the consequence, and what would happen if the reader did nothing
you have tested the prototype with someone who wasn't told what to do first
you have completed this week's Misbehaviour, Make Me Do Something

nodes.title: The Character Refuses
nodes.description: Every student starts with the same line. The character refuses to do what it says — and the story has to respond.
spec: your sequence begins with the line "And then the character opened the door." and the character refuses to open it
the refusal is understandable from the work, without relying on the word "no"
you can name what changed because of the refusal
you have completed this week's Misbehaviour, Say No

nodes.title: The Book Knows It’s a Book
nodes.description: Choose one part of the book readers normally ignore, and make the story need it.
spec: you have chosen one normally ignored book feature and built a short prototype where the story needs it
your prototype shows the feature's normal role, how the work recognises it, how it is used, and what changes as a result
the feature passes the removal test — taking it out damages the idea, it doesn't just remove decoration
you have completed this week's Misbehaviour, Use Something Nobody Reads

nodes.title: Make It Misbehave
nodes.description: Remove one trick from your current work and see what the reader loses — and whether the work is better without it.
spec: you have identified the main rule your current work breaks, what the break is meant to do, and any other tricks or devices currently present
you created an actual version of the work without one chosen trick, not just a description of the difference
you tested both versions with a peer using rule → break → effect and compared their reading with your intention
you have made and briefly justified one revision decision — keep, remove, reduce, clarify, or replace — and completed this week's Misbehaviour, Kill Your Favourite Trick

nodes.title: Assignment 3: The Badly Behaved Book
nodes.description: The final, resolved picture-book work, refined through at least one round of reader testing
spec: an original, resolved experimental picture-book work, in any suitable format
at least one documented cycle of prototype, reader test, and revision
if more than one convention is broken, they support each other rather than padding a checklist
a Reader Note of 400 words maximum covering intended experience, what happened in testing, what changed, and why the final work misbehaves

marking.description: Judged as a coherent reading experience rather than a checklist — whether the chosen misbehaviours support each other, whether a genuine cycle of prototype, reader test, and revision is evident, and whether the Reader Note explains what changed and why.

nodes.title: Assignment 1: One Rule, Broken
nodes.description: A short prototype that breaks exactly one picture-book convention on purpose
spec: approximately 4–6 pages or spread-equivalents
exactly one convention is broken, deliberately and legibly
a short explanation (roughly 150–250 words) names the rule, how it was broken, and the intended reader effect

criteria.name: Clarity of the single rule broken
Written explanation of rule, break, and effect

nodes.title: Assignment 2: Read Me Again
nodes.description: A prototype whose reading changes when a reader experiences it a second time
spec: approximately 6–10 pages or spread-equivalents
tested with roughly 2–3 readers, without explaining the trick first
lightweight evidence of what readers noticed, missed, misunderstood, or reconsidered
a design response of roughly 300 words comparing expected and observed reader response

criteria.name: Design of the change between first and second reading
Design response comparing expected and observed reading

nodes.title: Weekly Misbehaviour
nodes.description: A running practice of small experiments — the toolbox every later assessment draws on
spec: at least 10 of the 12 weekly prompts are submitted
each entry names the one idea it was testing
an unsuccessful experiment still states its intention clearly

marking.description: Marked on completion rather than polish. Submitting at least 10 of the 12 weekly prompts earns the full weight; an experiment that does not work can still count, provided the intention behind it is clear.

nodes.title: How Should a Picture Book Behave?
nodes.description: The conventions a picture book usually keeps invisible, and why you have to see them before you can break them.

nodes.title: The Picture Isn’t What You Think
nodes.description: A picture doesn't just show a scene — every framing choice changes what the reader assumes about it.

nodes.title: Words and Pictures Disagree
nodes.description: The same sentence can mean something different depending on what the picture does with it.

nodes.title: The Story Is Lying
nodes.description: Controlling what a reader believes, and making sure they can find the clues once they know better.

nodes.title: The Story Behind the Story
nodes.description: A second story can develop quietly in the background while the obvious story continues in front of it.

nodes.title: The Page Is a Place
nodes.description: The edge, the gutter, the margin and the text block aren't empty layout — they can become part of the story.

nodes.title: Don’t Turn the Page
nodes.description: The page turn hides the next moment until the reader chooses to look — and that gap can be designed.

nodes.title: Read It the Wrong Way
nodes.description: A book usually suggests one correct reading order. Changing that order can change the story, not just scramble it.

nodes.title: The Reader Did It
nodes.description: Not just turning pages or choosing a path — an action the reader has to perform before the story can continue.

nodes.title: The Character Refuses
nodes.description: A character is supposed to do what the narrator, the text, or the reader expects. Week 10 asks what happens when a character refuses.

nodes.title: The Book Knows It’s a Book
nodes.description: Cover, spine, endpaper, page number and gutter are normally infrastructure. Week 11 asks what happens when the story notices them.

nodes.title: Make It Misbehave
nodes.description: The course stops adding tricks and starts asking which ones a work actually needs — judged by removing them one at a time.

course.title: Learning Korean Culture with 12 Korean Dramas
course.description: A weekly seminar using twelve Korean television dramas, from royal-court melodrama to barracks comedy, as primary sources for studying Korean history, society and popular culture, and for practising the difference between what a drama shows and what it dramatises.

nodes.title: Screening 1: Jewel in the Palace
nodes.description: The opening screening --- royal-kitchen politics, and the first pass at telling a drama's history from its invention
spec: you have watched the assigned Jewel in the Palace episodes before arriving
you can name one dish or kitchen ritual the episode uses to mark rank
you can point to one moment that felt invented rather than recorded, and say why

meta.posterAlt: Promotional poster for Jewel in the Palace, showing a woman in a teal and navy hanbok with a red hair ribbon, in profile against a deep red background

nodes.title: Screening 2: KPop Demon Hunters
nodes.description: A girl group, a monster plot, and the industry underneath both
spec: you have watched the assigned episodes before arriving
you can describe one production choice (staging, styling, choreography) and what it's designed to do for an audience outside Korea
you can distinguish the show's fantasy premise from a claim about the real K-pop industry

meta.posterAlt: Promotional poster for KPop Demon Hunters, showing three animated idol characters in white and gold stage outfits against a pastel gradient

nodes.title: Screening 3: Crash Landing on You
nodes.description: Romance across the DMZ, and the line between a love story and a political argument
spec: you have watched the assigned episodes before arriving
you can name one detail the drama gets right about everyday life on either side of the border
you can name one thing the drama simplifies for the romance to work

meta.posterAlt: Promotional poster for Crash Landing on You, showing the four leads standing together in front of the Seoul skyline at dusk

nodes.title: Screening 4: When Life Gives You Tangerines
nodes.description: A family across three generations, and what changes underneath a household that doesn't
spec: you have watched the assigned episodes before arriving
you can identify one expectation placed on a parent or child that a later generation in the drama no longer accepts
you can connect one family decision to the wider economic change happening around it

meta.posterAlt: Promotional poster for When Life Gives You Tangerines, showing a couple in vintage uniforms standing together in a field of yellow flowers

nodes.title: Screening 5: Coffee Prince
nodes.description: A gender-disguise plot from 2007, read for its assumptions rather than its jokes
spec: you have watched the assigned episodes before arriving
you can state the discussion's ground rule in your own words --- represents, does not verdict, a whole society's beliefs
you can name one assumption the disguise premise makes about its audience

meta.posterAlt: Promotional poster for The 1st Shop of Coffee Prince, showing the two leads seated together outdoors, one holding a cup of coffee

nodes.title: Screening 6: Misaeng
nodes.description: A contract worker's first year, and the office hierarchy the show renders in close detail
spec: you have watched the assigned episodes before arriving
you can describe the contract-versus-permanent distinction and why it matters to the plot
you can separate one social pattern the show depicts from one moment that reads more like stereotype

meta.posterAlt: Promotional poster for Misaeng, showing office coworkers celebrating with papers thrown in the air around a meeting table

nodes.title: Screening 7: SKY Castle
nodes.description: A satire of admissions pressure, and the real weight it's exaggerating
spec: you have watched the assigned episodes before arriving
you can name one moment the show plays for satire and say what real pressure it's exaggerating
you can connect the show's admissions obsession to a claim about social mobility or inequality

meta.posterAlt: Promotional poster for SKY Castle, showing five women in formal black attire posed together in a studio portrait

nodes.title: Screening 8: Mr. Sunshine
nodes.description: Colonial-period Korea, and the difference between a moving scene and a historical source
spec: you have watched the assigned episodes before arriving
you can name one historical fact the drama draws on, with a source other than the drama itself
you can name one moment that is dramatic invention rather than record

meta.posterAlt: Promotional poster for Mr. Sunshine, showing five leads in period hanbok and military dress standing in an ornate, dimly lit interior

nodes.title: Screening 9: Reply 1988
nodes.description: A neighbourhood's daily life under authoritarian rule, told with more warmth than politics
spec: you have watched the assigned episodes before arriving
you can name one detail of 1980s daily life the show uses to build its world
you can name one thing the show's nostalgia plays down or leaves out

meta.posterAlt: Promotional poster for Reply 1988, showing a large multigenerational family posed together in a narrow neighbourhood alley

nodes.title: Screening 10: The Art of Sarah
nodes.description: A counterfeit-luxury scam, and what its ease tells us about status and visibility rather than about "materialism" in general
spec: you have watched the assigned episodes before arriving
you can name one real brand or price the drama uses to ground its fictional scam
you can restate this week's caution in your own words --- a visible theme is not the same as a verdict on a society

meta.posterAlt: Collage-style promotional poster for The Art of Sarah, showing a woman's face partly obscured by a folded document, with a luxury handbag tagged like police evidence

nodes.title: Screening 11: My ID Is Gangnam Beauty
nodes.description: A transformation story, and the live debate about cosmetic surgery it walks straight into
spec: you have watched the assigned episodes before arriving
you can name one social pressure the show depicts beyond the surgery itself
you can restate this week's caution --- variation and debate, not a single national fact

meta.posterAlt: Promotional poster for My ID Is Gangnam Beauty, showing the smiling lead holding books in the foreground with two classmates behind her

nodes.title: Screening 12: New Recruit
nodes.description: Compulsory service played for comedy, and what the tone choice tells us about a shared national experience
spec: you have watched the assigned episodes before arriving
you can name one way the show's hierarchy echoes an institution from an earlier week (family, school, workplace)
you can say what playing conscription for comedy, rather than trauma, does for the audience

meta.posterAlt: Promotional poster for New Recruit, showing a group of soldiers in camouflage and berets against a dark, dust-lit background

nodes.title: Close analysis essay
nodes.description: A close reading of one week's drama, arguing for a specific claim about what it represents and what it dramatises
spec: submitted by the deadline, in the format named below
argues one specific claim about a single week's drama, rather than surveying the whole show
separates what the drama represents from what it dramatises, and says why the difference matters for your claim
cites specific scenes or moments as evidence, not general impressions

criteria.name: Use of evidence from the drama

nodes.title: Final comparative essay
nodes.description: A comparative essay across at least two dramas, arguing for a theme or pattern that runs across the semester
spec: submitted by the deadline, in the format named below
compares at least two dramas from the semester against a specific, stated theme or question
draws explicitly on concepts introduced across the weeks it uses, not just plot description
reaches its own position, rather than only summarising each drama in turn

nodes.title: Weekly viewing responses
nodes.description: Short reactions to each week's drama and its questions, submitted across the semester rather than all at once
spec: a short response is submitted for most weeks, in the format named below
each response engages with that week's questions specifically, not just a plot summary
the responses read as your own reaction, not a restatement of the lecture

nodes.title: Jewel in the Palace: Korean Food Culture and Traditional Medicine

nodes.title: KPop Demon Hunters: K-pop and Korean Popular Culture
nodes.description: Why K-pop travels, and what its production model reveals about Korean popular culture and identity on a global stage

nodes.title: Crash Landing on You: Korean Division, North and South
nodes.description: A romance across the DMZ, and what it romanticises about a division that isn't a plot device

nodes.title: When Life Gives You Tangerines: Family and Generational Culture
nodes.description: A multigenerational Jeju family drama, and how duty, marriage, and independence have shifted between generations

nodes.title: Coffee Prince: Changing Attitudes Toward Sexuality and Gender
nodes.description: A gender-disguise romance from the 2000s, read for what it assumed its audience already believed

nodes.title: Misaeng: Incomplete Life and Korean Workplace Culture
nodes.description: A contract worker at a trading company, and what the show gets right about hierarchy, seniority, and hours

nodes.title: SKY Castle: Korea's Education Fever
nodes.description: Private tutors, university admissions, and the extremes a satire has to reach to feel exaggerated

nodes.title: Mr. Sunshine: Korean Independence and the Colonial Period

course.title: Urban Design Studio: Foundations of the Good City
course.description: A second-year design studio that treats Cities: Skylines II as a legitimate planning tool. Build a district across the semester, defend every zoning, transit and budget choice at crit, and learn why no design decision is free of tradeoffs.

nodes.title: Site Selection and the First Grid
nodes.description: Choose the studio site, cut a first road grid, and walk the terrain in-simulation before committing to anything that is expensive to undo.
spec: You have either a capable machine or a booked design-lab machine with Cities: Skylines II and the standard map installed; use no simulation-altering mods, no unlimited money and no unlock-all.
The Kerrow Basin standard map is loaded in a new save, not regenerated, with no roads placed.
You can name the three metrics — fiscal performance, mobility performance, livability — and say which panel each one is read in.
You have somewhere off this machine to put a save file, and you can put one there today.
You have blank paper or a document open for the one-page site report, which is produced during the session and not afterwards.

nodes.title: Block Pattern and the Walkability Desk Crit
nodes.description: Lay out one neighbourhood's block pattern, then defend it at desk crit against a single question: what is it actually like to walk here?
spec: One residential quarter is laid out in your Week 1 save at a block dimension you can state in metres.

You bring the unzoned path-count table for the tested 480 × 480 m block: independent routes between two named corners and the frontage metres the zoning tool can reach — there is no unzoned traffic-volume overlay, because an empty network has no local origins.
You bring the close-one-link redundancy test as two route counts: independent routes between the same two corners before the busiest topological link is removed on paper, and after.
You bring the road length and occupied-dwelling count you divided to derive road metres per dwelling, plus the road upkeep figure from the economy panel as a separate reading.
You can state the block dimension you chose in metres and say what you were trying to buy with that number.
You bring a frontage inventory with the count of road-reachable cells and its counting method, and establish one named dwelling address for Week 3.

nodes.title: Zoning the First District
nodes.description: Zone the district, then put land value and commute distance side by side and account for the gap between what you hoped for and what the readout says.
spec: Your Week 2 save opens with the Brayhurst quarter built at a committed block dimension and zoned low-density residential.
You can turn on the wind arrows inside the air pollution view and state the map's prevailing wind direction without looking it up.
You have chosen one dwelling by address in your quarter, and every commute distance you quote this week is measured from it.

You build Scheme A (separated, the assessed branch) in the assessed save and Scheme B (adjacent, a counterfactual) in a sandbox, then read ground, air, water and noise pollution plus traffic volume on each at in-game 08:00.
You bring a sandbox save you are willing to build a second, uncommitted zoning scheme in.

nodes.title: Upzoning the Amenity Core
nodes.description: Upzone around a central amenity and test how far its radius really reaches. First assessed pin-up of the semester, with the visiting critic on the jury.
spec: Your Neighbourhood Unit Plan is uploaded by 12:00 on 15 March and hanging on the wall by 13:00.
You arrive with the save `<student ID>-w04` loaded and advanced to in-game 08:00, not a screenshot of it — the upzoning and clinic branches already done as pre-deadline homework.
Your hung set includes the Land Value info view over the cell, the coverage radius of every service building you sited, and the traffic volume layer along the Kerrow corridor boundary.
The card at the bottom of your bay states what the cell costs per month and what it returns per month, as two figures in ₡.
You name, out loud at the jury, which two of the three metrics your plan traded and the element of the plan where that trade is visible.
You arrive with the issued three-cell clinic branches already made as pre-deadline homework; this session does not run them.

nodes.title: Designing the Transit Spine
nodes.description: Route the district's transit spine — where the line runs, how often, and how many residents end up genuinely within reach of it.
spec: You arrive with the save `<student ID>-w04` loaded and advanced to in-game 08:00, not a screenshot of it.
You bring the canonical straight bus alignment and one loop comparator, each with its manually timed round trip and stop count; the straight alignment is the line every student builds.
The headway you set is stated together with the arithmetic that produced it: round-trip time divided by headway, rounded up to whole vehicles.
You record allocated operating cost and fare revenue as separate worksheet figures alongside the live line-panel fields, without describing worksheet values as native readouts.
You measure the 400 m network catchment around each of your six stops and name the parts of the district your alignment leaves outside it, stated against the reference alignment's 62%.

nodes.title: Peak-Load Stress Test
nodes.description: Drive the road network to peak load and watch where it gives way, then argue the fix: a wider road, a better line, or fewer trips needing to be made.
spec: You arrive with the save `<student ID>-w05` loaded and the Transportation Overview open, not a screenshot of either.
Before you change anything, you record the raw peak count, lane count, supplied saturation-flow assumption and observed green fraction used to calculate Wickstead demand divided by assumed capacity.
The widening's route timing is on your sheet for three states — the first morning, the issued three-week checkpoint and the issued six-week checkpoint — each labelled with its source save and date.
Your decomposition table treats the four proposed refill sources as hypotheses, recording an estimate or `not estimable`, the observation used and every conversion assumption.
You leave a position statement of no more than 150 words on the wall and an off-machine copy of `<student ID>-w06`.

nodes.title: Utilities Clinic
nodes.description: Build and upgrade the water, sewage and power networks, then resolve a service failure that has already begun cascading through the district.
spec: You arrive with your Week 6 save unmodified, the issued overload checkpoint and the failure chronology marked at the first entry that would make you investigate.
You distinguish water production shortfall, sewage-treatment overload and river-pollution exposure using their actual panels, without claiming pipe pressure or a boil-notice state.
Your group clinic gives every student a named diagnostic role and compares the same baseline, water-upgrade and treatment-upgrade checkpoints.
You leave with both facility increments costed, a chosen order on the reverse-salient card, and your personal save preserved rather than overwritten by the reference scenario.
Every reading is labelled live UI, manual observation, worksheet calculation or reference-scenario value.

nodes.title: Budget Under Cutback
nodes.description: Balance the district budget against an imposed service cutback, and say out loud — on the record — what you have chosen not to fund.
spec: You arrive with the issued district allocation worksheet totalled; it is explicitly a course allocation of citywide costs, not a native district budget.
You arrive with a sealed one-line prediction naming the budget line you expect to cut and the metric you expect it to cost.
You compose a closure worth 22% of the worksheet's total eligible allocated outlay, once, while keeping both Week 7 utility increments funded in the allocation rather than cut.
You record your unfunded lines in the set form on the corridor budget sheet and signed unfunded list, using a spoken, written, recorded or seated equivalent.
You test the closure against the nearest issued reference branch, label the branch on every reading, and record where citywide controls cannot implement the district allocation exactly.

nodes.title: The Public Realm Build
nodes.description: Build the district's parks, plazas and street-level public space. Assessed pin-up, judged on what the public realm does rather than how it renders.
spec: Your screenshots and defence memo are uploaded by 12:00 and your printed set is on the wall before the hang closes at 13:25.
Every public space on your wall carries a monthly upkeep figure funded from your column of the corridor budget sheet.
Your signed unfunded list is pinned as the last sheet of your memo, with the Week 8 lines still on it.
You can state the cost per attributed happiness point in the reference worksheet and explain why simultaneous interventions make it an association rather than a causal return.
You bring one pedestrian count taken at 19:00 using the issued weather state, camera, polygon and one-minute observation window.

nodes.title: Hazard Scenario
nodes.description: Stress-test the district against a hazard it was never designed for, and separate what failed from what merely looked alarming.
spec: You arrive with the Week 9 save and the fire-hazard and electricity views already checked over your own district, wind read from the arrows inside the electricity view.
You branch your own district as your Week 10 save before any checkpoint is loaded, and nothing you load this afternoon alters it.
You read the issued d0, d3, d6 and recovered checkpoints rather than simulating a 19-day live run, and you close them without saving any of them as your own.
Your fault sheet separates what broke from what recovered, and every entry names its checkpoint.
Every Week 10 figure you quote afterwards names the checkpoint it was taken on.

nodes.title: Reading the Land-Value Curve
nodes.description: Read the district's land-value history since Week 1 against everything that curve does not record — who moved, who could not, and who was never modelled.
spec: You arrive with ten weekly saves (`w01`–`w10`) as a recovery path, plus the pre-extracted land-value series; today's save is the eleventh.
You plot the district land-value curve by hand from the pack (reference-scenario values, or a reconstructed row from your own save), 0–100 scale, with Week 10 left as a gap.
Every segment of your curve is annotated as a temporal association or hypothesis, or marked as unattributed — not as a proven single cause.
You leave with one written sentence naming what the four-block decision traded, which metric it moved, and which population it moved for.
Your omissions appendix is drafted to all four headings before you leave the room.

nodes.title: Final Jury
nodes.description: The comprehensive plan, presented and defended end to end to a full jury. Twelve weeks of district decisions, argued as one position.
spec: The A3 brief is the sole authority for memo, appendix, boards, screenshots, save and clocks; this session is the jury.
Your boards are hung in roster order before 12:50; the presentation order is drawn at 12:50 and does not rearrange the wall.
A metric card is permitted; spatial planning evidence on the boards is required, and oral polish without it does not carry the mark.
Transit share and walk share keep separate observation denominators and are not added; the reserve-versus-link forecast is a worksheet.
The last question of your slot is the fourth question: the Week 10 fire load case (`d3` against `recovered`) and what the model could not show.

nodes.title: Neighbourhood Unit Plan
nodes.description: Plan and defend a single neighbourhood unit — its block pattern, its zoning, and the amenity everything else is arranged around. First assessed pin-up of the semester.
spec: Your defence memo is no more than 800 words and names the two metrics you traded and the element of the plan where the trade is visible.
Your memo cites the Week 1 site report, the Week 2 block dimension and its upkeep, and the Week 3 scheme and named front door.

Your screenshots are captioned with in-game day and 08:00, and include the land value overlay over the cell, the coverage radius of every service building you sited (each captured with that building selected), and the traffic volume layer at the Kerrow corridor boundary.
The hung A3 shows the district-tool boundary, the amenity core at Pelling Cross, and the Kerrow corridor drawn where it actually runs, with the three required views printed beneath it.
The bay card states the cell's monthly cost and monthly return in ₡, from the issued district-cost worksheet.
The save `<student ID>-w04` matches the screenshots and the hung plan.

meta.heroImageAlt: A circular neighbourhood plan with twelve residential blocks around a tree-lined shared amenity, a walking catchment and a transit corridor.
meta.cardImageAlt: A circular neighbourhood plan with twelve residential blocks around a tree-lined shared amenity, a walking catchment and a transit corridor.

nodes.title: Public Realm and Infrastructure Plan
nodes.description: The district after the break: its parks, plazas and streets planned together with the utility networks beneath them, and costed against a budget that will not stretch.
spec: You submit 8–12 in-simulation screenshots captioned with in-game day and time, including an attractiveness overlay, a land value overlay, a water or sewage info-view, and a 19:00 street-level view with a counted, captioned polygon population.

Your defence memo is no more than 1,200 words, structured against livability, fiscal performance and mobility performance in that order, and accounts for the public realm spend while keeping both Week 7 utility increments funded.
Every public space you proposed carries one costed monthly line, funded from the Week 8 closure, with any happiness or land-value movement labelled as associated rather than isolated cause.
The signed unfunded list from Week 8 is the memo's last sheet.
The save `<student ID>-w09` matches the wall.

nodes.title: Comprehensive City Plan
nodes.description: The capstone: the whole district argued as one plan — every zoning, transit, budget and public-realm decision since Week 1, defended end to end at the final jury.
spec: The jury copy of your defence memo, with the omissions appendix at the front, reaches both chairs by Friday 21 May 12:00 — three days before the artefact deadline.
Your defence memo is no more than 1,600 words (the omissions appendix does not count) and states a claim, the grounds, the warrant, the qualifier as a number, and the rebuttal.
Your screenshots cover full extent roads only, the land value overlay, the corridor at neighbourhood scale, one street-level block, and the three metric readouts, captioned in-game day and 08:00.
Your boards carry spatial planning evidence: named overlays, the corridor budget sheet column, the unfunded list, and the Week 10 exposure statement.
Transit share and walk share are reported against separate observation denominators, never added together.
You answer, for every slot, whether the district holds under Week 10's fire load case and what the model could not show.

marking.description: Judged as a whole rather than criterion by criterion. The jury reads the plan against all three studio metrics at once — livability, fiscal performance and mobility performance — and asks a fourth question the earlier briefs do not: whether the district still holds up under the hazards of Week 10, and whether the plan is honest about what the simulation was never able to show it.

nodes.title: Site Analysis and the Blank Map
nodes.description: Terrain, climate and constraint as the first design move — reading a site before a single road goes down, and naming the three metrics the studio is marked against all semester.

nodes.title: The Grid vs. the Organic Street
nodes.description: Hippodamus's grid, the medieval street and the Radburn superblock — three answers to the same question about what shape a block should be, and what each one does to a walk.

nodes.title: Zoning and the Myth of Separation
nodes.description: Where Euclidean zoning came from, what it was built to prevent, and what separating uses costs a district in commute distance and land value.

nodes.title: Density and the 15-Minute City
nodes.description: Transit-oriented density and the amenity radius — how far a resident will actually walk, and what therefore has to sit inside the circle.

nodes.title: Moving People: Transit-Oriented Design
nodes.description: Headways, network legibility and the transfer penalty — why a line nobody can read at a glance is a line nobody rides.

nodes.title: Traffic Engineering and Its Discontents
nodes.description: Induced demand, the one-way-street fix, and the uncomfortable arithmetic of why the lane you add fills up again.

nodes.title: Infrastructure You Don't See
nodes.description: Water, sewage and power as capacity-constrained networks — where headroom runs out, and how one quiet failure cascades into the next.

nodes.title: Fiscal Realism: Taxes, Budgets and the Limits of Growth
nodes.description: Land value capture and the service-funding tradeoff — what a district can actually afford, and what it gives up in order to afford it.

nodes.title: Parks, Plazas and the Public Realm
nodes.description: Jacobs on eyes-on-the-street, and the third place — what public space is doing when it works, and how to read a plaza that does not.

nodes.title: Resilience: Hazards, Pollution and Climate
nodes.description: Hazard, pollution and climate as design constraints rather than events — planning for the conditions a district meets once and remembers for a decade.

nodes.title: What the Model Can't Show You
nodes.description: Land ownership, displacement, informal housing and political contest — the things the simulation abstracts away, and why knowing your model's edges is design literacy.

nodes.title: Capstone Review: The Comprehensive Plan
nodes.description: The comprehensive plan as an argument — drawing twelve weeks of district decisions into one whole a jury can be walked through and can push back on.

course.title: Patterns of Change: Taiji, Bagua, and the Visual Logic of Transformation
course.description: A semiotics course on how a small set of visual signs can encode change itself, not just static categories: from a single yin-yang line, through trigrams and hexagrams, to how their meanings were built, arranged, and reinterpreted across history.

nodes.title: Signs That Move — Framing the Question
nodes.description: What does a sign system need to represent change, not just categories?
spec: you can describe, for at least one comparison sign system, what makes it good or bad at representing a process rather than a fixed state
you can state this course's central question in your own words

nodes.title: One Splits into Two — Taiji and the Yin-Yang Line
nodes.description: What is the smallest visual distinction that can carry meaning?
spec: you can draw a broken (yin) and unbroken (yang) line and explain why one binary distinction is enough to start building a notation
you can place Taiji as the first term in the documented Taiji → Liangyi → Sixiang → Bagua sequence, without presenting it as a single fixed meaning

nodes.title: Doubling the Line — Bigrams and the Logic of Combination
nodes.description: What happens when you combine binary signs, and how far does combination scale?
spec: you can enumerate all four two-line combinations (bigrams) from the yin/yang line
you can explain why "Sixiang" in this course's sequence is not the same thing as the Four Symbols direction-guardian tradition

nodes.title: Eight from Three — Constructing the Bagua
nodes.description: How do three lines generate a complete symbol set?
spec: you can construct all eight trigrams from three stacked yin/yang lines
you can name the natural image the Shuogua zhuan attributes to at least three trigrams

nodes.title: Opposites and Neighbors — Relationships Among the Trigrams
nodes.description: How do the eight trigrams relate to each other, independent of how they are arranged?
spec: you can identify a trigram's line-inverse (every yin flipped to yang and back) and name the four inverse pairs among the eight trigrams
you can explain why a line-inverse relationship holds regardless of how the trigrams are arranged in space

nodes.title: An Inner Order — The Xiantian Arrangement
nodes.description: How did Shao Yong organize the eight trigrams into a symmetrical order?
spec: you can describe what makes the Xiantian arrangement symmetrical, concretely, in terms of the inverse pairs from week 5
you can distinguish the Fuxi legend (traditional attribution) from Shao Yong's Song-dynasty construction of the system (historically attested)

nodes.title: An Outer Order — The Houtian Arrangement and Correlative Cosmology
nodes.description: How does a second, different ordering encode a different logic over the same eight trigrams?
spec: you can state at least one concrete difference between the Xiantian and Houtian arrangements
you can trace the Houtian arrangement's direction/season correlations back to the Shuogua zhuan

nodes.title: Lines That Move — Hexagrams and Changing Lines
nodes.description: How does the notation encode transformation itself, not just a static state?
spec: you can stack two trigrams into a hexagram and identify each of its six lines
you can apply the changing-line rule to derive a new hexagram from a starting one

nodes.title: From Diagram to Text — The Zhouyi and Its Layers
nodes.description: How reliable is what we actually know about this text's origins?
spec: you can describe the Zhouyi as a layered, composite text rather than a single-author work of known date
you can distinguish a specific scholar's dating argument from the broader scholarly uncertainty about the text's age
you can name at least one later interpretive tradition (numerological or philosophical) built on top of the Zhouyi, and explain why it is a reception, not the core text's original content

nodes.title: One Symbol, Two Histories — Zhou Dunyi's Taijitu and the Swirling Symbol
nodes.description: How did a change in visual form change how the idea was communicated?
spec: you can distinguish Zhou Dunyi's 11th-century Taijitu from the later swirling black-and-white symbol as two historically separate images
you can name the five tiers of Zhou Dunyi's diagram in order
you can explain, for this specific case, how a redesigned visual form changed how the idea was communicated rather than merely restating it in new clothing

nodes.title: Crossing Worlds — Leibniz, Binary Arithmetic, and Global Afterlives
nodes.description: What actually happened when this notation reached Europe, and how does that compare with the popular version of the story?
spec: you can state the documented sequence of the Leibniz–Bouvet exchange in the order it happened
you can identify at least one way the popular "I Ching predicted binary computing" story overstates the documented episode

nodes.title: Reading Symbols Critically — Capstone
nodes.description: How do you tell a well-supported claim about a sign system from an overstated one, and does the toolkit transfer to a system you've never seen?
spec: you can evaluate a modern popular claim about this course's sign system (feng shui, "quantum yin-yang," or similar) against the sourcing standard used all semester
you can apply the same toolkit — construction, transformation, arrangement, sourcing discipline — to a sign system outside this course

nodes.title: Assignment 1
nodes.description: Construct a hexagram by hand, apply the changing-line rule, and compare the Xiantian and Houtian arrangements — the direct test of weeks 1–8's construction, transformation, and arrangement content
spec: submitted by the deadline, in the format named below
every trigram and hexagram is built from the line rule, not copied from a reference diagram
the changing-line derivation is shown as a step, not just the final answer
for at least one trigram used in the brief, its Xiantian and Houtian positions are both stated, with one concrete difference between what the two arrangements do with it

criteria.name: Correct application of the changing-line rule
Correct comparison of the Xiantian and Houtian arrangements

nodes.title: Final project
nodes.description: The capstone — critically evaluate a modern popular claim about this course's sign system, then transfer the same toolkit to one it never covered
spec: submitted by the deadline, in the format named below
the critical evaluation cites primary or academic sources, not tertiary wikis, for every factual claim it relies on

the critical evaluation labels at least three specific claims it discusses as historically attested fact, traditional/legendary attribution, or later interpretation/modern analogy, using this course's three evidence registers
the transfer analysis names which parts of this course's toolkit it is applying, and where the unfamiliar system's structure differs

marking.description: Judged as a whole against the brief, with particular attention to whether the critical evaluation is sourced rather than asserted, whether at least three specific claims are correctly labelled by evidence register (fact, attribution, or interpretation) rather than left unmarked, and whether the transfer analysis genuinely applies this course's toolkit (construction rules, structural relationships, arrangement, fact-versus-interpretation discipline) rather than restating facts about the new system in isolation.

course.title: Love, Markets, and Other Failures
course.description: Treats falling in love as a market, with all the frictions, information problems, and eventual failures that implies.

nodes.title: Market Case Studies
nodes.description: Find the frictions in a market that isn't romance, before the course turns the same lens on one that is
spec: you name a real market that isn't romantic (housing, hiring, college admissions, or one of your own)
you can point to at least one specific friction in it (a search cost, an information asymmetry, a screening mechanism)
you can say, out loud, what "the market fails" would mean for your example

nodes.title: Map Your Search Technology
nodes.description: Model a fictional persona's discovery channel as a cost function, not as a list of tips
spec: you've modeled a fictional persona's discovery channel as a cost function — rough cost per candidate, signal quality, false-positive rate — even if the numbers are guesses, they're written down
you've done the same for a second, different channel for the same persona, so two cost functions sit side by side, not one
you can point to the specific number that differs between the two and say which stopping rule it flips, not just that "the strategy changes"

nodes.title: Signal or Noise?
nodes.description: Sort a batch of fictional profile claims into cheap talk and costly signal, and defend the line
spec: every claim in your batch is sorted into cheap talk or costly signal
each sort comes with one sentence on what would have made it expensive to fake
you can name one claim you initially misclassified and why

nodes.title: Lemon Lot
nodes.description: A market-for-lemons exercise — choose who to "buy" under deliberately incomplete information
spec: you made a choice among the fictional personas given only partial information
you can state which piece of missing information you'd have paid the most to have
you can connect your choice to why the pool you were shown looked the way it did

nodes.title: Design a Screening Test
nodes.description: Groups design a screening mechanism that separates types by self-selection — and Assignment 1 is due
spec: your group's mechanism offers a menu, not a direct question
you can explain why a dishonest type would rationally choose differently from an honest one under your menu
Assignment 1 is submitted before the tutorial starts

nodes.title: Secretary Problem Simulator
nodes.description: Play the optimal-stopping game against your own intuition, then check it against the 1/e rule
spec: you played at least two full rounds of the simulator with different stopping strategies
you can state your own stopping threshold before being told the optimal one
you can explain, after seeing the results, why the optimal threshold beat your intuition (or didn't)

nodes.title: Opening Moves
nodes.description: Practice drills in the midterm's own format, the week the midterm is sat
spec: you've attempted at least five practice items in the midterm's format
you can name the concept (war of attrition, coordination under incomplete information, signaling cost) each drill was testing
the midterm itself is sat in this session

nodes.title: Run Gale–Shapley by Hand
nodes.description: Execute the stable matching algorithm on a small preference table, from both sides
spec: you ran the algorithm to completion on a supplied preference table
you ran it again with the proposing side reversed
you can point to at least one person whose outcome changed between the two runs

nodes.title: Negotiate the Bins
nodes.description: A structured Nash-bargaining role-play over a shared-resource dilemma
spec: you and your partner reached a split, and can state it as a number, not a vibe
you can each name your outside option and how it shaped the split
the split you reached is at least defensible against the Nash bargaining solution given the outside options you stated

nodes.title: Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma Tournament
nodes.description: The classic in-class tournament — submit a strategy, play it against everyone else's, repeatedly
spec: you submitted a strategy before round one started
you can state your strategy's rule in one sentence
you can name which strategy won and, in outline, why

nodes.title: Redesign the Rulebook
nodes.description: Workshop time on Assignment 2 — checking a proposed rule for incentive compatibility before you submit it
spec: you bring a draft rule from your Assignment 2 redesign
you can state, for your own rule, one way a rational participant could game it
after workshopping, your rule has changed in at least one specific way

nodes.title: Post-Mortem
nodes.description: A structured retrospective critiquing the market framework itself, ahead of the capstone
spec: you name one thing the market model explained well this semester
you name one thing it visibly failed to explain, for a case you can point to
you can state the difference between those two without hedging into "it depends"

nodes.title: Assignment 1: Design a Signal
nodes.description: Build a fictional dating persona and defend which of its claims are costly signals versus cheap talk
spec: submitted by the deadline, in the format named below
every persona in the submission is fictional — no real profile, yours or anyone else's, is used or referenced
each claim in the profile is labeled cheap talk or costly signal, with a defense that would survive a challenge

levels.label: Perfect (HD)
levels.description: Every claim is a deliberately engineered costly signal or a deliberately obvious cheap-talk foil; the profile reads as a genuine artefact, not an exercise.

levels.label: Excellent (HD)

levels.label: Very Good (D)

levels.label: Satisfactory (P)
levels.description: Clear attempt at costly signals, though some are weak or easy to fake.

levels.label: Borderline (P)
levels.description: Basic profile; most claims are unclassified cheap talk dressed up as signals.

levels.label: Unsatisfactory (F)
levels.description: Superficial profile with little evidence of deliberate signal design.

levels.label: Poor (F)
levels.description: Profile reads as generic, with no discernible signal/cheap-talk distinction attempted.

levels.label: Not Shown (0)
levels.description: No profile submitted.

levels.label: Perfect (HD)
levels.description: Every claim's classification is defended with a specific, testable reason that would survive a determined challenge.

levels.label: Excellent (HD)
levels.description: Sophisticated defenses that anticipate and pre-empt likely challenges.

levels.label: Very Good (D)

levels.label: Good (C)

levels.label: Satisfactory (P)

criteria.name: The profile is charming, not just accurate

levels.label: Perfect (HD)
levels.description: The profile would genuinely get a match — every line is engaging as well as classifiable, no filler.

levels.label: Excellent (HD)
