nodes.title: Assignment 2: Redesign the Rulebook
nodes.description: Propose an incentive-compatible redesign of a matching or bargaining mechanism, and show it survives being gamed
spec: submitted by the deadline, in the format named below
the mechanism you propose is stated as a rule, not a hope ("be honest") — a rational, self-interested participant must still be able to follow it to the letter
you demonstrate at least one specific attempt to game your own rule, and how the design survives it
you name the specific concept (incentive compatibility, mechanism design, screening, etc.) each part of your argument is applying — not just an answer

levels.label: Perfect (HD)
levels.description: The rule is stated with such precision that a rational, self-interested participant has no better strategy than the intended one — genuinely incentive-compatible, not just well-intentioned.

levels.label: Excellent (HD)
levels.description: Rule is precisely specified and the incentive-compatibility argument is rigorous and specific to the case.

levels.label: Very Good (D)
levels.description: Rule is clearly stated as an incentive structure, with a solid argument for why self-interest aligns with it.

levels.label: Good (C)
levels.description: Thoughtful redesign that functions as a real mechanism, not just advice.

levels.label: Satisfactory (P)
levels.description: Rule is stated as a mechanism, though the incentive argument is thin in places.

levels.label: Borderline (P)
levels.description: Redesign is mostly a restatement of good intentions ("be honest") rather than a rule with teeth.

levels.label: Unsatisfactory (F)
levels.description: Rule leaves obvious room for self-interested deviation with no penalty or structure to prevent it.

levels.label: Poor (F)

levels.label: Not Shown (0)

criteria.name: You show, concretely, how it survives an attempt to game it

levels.label: Perfect (HD)

levels.label: Excellent (HD)

levels.label: Very Good (D)

levels.label: Good (C)

levels.label: Satisfactory (P)

levels.label: Borderline (P)

levels.label: Unsatisfactory (F)

levels.label: Poor (F)
levels.description: No evidence the rule was pressure-tested at all.

levels.label: Not Shown (0)

criteria.name: Your mechanism has a name worth citing

levels.label: Unsatisfactory (F)

nodes.title: What is a copy?

nodes.title: Materials don't lie (usually)

nodes.title: Forging the hand — text, signatures and the tell in language

nodes.title: Currency and the state's own arms race

nodes.title: The market for authenticity

nodes.title: Reading a Box - Three Design Logics
nodes.description: Three real packages, three different things each one was actually built to do — and the claim this course spends twelve weeks testing

nodes.title: Corrugated Board - What the Flute Buys You
nodes.description: Flute type is a cost-and-protection trade-off with no sustainability content of its own — the first number behind week 1's three logics
spec: A-flute: about 4.8mm thick, about 33 flutes per foot — the best cushioning and stacking strength of the common flutes (see linked source)
B-flute: about 3.2mm thick, about 47 flutes per foot — the strongest flat-crush resistance of the common flutes (see linked source)
C-flute: about 4.0mm thick, about 39 flutes per foot — used in roughly 80% of global corrugated shipping containers (see linked source)
E-flute: about 1.6mm thick, about 90 flutes per foot — built for a smooth external print surface, not for cushioning (see linked source)
Double-wall board (e.g. BC-flute) combines two flute profiles, for heavier or more fragile shipments (see linked source)

nodes.title: Proving It Survives - ISTA 3A
nodes.description: What "survives shipping" is actually tested against, and why the test exists to protect a return/liability cost, not the planet
spec: ISTA 3A applies to packaged products up to 70kg, across standard, small, flat, and elongated package types (see linked source)
the procedure runs atmospheric preconditioning, then 9 drops followed by 8 more drops (see linked source)
it also runs random vibration testing, with and without a top load, plus an optional low-pressure vibration test (see linked source)
rotational edge and flat drops, concentrated and bridge impact tests, and a leak test for liquid contents complete the standard (see linked source)

nodes.title: Paying by Air - The Cubic Weight Formula
nodes.description: The formula a courier actually bills against, and the number that turns week 1's oversized lululemon box into a real line item
spec: cubic weight (kg) = length (m) x width (m) x height (m) x 250 (see linked source)
chargeable weight is whichever is greater: cubic weight or actual weight (see linked source)
the cubic-weight comparison typically applies once a parcel's actual weight is over 1kg (see linked source)

nodes.title: Reading an Industry's Own Data - The Fibre Box LCA
nodes.description: A rigorous, peer-reviewed life-cycle study, published by the trade association for the material it favours — this week's central critical-reading exercise
spec: corrugated packaging has a 70-75% recycling rate, compared with about 8% for polypropylene containers (see linked source)
the industry reports roughly a 50% reduction in per-unit greenhouse gas emissions between 2006 and 2020 (see linked source)
the methodology follows ISO 14040/14044, was conducted by the independent firm Anthesis Group, and was peer-reviewed (see linked source)

nodes.title: Midpoint - What Are They Actually Optimising For?
nodes.description: No new facts this week — revisit Apple, lululemon and OnTheList with four weeks of formulas and standards behind you

nodes.title: The Cost of Coming Back - Returns Economics
nodes.description: An e-commerce return isn't free once it leaves the warehouse — the return-rate and reverse-logistics numbers behind the other half of the throughline claim
spec: the overall e-commerce return rate is about 19.3% (see linked source)
return rates vary by category: apparel 20-40%, footwear 17-30%, electronics 8-15%, beauty 4-12%, jewelry 12-15% (see linked source)
reverse-logistics and restocking costs for electronics run about $30-65 per item, and can exceed the item's own margin for furniture or other oversized goods (see linked source)
fit and sizing account for about 50% of apparel returns (see linked source)
some brands issue a refund without requiring the item back — a 'keep-it' refund — once the reverse-logistics cost would exceed the item's value (see linked source)

nodes.title: Designing the Reveal - Nudge Theory and the Unboxing Moment
nodes.description: Thaler and Sunstein's choice-architecture framework, and what it does and doesn't explain about why brand packaging is built the way it is
spec: choice architecture ('nudge theory') originates from Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein's book Nudge: Improving Decisions About Health, Wealth, and Happiness (Yale University Press, 2008) — cited here by title, authors and publisher rather than a link, since no specific web source was verified for this week

nodes.title: Three Original Declarations - Shipping Under a Rule You Didn't Write

the declaration must also state the IATA packing instruction number used for that shipment (see linked source)
three original dangerous goods declarations are required per hazardous package (see linked source)

nodes.title: Designed for One, Used by Everyone - OXO Good Grips
nodes.description: Betsey Farber's arthritis, a bad vegetable peeler, and the origin of universal design as a case this course's logics haven't optimised for
spec: Betsey Farber's arthritis made a standard vegetable peeler painful to use in the late 1980s, prompting her and Sam Farber to develop an ergonomic alternative with the design firm Smart Design (see linked source)
the result was framed as universal design — accessible to and usable by as many people as possible, not a product designed only for people with arthritis (see linked source)
the peeler won design awards and is now in the Museum of Modern Art's permanent collection (see linked source)

course.title: Your Call Is Important to Us
course.description: Everybody waits, but not equally. This course studies queues as designed systems, using SlopU's Office of Everything as a running case, to learn what waiting measures, who it favours, and how a service should speak about it.

nodes.title: Watch a queue
nodes.description: A close observation exercise on a real waiting system, kept separate from any assumption about why it works the way it does.
spec: you have picked one real, observable waiting system to follow for the first three weeks (a café, a pharmacy, a printer room, a help desk — your choice, as long as you can watch it more than once)
you have a written record of one observation session that separates what you saw from what you assumed
you can state, in one sentence, when you think the wait actually began for the person you watched

nodes.title: Find what the average hides
nodes.description: Work the Office of Everything's own ticket log against its "average wait" memo, then apply the same check to the system you are tracking yourself.
spec: you have computed the mean and the median of the Office of Everything's week-2 ticket log and can explain why they differ
you have named, in writing, which kind of request the memo's average is quietly averaging away
you have taken a second timed observation of your own real waiting system, this time recording individual wait times rather than a general impression

nodes.title: Recompute with and without the outlier
nodes.description: Rehearse the Queue Autopsy's core technique on the Office of Everything's data, then apply it to your own observed system before writing it up.
spec: you have recomputed the week-2 Office of Everything numbers twice, once with the 26-minute ticket included and once with it removed, and can state the size of the difference
you have compared a separate service-time model under its declared 26-minute and 2-minute dispute durations, distinguishing this intervention from deleting a recorded wait
you have analysed your longest recorded wait without inventing an outlier
you have a short written note distinguishing what you observed about that moment from what you are inferring caused it

nodes.title: Answer the complaint on FCFS's own terms
nodes.description: Work out exactly what the students' association complaint is asking the Office to change, and who would carry the cost of that change.
spec: you have restated the complaint as a specific, checkable proposal for ordering the queue, not just a general objection
you have named at least one group of people that proposal would make wait longer, not only the group it would help
you have written one paragraph arguing for or against the change, on the Office's own file, without appealing to a source outside this course

nodes.title: Test the Quick Enquiries draft for starvation
nodes.description: Apply the Office's draft shortest-job-first notice to a busier ticket log and check whether the longest case ever gets served.
spec: you have simulated, by hand, the Quick Enquiries draft policy against a log where short requests keep arriving
you can state whether the long-dispute ticket is served, and if so, how much later than under plain FCFS
you have written one sentence naming who benefits from the draft policy and one sentence naming who it leaves worse off

nodes.title: Compare three policies on one log
nodes.description: Run FCFS, Quick Enquiries and the Priority Lane against the same ticket log, then choose and defend one policy for the Office of Everything.
spec: you have computed each ticket's wait under all three policies on the same log
you have chosen one policy and written a defence of it that names who it favours and who it disadvantages
you have noted, in writing, one way the Priority Lane could be misused given that urgency is self-declared

nodes.title: Design what the wait sign should say
nodes.description: Replace the Office's frozen "estimated wait: 5 minutes" sign with an honest form of words, given only the information the counter actually has.
spec: you have listed exactly what information the Office's counter could actually know at the moment someone takes a ticket
you have drafted specific wording for the sign, using only that information, for both a short queue and a long one
you have written one sentence on what your wording deliberately chooses not to promise, and why

nodes.title: Specify the evidence for "stuck"
nodes.description: Work out what a person waiting in the Thursday display-board incident could actually have used to tell a stuck queue from a slow one.
spec: you have listed the evidence actually available to someone waiting in the Thursday incident, separate from what staff behind the counter knew
you have written a specific rule for how long that evidence should be absent before someone reasonably concludes the queue is stuck
you have applied the same question to your own observed system: what would tell you it had stopped, rather than merely slowed?

nodes.title: Account for the 15% who left
nodes.description: Test what unrecorded departures leave unknown about waiting, and check your own system for the same measurement gap.
spec: you have stated, in writing, why a 4-minute average computed from served tickets only is not automatically the true average wait
you have calculated the mean elapsed time until service or departure under three explicit assumptions about unrecorded departure times
you have distinguished those assumptions from observed evidence
you have checked whether your own observed system could hide reneging the same way, and said what evidence would reveal it if so

nodes.title: Audit the Priority Lane's usage release
nodes.description: Read the Office's released Priority Lane dataset against its stated purpose, and state plainly what it does and doesn't let you conclude.
spec: you have stated each category's share of all requests and its share of Priority Lane declarations, and said which categories are over- or under-represented among declarations relative to their share of demand

you have reported the release's aggregate six-minute wait-time figure separately from the category-share analysis, and written one sentence stating why it is not evidence of what any single category saved or of what caused the difference
you have named at least two specific pieces of evidence this release does not include that would be needed to explain the six-minute figure
you have written a conclusion limited to what the released data actually supports, without claiming any category's declarations were truthful or that the lane measures urgency
you have named one additional field the Office could release that would make a future audit more informative, and said what it would let you check

nodes.title: Trace the worst day back to one decision
nodes.description: Work through the Office's compounding-failure incident and argue for the single earlier design decision most responsible for how badly it went.
spec: you have listed the separate contributing factors in the worst-day incident and marked which were bad luck and which were consequences of an earlier design choice
you have named one specific decision from an earlier week as the one you would change first, with a reason
you have stated what changing that decision would probably have cost on an ordinary day, not only what it would have saved on the worst one

nodes.title: Redesign the counter and prepare its defence
nodes.description: Bring the semester's decisions together into one redesign of the Office of Everything, and prepare to defend each choice under questioning.
spec: you have written a specific redesign of the Office of Everything's front counter that states its ordering policy, its wait-communication rule, its stuck/slow signal, and how it accounts for cancellations
you have identified, for each major decision, the alternative you did not choose and why
you have prepared a short defence of the one decision you expect to be challenged on hardest, including what you would concede if the challenge were right

nodes.title: Policy Trial
nodes.description: A comparison of two queue-ordering policies against the same declared dataset, ending in a defended choice between them.
spec: the dataset used for the comparison is declared in full, so a marker can check the working
the same dataset is used for both policies, with no change to it between trials
the comparison reports results for both policies, not only the one ultimately chosen
the written defence names at least one group the chosen policy disadvantages, not only the group it favours

criteria.name: Fair comparison of both policies on the same data
Defence names who benefits and who waits longer

nodes.title: Queue Autopsy
nodes.description: A close analysis of one real waiting system, separating what you observed from what you assumed, and accounting honestly for its slowest case.
spec: the system named is real and public, with repeated observations made personally or supplied through the approved accessibility arrangement
observation and assumption are kept in visibly separate sections, not blended into one narrative

the write-up reports the full sample and recomputes its mean with one longest recorded wait omitted, stating when no conspicuous outlier was observed and avoiding causal conclusions from this deletion

no general external source substitutes for the real observation record, whether personally collected or approved for accessibility; interpretation sources are cited, and claims about the system itself are kept to what your observation actually supports

criteria.name: Wait-time analysis and sensitivity to the longest recorded wait
Scope and clarity of the write-up

nodes.title: The Honest Queue
nodes.description: A full redesign of the SlopU Office of Everything's front counter, defended against normal demand, congestion, uncertainty, failure and cancellation.
spec: the redesign states a specific ordering policy for normal demand, not only a principle
it states what the counter honestly tells someone about how long they will wait, consistent with week 7's standard
it specifies evidence that would distinguish a genuine stall from an ordinary slow period, per week 8
it accounts for people who leave before being served, per week 9
it addresses the Priority Lane directly, using the week 10 audit as evidence for keeping, changing or removing it
it names, for at least one major decision, the alternative rejected and why
it identifies what would happen to the redesign under the week 11 worst-day conditions and does not claim the failure could not recur

marking.description: The redesign is judged as a whole against the requirements below, not as a checklist scored piece by piece. A strong submission makes specific, defensible decisions on each requirement and is honest about what those decisions cost; a submission that is thorough on some requirements and silent on others is judged on its weakest point, since an Office of Everything that only works under normal demand is not the one this course asked for.

course.title: The Economics of Waiting
course.description: Queues are not accidents. Every line you have stood in was designed by someone who decided whose time was worth less. Twelve weeks on how queues form, what waiting costs, and who pays when the rules change.

nodes.title: Lab 1 — Ninety Seconds of Looking
nodes.description: Stand in front of a real queue and write down the rule it is running. Harder than it sounds, and the whole course starts here.
spec: you have watched one real queue, in person, for at least ninety seconds
you can state its discipline as an instruction a new staff member could follow
you have found one thing about its layout that costs time

nodes.title: Lab 2 — Breaking a Queue on Purpose
nodes.description: Run a queue by hand with dice, then add variance and watch it fall over without adding a single customer.
spec: you have run a physical queue simulation for at least fifty ticks
your two runs differ only in variance, not in average load
you can state, from your own data, what happened to the queue at high rho

nodes.title: Lab 3 — Census Clinic
nodes.description: Bring your assignment data in progress. We break it, together, before the deadline rather than after.
spec: you arrive with at least twenty minutes of real observations already collected
you can say where your queue starts, in a way another observer could apply
you have identified one assumption of Little's Law your data may violate

nodes.title: Lab 4 — The Wait Bill
nodes.description: Put a number on the waiting your system produces, three different ways, and then argue about which number you would be willing to publish.
spec: you have costed one real queue's waiting three ways, with the assumptions written down
you can say who bears the cost and who currently sees it
you have taken a position on equal versus differentiated valuation, and defended it aloud

nodes.title: Lab 5 — One Line or Six
nodes.description: Run the bank experiment with real humans, and find out why the fairer system is the one people complain about on sight.
spec: you have run both configurations with the same arrival script
you have recorded individual waits, not just the average
you can state which configuration your own body preferred, and why that differed from the data

nodes.title: Lab 6 — Starving the Long Job
nodes.description: Build a scheduler that starves someone, watch it happen, then fix it and measure exactly what the fix cost you.
spec: you have produced a run in which a long job is starved for the full window
you have implemented one ageing rule and measured its effect on both mean and tail
you can state the exchange rate between mean wait and worst-case wait for your system

nodes.title: Lab 7 — Triage Under Pressure
nodes.description: Sort forty cases into five categories in ninety seconds each, then find out how you did and where your errors clustered.
spec: you have triaged forty case cards under time pressure, individually
you have compared your categories against the reference and against your group
you can describe one pattern in your own errors that was not random

nodes.title: Lab 8 — Open the Fast Lane
nodes.description: Add a paid lane to a working simulation and measure precisely who pays for it.
spec: you have run the same system with and without a priority lane
you have measured the effect separately for both groups, not for the population as a whole
you have found the uptake level at which the paid lane stops being worth buying

nodes.title: Lab 9 — Where Did the Wait Go?
nodes.description: Audit a real appointment system's published waiting time and find the boundary it drew to get that number.
spec: you have found a published waiting-time statistic from a real organisation
you can state the exact boundary its clock starts and stops at
you have estimated the wait a user experiences under a boundary you chose instead

nodes.title: Lab 10 — Board the Aircraft
nodes.description: Four boarding strategies, one cabin, twenty-four people and a stopwatch. Then the same four in software, and an argument about why the numbers disagree.
spec: you have physically boarded a mock cabin under at least three strategies
you have compared your physical timings against a simulation of the same strategies
you can name one effect present in the room and absent from the model

nodes.title: Lab 11 — Break the Rule
nodes.description: Attack a queueing system from the inside. Find the exploit, cost it, then design the version that survives you.
spec: you have found a concrete exploit against a real ordering rule
you have estimated what the exploit is worth to the person using it
you have proposed a counter and stated what it costs everyone else

nodes.title: Lab 12 — What Is It For?
nodes.description: Defend your design brief against the room, and answer the one question the whole semester has been building to.
spec: you can present your design in four minutes without notes
you can state in one sentence what your queue optimises for
you have heard the strongest version of the alternative you rejected, from someone else

nodes.title: Weekly Quizzes
nodes.description: A short quiz at the start of every lecture, on that lecture and nothing else. The best 7 of 12 scores count, worth 20% of the course between them.
spec: one quiz at the start of every teaching week, on that week's content only
delivered by QR code, closed before the next lecture begins
a two-minute window with in-person discussion allowed, a thirty-second window online
the best 7 of 12 scores counted; the rest carry no penalty

marking.description: Marked automatically the moment each quiz closes — correct or not, no partial credit, no re-mark. The best seven of the twelve weekly scores count toward the grade; the other five carry no penalty beyond that quiz's own mark.

nodes.title: Queue Census
nodes.description: Go and stand in a real queue with a stopwatch. Measure it properly, model it with Little's Law, and report the gap between the two.
spec: one real queue, observed in person, for at least forty continuous minutes
raw counts submitted as data, not only as conclusions
an estimate of L, λ and W, and a stated reason for trusting or distrusting each
a discrepancy identified, and an explanation offered for it

nodes.title: The Ordering Rule
nodes.description: Find a system, name the rule it uses to decide who goes first, change it, and say plainly who is worse off afterwards.
spec: a real system, with its current ordering rule stated precisely enough to implement
one specific change to that rule, not a wish for more capacity
a named group who is worse off after your change, and by roughly how much
the objection you find hardest to answer, answered

nodes.title: Simulation Report
nodes.description: Run two ordering rules against the same arrival stream, and report what the numbers did — including the part you did not expect.
spec: two disciplines compared on the same arrival stream, with the seed stated
at least one distributional result, not only a comparison of means
a sensitivity check — one parameter moved, and the effect reported
a statement of what the model leaves out and why that matters

nodes.title: Final Design Brief
nodes.description: Redesign one real queue end to end, and defend it against the best version of the alternative you rejected.
spec: one real queue, chosen by you, that you can gather evidence about
a diagnosis grounded in measurement or documented evidence, not intuition
a design specified to the level of an ordering rule and its exceptions
a named alternative, argued at its strongest, and then rejected with reasons
an explicit statement of what your design optimises, and what it gives up

marking.description: The design brief is read as a single argument. The question is whether a person responsible for this system could act on it — whether the problem is diagnosed with evidence, the design is specific enough to build, the losers are named without flinching, and the rejected alternative has been given its strongest form rather than its most convenient one.

nodes.title: The Queue You Didn't Notice
nodes.description: Every queue you have ever stood in was designed. This week is about learning to see the decision instead of the line.

meta.idea: A queue is a designed object, and somebody chose the rule it runs on.

nodes.title: Variability, Not Busyness
nodes.description: Queues do not form because a system is busy. They form because it is unpredictable — and the closer to capacity it runs, the worse that gets.

meta.idea: Variability creates queues, and congestion grows non-linearly as load approaches capacity.

nodes.title: Little's Law
nodes.description: One equation, provable in a page, that lets you measure a queue you have no access to — and catches most people's intuition out.

meta.idea: L equals lambda times W, so any two of length, throughput and wait give you the third.

nodes.title: The Cost of Waiting
nodes.description: Waiting is a real cost that almost never appears in anyone's accounts — which is precisely why systems produce so much of it.

meta.idea: Waiting is an unpriced cost borne by the queue and invisible to the organisation causing it.

nodes.title: First Come, First Served
nodes.description: The rule you have believed in since you were four years old, examined for the first time — including what it costs and what it quietly gets wrong.

meta.idea: FCFS is a choice with a specific fairness claim and a measurable efficiency price.

nodes.title: Shortest Job First
nodes.description: Reorder the same people and the average wait falls, with no extra staff and no extra hours. The free lunch is real. Somebody still pays for it.

meta.idea: Ordering by job length provably minimises mean wait, and starves the long jobs to do it.

nodes.title: Triage: Order by Need
nodes.description: The one place we already accept that arrival order is indefensible — and a live disagreement between the two people teaching it.

meta.idea: Ordering by urgency saves lives and depends entirely on the quality of a ninety-second judgement.

nodes.title: Pay to Skip: Order by Price
nodes.description: Every queue already sorts by willingness to pay — in time. Charging money instead is the most efficient and least popular thing in the course.

meta.idea: Prices sort by willingness to pay while queues sort by willingness to wait, and the two select different people.

nodes.title: Don't Queue At All
nodes.description: Appointments, reservations and virtual queues do not remove the wait. They move it somewhere you cannot see — which is sometimes exactly right.

meta.idea: Appointment and virtual systems relocate waiting rather than eliminating it, and the relocation has its own winners.

nodes.title: Queues in Networks
nodes.description: The set-piece. Everything from weeks 2, 6 and 8 applied to the aircraft we left in week 2 — and the discovery that fixing one queue can break the system.

meta.idea: Queues connected to other queues behave unlike any of them alone, and local optimisation can make the whole worse.

nodes.title: Queues That Know You're Waiting
nodes.description: People are not jobs. They balk, they renege, they game the rule, and they react to being told how long they will wait — which changes how long they wait.

meta.idea: Queues made of people are feedback systems, and information about the wait alters the wait.

nodes.title: There Is No Neutral Queue
nodes.description: Mean, tail, fairness or revenue — a queue can only optimise one. The closing lecture, on the system where society had to choose out loud.

meta.idea: Every queue optimises something, the objectives conflict, and choosing between them is a political act.

nodes.title: A typed consultation state model

course.title: Still Loading: The Design of Progress Bars
course.description: A progress bar is a promise made under uncertainty. Twelve weeks on one file-upload interface: what it may claim about progress, time remaining and completion, and what it has to admit it cannot know.

nodes.title: What does 99% promise?
nodes.description: The opening autopsy. Take a waiting interface you did not build, list every claim it makes, and find the ones that cannot have a source.
spec: every claim visible in the recording appears in your table
each claim carries a verdict, and "not determinable from outside" is used where it is true
the course prototype runs locally and you can trigger a simulated upload

meta.question: Looking only at what is on the screen, what has this interface claimed?

readings.title: Response Times: The 3 Important Limits
readings.why: Where the thresholds that force a waiting interface to exist come from — about one second before a user notices a delay, about ten before they lose the thread. This week's case sits well past both.

readings.title: Progress Indicators Make a Slow System Less Insufferable
readings.why: The standard argument for progress bars. Read it as the position the rest of this course argues with: it is about how waiting feels, and says very little about whether the indicator is telling the truth.

nodes.title: What counts as done?
nodes.description: The upload has two states and one of them is a lie. Find out how many states you actually have, and which of them a user is entitled to hear about.
spec: every state your interface can be in is named in code, and reachable from the simulator controls
the debug readout never shows a state that is not in the enumeration
the completion criterion is written down in one sentence, next to the state that claims it

meta.question: What has to be true before the interface is allowed to say "complete"?

readings.title: Uploading and copying objects using multipart upload
readings.why: A real upload lifecycle written by the people who operate it: initiate, upload parts, complete, and the states in between where a part exists but the object does not. Read the Multipart upload process section.

readings.title: The <progress> element
readings.why: Worth reading before you write your own. The platform already has a determinate/indeterminate distinction in one attribute, and it maps onto the state question more closely than most people expect.

nodes.title: Where is the denominator?
nodes.description: Percent of what? Build the same upload twice — counted in bytes, counted in stages — and measure where the two disagree.
spec: a byte-counted bar and a stage-counted bar run against the same simulated upload
both readings are logged on the same timeline, and the largest disagreement between them is recorded as a number
the page states which denominator the prototype ships with, and names what that denominator excludes

meta.question: When your bar says 40%, forty per cent of what has happened?

readings.title: ProgressEvent.lengthComputable
readings.why: Two paragraphs holding the whole of this week's question: the platform hands you a boolean saying whether a denominator exists, and total is meaningless when it is false.

readings.title: XMLHttpRequest: progress event
readings.why: What a browser actually reports during an upload, at what granularity. Note what is not in it: nothing about what the server does after receiving the bytes.

nodes.title: No idea how long
nodes.description: Three honest ways to say "still going" when there is no denominator at all, and the rule that none of them may imply a fraction.
spec: three indeterminate treatments run against an upload of unknown size — liveness, elapsed, and named stage
no treatment admits a fractional reading anywhere, including the document title
a written rule states which treatment is permitted in which circumstance

meta.question: What should the interface show when there is nothing to divide?

readings.title: The <progress> element
readings.why: Re-read the value attribute paragraph specifically. Omitting value is how the platform spells indeterminate, and it is deliberately not the same as value="0".

readings.title: Skeleton Screens
readings.why: A widely used indeterminate treatment, argued for on perception grounds. Read it against this week's constraint and decide whether a skeleton admits a fractional reading — the article does not ask that, which is why it is worth arguing with.

nodes.title: Why the estimate keeps jumping
nodes.description: Three estimators over one recorded transfer. Measure how much each one contradicts itself, then decide what to round to.
spec: three estimators run over the same supplied transfer trace
each estimator's instability is recorded as a number, by the same measure
the prototype names the estimator it ships, its rounding rule and its refresh interval, on screen

meta.question: You have a denominator. What can you honestly say about time?

readings.title: Exponential smoothing
readings.why: Read the Basic (simple) exponential smoothing section only. The one-line recurrence is the whole of the third estimator, and the article is explicit about what the smoothing factor assumes.

readings.title: curl man page — the progress meter
readings.why: Search for --progress-bar. A thirty-year-old progress meter shipping on millions of machines, documented unusually bluntly about what the display can and cannot promise. Worth seeing a design that chose austerity.

nodes.title: Motion, and how long it felt
nodes.description: Three animations over identical twenty-second waits, ranked by the class, and a careful account of why that ranking is weak evidence.
spec: three motion treatments run over waits of identical duration
the class ranking is recorded exactly as collected, with no adjustment
the write-up names at least three specific reasons the ranking is weak evidence

meta.question: Does how the bar moves change how long the wait feels, and how would you know?

readings.title: Progress Bars (research summary)
readings.why: The researchers' own summary of the perceived-duration experiments, including effect sizes. Read the numbers rather than the headline: notice how large a difference had to be before it was detectable, and compare that with what you could detect today.

readings.title: Response Times: The 3 Important Limits
readings.why: Re-read in week 6. These thresholds are an order of magnitude larger than the perceived-duration effects above — a useful sense of proportion before deciding how much easing is worth.

nodes.title: Understood without the animation
nodes.description: The audit workshop. Turn off the motion, put the mouse away, and find out whether your interface was ever carrying its information in text.
spec: the whole upload path, from choosing a file to reading the outcome, is reachable and operable from the keyboard
every state change a sighted user can see has a text form a screen reader reaches, and percentage ticks are not announced individually
a prefers-reduced-motion variant exists and loses no information the default variant carried
the audit sheet records failures as failures

meta.question: Does your interface still work with the motion off, the mouse gone, and the screen unseen?

readings.title: ARIA: progressbar role
readings.why: The required and optional attributes, and what a missing aria-valuenow means. Audit line 2.

readings.title: aria-valuetext
readings.why: For when the number needs words around it — which, on a staged upload, is most of the time.

readings.title: Understanding SC 4.1.3: Status Messages
readings.why: The success criterion behind audit line 3. Read the Intent section; the examples are a good model for what counts as a status change worth announcing.

readings.title: prefers-reduced-motion
readings.why: The mechanics for audit line 4. Note that no-preference is a separate value from the query not matching.

nodes.title: Stuck, timed out, disconnected
nodes.description: Three ways a transfer stops without finishing, and the sentences that have to be true when it does.
spec: stall, timeout and disconnection are separately reproducible from the simulator controls
each state's message names what happened, what it means for the file, and what happens next
no failure state leaves a progress indicator still implying progress
failure states reach the live region, not only the screen

meta.question: Nothing has moved for thirty seconds. What do you say?

readings.title: Understanding SC 2.2.1: Timing Adjustable
readings.why: A timeout is a time limit imposed on a user, and this is the criterion that governs it. The exceptions matter as much as the rule.

readings.title: Alert pattern
readings.why: When a failure warrants an assertive announcement rather than week 7's polite live region. The guidance on not stealing focus is the part that applies here.

readings.title: AbortSignal.timeout()
readings.why: The platform's own timeout mechanism, and useful before week 9 — it is the same object that will implement your Cancel.

nodes.title: Cancel and retry
nodes.description: Two buttons that make promises. Write the promise down first, then find out whether your code keeps it.
spec: cancel and retry each carry a written guarantee, stated in one sentence above the handler
one test per guarantee, asserting the guarantee rather than the current behaviour
the interface tells the user which guarantee applies before they commit to the action

meta.question: When the user presses Cancel, what exactly have you promised them?

readings.title: AbortController
readings.why: The platform's cancellation primitive. Read what abort() guarantees and, more importantly, what it does not: it stops the client listening, which is not the server stopping work.

readings.title: Multipart upload — aborting
readings.why: The Aborting a multipart upload part specifically. A real service documenting that parts persist and cost money until explicitly aborted — precisely the failure the Cancel guarantee is written to exclude.

nodes.title: Numbers without sources
nodes.description: Week 1 turned inward. Every number, phrase and movement on your own screen, traced back to the event that produced it, or deleted.
spec: every number, string and motion currently rendered appears as a row in the register
each row names the event that produces it, or records that none does
each row carries a verdict of holds, removed, or kept with reason
a "kept with reason" row gives a reason a reader can disagree with

meta.question: Which of the promises your interface makes can you actually keep?

readings.title: Meter pattern
readings.why: Short and pointed for this week: a meter reports a measurement, a progressbar reports progress toward completion, and using one for the other misstates what the value means. Check your register for a value that is really a meter.

readings.title: Performance.now()
readings.why: Read this if any of your rows traced back to a timer. It documents what a clock reading is, and why it is not evidence that work occurred.

nodes.title: Watching someone wait
nodes.description: Three classmates, fifteen minutes each, one stall they were not warned about. Then the harder part — deciding which of what you saw is worth acting on.
spec: three observation records exist, holding what people did and said rather than what you concluded they meant
three handling decisions are proposed, each naming the observation behind it
at most three changes are made to the prototype, and a decision to change nothing is recorded with its reason
the write-up states what this observation cannot establish, in terms specific to this session

meta.question: What did watching three people tell you that you could not have worked out at your own desk?

readings.title: Why You Only Need to Test with 5 Users
readings.why: The standard argument for small-n usability testing. Read it critically and note the scope of the claim: it is about the share of findable usability problems surfaced, not about how often anything happens in a population — exactly this week's existence-proof-versus-rate line.

readings.title: Progress Bars (research summary)
readings.why: Re-read after week 6. Compare the participant numbers and controls in that work against what you ran today, and you have the size of the gap between an experiment and an afternoon.

nodes.title: The last percent
nodes.description: Eight minutes each. Drive the interface through success, stall and failure, then defend one claim you knowingly kept.
spec: the demonstration drives the deployed interface through success, a stall and a failure, live
the presenter names one claim kept without a source event and gives the reason
two challenges from the room are answered from evidence, without appeal to how something feels

meta.question: Can you defend every number left on your screen?

nodes.title: Honest Waiting Kit
nodes.description: The finished interface, plus the three documents that make it checkable — a state reference, an evaluation record, and a register of every claim left on screen.
spec: every named failure is reproducible by a marker from the exposed simulator controls
cancel and retry keep the guarantees written above their handlers
every number, string and motion on screen appears in the claims register with a verdict
conclusions in the evaluation record are proportionate to the evidence recorded on the sheets
the interface never displays progress it is not making

nodes.title: Progress Bar Autopsy
nodes.description: Take a waiting interface you did not build, list every claim it makes, and say what evidence each one could possibly have.
spec: every claim visible in your recording appears as a row in the table
each row carries a verdict, and unsourceable claims are named as such
the inferred state model accounts for the behaviour in the recording, including transitions it does not show
the limits section states what black-box observation could not establish

nodes.title: Waiting Interface Prototype
nodes.description: The first half of the semester, shipped — a determinate bar, an honest estimate, an indeterminate case with no fractions, and an accessibility audit that records its failures.
spec: all four conditions are reproducible by a marker using the exposed simulator controls
the unknown-size condition shows no fractional reading anywhere, including the document title
the shipped estimator, its rounding rule and its refresh interval are stated on screen
the audit sheet is complete, and a line recorded as a pass survives a marker trying to break it

nodes.title: What 99% Promises
nodes.description: The one analytic move this course runs for twelve weeks — claim, source event, verdict — and why a local simulator is an instrument rather than a convenience.

nodes.title: Saying Nothing, Precisely
nodes.description: The difference between not knowing how long and having nothing to say, and the three honest registers available when there is no denominator.

nodes.title: Reading an Interface Without Looking at It
nodes.description: Status as text and semantics rather than as picture — ARIA values when there is no value, live regions that do not flood, and what reduced motion reveals about what your animation was carrying.

nodes.title: Three People Is Not a Study
nodes.description: What a handful of observations can establish, what it cannot, and why "the evidence does not support a change" is a finding rather than a failure.

nodes.title: Idris Fenn
nodes.description: Tutor. Runs the eight studios with no lecture, and wrote the simulator every exercise in the course runs against.

meta.affiliation: Slop University School of Invented Disciplines
meta.contact: In the studio every Thursday, 14:00–17:00. That is the fastest way to reach him.

nodes.title: Marisol Quaye
nodes.description: Convenor. Spent eleven years building upload and sync interfaces before deciding the interesting problem was what they were allowed to say.

meta.affiliation: Slop University School of Invented Disciplines
meta.contact: Ask in the Thursday studio. Email for anything that cannot wait until then.

nodes.title: Policies and support
nodes.description: Extensions, academic integrity, the week 11 consent arrangements, and what the course prototype is and is not allowed to do.

course.title: Is It Me or Is It the Game?
course.description: You died to the boss again. Either you are too slow or the boss is too big, and arguing will not settle it. This course finds out by simulation, in one two-minute game, Close Quarters: build the instrument, simulate the players, read the distribution, defend one number. Nobody plays until week ten.

nodes.title: Three predictions
nodes.description: Read the specimen's rules, then turn three opinions about its balance into predictions that a measurement could prove wrong.
spec: three balance claims about Close Quarters, each rewritten with a number and a unit
each one says how many runs it is about and what result would prove it wrong
none of them needed the game to be played

meta.measures: three predictions, each with a number, a unit and a run count

nodes.title: One headless run
nodes.description: Get the specimen running on your own machine with no window open, and time it.
spec: one seeded run of Close Quarters completed with no browser open
its wall time in ms, how it ended, and the second it ended on
the same seed run twice, with identical results shown side by side

meta.measures: wall time of one simulated run, in ms

nodes.title: A player with reaction time
nodes.description: Write two simulated players for the specimen, give one of them a reaction time, and compare their win rates over the same seeds.
spec: two policies for Close Quarters, each a function from the run's state to a direction
one of them re-decides no more often than every 150 ms
wins out of 15 for each, over the same fifteen seeds

meta.measures: wins out of 15 for a perfect player and for a delayed one

nodes.title: How many runs
nodes.description: Watch how far your median still moves as runs are added, and decide how much movement you are willing to live with.
spec: median survival of your delayed player at 1, 5, 15, 51, 101 and 501 runs
the shortest and longest run among the 501
the run count you will quote from now on, and the median at that count on a second set of 51 seeds

meta.measures: the run count you will quote from now on, and the smallest difference you will claim with it

nodes.title: Step one number
nodes.description: Pick one constant in the specimen's rules, step it evenly across six values, and find out whether difficulty followed.
spec: one constant from the rules, stepped evenly across six values in your own fork
wins out of 51 and median survival at each value, from the same seeds
one sentence naming where the cliff is, or stating that there is none

meta.measures: wins out of 51 and median survival at six evenly spaced values of one constant

nodes.title: Take one away
nodes.description: Ban each of the specimen's seven upgrade cards in turn and measure what your simulated player loses.
spec: a baseline of wins out of 51 with ordinary card choices
seven more rows, one per card, with that card never taken
the card you expected to matter most, written down before you ran anything

meta.measures: wins lost out of 51 when each of seven cards is banned

nodes.title: Size a gate
nodes.description: Work out from measured damage output how much health a boss needs in order to stop the player it is meant to stop, then check the arithmetic by simulation.
spec: damage per second of a player holding ten upgrades, measured and not assumed
the boss health that follows from it for a 26 s window, with the multiplication shown
pass rates out of 51 for players holding eight, ten and twelve upgrades against that boss

meta.measures: the health in hp of a boss that stops players holding fewer than ten upgrades

nodes.title: Break the game
nodes.description: Write the laziest, strangest and most cowardly simulated players you can, and find out whether any of them beats playing properly.
spec: three strategies nobody would call playing properly, each as a policy function
median survival and wins out of 51 for each, beside the intended strategy
if one of them wins, the single constant you would change and its new value

meta.measures: median survival and wins out of 51 for three degenerate strategies

nodes.title: Find the ceiling
nodes.description: Test your own instrument for saturation by comparing how much your metric moves between builds with how much it moves between sets of seeds.
spec: your main metric for the best and the worst build you have found, 51 runs each
the same metric for one build on two different sets of 51 seeds
a verdict of measuring or saturated, and what you would switch to if saturated

meta.measures: spread of your metric between best and worst build, against its spread between two seed sets

nodes.title: Play it
nodes.description: Ten minutes with the specimen in your hands, a list of what your simulation never told you, and one item turned into a check.
spec: a dated list of what you noticed in ten minutes of play, written while playing
each item marked as something your instrument could or could not have shown
one "could not" item rebuilt as a policy, a metric or a test that now can

meta.measures: the number of findings from ten minutes of play that no simulation of yours could have produced

nodes.title: Three kinds of player
nodes.description: Build three simulated players of different skill and find out which of them the specimen is actually made for.
spec: three simulated players that differ in at least reaction time, each described in a sentence
for each, how many of 51 runs get past the first boss, the second boss, and win
the player you think the game is built for, with the row that made you think so

meta.measures: the share of 51 runs that gets past each boss, for three players of different skill

nodes.title: Defence rehearsal
nodes.description: A dry run of the final defence in front of three classmates whose job is to find the missing step.
spec: one constant, its old value and its new value
wins out of 51 and median survival before and after, for at least two kinds of player
each of the seven parts of a defence present, in order, in under ten minutes

meta.measures: one constant, its old and new value, and wins out of 51 before and after

nodes.title: Final: Defend a number
nodes.description: One change to one constant in the specimen, defended in seven parts in under ten minutes.
spec: one constant, its old value and its new value
the seven parts from week twelve, each present and in order
wins out of 51 and median survival before and after, for at least two kinds of player
every quoted number traceable to a quiz answer or a reproducible command

meta.produces: one number, and the case for it

criteria.name: All seven parts of a defence present, in order, inside ten minutes
The instrument could have said no, and you show how you know
Results for more than one kind of player
What you felt when you played it, and whether it agrees with the numbers

nodes.title: Assignment 2: Nothing broke
nodes.description: Take one value from your Assignment 1 curve and show that moving the game there did not kill an option or hand the win to a lazy player.
spec: one proposed value for your Assignment 1 constant, with the reason you picked it
wins lost out of 51 for each of the seven cards, at the old value and at the new one
three or more degenerate strategies run at both values, beside the intended one
a statement of what you would have had to see to abandon the change

meta.produces: a proposed value for one constant, with its side effects measured

criteria.name: Restricted-play table for all seven cards, before and after
At least three lazy strategies, before and after
What you concluded, and what result would have changed your mind

nodes.title: Assignment 1: One constant, six values
nodes.description: Step one number in the specimen's rules evenly across six values and show what difficulty did in response.
spec: one constant from the rules, not reaction time and not the boss's time limit
your predicted curve, dated before your first run
wins out of 51 and median survival at six evenly spaced values, from fixed seeds
a paragraph on where the curve bends and what in the rules causes it

meta.produces: a curve of wins out of 51 against one constant, and the location of its cliff

criteria.name: The prediction, written before anything was measured
The measurement: six even values, 51 runs each, the same seeds throughout
Reading the curve, where it bends and why

nodes.title: Tutorial quizzes
nodes.description: Twelve five-minute quizzes, one at the end of every tutorial. Each asks for the number you just measured. Best ten count, 2% each.
spec: one quiz in every tutorial from week 1 to week 12, sat in the room on the day
every quiz asks for a number with a unit and the number of runs behind it
the week 10 quiz is the raw list written while playing, unedited

meta.produces: twelve dated numbers, one a week, that your defence is checked against

marking.description: Each quiz is marked out of 2. One mark for the number, with its unit and its run count. One mark for the sentence that says what you expected before you measured. The two lowest quizzes are dropped. A quiz is not marked on whether the number was good news.

nodes.title: A complaint about balance is a prediction
nodes.description: Nobody has written it down yet. This week you write down three predictions of your own, each with a number, about a game you may not play until week ten.

meta.bearing: There is no answer until someone says how many runs out of how many. Once counted, “you can skip the upgrades and still get through the first boss” was wrong in all 15 runs.

reading.title: Game Metrics Without Players: Strategies for Understanding Game Artifacts

nodes.title: A game that needs a screen cannot be measured
nodes.description: If a game's rules cannot run without its renderer, nothing about it can be measured. This week the specimen runs with no window open, in 6 ms.

meta.bearing: You cannot tell by playing alone. In the two minutes a person spends on one run, the rules on their own get through about twenty thousand.

nodes.title: A perfect player describes nobody
nodes.description: A perfect bot wins 12 runs out of 15 and tells you nothing about a person. This week the simulated player gets a reaction time, and the wins go away.

meta.bearing: It was the player. Leave the game alone, make the player wait about 150 ms before turning and aim a little off, and the same seeds give 1 win.

reading.authors: Aaron Isaksen, Dan Gopstein and Andy Nealen
reading.title: Exploring Game Space Using Survival Analysis

nodes.title: One run tells you nothing
nodes.description: The same player on the same game ends anywhere between 29.8 s and 120 s. This week is about how many runs a claim needs before it is worth saying out loud.

meta.bearing: A single death is one draw from the dice. One run said 69.3 s; the median of fifteen said 81.5 s, and nothing had changed but the seeds.

nodes.title: Even steps, uneven difficulty
nodes.description: Turn one dial in equal steps and the game does not get harder in equal steps. The first 50 ms costs 26 wins. A later 50 ms costs 0.4 s.

meta.bearing: It is you, unevenly. Give each boss anywhere from 18 s to 34 s on its clock and the 100 ms player still wins 12 of 51; at the usual 26 s, a player 50 ms quicker wins 38.

nodes.title: A dead option looks like a live one
nodes.description: A choice that does nothing looks exactly like a choice that matters. This week you measure what each of the specimen's seven upgrades is worth, by taking it away.

meta.bearing: Ban pickup reach, the card that looks least like a weapon, and wins fall from 12 of 51 to 1. What a card is worth comes from the game's rules.

reading.authors: Alexander Jaffe, Alex Miller, Erik Andersen, Yun-En Liu, Anna Karlin and Zoran Popović
reading.title: Evaluating Competitive Game Balance with Restricted Play

nodes.title: A gate everyone passes asks no question
nodes.description: A gate is a point the player must be strong enough to pass. Its size is not a design opinion. It is a multiplication, and the first version got it wrong.

meta.bearing: The game, and you can tell before anyone fights: the opening weapon alone does 20 damage a second for 26 s, so beating a boss under 520 hp says nothing about you.

nodes.title: The lazy strategy must lose
nodes.description: If one way of playing beats every other, the rest of the design is decoration. For a while the best way to play the specimen was to run away.

meta.bearing: Write the laziest player you can: if it beats the intended way to play, the game is at fault. Running away once did, in an older version of the game: 102 s against 87 s.

nodes.title: A metric that cannot fail is noise
nodes.description: Nine different builds, 34 kills each. A metric that gives every subject the same score is not measuring them, and it will not tell you so.

meta.bearing: The metric may not be able to say. Extra damage took the runs that kill the first boss from 0 to 43 of 51, while median survival stayed within a few seconds of 65 s.

reading.authors: Stefan Freyr Gudmundsson, Philipp Eisen, Erik Poromaa, Alex Nodet, Sami Purmonen, Bartlomiej Kozakowski, Richard Meurling and Lele Cao
reading.title: Human-Like Playtesting with Deep Learning
reading.venue: IEEE Conference on Computational Intelligence and Games, 2018

nodes.title: Playing finds what simulation never asked
nodes.description: This is the week you finally play the game. Ten minutes with your hands finds things that nine weeks of simulated runs did not.

meta.bearing: Some of the answer only a person finds. Standing still with the old shard weapon killed nothing, and no simulated run showed it, because the simulated player was always moving.

nodes.title: Every boss is easy for somebody
nodes.description: Difficulty is not one number. The same first boss lets 50 runs in 51 past, or 10 in 51, depending on who is holding the controls.

meta.bearing: That depends on the player. At a 200 ms reaction time, 46 of 51 runs reach the first boss and 18 outlast its clock; whether to lose that player is the designer's call.

reading.authors: Shaghayegh Roohi, Asko Relas, Jari Takatalo, Henri Heiskanen and Perttu Hämäläinen
reading.title: Predicting Game Difficulty and Churn Without Players

nodes.title: A change is finished when it can be checked
nodes.description: The semester ends with one change to one constant, and everything you have learned to say about why it is the right one.

meta.bearing: Your answer is the constant's new value beside its old one, measured on the same 51 fixed seeds, so anyone can run it again and show you are wrong.

nodes.title: Tamsin Okoro
nodes.description: Nine years as a systems designer on action and survival games, most of them spent in meetings about whether a boss was too hard.

nodes.title: Policies and support
nodes.description: The rules of the course, most of which are rules about numbers, and where to go when something is in the way.

course.title: The Sandwich Must Hold
course.description: A sandwich is a temporary structure whose failure is eaten. This course treats lunch as a material system: how layers carry load, exchange moisture, and come apart under compression, handling and transport. No culinary experience is expected and taste is not assessed.

nodes.title: What Counts as a Sandwich?
nodes.description: The opening classification problem — whether a sandwich is defined by its shape, its materials, its function, or the way it is used
spec: you can state the criterion your classification depends on
you can name one specimen your criterion admits that you would rather it excluded
you have recorded one disputed specimen with a photograph, sketch or supplied case

nodes.title: Bread Is a Beam
nodes.description: The outer layer treated as structure — how it carries load across a span, where it fails first, and what it does after the load is removed
spec: you can identify the span, the supports and the loaded region of a specimen
you have recorded a deflection measurement and the condition it was taken under
you can distinguish elastic recovery from permanent deformation in your own record

nodes.title: Grip, Friction and Slip
nodes.description: Resistance at an interface treated as a measurable quantity — what holds two layers together, and the angle at which it stops
spec: you can state the angle of first movement for each interface you tested
you have recorded the normal load applied and whether it moved that angle
you can name which surface of a pairing you hold responsible, and on what evidence

nodes.title: Moisture Is a Load
nodes.description: Liquid entering a porous layer as a structural event — where the front is, how fast it slows, and what it takes away
spec: you have three timed positions of the moisture front recorded on one overlay
you can state where the specimen lost geometry relative to the front
you can separate the weight of the liquid from the stiffness change it caused

nodes.title: Load-Bearing Fillings
nodes.description: Every layer sorted into two categories — the ones carrying force to a support, and the ones being carried by the rest
spec: you can trace one continuous load path from the loaded region to a support
you have classified every layer of a specimen as support or payload
you can defend one classification a second person would dispute

nodes.title: Sauce at the Interface
nodes.description: The layer between two others read as a bond or a bearing, and the thickness at which it stops being the first
spec: you can name the failure mode as adhesive at a stated face or cohesive within the film
you have three sequential frames covering one event, with the interval between them
you can state one alternative reading of the same frames and why you rejected it

nodes.title: Thermal Conflict
nodes.description: Temperature treated as a time-dependent load — the gradient across an assembly, where it deposits liquid, and what remains once it has gone
spec: you can name the two zones your thermal gradient runs between
you have three timed observations of one condition, each with its measurement location
you can separate a change caused by temperature from one caused by elapsed time

nodes.title: The Order of Layers
nodes.description: Assembly order treated as a structural variable — which interfaces exist, which face is exposed, and which layer ends up carrying the load
spec: you can list every interface in your assembly and the two layers forming it
you have built one material set in two orders with an adjacency note per interface
you can name one behaviour that changed with order alone, and where it changed

nodes.title: Cutting Geometry
nodes.description: The cut treated as a second design — continuity removed, new free edges opened, and span, support and load concentration all moved
spec: you can mark span and support positions before and after a cut on one drawing
you have measured the exposed cut face for two cut angles across the same width
you can name the interface a cut opened and where load now concentrates

nodes.title: Packaging Is Part of the Structure
nodes.description: Packaging treated as a loaded member — where it braces, where it compresses, and what transport adds that the bench cannot
spec: you can state which function your packaging performs first — brace, compress or enclose
you have recorded a route trace with tilt angle, applied load and handling count
you can say whether the packaging moved the point of first failure or only concealed it

nodes.title: Failure Autopsy
nodes.description: Reconstructing a failure sequence from incomplete evidence, and keeping resemblance separate from established cause
spec: you have inventoried the evidence with observed, inferred and unknown kept separate
you can present a causal chain that branches wherever the evidence does not decide
you can name one competing explanation you could not eliminate, and what would eliminate it

nodes.title: The Final Stress Test
nodes.description: One declared load case, one documented failure, one justified revision, and the defence that holds them together
spec: you have declared the load case in writing before testing against it
you can identify the point of first failure and the revision it prompted
you can defend the final result against the declared case, including where it still fails

nodes.title: Component Test
nodes.description: One declared structural variable, tested under at least three conditions, with a protocol another person could repeat without asking you anything
spec: one variable is declared, and it is the only thing that changes between conditions
at least three conditions are tested, with a control where the question supports one
the protocol is written so a second person could repeat the test unaided
the limitations name at least one thing the test could not hold constant

nodes.title: Failure Autopsy
nodes.description: One case from the supplied failure-case pack, reconstructed into the most defensible sequence the incomplete evidence will actually carry
spec: the evidence inventory states what the pack contains and what it does not
every causal claim is traceable to a numbered item in that inventory
at least one competing explanation is tested against the same evidence
unresolved uncertainty is recorded rather than closed by assertion

nodes.title: Sandwich Field Log
nodes.description: Four specimens recorded as structures, with what was observed held apart from what was inferred and what remains unknown
spec: four specimens are recorded, each with an annotated photograph or diagram
every entry names a structural classification and the criterion it rests on
every entry separates Observed, Inferred and Unknown as three statements
no specimen's analysis exceeds 250 words

nodes.title: The Sandwich Must Hold
nodes.description: One declared load case, one system designed against it, and the record of the test, the failure, the revision and the defence
spec: one load case is declared before the first test, and the design answers that case
the protocol, its evidence and at least one documented failure are all present
one revision is justified by the failure it responds to, with evidence either side
the final defence states the conditions the design is not claimed to survive

nodes.title: Moisture Is a Load
nodes.description: The Week 4 lecture — how liquid progressively compromises a boundary, and how to design a comparison that can say so

nodes.title: The Order of Layers
nodes.description: The Week 8 lecture — assembly order as a structural variable, and how to build one material set twice so that the ordering is the only thing under test

nodes.title: A Sandwich Is a Structure

nodes.title: Beams, Spans and Recovery
nodes.description: Week 2 — the outer layer as a structural member, and the difference between bending that comes back and bending that does not
