course.title: Back of the Envelope
course.description: The course turns on one question: how wrong can you be, and still be useful? Students learn to build and defend estimates from incomplete evidence, make their assumptions and uncertainty visible, and judge how much precision a decision actually needs. No statistics prerequisite.

nodes.title: The Right Number of Digits
nodes.description: The first session — a published population figure resolved to the last person, and the four different questions its digits invite you to confuse
spec: you can say how precise an answer a decision needs before you calculate anything
you can name at least one assumption sitting underneath a published figure
you have committed a range to paper before looking, and can say why published coverage evidence is not that range's error bar

nodes.title: Taking It Apart
nodes.description: The one week you build a number out of nothing — and then discover that your number and the official one were counting different things
spec: every link in your chain is written down as a number with a reason beside it
someone else has audited your units, and whatever they found is marked or repaired on the page
you can say what your number was a number of, precisely enough to disagree with

nodes.title: Naming Your Assumptions
nodes.description: A case file rather than an exercise — one 1957 estimate, one 1973 outcome, and the question of which assumption was holding the first one up
spec: your ledger separates what the sources say from what you are inferring
you can rank assumptions by consequence, not by likelihood, and say why the two differ
you can name one assumption that was load-bearing, and say whether it was checkable at the time or still unresolved

nodes.title: A Number With a Shape
nodes.description: A national agency publishes its uncertainty on purpose, in a grammar you can borrow — two numbers, a percentage, and a statement of what each one means
spec: you can read a published range and say what each of its numbers claims
three of your own point estimates now carry a range and a stated confidence
you committed a range before looking up the answer, and wrote down what would have made it miss

nodes.title: Borrowed Numbers
nodes.description: Almost every number you will use was collected to answer somebody else’s question — today you write down what stands between their question and yours
spec: you can state, in one sentence each, what a dataset measures and what you wanted it to measure
your bridge from proxy to target is written as separate claims, not as one leap
you have named a condition under which your bridge stops holding, and how you would notice

nodes.title: Conflicting Evidence
nodes.description: Two Australian agencies count homelessness and get different answers — the work is diagnosing which question each of them answered
spec: you can name which axis a disagreement between two sources actually sits on
your diagnosis separates what the publications state from what you are inferring
you can choose a source for a stated purpose and say what you would refuse to claim with it

nodes.title: The Number Someone Wants
nodes.description: A real business case that came out below one, an evaluation that says exactly where the pressure went, and an hour spent finding out what you would have done
spec: your pressure log records every request, the move you made, and the reason for it
you can distinguish a revision justified by new evidence or exposed reasoning from one justified by who asked
you can point to an asymmetry in a real appraisal and say which way it pushed the answer

nodes.title: Ask the Room
nodes.description: Two rounds of estimates from the same people under two different protocols, and a national polling failure that has the same shape as the second round
spec: you can say what the room’s two aggregates did, and why they differed
you can name what the second round’s estimates had in common
you can point to one estimate of your own whose inputs were shared with everyone else’s

nodes.title: Who Carries the Cost
nodes.description: A debt-recovery scheme acted on an estimate at scale, and the question that outlasts whether the estimate itself was any good — who pays when it is wrong
spec: you can name the direction in which the scheme's error fell, and who was made to disprove it
your who-bears ledger covers both directions of the error, not only the one that happened
your stakes note names who bears the cost of your own Client Estimate in each direction, and whether it is the same party

nodes.title: A Number About Tomorrow
nodes.description: Every target so far already existed. Today's does not — a dated commitment from the Reserve Bank, what happened instead, and a forecast you seal shut
spec: you can state exactly what the Reserve Bank committed to, in its own words, and exactly what happened instead
your class forecast is sealed before the target date, with a low bound, a high bound, a plain-language confidence, and a miss-line
you can name the single Bureau of Meteorology product that will resolve the forecast, and roughly when it will do so

nodes.title: Estimate Court
nodes.description: The written estimate and its disclosure are already submitted. Today a panel reads them, asks one shared question, and follows up on whatever it likes
spec: you can name one disclosed assumption a panellist actually challenged, and whether you accepted, rejected, or widened in response
you can say why a well-justified concession is not, by itself, a lower mark than holding your ground
your account of any change names the new information or reasoning that justified it, not just that a challenge occurred

nodes.title: Your Own Track Record
nodes.description: The whole semester's set of ranges, read together for the particular way you tend to be wrong — a shape no single estimate could ever have shown you
spec: your calibration audit is a plain count of resolved entries against stated confidence, with no formula behind it
your pattern claim cites at least four dated entries, and your counter-case engages whatever in the record complicates it
your peer note comes from a real search for counterevidence, and names a missed pattern, a genuinely non-fitting entry, or the claim's limits and what would threaten it

nodes.title: Calibration Diary
nodes.description: A semester-long record of ranges committed before you knew the answer, audited at the end for pattern rather than for how often you were right
spec: the diary holds at least 15 entries, at least 12 resolved, each recorded before its answer was known
the pattern claim is supported by specific, dated entries rather than by impression
the counter-case engages whatever in the record complicates the claimed pattern, and the forward commitment is checkable

nodes.title: Client Estimate & Estimate Court
nodes.description: One real, already-settled target shared by the whole cohort, and a live cross-examination of the estimate you built to answer it
spec: the estimate is decomposed into a chain, with an assumption ledger ranked by consequence
the range and confidence are stated in plain language, and the proxy-to-target bridge names its breaking condition

the pre-hearing disclosure states every material assumption the opinion rests on, and the post-Court revision distinguishes what changed in the evidence or the reasoning from what changed only in the room

nodes.title: The digits are a claim you did not make
nodes.description: Why written precision overstates what is known, and why the first question in any estimate is what the decision needs

nodes.title: A number is a chain, not a guess
nodes.description: Why breaking a quantity into parts beats guessing it whole, and why defining the target is part of the estimate rather than a preliminary to it

nodes.title: The assumption you didn’t notice you made
nodes.description: Why an estimate’s fragility concentrates in a few inputs, why people audit the wrong ones, and why hindsight makes this look easier than it was

nodes.title: A range says more than a number
nodes.description: What a point estimate hides, why a national agency publishes its uncertainty on purpose, and how to choose a width honestly

nodes.title: Measured well, about something else
nodes.description: Why most evidence is borrowed, the three ways a proxy fails, and why a proxy relationship can decay without anybody noticing

nodes.title: Disagreement is information
nodes.description: Why splitting the difference destroys evidence, the small set of axes real disagreements sit on, and why nobody warns you at the moment you need it

nodes.title: Revision, and its imitation
nodes.description: How pressure actually arrives, the test that separates an honest change from a concession, and why the defences have to be built early

nodes.title: What your estimates have in common
nodes.description: The single mechanism that makes combining estimates work, what happens when it is absent, and why agreement is not evidence

nodes.title: Accurate on average is not the same question
nodes.description: Why expected accuracy stops being the point once an estimate gets acted on, and the two questions the rest of the course has kept merged

nodes.title: The one thing forecasting adds
nodes.description: Why a claim about the future needs no new machinery beyond what you already have, and the one structural difference that changes everything

nodes.title: What prose cannot force you to say
nodes.description: Why a written justification can hide exactly the weakness a live question exposes in seconds, and what the Court is actually testing for

nodes.title: One miss tells you nothing. Fifteen might.
nodes.description: Why no single estimate can reveal whether you are a good estimator, and what an accumulated, precommitted record can show instead

nodes.title: Policies and support
nodes.description: The course-wide rules for late work, extensions, academic integrity and getting help.

course.title: Weaponised Etiquette
course.description: Weaponised Etiquette studies the unwritten rules of public space by breaking them on purpose. Each week isolates one social contract — queues, elevators, coughs, seats — and catalogues how it is already being violated. Case studies, not confessions.

nodes.title: Live Practicum
nodes.description: The supervised session where you perform one deliberate, exaggerated violation in front of your cohort and debrief it in real time.

nodes.title: Midpoint Crit
nodes.description: Bring your first four case studies and have the method stress-tested by the room before you commit to the back half of the course.

nodes.title: Orientation
nodes.description: Where the course's method gets rehearsed for the first time, on a deliberately low-stakes example, before anyone picks a real topic.

nodes.title: Assignment 1
nodes.description: A report investigating a rude or improper public behaviour you personally observed or experienced, analysed with the course's own method.

criteria.name: Analytical use of the observe/isolate/describe method
Engagement with relevant literature and citations
Referencing standard and academic-integrity compliance (including AI-use disclosure)

nodes.title: Assignment 2
nodes.description: A report designing and explaining several signs or notices intended to nudge people who see them toward more ethical public behaviour.

criteria.name: Clarity and specificity of each sign's target behaviour
Range and originality across the set of signs

nodes.title: Final Exam
nodes.description: Forty practice questions covering the course's method and case studies, plus a short description of what the real exam will actually look like.

marking.description: Marked on accurate, precise application of the observe/isolate/describe method to both studied and novel scenarios across the whole course, not on rote recall of any single week.

nodes.title: Tutorial Participation
nodes.description: Attendance and engagement across the semester's tutorials, marked holistically rather than tutorial by tutorial.

marking.description: Marked on attendance and engagement across the semester's tutorials as a whole, not on any single week — turning up and taking part consistently earns full marks; consistent absence or disengagement is what costs marks here, not the quality of any one week's contribution.

nodes.title: Weekly Quizzes
nodes.description: A short multiple-choice quiz for each week, marked holistically across the semester rather than quiz by quiz.

marking.description: Marked on completion and accuracy across the semester's quizzes taken as a whole, not on any single week's result — a strong overall completion and accuracy rate earns full marks, so one weaker week doesn't disproportionately affect the mark.

nodes.title: Week 1: A Short History of Public Misconduct
nodes.description: What this course studies, why it studies it as a discipline rather than a complaint, and the method every later week reuses.

nodes.title: Week 2: The Classroom as a Contested Acoustic Jurisdiction
nodes.description: One room, two entirely different kinds of violation — a cough at the fully deniable end, an answered phone call at the fully overt end.

nodes.title: Week 3: Socio-Political Dynamics of Confinement in Vertical Transit
nodes.description: A box with one door, one button panel, and no way to leave — read as the purest small-scale power structure in the built environment.

nodes.title: Week 4: An Acoustic-Ethnographic Inquiry into the Reading Room
nodes.description: How sound actually travels through a reading room, and why "shush" is such an unreliable countermeasure.

nodes.title: Week 5: Socio-Political Dynamics of Seat-Saving in Contemporary Cafés
nodes.description: A jacket on a chair is a territorial claim with no legal standing and near-total local enforcement. This week asks why that works, and when it stops. Assignment 1 due this week.

nodes.title: Week 6: Spatial Sovereignty and the Unpriced Transit Commons
nodes.description: Armrests, poles, and the seat next to yours — a jurisdictional survey of how much space one passenger can annex before another one objects.

nodes.title: Week 7: A Phenomenological Inquiry into Queueing and Threshold Litter in Unmarked Commons
nodes.description: Two space-agnostic public-commons cases, elevated to civilisational infrastructure — a queue held together by nothing but mutual glaring, and litter that piles up in the last few metres before a bin. An early heads-up — Assignment 2 is due in Week 9.

nodes.title: Week 8: A Fluid-Dynamics Inquiry into Discontinuity Propagation in Ambulatory Flow
nodes.description: Stopping dead in a moving crowd to check your phone, and the pile-up that follows — read as a fluid-dynamics problem with a person at the front.

nodes.title: Week 9: Towards a Unified Theory of Deniable Discourtesy
nodes.description: A meta-analytic synthesis week — no new case, just the bad-manner/good-manner method turned back on three earlier cases to see whether it actually generalises, or merely repeats itself with new nouns. Assignment 2 due this week.

nodes.title: Week 10: A Phenomenological Inquiry into Acoustic Self-Deception in the Public Restroom
nodes.description: The one public space designed around pretending nobody can hear anything — and what happens when that pretence is dropped.

nodes.title: Week 11: Practicum — Performing the Exaggeration
nodes.description: Nine weeks of cataloguing other people's violations; this week you commit one, on purpose, under supervision, and describe it honestly afterward.

nodes.title: Week 12: Capstone — Writing Up an Anti-Manners Report
nodes.description: Turning eleven weeks of case studies and one live performance into a single analytical argument, and reviewing that argument in practice questions ahead of the Final Exam.

nodes.title: Week 1 Tutorial: Observing the Method for the First Time
nodes.description: The observe/isolate/describe method, rehearsed once on a norm nobody in the room has any stake in, before anyone picks a real topic.

nodes.title: Week 2 Tutorial: Deniable to Overt
nodes.description: Applying the timing/target/aftermath framework to a cough, then contrasting it against a classroom violation nobody could call an accident.

nodes.title: Week 3 Tutorial: Watching the Panel and the Door
nodes.description: A short field observation of an elevator boarding sequence, framed by the lecture's fixed-capacity, high-density reading of the space.

nodes.title: Week 4 Tutorial: Measuring the Room's Noise Floor
nodes.description: Logging a quiet room's actual noise floor for ten minutes, to test the lecture's claim that a shush is often louder than what it answers.

nodes.title: Week 5 Tutorial: Pricing a Saved Seat
nodes.description: Observing how the same seat-saving claim reads differently depending on how full the room is, ahead of Assignment 1.

nodes.title: Week 6 Tutorial: Claimed Space on a Moving Vehicle
nodes.description: Comparing transport's constantly-recalculated claimed space against Week 5's seat-saving, ahead of the Midpoint Crit.

nodes.title: Week 7 Tutorial: Two Commons, No Fixed Venue
nodes.description: Locating where a queue's implicit agreement is strongest and weakest, and walking a route to observe threshold litter, ahead of Assignment 2.

nodes.title: Week 8 Tutorial: Measuring a Pile-Up
nodes.description: Timing how far a sudden stop propagates through a moving crowd, treating pedestrian flow as a fluid-dynamics problem.

nodes.title: Week 9 Tutorial: Re-Testing the Isolate–Contest–Verdict Protocol
nodes.description: Applying the Isolate–Contest–Verdict (ICV) Protocol to a case you already know the answer to, ahead of Assignment 2.

nodes.title: Week 10 Tutorial: Naming a Breach
nodes.description: Examining the public restroom's silence pretence, and what it actually costs to name a breach of it out loud.

nodes.title: Week 11 Tutorial: Rehearsing the Performance
nodes.description: Preparing and debriefing the one deliberate violation the course asks you to actually commit, under supervision, in the Live Practicum.

nodes.title: Week 12 Tutorial: Drafting the Capstone Claim
nodes.description: Turning a semester of case studies into one testable claim, rehearsed against the Week 1 method ahead of the Final Exam.

nodes.title: Week 1 Quiz
nodes.description: Checking whether the course's core method actually landed.

questions.question: What are the three steps of the course's method, in order?
options: Observe, isolate, describe
Complain, escalate, report
Notice, judge, publish
Isolate, observe, punish

questions.question: According to Week 1, what is the Live Practicum for?
options: To perform a technique yourself, under supervision, rather than only observing others
To collect anonymous complaints from the public
To grade classmates on their manners
To replace the Final Exam

questions.question: The lecture compares the course's method to an engineer studying a bridge. What is the point of the comparison?
options: You understand a norm's limit by finding out how much it takes to break it, not by reading a rule
Etiquette rules are exactly as precise as engineering specifications
Bridges and elevators are both covered in Week 3
Engineers make the best case-study subjects

nodes.title: Week 2 Quiz
nodes.description: Checking whether this week's deniable-to-overt classroom spectrum landed.

questions.question: What is the key difference between where the cough sits on the deniable-to-overt spectrum and where the phone call sits?
options: The cough stays technically indistinguishable from an accident; the phone call involves a visible, undeniable choice
There is no difference — both are equally deniable
The phone call is illegal and the cough is not
The cough only happens in classrooms and the phone call happens everywhere

questions.question: Which three signals does the lecture say a room actually reads when judging a cough?
options: Timing, target, aftermath
Volume, location, weather
Age, gender, seating position
Duration, pitch, echo

questions.question: Since intent is never in doubt for the phone-call case, what does the lecture say the room actually argues about instead?
options: Proportionality — how much disruption a given choice was worth, and to whom
Whether the call was actually the student's own phone
Whether phones should be banned from lecture theatres entirely
Nothing — the room has no reaction to overt violations

questions.question: In this week's Bad manner / Good manner pairs, what does the good-manner version actually cost the person doing it?
options: Very little — a quiet sentence or a few steps into the corridor, smaller than the disruption just avoided
A formal apology to everyone nearby
A fine or other legal penalty
Nothing changes between the two versions

nodes.title: Week 3 Quiz
nodes.description: Checking whether this week's elevator power-dynamics reading landed.

questions.question: What four properties does the lecture say make the elevator such a rigid etiquette system?
options: Fixed capacity, fixed exits, short duration, high density
Loud, dark, slow, crowded
Public, free, automated, silent
Old, mechanical, shared, timed

questions.question: In this week's Bad manner / Good manner pair, what is the actual cost comparison being made?
options: A few shared seconds for everyone already inside, versus the full wait for the next car carried alone by the latecomer
The cost of pressing a button versus not pressing it
Nothing — both options cost the same
The building's electricity bill for running the elevator

questions.question: According to the lecture, when is an elevator's etiquette actually settled?
options: Silently, in the first two seconds, by people who never discuss it
By a posted sign inside the car
Only after someone complains to building management
By whoever pressed the call button first

questions.question: Why does holding the close-door button on someone jogging toward the lift count as deniable, in the course's sense?
options: It's always possible to claim you simply didn't see them — the act can be waved off as an accident even when it wasn't one
Elevator doors are legally required to close on a fixed timer
No security camera can see inside the car
Deniability doesn't apply inside an elevator

questions.question: A passenger reaches past you to press a floor without asking. Is this the isolated act, or the aftermath, in the method's terms?
options: The isolated act — the aftermath is however the car reacts to it next
The aftermath — pressing a button is never an isolated act
Neither — the method doesn't apply to button presses
Both at once, by definition

nodes.title: Week 4 Quiz
nodes.description: Checking whether this week's noise-propagation reading landed.

questions.question: Why does the lecture call a library's noise floor "a design goal, not an accident"?
options: The space is built specifically to keep ambient noise low
Libraries are always completely empty
Sound cannot travel indoors
Every library has a legally enforced noise rule

questions.question: What does the lecture say makes the shush unusual as a countermeasure?
options: It is often louder, socially, than the noise it responds to
It is silent and therefore has no effect
It requires a librarian's authority to use
It only works when amplified over a microphone

questions.question: What actually enforces "the library is quiet" as a norm, according to the lecture?
options: Mostly glares — there is no real enforcing authority most of the time
A posted decibel limit checked by staff
A local noise ordinance
Nothing; the norm isn't actually enforced at all

questions.question: A five-minute phone call goes unchallenged; a ten-second shush in response draws visible reactions across the whole floor. What does this asymmetry tell you about how the room enforces its own norms?
options: Enforcement itself carries a bigger, more visible social cost than the violation it's answering — part of why norms like this are so rarely enforced directly
It shows the phone call was actually the quieter of the two sounds
It shows shushing is legally protected speech and phone calls are not
It shows the room has no functioning norm at all

nodes.title: Week 5 Quiz
nodes.description: Checking whether this week's seat-saving-as-property reading landed.

questions.question: According to the lecture, what actually enforces a seat-saving claim like a jacket on a chair?
options: Nothing but the expectation that other people will honour it
A café's posted policy
A physical lock or barrier
A numbered ticket tied to the seat

questions.question: What variable does the lecture say changes whether a seat-saving claim is read as legitimate?
options: Scarcity — how full the room is
The brand of jacket used
The time of day, and nothing else
Whether the café offers table service

questions.question: In this week's Bad manner / Good manner pair, what is the key difference in the good-manner version?
options: The customer orders first, then takes a table only once they have something to sit down with
The customer never sits down at all
The customer asks staff to guard the table
The customer brings a second jacket to double the claim

questions.question: Why does this week say "he saved a seat" is an incomplete description on its own, whatever the verdict turns out to be?
options: Because it jumps straight to a verdict without isolating the one variable that actually decides the case — how scarce seats were at that moment
Because it doesn't specify which chair was used
Because it fails to name the jacket's brand
Because it doesn't confirm whether the seat-saver eventually sat down

nodes.title: Week 6 Quiz
nodes.description: Checking whether this week's claimed-space-on-transport reading landed.

questions.question: What does the lecture mean by calling public transport an "unpriced commons"?
options: There's more space in a carriage than any timetable accounts for, and posture alone decides who gets it
Tickets are free on all public transport
Every seat is numbered and reserved in advance
"The commons" names one specific bus route

questions.question: How does the lecture say transport's claimed space differs from the Week 3 elevator's?
options: Transport keeps recalculating stop by stop; the elevator fixes everyone's position for the whole ride
They work identically in every respect
Elevators always have more available space than buses
Transport has assigned seating and elevators don't

questions.question: In this week's Bad manner / Good manner pair, what does the good-manner passenger do differently?
options: Pulls their legs in and moves their bag before anyone has to ask
Gets off at the very next stop
Asks every boarding passenger for permission to stay seated
Stands for the entire trip regardless of seat availability

questions.question: Name two things listed this week that cost another passenger something without breaking any actual rule.
options: Any two of: the bag on the empty seat, a wide pole grip, or headphone volume pitched to be heard rather than merely audible
Any two of: a delayed bus, a broken ticket machine, or a closed station exit
Any two of: eating on board, standing near the doors, or checking a phone
Any two of: loud music through open speakers, smoking on board, or blocking the doors

nodes.title: Week 7 Quiz
nodes.description: Checking whether this week's queueing-and-threshold-litter reading landed.

questions.question: Structurally, what does the lecture say a queue actually is?
options: Nothing but an agreement among strangers about whose turn it is, enforced by mutual glaring
A legal contract enforced by venue staff
A physical barrier like a rope or turnstile
A numbered-ticket system used at every counter

questions.question: What property do queueing and threshold litter share that justifies studying them in the same week?
options: Neither is tied to a single physical space — both recur wherever strangers share public space
Both are illegal in most jurisdictions
Both only happen at store counters
Both require a witness to be classified as a violation

questions.question: Why does the course call littering an "audience-less nuisance"?
options: The person who benefits from the act is rarely watched doing it
It is the only case study that is illegal
It never carries any social cost
It always happens indoors

questions.question: In this week's Bad manner / Good manner pairs, what does the good-manner version actually cost the person doing it?
options: Very little — asking "who's next?" or a few extra steps, smaller than the effort just avoided
A formal apology to everyone nearby
A fine or other legal penalty
Nothing changes between the two versions

nodes.title: Week 8 Quiz
nodes.description: Checking whether this week's pedestrian-flow reading landed.

questions.question: According to the lecture, what makes a sudden stop the "cleanest" disruption to measure?
options: It's one of the few genuinely instantaneous disruptions the course studies
It happens the exact same way every single time
It is always caught on camera
Nobody nearby is ever actually affected by it

questions.question: What two things does the lecture say determine how far a pile-up propagates?
options: Footpath width and crowd density
The stopper's height and weight
Time of day and the weather
Whether the stop happens near a public bin

questions.question: Whose own research does the lecture say this week's material draws on directly?
options: Mr. Osei's
Dr. Vance's
Ms. Halvorsen's
An anonymous public survey

questions.question: Two people both stop to check a phone notification on a crowded footpath — one mid-flow, one stepped aside first. Why does only one of them cause a pile-up?
options: Stepping aside removes the stop from the main flow entirely, so nobody behind has to react to it
The one mid-flow was walking slower to begin with
Pile-ups are random and unrelated to where someone stops
Only stops longer than one minute cause any disruption at all

nodes.title: Week 9 Quiz
nodes.description: Checking whether this week's method-generalisation reading landed.

questions.question: This week doesn't introduce a new physical space. What does it do instead?
options: Re-applies the course's method to three cases already built earlier in the course
Introduces a fourth new common-manners case
Retires the Bad manner / Good manner framework
Focuses entirely on legal enforcement of etiquette

questions.question: What two questions does this week ask of each revisited case?
options: What makes the act deniable or contestable, and what the Good manner version actually costs
Who is legally liable, and what the penalty should be
How often the act occurs, and where
Whether the act is illegal, and whether it is enforced

questions.question: Across the three revisited cases (elevator, seat-saving, transit space), what does the Good manner version consistently share?
options: It costs less than the harm the Bad manner version imposes on someone else
It always requires a formal apology
It always involves reporting the incident to staff
It eliminates the norm entirely

questions.question: Why does the lecture say re-testing a method on cases you already understand is still meaningful?
options: A method that only works on the case it was built for hasn't actually been tested
Because those cases are the hardest in the whole course
Because the earlier weeks' verdicts were wrong
It isn't meaningful — it's just a review for its own sake

questions.question: What does the Isolate–Contest–Verdict (ICV) Protocol actually add to the method used in Weeks 2 through 8?
options: A name — the three steps themselves are identical
A fourth step, verification, not used in earlier weeks
A legal enforcement mechanism
A numeric score replacing the Bad manner / Good manner verdict

nodes.title: Week 10 Quiz
nodes.description: Checking whether this week's restroom-silence-pretence reading landed.

questions.question: What norm does the lecture say the public restroom runs on?
options: Everyone present agrees, by unspoken consensus, to act as though the room is silent
A posted sign requiring silence at all times
No norm at all — restrooms are entirely unregulated spaces
A norm enforced by attendants on duty

questions.question: According to the lecture, what does the tap-as-mask have in common with the Week 4 shush?

nodes.title: Resources & Policies
nodes.description: Readings, referencing, and where slides live — plus the course-wide rules for late work, extensions, academic integrity, and the scope of what this course actually asks you to do.

course.title: Dashboard Language: How Cars Talk to Drivers
course.description: A design course on how a car talks to the person behind the wheel — through needles, lights, icons, chimes, text and heads-up displays — and what happens to that conversation when it goes wrong.

nodes.title: Orientation — reading your own dashboard
nodes.description: A first pass at classifying one real dashboard element before the course gives you vocabulary for it
spec: you can name one dashboard element and say what channel it uses (needle, light, icon, chime, text, or some combination)
you can state what the element is trying to communicate and to whom it assumes it is speaking
you can say what would go wrong if that element used a different channel instead

nodes.title: Reading the needle
nodes.description: A hands-on comparison of gauge placement and priority across three real dashboards
spec: Bring driver's-eye photographs or manuals of at least three different cars' instrument clusters, from different categories of car.
For each cluster, identify the centred, largest instrument and state, in one sentence, what its placement claims matters most to the driver.
Produce a short written argument (150+ words) comparing at least two of the layouts and defending which driver each layout best serves.

nodes.title: Classify your own idiot light
nodes.description: Bring a real telltale from a car you have access to and argue whether it's genuinely binary or a continuous measurement flattened into one light
spec: you can name a real telltale and the underlying signal it is switched from (a sensor reading, a voltage, a pressure, a code)
you can state where a threshold sits in that underlying signal, and what information disappears on the "fine" side of it
you can argue, with a reason, whether that telltale should stay binary or would be better served by more than one state

nodes.title: Reading icons cold
nodes.description: Students guess the meaning of unlabelled dashboard icons before checking their guesses against the ISO standard
spec: you can name at least one icon you guessed wrong and explain why it misled you
you can distinguish an icon that is legible on its own from one that only works because you already knew the answer
you can point to one place in your own Alert Audit draft where an icon's meaning depends on prior knowledge rather than its shape

nodes.title: Simulating colour-blindness on a real cluster
nodes.description: Running a photographed instrument cluster through a colour-blindness simulator to find out which telltales collapse into each other
spec: you can name at least one telltale pair that becomes ambiguous or indistinguishable under a red-green colour-blindness simulation
you can point to a non-colour feature (shape, fill, position, icon) that would have disambiguated that pair, and say whether the real dashboard actually provides it
you can state, in one sentence, what a driver with that colour-blindness loses compared with a driver without it

nodes.title: Ranking alerts by ear alone
nodes.description: Students listen blind to a set of real dashboard alert sounds and try to rank them by intended urgency using only what they hear
spec: you can justify your urgency ranking using specific sound properties (pitch, tempo, repetition, timbre), not just gut feeling
you can name at least one alert whose sound felt more or less urgent than the situation it signals actually warrants
you can describe, in words, the difference between two alerts a non-designer would call "basically the same beeping"

nodes.title: Writing the sentence an icon implies
nodes.description: Taking a telltale from earlier in the course, writing the plain-language message it implies, then translating that message and measuring what breaks
spec: you can produce a one-sentence plain-language message for a specific icon telltale that a driver with no prior training could act on correctly
you can produce a translation of that sentence into a second language and name one specific word or phrase where the translation adds, loses, or changes precision
you can state, in one sentence, which of the two versions (icon or sentence) a driver under time pressure is better served by, and why

nodes.title: Where does the arrow go?
nodes.description: Students place a lane-departure and a following-distance warning on a printed windscreen photo and argue about how far into central vision an alert is allowed to intrude
spec: you can point to a specific location on the windscreen photo for both the lane-departure and following-distance warning, and justify each placement
you can state, in one sentence, the trade-off between placing a warning low and peripheral versus placing it high and central
you can name one thing your placement would break if the driver's seat height or eye position changed

nodes.title: Report or narrate? Sorting real ADAS alerts
nodes.description: Students sort real driver-assistance alerts into "reports a state" and "narrates a decision," then argue about which kind is harder to design well
spec: you can place at least six real driver-assistance alerts into "reports a state" or "narrates a decision" and justify each placement in one sentence
you can name one alert your group disagreed on, and explain what made it genuinely ambiguous rather than a simple mistake
you can state, in one sentence, which category your group judged harder to design well, and why

nodes.title: Your personal false-alarm threshold
nodes.description: Students estimate the false-alarm rate at which they'd personally start ignoring or disabling a given alert, then compare answers to see how much the threshold varies person to person
spec: you can state a specific false-alarm rate (e.g. "1 in 5") at which you personally said you'd disable each of the two alerts, with a reason
you can name one factor besides raw false-alarm rate that changed your own threshold (e.g. how the alert fires, when, or what it costs to silence)
you can describe how your answer compared to at least one other student's, and why the gap exists

nodes.title: One alert, two markets
nodes.description: Students research how a single dashboard alert is regulated or implemented differently in two countries, then argue which version actually serves the driver better
spec: you can name the alert you researched and the two specific markets you compared, citing where each requirement or feature comes from
you can state, in one sentence, the concrete difference between the two implementations (present vs absent, standard vs optional, or a different threshold or timeline)
you can argue which version better serves the driver, and name the trade-off the "worse" version is actually optimising for

nodes.title: Final crit — the alert vocabulary as a system
nodes.description: A structured peer crit of near-final drafts of the capstone assessment, testing whether each student's alert vocabulary holds together as a coherent system before it's submitted
spec: you presented your vocabulary's urgency hierarchy to a partner and can name one gap or inconsistency they found in it
you gave written feedback on a partner's vocabulary that names a specific failure mode (a false alarm, an overloaded driver, a channel that fails) their design doesn't yet handle
you can state one concrete change you're making to your own submission as a direct result of today's crit

nodes.title: The Alert Audit
nodes.description: A close reading of one real dashboard's full alert vocabulary, and a judgement on how well its parts hang together
spec: every gauge, light, icon, chime and text message on the chosen dashboard is catalogued, not just the interesting ones
each entry says what channel it uses (visual, audible, textual) and what it assumes about the driver's attention or knowledge
the audit names at least one place where the vocabulary is inconsistent with itself

criteria.name: Coverage and accuracy of the audit

nodes.title: The Instrument Cluster You'd Trust
nodes.description: The capstone — design a complete alert vocabulary for a vehicle of your choosing, and defend it as a system rather than a pile of good ideas
spec: the vehicle and its operating context are stated precisely enough that a reader can judge whether the design fits it
the full alert vocabulary is specified — what triggers each alert, what channel(s) it uses, and how it relates in urgency to every other alert in the system
the submission argues for the system as a whole, addressing at least one likely failure mode (a false alarm, an overloaded driver, a channel that fails) and how the design handles it

marking.description: Judged as a whole system, not as a checklist of channels covered. A strong submission demonstrates command of gauges, lights, icons, colour, sound, text, and — where the chosen vehicle warrants it — HUD or driver-assistance alerts, and argues for the vocabulary as a coherent whole rather than defending each choice in isolation. A submission that is excellent on individual alerts but incoherent between them will not score as highly as one that is merely good throughout but consistent.

nodes.title: Redesign a Warning
nodes.description: Take one existing dashboard alert apart and rebuild it across icon, colour, sound and text, with a rationale that survives an argument
spec: the original alert is identified precisely (make, model, fault, and how it is currently signalled)
the redesign specifies icon, colour, sound and (if used) text — not just one channel
the written rationale cites specific weeks' material by name, not just "we learned that..."

nodes.title: The dashboard as language
nodes.description: Why a dashboard is a designed language rather than a neutral report of facts, framed through the Jaguar E-Type and the Mercedes MBUX Hyperscreen

nodes.title: Needles and Gauges — The Analogue Century
nodes.description: Why continuous analogue gauges dominated dashboard design for a century, and what they assumed about the driver reading them

nodes.title: The idiot light
nodes.description: What a dashboard loses, and gains, when a continuous measurement becomes a single light — from the 1950s–60s US gauge-to-light shift to the modern check-engine light

nodes.title: Icons and symbols — building a shared vocabulary
nodes.description: How a tiny pictogram comes to mean the same thing across languages, literacy levels and decades, through the case of the tyre-pressure warning icon

nodes.title: Red, amber, green: the grammar of urgency
nodes.description: How three colours came to carry the entire weight of automotive urgency, and what happens to a driver for whom two of them look the same

nodes.title: Chimes, dings and voices — the sonic register
nodes.description: What makes a warning sound urgent without becoming alarming, examined through the seatbelt chime's regulatory escalation against Tesla's deliberately sparse chime set

nodes.title: From acronym to sentence: text on the dashboard
nodes.description: What a full sentence can tell a driver that an icon and a two-letter code never could, and the translation bill that arrives the moment the dashboard starts writing in words

nodes.title: Heads-up: the dashboard on the windscreen
nodes.description: What changes when an instrument stops living in the dashboard and starts living in the driver's own view of the road

nodes.title: The vocabulary of almost-autonomy
nodes.description: What an alert is actually claiming once the car can act on its own judgement, and why Volvo's City Safety (2008) is the moment the dashboard started narrating decisions instead of reporting symptoms

nodes.title: Cry wolf: trust and alarm fatigue
nodes.description: What happens to a warning system's credibility the tenth time it's wrong, and why the driver-assistance features most likely to matter are also the ones most likely to get switched off

nodes.title: The same car, different countries
nodes.description: Why the same vehicle platform ships with a different urgency vocabulary depending on which market it's sold into, and what that says about whose "urgent" a dashboard is actually built around

nodes.title: The next dashboard
nodes.description: If you were inventing this vocabulary today, with no legacy dashboard to imitate, what would you keep, and what would you throw out — and what happens once the vocabulary lives in software the manufacturer can change after the sale

course.title: Please Wait: The Design and Politics of Waiting
course.description: A queue is a machine for handing out waiting, and every queue is a decision about whose time counts for less. Twelve weeks measuring real lines, from supermarket tills to transplant lists to the scheduler in your laptop, and one queue you redesign and defend.

nodes.title: Choosing your queue
nodes.description: Two hours to commit to the queue you will still be measuring in week 12, and to find out why your first choice will not work.
spec: you leave with one queue, named, located, and accessible on two different days
you have stood next to it once
you know who to ask for permission, if permission is needed

nodes.title: The clipboard
nodes.description: Learning to record arrivals and services by hand, badly, and then learning what the errors were.
spec: you record 30 minutes of arrivals and services at a queue in the building
your counts are compared against a second observer's
you can state your own error rate

nodes.title: The long tail
nodes.description: Plotting your own service times and discovering that the average was hiding most of what matters.
spec: you plot a histogram of at least 60 service times from your own queue
you compute the coefficient of variation
you can say whether your queue is closer to a production line or a clinic

nodes.title: Counting servers
nodes.description: A walk around four queues in the same building to work out how many servers each one really has.
spec: you visit four queues as a group and classify each as pooled or not
for each, you name which of the five reasons not to pool applies
you count the servers, and defend the count

nodes.title: Watching the jump
nodes.description: Two hours recording every instance of somebody being served out of order, and what happened next.
spec: you record every out-of-order service at your own queue for one hour
each one is classified as sanctioned, negotiated or unnoticed
you estimate the cost in seconds to the people behind

nodes.title: The triage table
nodes.description: A tabletop exercise where your group writes a triage scale, then runs a surge through it and watches it fail.
spec: your group produces a written scale with categories, time promises and a rationale
you run 40 arrivals through it under normal load and under surge
you name the group your scale treats worst and say whether that is defensible

nodes.title: Filing for a number
nodes.description: Putting a measurement on a queue that publishes nothing, starting with a real request for its length.
spec: you identify one invisible queue and one organisation that holds its numbers
you draft a request for its length, rate and median wait
you produce an outside estimate of the same three quantities

nodes.title: The waiting room audit
nodes.description: Auditing one waiting space against the seven propositions, and separating the service from the anaesthetic.
spec: you audit one waiting space against all seven propositions
every intervention you find is classified as shortening the wait or hiding it
you interview at least one person who is waiting, with their consent

nodes.title: Reading a scheduler trace
nodes.description: Finding Little's Law, the utilisation wall and starvation in a real trace from a machine with nothing to hide.
spec: you extract arrival rate, mean residence and queue length from a supplied trace
you verify Little's Law holds in the trace to within one percent
you find at least one starved job and say what ageing would have done to it

nodes.title: The post-mortem
nodes.description: Working through a published inquiry into a queue that failed badly, and finding the week we would have caught it.
spec: your group works through one published inquiry or incident report
you identify the measurable quantity that was not measured
you name the week of this course that would have caught it

nodes.title: The redesign studio
nodes.description: You pitch your one change to three people whose job is to find the group it costs.
spec: you pitch your single change in five minutes with the arithmetic visible
three people attempt to find a group your change makes worse
you leave with either a defence or a different change

nodes.title: The defence
nodes.description: Eight minutes each, questions from the room, and in the best years the manager of the queue you have been measuring.
spec: you present your redesign in eight minutes and take questions for four
the arithmetic and the named loser both appear in the presentation
you answer at least one question you had not anticipated

nodes.title: The Measured Queue
nodes.description: Observe one real queue for at least 90 minutes and report its arrival rate, service rate, utilisation and mean wait, with the method behind each figure.
spec: one queue, chosen in the week 1 field session and registered by 17:00 Friday of week 1, not changed after week 2
at least 90 minutes of observation, in blocks of 30 minutes or more, across two different days
arrival rate, service rate, utilisation and mean wait, each reported with its unit, its sample size and the method that produced it
one histogram of service times
a section naming one quantity you could not obtain, and why
a report of at most 1500 words as a PDF, plus the raw observation sheets as a separate file

criteria.name: Correct use of Little's Law and the variability term
Honesty about what the numbers cannot tell you

nodes.title: The Queue Journal
nodes.description: Eleven weekly entries of 100 to 250 words on queues you were in or watched, plus a closing note, submitted once as a single document.
spec: one entry for each teaching week from week 1 to week 11
each entry between 100 and 250 words
each entry headed with its week number, the date of the queue and the date you wrote it
each entry names one thing you could measure about that queue and one thing you could not
a closing note of at most 300 words
one PDF, entries in week order

marking.description: Marked as one document rather than entry by entry. A journal in the upper band has an entry for every week, written close to the event, covering a range of different queues, and shows the vocabulary of the course arriving in the entries as each week teaches it. A journal in the middle band meets the format but repeats the same observation with different queues attached. A journal in the lower band has entries clustered in a few days of writing, generic descriptions that could apply to any queue, or fewer than nine entries. Missing weeks marked as missing cost less than reconstructed ones.

meta.latenessNote: This piece is not accepted late, because entries written after the deadline cannot be evidence of a weekly habit. Request an extension before the deadline instead.

nodes.title: The Redesign
nodes.description: A 2000 word proposal for one change to the queue you measured, with the predicted effect worked out, plus an eight minute defence in week 12.
spec: one change to the queue you measured for The Measured Queue
a predicted mean wait after the change, with the arithmetic shown in full
a named group who waits longer after the change, and by how much
a feasibility section addressing cost, staffing, space and who has to agree
a proposal of at most 2000 words as a PDF
a defence in the week 12 field session, eight minutes plus five minutes of questions

criteria.name: The prediction, and the working behind it
Feasibility against the real constraints of the site

meta.latenessNote: The written proposal takes the ordinary per-day penalty. The defence happens in the week 12 field session and cannot be submitted late, so if you cannot attend, request an extension rather than a late submission.

nodes.title: Whose Time It Was
nodes.description: An essay of 1200 to 1800 words arguing about how one queue distributes waiting, with evidence and the strongest case against you stated in full.
spec: 1200 to 1800 words, excluding the reference list
about one queue, which may be the one you measured in week 1 or one from weeks 5 to 7
a thesis stated in the first 150 words
at least one quantified claim about who waits longer, with its source
at least six sources, of which at least two are operating documents, published service standards or inquiry reports
the strongest counter-argument stated in its own best form before you answer it
submitted as a single PDF

criteria.name: Use of evidence, including your own measurements
Fair treatment of the strongest case against you

nodes.title: The line starts here
nodes.description: First-come-first-served is not the natural state of a queue. It is a policy somebody chose.

nodes.title: Little's Law
nodes.description: You can work out how long people are waiting without timing a single one of them.

nodes.title: Variability is the tax
nodes.description: A counter running at ninety-five percent of capacity is not a well-run counter. It is one bad morning from collapse.

nodes.title: One line or many
nodes.description: The banks changed to a single serpentine line and the supermarkets never did. Both were right.

nodes.title: Priority, and who pays for it
nodes.description: Every queue jump is paid for by somebody standing further back who was never told.

nodes.title: Triage
nodes.description: Emergency medicine solved the ethics of priority in public and wrote the answer down. It is worth reading.

nodes.title: The queues with no visible front
nodes.description: A visible line is a courtesy. The queues that decide the most about a life publish nothing.

nodes.title: The felt wait
nodes.description: An unexplained two minutes is longer than an explained five. That is not a failure of the customer.

nodes.title: Machines that wait
nodes.description: Your laptop is running a dozen queues right now and its scheduler faces exactly the problem the passport office does.

nodes.title: When the queue is the hazard
nodes.description: A crowd crush is a queueing failure, and the arithmetic that predicts it is the arithmetic from week 3.

nodes.title: Abolishing the queue
nodes.description: Appointments, lotteries and auctions do not remove waiting. They change who does it and what it costs them.

nodes.title: What you can see now
nodes.description: A last hour on what changes once you cannot stand in a line without reading it.

course.title: Getting Read
course.description: Most cold emails are deleted unread. This course treats that as a triage problem rather than a persuasion problem, and spends twelve weeks on the specific writing failures that get an email ignored, not opened, or reported.

nodes.title: Final: Doctrine and Defence
nodes.description: A one-page personal doctrine on what makes an email worth reading, defended against one email you'd actually send.

one real email defended against the doctrine, naming where it falls short if it does
the defence engages the legal and ethical floor from weeks 10 and 12, not just craft

nodes.title: Midterm Teardown
nodes.description: An audit of ten redacted real cold emails against the course's own failure taxonomy.
spec: ten emails audited, each assigned exactly one failure mode from weeks 1–7
each diagnosis is justified in the email's own text, not asserted
each entry proposes a specific fix, not a general improvement

criteria.name: Quality and specificity of the proposed fix

nodes.title: Weekly Rewrite Portfolio
nodes.description: A collected portfolio of rewrites, one named failure mode fixed per week, graded as a whole.
spec: one rewrite submitted for each of weeks 1–6, each naming the failure mode it fixes
each rewrite pairs the original (redacted if not your own) with the fixed version
a short note per rewrite explaining what specifically changed and why

marking.description: Graded on the portfolio as a whole rather than per email. Readers assess whether each rewrite correctly identifies its week's failure mode, whether the fix actually addresses it rather than just changing tone, and whether the diagnosis gets sharper across the weeks it covers.

course.title: Try Again, Later
course.description: A course about one decision, asked in a new context every week: something failed — should you try again, and how? From flaky HTTP clients to double-charged payments, we study when persistence helps and when it quietly makes things worse.

nodes.title: Reproducing the reflex
nodes.description: A read times out and the retry succeeds. Nothing was written and nothing broke, so the reflex gets learned before anyone examines it.

meta.failure_scenario: A read request times out once; a client retries it and the second attempt succeeds.
meta.imageAlt: A boomerang mid-flight, curving back toward the open hand that threw it

nodes.title: Charging twice on purpose
nodes.description: The same retry, aimed at a write: one charge becomes two, and the client cannot tell whether it already worked.

meta.failure_scenario: A payment write times out after the charge has already been committed server-side, and the client retries it.
meta.imageAlt: A rubber stamp striking the same receipt twice, the second impression landing just off the first

nodes.title: Becoming the outage
nodes.description: A two-second slowdown, a retry loop with no delay between attempts, and a client that keeps the dependency down long after the original problem passed.

meta.failure_scenario: A client with no delay between attempts retries into a dependency that is down for two seconds.
meta.imageAlt: A single tap turned fully open, overflowing a basin faster than the drain can take it

nodes.title: Synchronising a herd
nodes.description: Ten thousand clients, each correct alone, that fall over the dependency together the moment it recovers.

meta.failure_scenario: Ten thousand clients, each backing off correctly on its own, all retry on the same second.
meta.imageAlt: A tight cluster of identical alarm clocks, all their hands at the same hour, ringing together

nodes.title: Counting to twenty-seven
nodes.description: Twenty-seven attempts for one request, and why no single layer can see it happening.

meta.failure_scenario: Three layers of a call stack each retry a failing downstream call three times, independently.
meta.imageAlt: A pressure gauge with its needle pinned into a red zone near the top of the dial

nodes.title: Two people, one payout
nodes.description: The same failure with no code in it: two people, one payout, and a runbook standing in for a lock.

meta.failure_scenario: A failed payout is retried at 3am by two on-call operators working the same incident independently, with no queue or lock between them.
meta.imageAlt: Two hands, each dropping an identical coin into the same slot at once

nodes.title: Telling a no from a not yet
nodes.description: A 400 and a malformed message look exactly like a timeout at the moment they fail. Classifying failures before retrying them, and what goes wrong when the classification is wrong.

meta.failure_scenario: A queue consumer retries a malformed message forever and a client retries a 400 it will never pass, because neither can tell a permanent failure from a transient one.
meta.imageAlt: An envelope caught between two mail slots side by side, one bricked shut, the other open

nodes.title: Watching a breaker trip
nodes.description: A dependency down for minutes, and a breaker that refuses calls outright rather than letting every request find out for itself.

meta.failure_scenario: A dependency is down for an extended period, and every request still knocks on its door before giving up.
meta.imageAlt: An industrial circuit-breaker switch lever caught in its half-thrown middle position

nodes.title: Retrying into an empty room
nodes.description: The work finishes; the person who asked closed the tab ninety seconds ago.

meta.failure_scenario: A request is retried for ninety seconds against a caller that gave up after three, and the successful attempt returns to a connection that has already closed.
meta.imageAlt: A telephone ringing on a desk in an empty room, its chair pushed back and empty

nodes.title: Reading past the dashboard
nodes.description: A dependency degrades for six weeks, retries absorb every failure, and the success-rate dashboard never moves.

meta.failure_scenario: Retries quietly absorb a dependency degrading over six weeks, and the dashboard stays green while the retried latency climbs unmeasured.
meta.imageAlt: A house of cards standing perfectly still on a table that is visibly tilting to one side beneath it

nodes.title: Finding the point of no return
nodes.description: Some steps cannot be retried at all, which makes the decision an ordering problem instead.

meta.failure_scenario: A confirmation email has already been sent and a resource lock has already been released by the time a later step in the same request fails.
meta.imageAlt: A row of dominoes with the last one already fallen, out of order ahead of the ones still standing

nodes.title: Arguing the case
nodes.description: A retry policy that cites every mechanism from the last eleven weeks, the incident it produced, and a position you have to defend.

meta.failure_scenario: A retry policy citing every mechanism from the semester, handed over with the incident it produced and the outcome removed, to be argued for or against.
meta.imageAlt: A wooden signpost whose two blank arms are the same size and point in opposite directions

nodes.title: The case against retrying
nodes.description: A failure from earlier in the semester, read cold with the outcome removed — argue for or against having retried at all.
spec: takes a clear position, for or against having retried, rather than presenting both sides unresolved
names what that decision did to the dependency, to the caller's latency, and to the state a failed attempt left behind
proposes a measurement that would have told the decision-maker whether they were right, before the outcome was known
engages the strongest version of the opposing argument, not a weaker one it's easier to beat

marking.description: Judged as a single argument rather than a checklist: whether the case correctly identifies what the retry actually did — attempts arriving at the dependency, latency on the path that was already working, the state a failed attempt left behind, who could see it happening — whether it commits to a position instead of hedging between both, and whether the measurement it proposes would actually have settled the question at the time, not only in hindsight.

meta.imageAlt: A gavel resting on a closed case file

nodes.title: Retry audit
nodes.description: Find every retry in a real codebase and diagnose each one against the four weeks that got you here: safe to repeat, backed off, jittered, and survivable when ten thousand clients recover at once.
spec: every retry site the codebase actually contains is found, not a sample of the obvious ones
each site is diagnosed against the specific failure modes named in weeks 1 to 4, not a generic checklist
a fix is proposed for each site that fails a check, and the fix is one this course has actually covered
each proposed fix names its own limit — the latency, the storage, or the predictability it takes away from somebody
submitted by the deadline, as a single document with one entry per retry site

meta.imageAlt: A magnifying glass held over a tangled knot of cord

nodes.title: A retry policy you have to defend
nodes.description: Write a retry policy for a real service, then defend every number in it against a panel assigned to find the one you cannot justify.
spec: the policy names a real service and covers what happens on failure end to end, not one mechanism in isolation
it states a retry budget, a backoff strategy and a breaker condition, and says how they interact
every mechanism it adopts states its own limit: what that mechanism does to requests that would have succeeded without it, or what it needs from the client to work at all
it names at least one alternative design it rejected, and why
the defence responds to the specific challenge raised, not a rehearsed answer prepared in advance

criteria.name: Justification against the alternatives it rejects

meta.imageAlt: A wax seal stamped twice onto the same document, the second impression doubled over the first

nodes.title: A retried read is safe for a reason nobody writes down
nodes.description: Why the retry reflex gets learned on requests where it cannot do harm, and what changes as soon as the call writes something.

meta.imageAlt: A boomerang mid-flight, curving back toward the open hand that threw it

nodes.title: A non-idempotent retry is a hidden bug
nodes.description: Why a timeout cannot tell a client whether the write already happened, and what an idempotency key actually guarantees.

meta.imageAlt: A rubber stamp striking the same receipt twice, the second impression landing just off the first

nodes.title: Your retry loop is the outage now
nodes.description: Why more attempts, sooner, makes recovery slower, and why spacing retries out belongs in a library rather than at each call site.

meta.imageAlt: A single tap turned fully open, overflowing a basin faster than the drain can take it

nodes.title: Ten thousand correct clients make one spike
nodes.description: How individually correct backoff still adds up to a synchronised spike, and why jitter has to be mandatory rather than optional.

meta.imageAlt: A tight cluster of identical alarm clocks, all their hands at the same hour, ringing together

nodes.title: A budget beats a per-call count
nodes.description: Why retries compound multiplicatively across a call stack, and what a shared retry budget has to track to stop them.

meta.imageAlt: A pressure gauge with its needle pinned into a red zone near the top of the dial

nodes.title: A runbook fails the same ways a retry library does
nodes.description: Why some weeks have no client, library or platform to hand the decision to, and what a runbook has in common with a retry library.

meta.imageAlt: Two hands, each dropping an identical coin into the same slot at once

nodes.title: Not every failure can be retried away
nodes.description: How a status code and a poison message are the same problem, and where the judgement that separates them has to live.

meta.imageAlt: An envelope caught between two mail slots side by side, one bricked shut, the other open

nodes.title: A breaker stuck open protects nothing
nodes.description: Why a circuit breaker is shared state the platform has to hold, and why it needs to close again as much as it needs to open.

meta.imageAlt: An industrial circuit-breaker switch lever caught in its half-thrown middle position

nodes.title: Nobody is waiting for your third attempt
nodes.description: What a deadline bounds that an attempt count cannot, and why only the caller knows whether an answer is still wanted.

meta.imageAlt: A telephone ringing on a desk in an empty room, its chair pushed back and empty

nodes.title: A green dashboard hides a slow decline
nodes.description: Why success rate stays flat while a dependency degrades for six weeks, and what has to be reported beside it.

meta.imageAlt: A house of cards standing perfectly still on a table that is visibly tilting to one side beneath it

nodes.title: Some steps only happen once, by design
nodes.description: Why an irreversible step has no retry decision to make, and why the fix is ordering it to run last instead.

meta.imageAlt: A row of dominoes with the last one already fallen, out of order ahead of the ones still standing

nodes.title: Reading a retry policy's numbers against each other
nodes.description: How a policy holding every mechanism from the semester still fails, and why the last question of the course is a product one.

meta.imageAlt: A wooden signpost whose two blank arms are the same size and point in opposite directions
