course.title: Autocomplete Studies
course.description: A semester spent taking predictive text seriously: from T9 keypads to code completion to language models, tracing what it means for a machine to keep finishing your sentence, and what that has changed about how we write, code, and decide what to say next.

nodes.title: Build a T9 disambiguator
nodes.description: The first lab — turn a keypress sequence into a ranked list of real words, using nothing but a dictionary and a mapping of letters to keys
spec: given a sequence of keypresses, your program returns every dictionary word that sequence could spell
when more than one word matches, the results are ordered by some stated rule, not left in whatever order the dictionary happened to be in
you can explain, out loud, one word pair your dictionary gets wrong

nodes.title: Autocorrect post-mortem
nodes.description: A lab spent deliberately breaking an autocorrect implementation, then writing up why each break happened
spec: you have found at least three inputs that your chosen autocorrect implementation corrects wrong, and can reproduce each one on demand
for each, you can name the specific mechanism that produced the wrong correction, not just that it happened
you can describe one change that would fix your worst example without obviously breaking something else

nodes.title: Query completion audit
nodes.description: A lab auditing a real search box's autocomplete for suggestions its owner probably wouldn't choose to put there on purpose
spec: you have typed a defined list of neutral prefixes into a real search box and recorded exactly what it suggests
you can identify at least one suggestion that reveals something about the aggregate searcher rather than answering the prefix
you can state what rule, if any, the platform appears to be applying to filter suggestions, based on what you don't see

nodes.title: AAC scanning simulation
nodes.description: A lab spent composing sentences through a scanning-and-selection interface with a deliberately mediocre word predictor, to feel the cost of a bad list
spec: you have composed at least five sentences using only scanning selection, no direct typing
you can report how many selections each sentence took, with and without the predictor's suggestions
you can name one change to the predictor's word list that would have saved you selections on a specific sentence you composed

nodes.title: Assignment 1 clinic
nodes.description: A work session for Assignment 1, run as one-on-one check-ins rather than a taught lab, in the week the assignment is due
spec: you arrive with a build that runs, even if it's incomplete
you can point to the specific input your build handles worst, without being asked to demonstrate it
you leave with a written note of the one thing you changed as a result of the check-in, or a written note that nothing changed and why

nodes.title: Inbox smart-reply audit
nodes.description: A lab auditing your own email or messaging app's suggested replies against the messages that triggered them
spec: you have collected the suggested replies offered for at least ten real messages in your own inbox
you can identify at least one suggestion that was tonally wrong for the message it responded to, or say honestly that you found none
you can describe, in one sentence, what a wrong suggestion had in common with the ones that worked

nodes.title: Continuation-swap lab
nodes.description: A lab where pairs swap half-finished conversations and try to tell a model's continuation from a human one, then check their reasoning
spec: you have judged at least eight paired continuations and recorded your guess before seeing the answer for each
your written reasoning for at least two guesses cites a specific textual feature, not a vague impression
you can state your own hit rate, including the guesses you got wrong

nodes.title: Inpainting seams lab
nodes.description: A lab spent generating and then deliberately hunting for the seams in inpainted images, cataloguing which tells actually generalise
spec: you have generated at least six inpainted images using a masked region of your choosing
you have identified a visible flaw in at least two of them and can point to its exact location
your write-up sorts your flaws into categories rather than listing them individually

nodes.title: Forecast UI comparison
nodes.description: A lab comparing how three real forecast interfaces represent uncertainty for the same underlying kind of prediction
spec: you have screenshotted the same forecast, at the same moment, from at least three different interfaces covering the same domain
for each, you can state in one sentence how it represents (or fails to represent) uncertainty
you can rank the three by how honestly each one represents its own confidence, and defend the ranking

nodes.title: Co-writing exchange
nodes.description: A lab where you write a short piece with a predictive tool, log every suggestion you accepted or rejected, and trade logs with a partner
spec: you have produced a short piece of writing, under 400 words, using a predictive co-writing tool of your choice
you have a log recording every suggestion you were offered and whether you accepted, rejected, or edited it
you can state your own acceptance rate and one thing it surprised you about your own writing process

nodes.title: Feed reverse-engineering
nodes.description: A lab where you deliberately engage with a narrow slice of content on a fresh or logged-out feed and log how quickly the recommendations shift
spec: you have run the engagement experiment for at least fifteen minutes of active interaction, not fifteen minutes of elapsed time
you can report roughly how many interactions passed before the feed visibly shifted toward your chosen slice
you can name one piece of content the feed showed you that didn't fit the slice, and a plausible reason it appeared anyway

nodes.title: Closing crit
nodes.description: The last lab of the semester — short presentations of final project work in progress, judged against the persuasion framework from this week's lecture
spec: you present a five-minute account of your final project's current state, including what isn't finished
you name one suggestion you rejected during Week 10's co-writing exchange, and why, as the lecture asked
you can point to at least one place your own final project makes a suggestion, and say honestly whose interest it serves

nodes.title: Assignment 1: Build a predictive input system
nodes.description: A working predictive-text build in a domain of your choice, submitted with a short written account of exactly where and why it fails
spec: a working predictive-text system in a domain covered by weeks 1 through 4 (a keypad disambiguator, an autocorrector, a query completer, or an accessible-input predictor), runnable by the marker without your help
a written account, no more than 800 words, naming at least three specific inputs your build handles wrong, and explaining the mechanism behind each
the domain is not the T9 lab in its unmodified form — extend it, combine it with a second constraint, or pick a different week's domain entirely

criteria.name: The build works on its stated inputs
The failure-mode write-up is specific and evidenced
The chosen domain is harder than the minimum viable version

nodes.title: Assignment 2: Audit a deployed suggestion feature
nodes.description: A comparative audit of a real, currently deployed prediction or suggestion feature, using the fixed-input method practised across weeks 6 through 9
spec: a fixed set of at least ten inputs, run identically across at least two comparable interfaces or products in the same domain
a record of exactly what each interface returned, not a paraphrase of what it "generally" does
a stated judgement of whose interest the feature's design choices appear to serve, argued from the recorded evidence rather than asserted
the audited feature falls in the territory covered by weeks 6 through 9 (suggested replies, chat continuations, image completion, or forecast interfaces)

criteria.name: Findings are specific and evidenced, not asserted
The audit states who the feature's design appears to serve

nodes.title: Final project: The full audit
nodes.description: The capstone — take Assignment 2's audit and turn it into a complete, standalone case study of a real product's suggestion design
spec: it stands alone — a reader who has not seen Assignment 2 can follow it completely, including the feature it audits and the method used
it extends Assignment 2's audit rather than repeating it, with either a wider comparison set, a longer observation period, or a deeper mechanism analysis of the same feature
it applies the week 12 persuasion framework explicitly, arguing whose interest the audited feature's design serves and what evidence supports that claim
it proposes one concrete, specific change to the feature's design, not a general call for more transparency

marking.description: The final project is judged as a single piece of work: whether it reads as a complete, standalone audit rather than an extended assignment; whether its claims are backed by evidence gathered using the semester's methods rather than by general impressions of the feature; and whether it engages honestly with the persuasion framework from week 12 rather than treating the feature it audits as neutral by default. A project that is narrower than Assignment 2 but genuinely deeper marks higher than one that is broader but repeats the same kind of finding at greater length.

nodes.title: Multi-tap, T9, and the keypad that started it
nodes.description: The course's opening argument — that predictive text is a design lineage, not a recent invention, starting with the twelve-key keypad

nodes.title: Autocorrect and the comedy of failure
nodes.description: Why the same system that quietly fixes most of your typos occasionally produces something you'd never have written on purpose

nodes.title: Query completion and the autocomplete confession
nodes.description: What a search box's suggestions reveal about the people typing into it, and why that turned out to be a design problem

nodes.title: Prediction as access — AAC and assistive input
nodes.description: What predictive text looks like when it's the only way someone composes language at conversational speed, not a convenience layered on top of typing

nodes.title: Code completion, from IntelliSense to Copilot
nodes.description: Predictive text applied to a language with a grammar checker built in, and what changed when the completion stopped being confined to your own file

nodes.title: Smart replies and the suggested response
nodes.description: What it means for a system to write the polite part of a conversation for you, one tap at a time, and why that started to feel strange

nodes.title: Conversational completion — the chatbot as autocomplete
nodes.description: The first lecture back after the break, arguing that a conversational model is best understood as autocomplete operating at paragraph scale

nodes.title: Inpainting — completion in pixels
nodes.description: What autocomplete looks like when the missing continuation is a region of an image instead of the next word, and why the two turn out to be related

nodes.title: Forecast UIs and the uncertainty they hide
nodes.description: What a weather app, a poll tracker, and a stock chart have in common with autocomplete — and what each one does with the uncertainty a good forecast can't remove

nodes.title: Co-writing — authorship with a predictive collaborator
nodes.description: What happens to the idea of authorship once the sentence you're writing is being continued, word by word, by something that has read more than you have

nodes.title: The feed — recommendation as prediction
nodes.description: Why a recommendation feed is autocomplete for your attention rather than your sentence, and why that reframing changes what counts as a good guess

nodes.title: Persuasion by default — closing synthesis
nodes.description: A guest lecture on consent by autocomplete, closing the semester by reading every prior week as a question about whose interests a suggestion serves

nodes.title: Callum Voss
nodes.description: Tutor. Ten years writing code-completion tooling before deciding the interesting part was never the ranking model.

course.title: How and Why You're Dumb
course.description: An account of intelligence built from bacteria upward, then turned on the reader: what your mind discards in order to work at all, why it can't tell you what it discarded, and why every model you hold rests on assumptions you didn't choose.

nodes.title: A world too large
nodes.description: The constraint the whole course runs on, and the grading scheme you will use every week after this one.
spec: you can state the constraint any finite system faces, in one sentence, without using the word intelligence
you have found your own retinal blind spot and can say why you had never noticed it
you can assign an evidence grade to a claim and defend the grade rather than the claim

nodes.title: Measurement
nodes.description: What a sense organ is for, and the case that settles it — an animal with twelve colour channels that discriminates colour worse than a goldfish.
spec: you can describe E. coli chemotaxis without attributing a representation to it
you can explain why twelve photoreceptor types produce worse colour discrimination than four
your position statement is submitted

nodes.title: The trace
nodes.description: Memory without a nervous system, and the century-long mistake that comes with it — a finding discarded in 1906 because the replication used the wrong species.
spec: you can explain how Physarum navigates a U-shaped trap it cannot reason about
you can say why the Stentor replication failed and what that failure was actually evidence of
you can distinguish the plant learning literature that has held up from the part that has not

nodes.title: Association
nodes.description: The first mechanism that can be systematically fooled, and why nothing inside it can tell the difference between a cause and a reliable coincidence.
spec: you can state what associative learning has access to, and what it does not
you can explain why superstition is a prediction of the mechanism rather than a malfunction
you can say what the Clever Hans case established about experimental design

nodes.title: Structure not sensed
nodes.description: The internal map, and the result that suggests it was never really about space at all.
spec: you can explain what a cognitive map lets an animal do that association alone cannot
you can describe what Constantinescu and colleagues found, and why it reframes the previous eighty years
you can state one thing a map-holding system cannot detect about its own map

nodes.title: Prediction
nodes.description: The week the course turns over. Perception as mostly construction, and illusions as the mechanism working rather than failing.
spec: you can state the direction of information flow that predictive accounts propose, and what it explains
you can explain why an illusion is evidence for the mechanism rather than against it
you can give one substantive objection to the free energy framing

nodes.title: The self-model
nodes.description: The modeller starts modelling itself, and finds that introspection reports a summary rather than the process that produced it.
spec: you can explain why a self-model has to be lower-dimensional than the system it models
you can describe the choice blindness result and the objection that has been raised to it
you can say what the mirror test does and does not license

nodes.title: Small brains
nodes.description: Everything so far, running on a million neurons — and the collapse of the brain-size story that made it puzzling.
spec: you can explain why the small-brain puzzle largely dissolves once neurons are counted rather than mass
you can describe the stilts-and-stumps experiment and what it establishes
you can name one capacity in an insect that has no obvious function

nodes.title: Alien architecture
nodes.description: A nervous system built on a different plan, and a famous question that may be malformed.
spec: you can describe how octopus neural organisation differs from the vertebrate arrangement
you can state Nagel's question precisely, and Akins' objection to it
you can say what the colour-vision problem in cephalopods is

nodes.title: Offloaded
nodes.description: Cognition pushed outside the individual, and the discovery that a group's failures are not the sum of its members'.
spec: you can explain what cross inhibition does in a honeybee swarm and what it is analogous to
you can state the extended mind thesis and the coupling-constitution objection to it
you can say under what conditions social influence improves a group estimate and when it does not

nodes.title: The catalogue, and its own problem
nodes.description: The human case, and the week the course grades its own sources — most of the famous literature about how badly you reason has not replicated.
spec: you can distinguish bounded rationality, ecological rationality and the heuristics-and-biases programme
you can name three findings from the bias canon that have failed to replicate and say what replaced them
your revision and memo are submitted

nodes.title: The blind spot
nodes.description: Nothing is added. You apply eleven weeks of account to your own judgement, and the question from week 1 comes back in a form no card will find.
spec: you can explain why the classic Dunning-Kruger curve is partly a statistical artefact
you can state Agrippa's trilemma and say which horn you take
you can explain why fallibilism is not relativism

nodes.title: Calibrated quizzes
nodes.description: Ten short quizzes where you declare how sure you are, and being wrong while confident costs more than being wrong while hedging.
spec: at least eight of the ten quizzes are attempted
each answer carries a declared certainty level
the best strategy available to you is to report your actual confidence

nodes.title: Cognitive profile
nodes.description: A structured profile of one real organism's cognition, answering nine fixed sections, and closing on what that organism lets you see about people that you cannot see from inside.
spec: every one of the nine sections is answered
each substantive claim carries an evidence grade and a source
at least one demonstrated failure is identified as having no possible fix, with the reason
the comparison identifies a structural parallel with human cognition, not a difference in degree

criteria.name: Do the sections contain the kind of claim they ask for, especially what is stored rather than what is done
Are the structural limits correctly separated from the contingent failures
Does the comparison find a shared structure rather than ranking the two systems
Are the sources real, read, and graded defensibly

nodes.title: News and Views
nodes.description: A thousand words tracing a circulating claim back to its primary source, and reporting the gap between what the source says and what everyone repeats.
spec: the primary source is cited and was read, not paraphrased from secondary coverage
the claim as it circulates and the claim as published are both stated precisely
a non-specialist reader can follow it without the original paper open
between 900 and 1200 words

criteria.name: Did you reach the primary source and read it properly
Is the gap accurately characterised, including where there is no gap
Does it work as a piece of writing for a reader outside the subfield

nodes.title: Position statement and revision
nodes.description: Write down what you think intelligence is before you know anything, then revise it in week 11 and account for what moved. The memo is what gets marked.
spec: the position statement was submitted by the end of week 3
the original is resubmitted unaltered alongside the revision
every change in the memo cites the specific paper, week or argument that caused it
the memo names at least one claim you kept under pressure, and at least one weakness that remains

criteria.name: Did you identify the claims the course actually undermined
Is each change tied to something specific rather than to having read more
Did you leave alone what did not need changing, and can you say why
Do you name what is still weakest in the revised version

nodes.title: Too large to represent
nodes.description: The lecture sets the constraint and nothing else. A finite system inside a larger world cannot hold that world, so it holds a compression, and compressions lose things.

nodes.title: What a sense organ is for
nodes.description: Sensing is not reception. It is a commitment about which distinctions are worth paying for, and the mantis shrimp is the case that makes this undeniable.

nodes.title: Memory outside the head
nodes.description: How the past constrains the present with no neurons involved, and the ninety-year mistake that arrived with it.

nodes.title: Correlation, standing in for cause
nodes.description: The first mechanism that can be systematically misled, and the fact that nothing inside it can detect the difference.

nodes.title: The map, and what it was really for
nodes.description: Representing structure you are not currently sensing — and the 2016 result suggesting the machinery was never specifically spatial.

nodes.title: Perception as construction
nodes.description: The lecture where the direction of flow reverses, and most of what you take to be sensing turns out to be generation checked against input.

nodes.title: Modelling the modeller
nodes.description: Why a self-model must be a summary, and what that predicts about introspective reports.

nodes.title: A million neurons is plenty
nodes.description: The brain-size puzzle, and why counting the right thing makes most of it disappear.

nodes.title: Another architecture entirely
nodes.description: An animal whose nervous system is mostly not in its brain, and a famous question that may be the wrong shape.

nodes.title: Cognition outside the individual
nodes.description: Swarms, notebooks and committees — and the finding that a group's failures are not its members' failures added up.

nodes.title: The catalogue, graded by its own scheme
nodes.description: Three separate research programmes that got merged into one slogan, and how much of the famous version did not replicate.

nodes.title: The blind spot
nodes.description: Nothing new. The account from eleven weeks, aimed at the person holding it, and the week 1 question in a form no card will find.

course.title: The Formal Theory of Poker
course.description: A formal treatment of poker: hand combinatorics, equity, game-theoretic equilibria and bankroll mathematics, testing how much of 'good instincts' at the table actually survives translation into a provable claim.

nodes.title: Getting started
nodes.description: The first Problem Session — no assignment is due yet, so it's spent agreeing on notation and working the week 1 example by hand together
spec: you can state, in your own words, what makes a claim "formalized" under this course's definition
you have re-derived the week 1 worked example's equity figure by hand, not just read it

nodes.title: Counting practice
nodes.description: The second Problem Session — deriving the week 2 combo and class counts by hand, then reusing the technique on a smaller counting problem
spec: you can independently derive the 1,326-combo and 169-class counts, not just recite them
given two specific starting cards, you can say which combo-count bucket (pair, suited, offsuit) they belong to and why

nodes.title: Pot odds practice
nodes.description: The third Problem Session — rebuilding the deck's flagship hand from scratch, from outs count through to a call-or-fold verdict in dollars
spec: given a hand and board, you can count outs correctly, including your own hole cards in what gets removed from the deck
you can compute a pot-odds threshold and an EV-of-call figure for a hand that was not shown in lecture

nodes.title: Variance workshop
nodes.description: Recomputing the flagship hand's EV at a bigger pot, then measuring the variance and sample-size effects a bare EV figure never shows
spec: given a decision's outcomes and probabilities, you can compute EV and variance directly from the two-outcome formula, not just recall them
you can explain why a positive-EV play loses on most individual attempts, using this week's own numbers as the example

nodes.title: Value of information workshop
nodes.description: Rebuilding the lecture's blind-vs-informed EV comparison, then building a second toy example from scratch with new numbers
spec: given a two-action, two-state payoff table, you can compute both the best blind action's EV and the best informed EV, and their difference
you can explain, without the lecture's numbers in front of you, why the informed side can never be worse than the blind side

nodes.title: Bayesian updating workshop
nodes.description: Rebuilding the flagship Bayes update from scratch, then updating on a second signal to see the posterior move again
spec: given a prior and two conditional likelihoods, you can compute the Bayesian posterior and re-derive EV(call) from it
you can update a posterior a second time on a new signal, using the first posterior as the new prior

nodes.title: Indifference equations practice
nodes.description: Re-deriving optimal bluff frequency and MDF from scratch, then solving both at a new bet size to check the method, not just the memorized ratio
spec: given a pot and a bet size, you can set up and solve both indifference equations from scratch to get optimal bluff frequency and MDF
you can explain in words why an indifference condition, not a single best action, is the right target when facing a mixed strategy

nodes.title: Exploitability workshop
nodes.description: Computing best responses and exploitability numbers for opponent frequencies not covered in lecture, to check the formulas generalize
spec: given an opponent's fixed bluff frequency, you can determine the pure best response and its EV without defaulting to the equilibrium mix
given a hero calling frequency, you can compute its exploitability and say in words what that dollar figure means

nodes.title: Multi-way equity workshop
nodes.description: Running the multi-opponent simulator on a hand nobody has seen, and auditing which other course results would need re-deriving with 3 players
spec: given a hand's 2-way equity, you can state the naive independence estimate for 2 and 3 opponents and explain why it's a lower bound, not an estimate, in the way this week's numbers show
you can identify, for a course result from an earlier week, whether it assumed exactly one opponent and if so what breaks with a second

nodes.title: ICM workshop
nodes.description: Running the recursive ICM calculation on a payout structure and stack distribution nobody has seen, then a two-player sanity check by hand
spec: given stacks and a payout structure, you can compute each player's finish-placement probabilities and $EV using the recursive definition, not the naive chip-proportional shortcut
you can explain, in words, why a short stack's ICM $EV usually exceeds its chip-proportional share and a chip leader's usually falls short

nodes.title: Kelly criterion workshop
nodes.description: Computing Kelly fractions and growth rates for bets not covered in lecture, then locating the actual peak of the growth-rate curve by hand
spec: given a win probability and payout odds, you can compute the Kelly fraction and the resulting per-bet growth rate from the formulas
you can explain why doubling a Kelly-optimal stake can turn positive long-run growth negative even though every single bet stays +EV

nodes.title: Capstone review
nodes.description: Working through the Kuhn poker solve by hand at a small scale, then a closing discussion of what the semester's tools did and didn't capture
spec: given a small extensive-form toy game's information sets, you can explain what regret minimization is doing at each one, in terms of week 7's indifference-equation logic
you can state, for each of the four week 1 folk claims, whether this course resolved it fully, partially, or mostly built the tool without running the specific case — and why

nodes.title: Final Exam
nodes.description: A comprehensive closed-book exam, weighted towards the equilibrium and tournament-equity material that only makes sense once the earlier weeks are in place.
spec: sat during the scheduled slot named above
final answers are correct
at least one answer draws an explicit connection across two or more weeks' material, not just within a single week's method

nodes.title: Midterm
nodes.description: A closed-book written exam covering the first six weeks, from hand combinatorics through Bayesian range reading.
spec: sat during the scheduled slot named above
final answers are correct
the method used to reach each one is shown, not just asserted

nodes.title: Weekly Assignments
nodes.description: Ten short problem sets across the semester, each asking for one computed quantity and the working that produced it.
spec: submitted by that week's deadline, in the format named below
the final numeric answer is correct
the method used to reach it is shown, not just asserted

nodes.title: What formalizing an instinct even means
nodes.description: Orientation — a short history of poker theory, what this course means by "formalize," and the folk claims we'll spend the semester cashing in

nodes.title: Counting the deck
nodes.description: Combinatorics before probability — how many starting hands there really are, and why the answer depends on what you're counting

nodes.title: Pot Odds, Equity, and the Calling Decision
nodes.description: Reopening week 1's rule of 4 and 2 — its exact error, outs-counting by draw type, and one real hand priced from equity through to a dollar EV

nodes.title: Expected value and variance
nodes.description: Formalizing EV beyond one hand, why a correct call still loses most of the time it's made, and why sample size is doing more work than it looks

nodes.title: Position and the value of information
nodes.description: A clean decision-theory result — the value of perfect information — used to put a number on why acting last is worth something

nodes.title: Range reading and Bayesian updating
nodes.description: Turning a partial signal — a bet size, not a revealed hand — into an updated probability, and watching it flip last week's call into a fold

nodes.title: Mixed strategies and the algebra of bluffing
nodes.description: Deriving optimal bluffing frequency and minimum defense frequency from indifference conditions, in the simplest toy game that has both

nodes.title: GTO versus exploitative play
nodes.description: What "unexploitable" actually means, formalized as a zero-exploitability property of week 7's equilibrium, versus the higher-EV but riskier alternative of deviating to exploit a fixed opponent

nodes.title: Multi-way pots
nodes.description: Which of this course's two-player results survive a third player at the table, tested against a real Monte Carlo simulation rather than assumed

nodes.title: Tournament equity and the Independent Chip Model
nodes.description: Why a chip isn't worth a dollar once elimination is on the table, made precise with the standard recursive ICM calculation and checked against the naive chip-proportional model it's often confused with

nodes.title: Bankroll management and the Kelly criterion
nodes.description: Why the size of a bet matters even when its EV is fixed and positive, formalized as maximizing long-run exponential growth rather than per-bet expectation

nodes.title: Capstone: how much of good poker intuition can be formalized
nodes.description: Grading the semester's own four promises, solving the real Kuhn poker equilibrium and checking it against the published result, and naming what stayed outside every tool this course built

course.title: How to Hear the Universe
course.description: A studio course in astronomical data sonification: trace signals from telescope to speaker, design accountable mappings, and build a listening instrument that never hides its data.

nodes.title: One curve, two readings
nodes.description: Compare pitch and rhythm mappings while the source values remain fixed.
spec: the same ten values drive both versions
each mapping rule includes domain, range and timing
the annotation names one revealed pattern and one hidden feature

meta.output: an annotated comparison of two mappings

nodes.title: Draw the provenance chain
nodes.description: Trace a small light curve from detector images to a playable sequence.
spec: observed and derived quantities use different labels
every transformation states its input and output units
presentation choices are separated from calibration

meta.output: a provenance diagram with transformations labelled

nodes.title: Mapping shoot-out
nodes.description: Test linear, logarithmic and quantised mappings against a recognition task.
spec: three mappings use the same input sequence
at least three listeners attempt the same recognition task
the selected rule is justified with observations rather than taste

meta.output: a tested mapping matrix and selected rule

nodes.title: Fold a pulsar
nodes.description: Align repeated pulses and compare raw timing with a folded profile.
spec: the pulsar and catalogue source are identified
the period used for folding is stated
raw and folded versions remain distinguishable

meta.output: a pulsar profile and an audification note

nodes.title: Noise or event?
nodes.description: Annotate a dynamic spectrum before choosing what the sonification will retain.
spec: time, frequency and intensity axes retain units
suspected interference is marked but not silently removed
unknown features remain labelled unknown

nodes.title: Chirp under inspection
nodes.description: Compare raw, filtered and shifted renderings of a gravitational-wave event.
spec: all versions point to the same source event
filtering, amplification and shifting are disclosed separately
the comparison distinguishes detection evidence from audibility

meta.output: a blind comparison of three chirp transformations

nodes.title: Scan an X-ray field
nodes.description: Prototype a spatial scan of an astronomical image with progress cues.
spec: scan origin, direction and duration are explicit
spatial and intensity mappings use independent sound dimensions
a non-audio image description accompanies the storyboard

meta.output: a storyboard for an image sonification

nodes.title: Find the shifted line
nodes.description: Design reference cues that make two emission spectra comparable by ear.
spec: wavelength and flux transformations are documented
the reference cue does not obscure the measured lines
listeners answer a defined comparison question

nodes.title: Make uncertainty audible
nodes.description: Compare error voices, roughness and explicit gaps on one light curve.
spec: missing data is distinct from a measured zero
the uncertainty channel can be switched off for comparison
the prototype includes the original values and error fields

meta.output: an uncertainty prototype with a recognition result

nodes.title: Design without sound
nodes.description: Ensure the scientific task remains possible through text, table and visual channels.
spec: every transport control works with a keyboard
no scientific fact is available only through sound
motion, playback and volume remain user controlled

meta.output: a multimodal access audit and revision

nodes.title: The honesty audit
nodes.description: Identify where an instrument's musical framing may overstate its evidence.
spec: every cleaning and scaling operation is listed
compositional additions are labelled as additions
one potentially misleading choice is removed or defended

meta.output: a completed disclosure checklist and revised prototype

nodes.title: Open the listening room
nodes.description: Run the final instrument with public listeners and capture evidence for one revision.
spec: a first-time visitor can begin and stop without assistance
source, mapping, uncertainty and non-audio representation are visible
feedback answers the stated scientific listening task

meta.output: a public instrument and observed listening record

nodes.title: Cosmic Listening Instrument
nodes.description: Design, test and publish an interactive instrument that makes one astronomical pattern audible and accountable.
spec: the public URL works without a login in current Chrome at desktop and phone widths
a listener can inspect source values, mapping, uncertainty and all processing
play, pause or stop and the primary exploration path work by keyboard
the scientific task remains possible without audio
the submission includes evidence from at least five first-time users

nodes.title: Listening Notebook
nodes.description: Four compact experiments that establish a vocabulary for source, mapping and listening evidence.
spec: four entries of 250–350 words are combined in one accessible PDF or web page
every entry includes data values, a reconstructable mapping rule and a non-audio representation
sources, software and assistance are attributed

nodes.title: Pulsar Signal Study
nodes.description: Analyse one periodic radio signal and defend the transformations used to make its timing audible.
spec: the selected pulsar, catalogue record, period and data source are identified
raw-timing and folded-profile renderings are included and clearly distinguished
a 900–1200 word study explains processing, mapping and limitations

nodes.title: Sonification Critique
nodes.description: Audit a published astronomical sonification by reconstructing its mapping and testing its claim.
spec: the chosen work uses astronomical data and has a citable public source
the critique separates source features from processing and musical additions
a 1200–1500 word accessible document includes one concrete redesign

nodes.title: Can space be heard?
nodes.description: Separate physical sound, electromagnetic measurement and designed sonification.

meta.question: What exactly are we hearing when an astronomical dataset becomes sound?

nodes.title: From telescope to speaker
nodes.description: Follow a measurement through calibration, reduction, representation and playback.

meta.question: Which transformations happen before a telescope measurement reaches a listener?

nodes.title: Mapping numbers to sound
nodes.description: Design and compare mappings across pitch, loudness, timbre, time and stereo position.

meta.question: When does a sonic mapping preserve an order, difference or pattern in the data?

nodes.title: The clocks of pulsars
nodes.description: Use periodic radio pulses to distinguish audification from musical quantisation.

meta.question: How can timing reveal a pulsar without turning its regularity into a beat fiction?

nodes.title: The noisy Sun
nodes.description: Hear bursts, baselines and interference without treating every spike as a solar event.

meta.question: How do we distinguish a solar radio event from noise, interference and instrument drift?

nodes.title: The gravitational-wave chirp
nodes.description: Reconstruct why a compact-binary signal rises in frequency and how it enters hearing.

meta.question: Why does a gravitational-wave event sound like a chirp, and which parts are transformed?

nodes.title: Listening to light
nodes.description: Traverse an astronomical image while keeping spatial position and intensity legible.

meta.question: What can an image scan communicate when the listener cannot see the source image?

nodes.title: Spectra, colour and redshift
nodes.description: Translate spectral lines while preserving wavelength, intensity and scale.

meta.question: Can a listener compare spectra without confusing wavelength with musical harmony?

nodes.title: Noise, gaps and uncertainty
nodes.description: Make missing samples and confidence limits part of the listening experience.

meta.dataObject: light curve with error bars and gaps

nodes.title: Accessibility beyond the graph
nodes.description: Treat sonification as one coordinated representation, not an automatic accessibility fix.

meta.question: Who gains and who is excluded when sound becomes the primary representation?

nodes.title: When sonification lies
nodes.description: Audit aesthetic choices, omitted values and suggestive musical framing.

meta.question: At what point does a compelling listening experience become a misleading scientific claim?

nodes.title: The cosmic listening room
nodes.description: Present a public instrument, invite structured listening and defend every transformation.

meta.question: Can a public listener understand both the astronomical pattern and how its sound was made?

course.title: Via Negativa: Practices of Subtraction
course.description: A studio in what disciplines gain by leaving something out: twelve weeks moving from apophatic theology and literati ink painting to film editing, minimalist design and the null hypothesis, each week asking what the cut was for. Practice-based, discussion-heavy, and suspicious of its own restraint.

nodes.title: Orientation
nodes.description: The first seminar --- no assigned cuts to argue over yet, just the semester's ground rules and a warm-up exercise in noticing them

nodes.title: Painting and silence
nodes.description: Putting Ni Zan's blank silk next to Cage's rest --- do two disciplines' favourite omissions actually argue the same thing?

nodes.title: The cut
nodes.description: A screening-room seminar --- watching the same scene continuity-cut and montage-cut, then walking Pawson's monastery on video

nodes.title: The limits of restraint
nodes.description: The closing seminar --- pitching final-project arguments to the room and pressure-testing them against the semester's own counter-examples

nodes.title: The null result
nodes.description: A seminar built around a real file-drawer case study, and a working session for "A Practice in Subtraction," due at the end of next week

nodes.title: The sentence not written
nodes.description: Arguing Hemingway's and Lish's cuts against each other, and workshopping Commonplace Books due at the end of this same week

nodes.title: A Practice in Subtraction
nodes.description: A studio piece, in a medium of your choosing, built around one deliberate and defensible omission
spec: a finished piece in one medium, plus a written defence of at least 300 words
the defence names the specific thing left out and argues why leaving it out was the harder, better decision than including it

nodes.title: Commonplace Book of Cuts
nodes.description: A running collection of omissions you noticed in the wild, kept from week one and submitted at the end of week five
spec: at least 8 dated entries, spanning at least 4 different disciplines
every entry names a specific, locatable instance --- not a general claim about a whole genre or field

marking.description: Marked on the range and specificity of what you noticed, not on volume --- eight well-argued entries from genuinely different domains outperform twenty samey ones. Each entry needs the omission named precisely enough that another reader could go find it, plus one to three sentences on what it cost and what it bought. An entry that only asserts a cut without pointing at a specific, checkable instance of it will be marked down.

nodes.title: The Argument by Omission
nodes.description: The final project --- a piece of persuasive writing, design or media whose force depends on something it deliberately never says
spec: a persuasive piece in any medium, plus a 600-1000 word critical commentary
the commentary names the specific omission the argument depends on and engages at least three weeks of the semester's material by name
the commentary directly addresses week 12's counter-case --- why this particular omission earns its keep rather than merely hiding a weak spot

nodes.title: Via negativa
nodes.description: The opening lecture — the thesis for the whole semester, stated once, and the case for taking a course built entirely out of other people's cuts

nodes.title: The apophatic turn
nodes.description: Pseudo-Dionysius, Maimonides and the Cloud of Unknowing --- a tradition that got more precise about God by refusing every positive sentence about him

nodes.title: Blank silk
nodes.description: Yuan-dynasty ink painting and the unpainted ground --- what a scroll's empty silk is doing when it's doing more than half the composition

nodes.title: The rest
nodes.description: Silence as a compositional element, from the rest on a stave to Cage's four minutes and thirty-three seconds of nothing being played on purpose

nodes.title: The iceberg theory
nodes.description: Hemingway's "the dignity of movement of an iceberg" and the minimalist fiction that took the metaphor as a literal compositional method

nodes.title: The invisible cut
nodes.description: Continuity editing and the century-long project of making a cut feel like it never happened --- and what's lost when it succeeds too well

nodes.title: Negative space
nodes.description: What a building or a page does with the room it refuses to fill, from Pawson's monastery to a logo that draws an arrow out of two letters

nodes.title: Less is a verb
nodes.description: Dieter Rams's ten principles, Bauhaus functionalism, and the difference between a design that removed something and one that never had it

nodes.title: The null result
nodes.description: Why "we found nothing" is the hardest sentence in science to publish, and what a discipline loses when it only keeps its positive results

nodes.title: Proof by elimination
nodes.description: Occam's razor, reductio ad absurdum, and a mathematics tradition that treats the shortest correct proof as a mark of taste, not just economy

nodes.title: The unsaid argument
nodes.description: Redacted documents, unpriced externalities and the political speech that persuades by what it declines to mention

nodes.title: What this course left out
nodes.description: The closing lecture, turning eleven weeks of praising subtraction back on itself --- what does the thesis conveniently fail to explain?

course.title: Designing Things People Hate
course.description: Interfaces, objects and systems shape behaviour on purpose. This course teaches you to read that design, build it deliberately badly, test whether the bad version actually works, then fix it.

nodes.title: The Hate Wall
nodes.description: The first session — a quick orientation, then the class's first pass at naming what actually makes something hateable
spec: you arrive with three things you already hate using, each named specifically enough that a stranger could recognise it
for each one, you can point to the exact moment it turns from fine to frustrating
all three examples are added to the class's shared Hate Catalogue by the end of the session

nodes.title: Follow the Incentive

nodes.title: Make Me Click It

you have translated one entry from a plain complaint into a claim about a specific mechanism
your Hate Catalogue is submitted as Assessment 1 by the due date

nodes.title: Dark Pattern Detective
nodes.description: Naming the dark arts — confirmshaming, forced continuity, bait-and-switch — and what behaviour each one is actually trying to produce

you have found examples the class has not already flagged

nodes.title: Make It Worse
nodes.description: The semester's first build — take a working interface and make it significantly worse, without breaking it
spec: your redesign still functions end to end — nothing is actually broken
you can name the specific friction you introduced (cognitive load, hidden information, ambiguity, unnecessary decisions, waiting, harder error recovery) for each change
you can state, in one sentence per change, what behaviour you expect it to produce

nodes.title: Friction Lab
nodes.description: Not all difficulty is equal — redesigning one task three ways and comparing what each version costs the user. Assessment 2 is due this week
spec: you have a low-friction, an annoying, and an extremely high-friction version of the same task
you can distinguish, for at least one version, useful friction from friction that only serves your assignment
The Worst Interface is submitted by the due date

nodes.title: Hostile Object Safari
nodes.description: Leaving the screen — doors, chairs, packaging and vending machines that tell you the wrong thing about how to use them
spec: you document five physical objects, each with what it looks like you should do and what you actually have to do
at least one of your five is not a door (doors are the easy answer)
you can explain, for each, why the gap is confusing rather than just inconvenient

nodes.title: The Maze
nodes.description: A single objective — change your address — buried inside a process built from conflicting instructions and repeated forms
spec: you attempt the objective as given, before reading ahead to the analysis
you can point to the specific step where the process actually failed you, not just where it felt tedious
you can name what a beautiful interface on top of this process would not have fixed

nodes.title: Human Guinea Pigs
nodes.description: Testing whether your week-5 interface actually produces the frustration you designed it to. Hostile Design Experiment due this week
spec: you test your week-5 interface on at least one participant who was not told what is being measured
you record what you predicted versus what actually happened, including anything the participant did that you did not anticipate
the Hostile Design Experiment is submitted by the due date

nodes.title: Defend the Indefensible
nodes.description: Is bad design actually bad? Each student defends a hated design from the Hate Catalogue as if it were good
spec: you are assigned a design you did not originally submit to the Hate Catalogue
you argue in its favour even where you personally still find it frustrating
you can name at least one legitimate goal the design might actually be serving

nodes.title: Redemption Studio
nodes.description: Returning to your original bad system to fix it, without destroying whatever legitimate goal it was actually serving
spec: your redesign names what the user needs, what the organisation needs, and the constraint that produced the original problem
you present before, why it was bad, what caused it, the redesign, and what changed, in that order
a peer's critique of your redesign is recorded, not just delivered

nodes.title: The Worst Design Awards
nodes.description: Final presentations, run as an awards ceremony. The Redemption Project is due this week
spec: your Redemption Project is presented in a category the class has agreed on
you can answer, on the spot, what makes your chosen system genuinely bad
The Redemption Project is submitted by the due date

nodes.title: Hate Catalogue
nodes.description: Five examples of design that make people miserable, picked apart until you can say exactly why each one works
spec: the catalogue contains exactly five entries, each with a photo or screenshot and roughly 150–250 words of analysis
every entry names the user's goal, the specific problem, a likely stakeholder, a suspected reason it might be deliberate, and the mechanism doing the damage
at least two of the five entries come from something you noticed yourself, not an example already circulating online
the catalogue closes with a reflection naming a pattern that shows up more than once across the five entries

nodes.title: Hostile Design Experiment
nodes.description: Running your worst interface on real people, then finding out if it actually did what you designed it to do
spec: you test on 3–5 participants, none of whom are told what's actually being measured
your report states a specific research question before you present any results
you compare what you predicted in Assessment 2 against what participants actually did
the report runs roughly 800–1,000 words and is honest about what surprised you, not just what confirmed the theory

criteria.name: Analysis of the gap between prediction and result

nodes.title: The Redemption Project
nodes.description: Autopsy, defence, evidence and a redesign of one real system you actually hate, argued in that order
spec: it stands on its own, without you there to present it
all five parts are present — autopsy, defence, experiment, redesign, defence of the redesign
the redesign is argued to be better, not just different, with evidence from your own testing
the written report runs roughly 1,500–2,000 words, and the live presentation compresses it to what it was, why it existed, what the evidence showed, and what you changed

marking.description: Judged as a whole against the brief — whether the autopsy correctly identifies the mechanism, whether the defence takes the original design's goals seriously rather than strawmanning them, whether the experiment produces real evidence about the original system, whether the redesign keeps the original's legitimate goals intact, and whether the final defence argues convincingly that the new version is actually better, not just nicer to look at.

nodes.title: The Worst Interface
nodes.description: A working interface you make deliberately worse on purpose, with the receipts for exactly why
spec: the interaction you redesign is an ordinary one (checkout, booking, subscription, cancellation, or similar) and still works end to end
you name one specific hostile goal before you change anything, and every design decision serves that goal
the 600–800 word write-up explains what you changed, why you expect each change to work, and which course concepts back it up
the original or a neutral baseline is included so a marker can compare it directly against your redesign

nodes.title: What Makes You Hate Something?
nodes.description: The opening lecture — why looking ugly and working badly are two different problems, and which one this course spends the semester on

meta.coverImageAlt: A ceramic mug cracked into a frowning face, leaking coffee onto the counter, next to the note "Looks fine. Works terribly."

nodes.title: The User Is Not the Customer
nodes.description: Why a system can work great for whoever pays for it and badly for whoever is stuck using it — and why "bad design" always has to name who it's bad for

meta.coverImageAlt: A crossroads signpost with arrows pointing to Business, Users, Shareholders, Designers and Society, next to the note "Different goals. Different experiences."

nodes.description: How defaults, fake scarcity and social proof quietly steer decisions you thought you made yourself

nodes.title: The Dark Arts of Interface Design
nodes.description: The dark patterns get names so you can spot them — but naming one is the easy part, not the useful part

course.title: Edible Matter: Thermodynamics, Transport and Soft-Matter Physics in the Chinese Kitchen
course.description: A third-year elective treating Chinese cooking as applied soft-matter physics. Across four stages, students measure, model and redesign real food systems (dough, gels, emulsions, crisp skins) using the same rheology, transport and thermodynamics used to characterise any soft material.

nodes.title: What Is Edible Matter?
nodes.description: Framing the course's central claim — a food's texture is a measurable material property, not a matter of taste. Anchored on tapioca pearls.
spec: state, in one sentence, what "QQ" (Q弹) texture means as a physical property
name the four material regimes a cooked food can occupy (fluid, viscoelastic solid, amorphous glass, crystalline/semi-crystalline solid) and give a Chinese food example of each
explain why "chewy" is not one property but at least two (elasticity and toughness)

nodes.title: Rheology I: Flow Behaviour
nodes.description: Why doubanjiang has to be pushed before it flows, and honey doesn't — Newtonian, power-law and Herschel-Bulkley models of shear flow.
spec: write the Herschel-Bulkley equation and identify which term is the yield stress
given a flow curve, say whether a fluid is shear-thinning, shear-thickening, or Newtonian
explain why "viscosity" is not a single number for most food pastes

nodes.title: Thermal Characterisation
nodes.description: Reading a braise as a heat-and-transition budget — specific heat, latent heat of transition, and what a thermal signature tells you about pork belly.
spec: distinguish sensible heat from latent heat of transition in a worked example
explain what a differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) trace shows and why a peak, not a point, marks a transition
identify two distinct thermal transitions that happen during a long braise

nodes.title: Polymer Networks I: Starch Gels
nodes.description: How liangpi goes from a pourable starch slurry to a sliceable sheet — gelatinisation, retrogradation, and the degree-of-gelatinisation model.
spec: explain gelatinisation and retrogradation as two distinct, sequential processes
define degree of gelatinisation and say what a partially-gelatinised sample implies for texture
name one variable (besides temperature) that changes how a starch gel sets

nodes.title: Protein Aggregation and Gelation
nodes.description: The moment soy milk becomes tofu — percolation, the gel point, and the Winter-Chambon criterion for when a liquid becomes a solid network.
spec: state the Winter-Chambon criterion for locating a gel point
explain what "percolation" means for a network of aggregating protein particles
say why the gel point is a moment, not a texture, and why that distinction matters

nodes.title: Colloids and Emulsions
nodes.description: Why a long-simmered bone broth turns milky and stays that way — Stokes' law and what actually stabilises a food emulsion.
spec: write Stokes' law for creaming velocity and identify which variable is easiest to control in a kitchen
explain why droplet size matters more than density difference for a stable food emulsion
state one reason Stokes' law is only an approximation for a real broth

nodes.title: Heat and Mass Transport
nodes.description: Why a xiaolongbao's filling is still cold when its wrapper is done — Fourier's law, the Biot number, and simultaneous heat and moisture transport.
spec: write Fourier's law for one-dimensional conduction and name each term
use the Biot number to decide whether a lumped (uniform-temperature) model is valid for a given food object
explain why steaming transfers both heat and moisture to a dumpling, not heat alone

nodes.title: Reaction Kinetics
nodes.description: Why Peking duck skin browns faster at a higher oven temperature than the temperature difference alone would suggest — the Arrhenius equation.
spec: write the Arrhenius equation and explain what activation energy controls
explain why a small increase in cooking temperature can cause a large increase in browning rate
compare the temperature-sensitivity of two different food reactions using the same model

nodes.title: Phase Transitions in Cooking
nodes.description: What actually happens inside a youtiao as it deep-fries — a moving moisture front and a crust crossing its glass transition.
spec: describe the two zones (crust, moist core) that form inside a piece of dough during frying and why a boundary moves between them
explain what a glass transition is and why crossing it is what makes a fried crust rigid
name the two variables a Gordon-Taylor-style model links for a food glass transition

nodes.title: Building Predictive Models
nodes.description: Fitting the Virtual Rheometer's models to noisy data — least squares, residuals, and how to tell a good model fit from a lucky one.
spec: explain what a residual is and what a residual-vs-shear-rate plot can reveal that R² alone cannot
state why fitting the Herschel-Bulkley model to Newtonian data does not, by itself, prove doubanjiang has a yield stress
use the Virtual Rheometer to fit at least two candidate models to the same specimen and justify picking one

nodes.title: The Crispness Design Space
nodes.description: Mapping temperature and moisture onto glassy, rubbery, crisp and softened regions — the state diagram behind why crackers go stale.
spec: locate a food's crisp region on a temperature-versus-moisture state diagram and explain why it is bounded on two sides
explain why a cracker left in humid air softens even at constant room temperature
use the Crispness Phase Diagram instrument to compare two specimens' stability margins

nodes.title: Inverse Material Design
nodes.description: Given a target texture, work backward through the course's models to choose a formulation and process — the capstone design problem.
spec: state the difference between a forward model (predict outcome from process) and an inverse problem (choose process from target outcome)
identify which two prior modules' models are needed to solve a stated crispness-shelf-life design target
propose a formulation or process change and justify it by tracing back through the specific equation it acts on

nodes.title: Inverse Material Design Project
nodes.description: The capstone — pose and solve an inverse design problem for a real Chinese food material, using the course's models run backward.
spec: submitted by the deadline as a single PDF, 2,500–3,500 words excluding references and appendices
states one specific, measurable target outcome with a tolerance, not a texture word alone
names the forward model(s) inverted and the free variables acted on, tracing back to specific equations

marking.description: Judged as a whole against the brief, with particular weight on whether the stated target outcome is genuinely measurable, whether the chosen forward models are appropriate to invert for it, and whether the submission is honest about where its inverted answer is a tested hypothesis rather than a guaranteed specification.

nodes.title: Laboratory Portfolio
nodes.description: A portfolio built from both virtual instruments plus two supplied-dataset analyses, demonstrating fitting, interpretation and honest provenance.
spec: submitted by the deadline as a single PDF portfolio with four labelled sections
includes at least one screenshot or exported figure from each of the two instruments
both supplied datasets are analysed with a stated method, not eyeballed

criteria.name: Virtual Rheometer task — model choice, fit quality, residuals
Crispness Phase Diagram task — state interpretation, stability margin
Assumptions and data provenance stated throughout

nodes.title: Material Characterisation Report
nodes.description: A short written report characterising one real Chinese food material using the thermal or mechanical models built in Stage 1.
spec: submitted by the deadline as a PDF report, 1,200–1,800 words excluding references
names one governing model from Modules 1–3 and states why it fits the chosen material
every reported value is labelled as measured, literature-derived, or illustrative

criteria.name: Correct use of a governing model from Stage 1
Honest treatment of assumptions and uncertainty
Clarity — units, variable definitions, labelled figures
Use of real, cited sources or clearly labelled illustrative values

nodes.title: Modelling Problem Sets
nodes.description: A set of worked problems applying the transport, kinetics and phase- transition models from Stages 2 and 3 to new numbers.
spec: submitted by the deadline as a single PDF with working shown for every problem
every numeric answer states its units
at least one problem's answer includes a stated assumption or limitation

criteria.name: Correct application of the relevant model
Discussion of sensitivity, limits, or edge cases

nodes.title: Opening Lecture: Why Treat Food as a Material
nodes.description: The course's central claim — texture is a measurable material property — and how the four-stage curriculum builds toward testing it.

nodes.title: Rheology I: Flow Behaviour
nodes.description: In-class walkthrough of Newtonian, power-law and Herschel-Bulkley flow — reading a flow curve to tell "thick" apart from "won't move until pushed."

nodes.title: Thermal Characterisation
nodes.description: Closing Stage 1 with the thermal toolkit — sensible heat, latent heat of transition, and reading a calorimetry trace as a two-transition story.

nodes.title: Stage 2 Overview: From Flow to Structure
nodes.description: Why the course moves from measuring behaviour to explaining it, and how a network's connectivity — not just its ingredients — sets a gel's texture.

nodes.title: Protein Aggregation and Gelation
nodes.description: Watching soy milk become tofu as a percolation event — the gel point as a moment in time, not a texture, and the Winter-Chambon criterion for it.

nodes.title: Colloids and Emulsions
nodes.description: Why a simmered broth turns milky and stays that way — Stokes' law, droplet size, and closing Stage 2's run of network-and-dispersion structures.

nodes.title: Stage 3 Overview: Transport, Kinetics and Transformation
nodes.description: Why cooking is best modelled as three coupled processes — heat and mass transport, reaction kinetics, and phase transition — not one vague "heat."

nodes.title: Reaction Kinetics
nodes.description: Why a small rise in oven temperature browns Peking duck skin much faster than the temperature difference alone suggests — the Arrhenius equation.

nodes.title: Phase Transitions in Cooking
nodes.description: What happens inside a youtiao as it deep-fries — a moving moisture front and a crust crossing its glass transition, closing Stage 3.

nodes.title: Stage 4 Overview: Prediction, Design, and the Crispness Deep-Dive
nodes.description: How Stage 4 turns Stage 3's models into predictions and then a design tool, with a full lecture on crispness as a metastable material state.

nodes.title: The Crispness Design Space
nodes.description: Turning Module 9's glass transition into a map — temperature and moisture bounding a crisp region on two sides, and why a cracker in humid air softens.

nodes.title: Inverse Material Design
nodes.description: The capstone design problem — given a target texture, work backward through the course's models to choose a formulation and a process.

course.title: Metamath 101
course.description: Metamath from nothing: the language, the programs that check it, the set.mm database, and proving in mmj2. Twelve weeks of lectures and labs, ending in a proof verifier you wrote yourself.

nodes.title: Install and verify
nodes.description: Get metamath-exe and mmj2 running on your own machine, download set.mm, and watch a verifier check every proof in it.
spec: metamath-exe starts on your machine and reads set.mm without error
`verify proof *` runs over set.mm and reports no errors
mmj2 starts, loads set.mm, and opens its Proof Assistant window

nodes.title: Read a small database, write a smaller one
nodes.description: Read miu.mm and peano.mm line by line, then write a database of about ten lines by hand and get a verifier to accept it.
spec: you can name each statement type in miu.mm and say what it declares
your own database of about ten lines reads into metamath-exe and passes `verify proof *`
it declares its constants and variables, states one axiom, and proves one theorem from it

nodes.title: First proof
nodes.description: The first proving lab: build a short propositional-logic proof in mmj2's Proof Assistant, unify it, and see the verifier accept it. This lab counts toward the lab-proof mark.
spec: your worksheet for the theorem handed out at the start unifies in mmj2 with no errors
every step cites a hypothesis, an axiom or an earlier theorem of set.mm by label
the worksheet is submitted by 5pm on Friday, as the lab proofs page says

nodes.title: Navigate and prove
nodes.description: Find a theorem in the Proof Explorer and read its proof step by step, then prove a propositional theorem of your own in mmj2 with set.mm loaded.
spec: you can open the assigned theorem's page in the Proof Explorer and name the axiom or earlier theorem each essential step applies
your proof of this week's assigned theorem verifies in mmj2 with no errors
the proof is submitted as the file mmj2 saved, before the deadline on the lab proofs page

nodes.title: mmj2 in depth
nodes.description: How mmj2 unifies a step, what a work variable is for, and how to grow a proof worksheet one step at a time until a theorem that needs several steps verifies.
spec: your proof of this week's assigned theorem, which needs several essential steps, verifies in mmj2 with no errors
the worksheet you submit has no work variables left in it
for one step of your proof you can show which earlier steps its hypotheses unified with, and what was substituted for each variable

nodes.title: Distinct variables
nodes.description: Prove a theorem whose proof needs a $d condition, then remove the condition and read the error the verifier reports.
spec: your proof of this week's assigned theorem verifies in mmj2 with no errors and carries the $d statements it needs
you can show the error metamath-exe reports when one of those $d statements is removed, and name the step and the axiom the message cites
your submission says, in one sentence, which substitution the removed $d was forbidding

nodes.title: A definition that fails
nodes.description: Add a definition to a copy of set.mm, run mmj2's definition check, watch it reject one, and fix it. The corrected definition starts your definition exercise.
spec: the definition check runs on your copy of set.mm with the recommended exclusions, and you kept its report
your own definition, added to that copy, fails the check at least once, and you kept that report too
your corrected definition passes the check, and one theorem about it verifies in mmj2 with no errors

nodes.title: Prove in iset.mm
nodes.description: The same theorem proved against set.mm and then iset.mm, to see where a classical proof needs excluded middle. Then the verifier project check-in: where your verifier should be by now.
spec: your proof of the chosen theorem verifies in mmj2 against set.mm with no errors
the same statement verifies against iset.mm, or you have named the step that needs excluded middle and the closest iset.mm replacement from the cross reference
your verifier runs on peano.mm at the check-in, and you can say which of the tests named that morning it passes

nodes.title: A longer proof
nodes.description: Plan a proof that needs several lemmas before typing any of it, then prove the lemmas in order in mmj2 and verify the whole file in metamath-exe.
spec: your plan names the target theorem and every lemma as a Metamath statement, and the tutor checked it before you typed a proof
each lemma's proof and the final proof verify in mmj2 with no errors
the file holding them passes `verify proof *` in metamath-exe with no errors, and you can say which axioms the final theorem depends on

nodes.title: Read MM0 against Metamath
nodes.description: Read the Metamath Zero translation of set.mm's axioms beside the axioms themselves, line by line, and say what each file states that the other leaves out.
spec: for each of ax-1, ax-2, ax-3 and ax-mp in set.mm you can point to the line of set.mm0 that states it
your half-page names two differences between the two files, each with a line from each file beside it
your week 10 lab proof verifies in mmj2 with no errors and is submitted by Friday

nodes.title: Verify a machine-found proof by hand
nodes.description: Take a short propositional proof found by exhaustive search, check every step on paper, then check it in mmj2 and with mmverify.py. The last lab that counts toward lab proofs.
spec: your hand check lists every step of the chosen proof with the axiom it applies and the statement it produces, ending in the file's "Result of proof"
the same proof, entered in mmj2 in a database whose only axioms are ax-1, ax-2, ax-3 and ax-mp, verifies with no errors
mmverify.py run on that database reports no errors

nodes.title: Retrospective
nodes.description: Demonstrate your verifier on peano.mm and on a file you have not seen, then show one proof from the semester. The last lab; the verifier project is due this week.
spec: your verifier runs in the lab on peano.mm and on the tutor's file, and gives the same pass or fail verdict as mmverify.py on each
you show one proof you wrote this semester and say, in a minute, what it proves and why you chose it
your verifier project is submitted by the time on its assessment page

nodes.title: The definition exercise
nodes.description: Write a definition, break it, and explain what the definition check caught. Set in week 7, due at the end of week 8.
spec: a definition of your own that passes mmj2's definition check in the database the lab names
a second version of it that fails the check, submitted alongside
a write-up of no more than 500 words saying what the check found and what would have gone wrong without it

criteria.name: The good definition passes the check
The bad definition fails it, and you can say why

nodes.title: Lab proofs
nodes.description: Nine weekly proofs, weeks 3 to 11, each due on the Friday of its week. The best eight count, and a proof counts when the verifier accepts it.
spec: each proof verifies in mmj2, against the database the lab names, with no errors
each proof is submitted as the file the lab names, by 5pm on the Friday of its week
the best eight of the nine proofs count, each for one eighth of the mark

nodes.title: The verifier project
nodes.description: Write your own Metamath verifier, in a language of your choice, and have it marked against a test suite the course provides. Set in week 5, due at the end of week 12; full details to follow.
spec: a verifier written by you, in a language other than C, C++, Rust, Java or Python, that reads a Metamath database and reports whether every proof in it is correct
it passes the core tests of the suite the course provides
it is shown running at the week 8 lab check-in, against the tests the check-in names
a short report on how you tested it

marking.description: Marked against a test suite the course provides, with bonus marks for features beyond the core. The suite and the marking scheme are published when the project is set in week 5.

nodes.title: What Metamath is, and where it lives
nodes.description: Metamath in the project's own words: the language, the website and its mirrors, the licence, the GitHub organisation, and three unrelated projects that share the name.

nodes.title: The language
nodes.description: What a .mm file is made of: the four-page specification in the Metamath book, a condensed introduction, two machine-readable grammars, and the $j annotations that tools read.

nodes.title: Verification
nodes.description: What a verifier does, the five verifiers that check every change to set.mm and the workflow that runs them, the conformance suites, and how many more verifiers exist.

nodes.title: set.mm and the Proof Explorer
nodes.description: The set.mm database, the web pages generated from it, the theorem list as its table of contents, how it cites books, and where its history is kept.

nodes.title: Proof assistants
nodes.description: The tools a student proves with — mmj2, metamath-lamp, Yamma, mmt1, metamath-exe's own assistant — and how they differ from the verifier you will write.

nodes.title: The axioms, and the metalogic behind $d
nodes.description: Where set.mm's axioms come from, why its statements are schemes rather than theorems, what a distinct-variable condition is, and the results and open problems around them.

nodes.title: Definitions and soundness
nodes.description: A Metamath definition is an axiom to the verifier, so a wrong one can make the database inconsistent without any proof failing. What the extra check is and which tool runs it.

nodes.title: Other databases
nodes.description: The Metamath databases beside set.mm: intuitionistic logic, higher-order logic, New Foundations, quantum logic, Peano arithmetic, the MIU system, Laws of Form, and the third-party ones on GitHub.

nodes.title: Formalisation in practice
nodes.description: What large Metamath proofs cost, from the ones that exist: GCH implies AC, the prime number theorem, Bertrand's postulate, a proof done on video, legibility research, and the 100 theorems scoreboard.

nodes.title: Descendants, translations and comparisons
nodes.description: The languages that grew out of Metamath, the programs that carry proofs into and out of it, and one published comparison that sets it beside sixteen other provers.

nodes.title: Machine learning on Metamath
nodes.description: The papers that trained programs to find Metamath proofs, in order from 2016 to 2025, the datasets and tools built for them, and a name collision to know about.

nodes.title: Miscellanea
nodes.description: The pieces that fit nowhere else: the Solitaire applet, the shortest Principia proofs, open problems, where the community talks, meetings, a video, the GitHub organisation, and one paragraph of history.

nodes.title: Noor Castellane

course.title: Meets Expectations: Surviving the Performance Review
course.description: A semester on how tech companies rate, rank and cut their staff, taught as the survival guide nobody gives graduates. Learn the tricks, learn why they work and who pays for them, then design a review that can't be gamed.

nodes.title: Welcome to calibration

nodes.title: Calibration
nodes.description: Your group's calibration meeting on the Assessment 2 packets, and the one page afterwards that explains the result using only what the room did.
spec: you posted your prediction by Wednesday midnight, in terms of the room and not the packets
you argued for your engineer in the room from the case you wrote, or you chaired it and kept the record; that is pass or fail
the room fitted its proposals to the curve for its size, and the record shows every move
the page is under 500 words and every claim about the room matches the chair's record
the page names at least three mechanisms, each tied to a record entry and a week
the page quotes your prediction, states the outcome, and explains the gap
the page names one change in the room that would have moved the below

criteria.name: The record. What happened, and it matches the chair's sheet
The mechanisms. At least three, each tied to a record entry and a week
The prediction and the gap. What you predicted, what happened, and why they differ
The counterfactual. One change in the room that moves the below to someone else

bands.expectation: The record has no errors against the chair's sheet. Three or more mechanisms each point at a specific entry and a week, and at least one is not the obvious one about speaking first. The gap paragraph says which mechanism beat the one you expected. The counterfactual is a single concrete change in the room, and a reader can see why it would move the below.

The record is accurate. Three mechanisms are named and tied to entries, but they overlap or one is thin. The gap is described rather than explained. The counterfactual is plausible but not tied to a mechanism.

The record has one or two mismatches with the sheet. The mechanisms are named but the same one is used more than once. The prediction is quoted and the outcome stated with no account of the difference. The counterfactual is vague.

The record is partial. One mechanism carries the whole page. The gap section says only that the prediction was right or wrong. The counterfactual changes a packet rather than the room, which is the one rule the page has.
Missed the room, which is the gate. Or a page that argues the ratings were wrong rather than explaining why they came out as they did. Or no prediction was posted before the room.

nodes.title: The manager's case
