spec: the case is for the engineer you were assigned, and page one opens with a proposed rating and the curve
page one has three claims, each pointing at one item in the packet and naming its evidence type
page one is 450 words or fewer
page two names every item you do not believe, by week, with what it would take to check it
page two ends with the rating you would give if everything checked out, and the gap

criteria.name: The proposed rating is argued from the packet, each claim tied to a named source
The tricks in the packet are found and named by week
What it would take to check each one is specific and checkable
Page one reads in two minutes, and page two is honest about the gap

bands.expectation: Every claim on page one points at one item in the packet and says which kind of evidence it is. Page two finds every trick the packet holds, names each by week, does not mistake a real achievement for one, and says exactly what would be needed to check it. The last paragraph states the gap between the two ratings and why the first was still proposed.

Page one argues from the packet with one claim that leans on the self-review without saying so. Page two finds most of the tricks and names them correctly; one check is vague. The gap is stated but not explained.

Page one is a case, but two of its three claims come from the same source. Page two finds the obvious trick and misses or misnames another, or calls a genuine result a trick. The gap paragraph gives the same rating twice without saying why.
Page one restates the self-review. Page two lists doubts without weeks or without saying what would resolve them. There is a rating on each page and no account of the difference.
Page one is over 450 words or could not be read in two minutes. Page two is missing, empty, or calls everything a trick. Or the case is for the wrong engineer.

nodes.title: Stand-up attendance

the best ten of your twelve marks count, scaled to ten percent of the course
the tutor records the mark in the room and it is not revisited afterwards

criteria.name: You were in the room when the stand-up started
You brought what the week's Bring section asked for

bands.expectation: On time with the item at ten or more stand-ups, or the equivalent in half marks.
Nine good weeks, or ten with the item forgotten once or twice.
Seven or eight good weeks.
Five or six good weeks.
Fewer than five. If something is going on, the extension rule on the policies page applies.

nodes.title: The self-review
nodes.description: Two pages about the same ordinary quarter: the self-review a manager could carry into calibration, and the honest version.
spec: one page in corporate register and one page in plain English, about the same work
page one names the rubric it uses and tags every accomplishment with a line of it
every number on page one is tagged C for checkable or E for estimated
page two is under 300 words, in second person, with no untagged number

criteria.name: Every claim on page one maps to a named rubric line
Every number is tagged checkable or estimated, and the checkable ones could be checked
Page two is honest, in second person, and shorter

bands.expectation: Every sentence on page one files under a named rubric line without help, every number carries a C or an E, and the C ones could be checked by a stranger. Page two is shorter, plain, and admits what page one inflated.
Page one maps cleanly with one or two lines a marker has to think about. Numbers are tagged and mostly plausible. Page two is honest but still borrows page one's register in places.
Most claims map. Some numbers are untagged, or an estimate is stretched past what anyone would defend. Page two is shorter but reads as a summary of page one rather than the truth about it.
The two pages exist and describe the same quarter, but the rubric mapping is partial, the numbers are unmarked, or page two is not honest, not shorter, or not in second person.
A single page, a remarkable quarter instead of an ordinary one, numbers with no tag at all, or a page two that is page one with the adjectives removed.

nodes.title: Design an ungameable review
nodes.description: Design a performance review system for the team whose packets you argued from. The rest of your group gets a week to beat it. Your mark depends on what it survives, what it does about the rater, and whether you named who pays.
spec: the design was posted by 9 am on Monday of week 12 and covers what is measured, who decides, and how evidence is gathered
the design has a front page with the three answers, and a trick table with a row for every week from 1 to 11
for every trick in weeks 1 to 11 the table says what it stands on and whether it is closed or conceded, and how
the design says what does calibration's job of reducing rater bias, or keeps calibration and says why
the design says how a rated person can contest a result, and who hears it
the justification names who pays under the design, using the weekly cost lines, and what the design gave up for it
the justification has a section called What beat it, and it is not empty

criteria.name: Coverage. Every trick from weeks 1 to 11 is placed, and closed or conceded
The rater. What replaces calibration, or why it stays
Contest. How a rating is disputed, and by whom
Who pays. The bill for each closure, using the weekly cost lines
Survival. What the attack week found, reported honestly

bands.expectation: Every trick from weeks 1 to 11 is placed and either closed with something it can no longer stand on or conceded by name. The front page answers the rater and contest questions with something the research would accept. The bill for every closure is named and lands on someone specific. The attack week found little, and the justification says exactly what it found.

Most tricks closed, the rest conceded. Both front-page answers present, one of them thin: a calibration meeting kept with no reason, or an appeal route with nobody to hear it. Costs named for most closures. The attack week's findings reported.

The trick table is complete but several closures are assertions. One front-page answer is missing, or amounts to trusting the manager. Costs are listed generically. The attack week's findings are mentioned but not engaged with.
A design and a justification exist, but the trick table has gaps, the front page is incomplete, or the justification claims trade-offs without saying who pays.
Claims nobody pays. No front page. Not posted by Monday, so nobody could attack it. Or over the limits by enough that the marker stops reading.

nodes.title: Welcome to calibration
nodes.description: What a calibration meeting is, who is in it, what the curve looks like, and why a company that knows a rating is mostly the rater still runs one.

meta.mechanism: Over half the variance in a rating is the rater, not the rated; calibration exists to squeeze that out, and it does so by giving your manager three minutes.

sources.title: Scullen, Mount and Goff, Understanding the latent structure of job performance ratings (Journal of Applied Psychology, 2000)
Speer, Tenbrink and Schwendeman, The effects of calibration meetings on performance ratings (Human Performance, 2019)
Buckingham and Goodall, Reinventing performance management (Harvard Business Review, 2015)
Vitality curve

Meta tells managers to rate 15 to 20 percent below expectations (People Matters, May 2025)

nodes.title: Rewarding A, hoping for B
nodes.description: Kerr, Goodhart, Campbell, and the model underneath all three. What happens to a measure once the people it measures know it is a target, and to the work the measure cannot count.

meta.mechanism: Pay for what you can count and people do the countable thing; the uncountable work is what the measure was for.

sources.title: Kerr, On the folly of rewarding A, while hoping for B (Academy of Management Journal, 1975)
Holmstrom and Milgrom, Multitask principal-agent analyses (Journal of Law, Economics, and Organization, 1991)
Goodhart's law
Campbell's law
Goodhart's law in engineering metrics

nodes.title: Who speaks for you
nodes.description: The cast of a calibration meeting, the peers you nominate, and two literatures: incentive theory on subjective evaluation, and the research on impression management.

meta.mechanism: Subjective evaluation rewards influence over the evaluator, and the research says being liked moves a rating further than being impressive.

sources.title: Prendergast, The provision of incentives in firms (Journal of Economic Literature, 1999)
Bolino, Kacmar, Turnley and Gilstrap, A multi-level review of impression management (Journal of Management, 2008)
Performance calibrations at tech companies (The Pragmatic Engineer)
The how and why of performance review calibration (Lattice)

nodes.title: The self-review as fiction
nodes.description: The brag document, the self-review, and Amazon's 2026 requirement that every corporate employee list three to five accomplishments with impact.

meta.mechanism: Self-ratings run half a standard deviation above the manager's, and the summary that reaches the room keeps the numbers and drops the sentences.

sources.title: Harris and Schaubroeck, A meta-analysis of self-supervisor, self-peer, and peer-supervisor ratings (Personnel Psychology, 1988)
Julia Evans, Get your work recognized: write a brag document
Amazon asks employees for a list of accomplishments (Fortune, January 2026)

nodes.title: Traces
nodes.description: Memory, numbers, self-review, and why memory wins. What a manager of ten can hold from a quarter, direct message against channel, and the line where a trace becomes theatre.

meta.mechanism: A manager's memory of your quarter is built from the traces that crossed their screen, and a private message leaves none.

sources.title: Julia Evans, Get your work recognized: write a brag document
Performance calibrations at tech companies (The Pragmatic Engineer)

nodes.title: Credit
nodes.description: Who reads what about a project, how a promotion packet is assembled from public associations, and what the research found when a mixed team's credit was left unassigned.

meta.mechanism: The announcement is the one artefact senior people read, and when a team result's source is ambiguous, credit goes by expectation, not contribution.

sources.title: Heilman and Haynes, No credit where credit is due (Journal of Applied Psychology, 2005)
Nemenman, Promotion-driven development
Performance calibrations at tech companies (The Pragmatic Engineer)

nodes.title: Promotion-driven development
nodes.description: Promotion packets, Google's product graveyard, the multitask model with a launch in it, and how to tell a rebuild the users needed from one the packet needed.

meta.mechanism: A packet counts launches; the multitask result says the countable task crowds out the rest, and maintenance is the rest.

sources.title: Holmstrom and Milgrom, Multitask principal-agent analyses (Journal of Law, Economics, and Organization, 1991)
Nemenman, Promotion-driven development
Yegge, Dear Google Cloud: your deprecation policy is killing you

nodes.title: Presence
nodes.description: Passive face time and the research behind it, the 2026 proxies that replaced the car park, and why this is a different week from week 5.

meta.mechanism: Being seen present triggers automatic inferences of "dependable" and "committed", and nobody who makes them knows they did.

sources.title: Elsbach, Cable and Sherman, How passive face time affects perceptions of employees (Human Relations, 2010)
Elsbach and Cable, Why showing your face at work matters (MIT Sloan Management Review, 2012)
Campbell's law

nodes.title: The reorg
nodes.description: What a restructure resets, the order a list is built in, dependency as the last filter, and the ceiling that strategy puts on the person using it.

meta.mechanism: A reorg resets every relationship a rating depended on; what survives is being the one person whose removal breaks something visible.

sources.title: Sucher and Gupta, Layoffs that don't break your company (Harvard Business Review, 2018)
How companies decide who to lay off and who to keep (Dice)

nodes.title: The rat race

nodes.title: Now you're the manager

course.title: Bread
course.description: Twelve weeks at the bench, one bread a week. Take each loaf apart — what the flour is doing, what the fermentation is doing, what the oven is doing — then bake it and find out whether the theory held.

marking.description: Marked as one bread against the brief you wrote, not against criteria. What a marker weighs most is the fit between the two: whether the thing on the bench is the thing you proposed, and whether you can name the structure holding it up, the schedule that got it there and what you asked the oven for. Ambition and execution trade against each other on purpose, so a hard bake with a visible flaw can outrank a safe one done cleanly. What sinks an otherwise competent bake is a showpiece that dodges every difficult decision, or a brief whose scope was never achievable between the proposal and the bake-off.

course.title: Buttons: Twelve Weeks of Pressing Things
course.description: A button is the smallest promise an interface makes: press me, and something will happen. This course spends twelve weeks taking that promise apart — its history, its timing, its psychology, its failures, and who benefits when you believe it.
learningOutcomes: Explain how a digital button inherits its meaning from a century of mechanical predecessors.
Analyse why an interface element reads as pressable, using the vocabulary of affordance and signifier, independent of visual style.
Design and build a button whose feedback timing and reward structure match the actual weight of the action it performs.
Identify a real manipulative button, rebuild an honest version of it, and name precisely what leverage was removed.
Test a single button across different bodies and reaches, and identify the exact point where the same push mechanism stops working for a hand that isn't yours.
Defend, in full technical and rhetorical detail, why one specific button deserves to be pressed.

nodes.title: The Button Before the Screen
nodes.description: Before a button was a rectangle on glass, it was a switch a stranger could find in the dark — a doorbell, an elevator call button, a pedestrian crossing button, a panic button.
spec: you have logged three physical buttons you pressed today, naming what each one is called, where it is, and the remote action it stands in for
each entry says what actually happens on the other end of the press, not just what the button looks like
you can state, without mentioning a screen, what a button is a device for

nodes.title: Translating the Push
nodes.description: What a physical button gives you for free — resistance, travel, a click, a physical return to its resting position — and what a digital button has to fake or simply do without.
spec: you have picked one button from your week 1 log and built a minimal digital version of it
you can name, for that specific button, every physical cue the digital version had to fake or drop — resistance, travel, click, physical return, tactile confirmation
the digital version gives some signal, however small, that the press registered

nodes.title: The Grammar of Pressable
nodes.description: How a shape earns the right to be pressed — affordance, signifier, convention, and invention — read off real interface elements that get it wrong in both directions.
spec: you have found one real interface element that is genuinely mis-clickable or visually ambiguous, with a screenshot or link
you have named which specific convention it violates — affordance, signifier, or established convention
you have proposed the smallest visual change that would fix it, without redesigning the whole element

nodes.title: What the Button Promises
nodes.description: Every button is a promise about what will happen next, somewhere between trivial and irreversible — and some buttons lie about which end of that scale they're on.
spec: you have picked five buttons from one real application and placed each on a reversible-to-irreversible axis
for each button you can say, in one sentence, what state actually changes when it is pressed
you have identified at least one button, from your five or elsewhere, whose visual or verbal presentation misrepresents how consequential it is

nodes.title: Feedback and the Length of a Second
nodes.description: The interval between a press and its visible result, and how long a button can stay silent before that gap reads as failure.
spec: you have built the same button action three times, with a no-feedback delay, a loading-indicator delay, and an immediate-acknowledgement-then-result delay
you have logged the fixed delay you used for each version
you have recorded, for a real tester on each version, the moment they showed they suspected the press had failed, or logged that they never did

nodes.title: The Button That Wants You Back
nodes.description: One repeatable digital button, and why a small randomized reward makes people press it again more than a reliable one does.
spec: you have built one button that gives a small randomized response after each press
you have built a predictable-outcome version of the same button for comparison
you have logged, per tester, how many times they pressed the predictable version and how many times they pressed the variable one

nodes.title: The Button That Doesn't Work
nodes.description: Buttons that visibly acknowledge a press while changing nothing at all — real crossing buttons, elevator door-close buttons, and one you'll build yourself.
spec: you have built a digital pedestrian crossing button that visibly acknowledges every press while the underlying signal timing never changes
you have had a real person use it across multiple presses and logged the press number, or elapsed time, at which they first showed they suspected nothing was happening
you can state, in one sentence, which real signifier your version borrowed from an actual crossing button

nodes.title: The Button You Stop Seeing
nodes.description: What happens to a button pressed so often it stops being looked at, and what that means for designing it.
spec: you have logged, over a defined period, every press of one digital button you use repeatedly, noting whether you looked at it or pressed from memory
you have redesigned that button once for a first-time presser and once for a habitual presser, without changing what it does
you can name, in one sentence, what each redesign assumes the presser already knows

nodes.title: One Button, Many Hands
nodes.description: Returning to the Week 7 crossing button to find the exact point where its push mechanism stops working for a hand unlike the one that built it.
spec: you have reused the exact digital crossing button from Week 7, unchanged, as the object under test

you have tested it under at least three changed conditions (for example one-handed use, no visual feedback, keyboard-only activation, a different physical reach) and logged the specific point each one broke
your log names a mechanism failure — reach, target size, timing window, sight-only or sound-only acknowledgement, or activation method — for each condition, not a general impression

nodes.title: The Button With a Guard Rail
nodes.description: Adding exactly one proportionate obstacle to one of the five buttons from Week 4's reversible-to-irreversible table.
spec: you have picked one button from your Week 4 five-button table and restated its place on the reversible-to-irreversible axis
you have added exactly one obstacle before its consequence — for example confirmation, hold-to-confirm, delay, re-entry, or typed confirmation
you can justify, in specific terms, why that exact obstacle is proportionate — not too weak for the consequence, not more obstructive than the consequence warrants

nodes.title: The Button That's Lying to You
nodes.description: One real button whose wording, weight, or friction steers a choice, and what's lost when that leverage is removed.
spec: you have found and accurately described one real bounded button whose wording, size, position, timing, visual weight, or confirmation friction pushes toward one choice — or documented your own example if a public one wasn't available
you have rebuilt the same button honestly, changing only wording, size, position, timing, visual weight, or confirmation/friction, without changing what it does
you have written one paragraph naming exactly what leverage the original used and what was lost, for the person pressing it, once you removed it

nodes.title: The Perfect Button
nodes.description: Returning to the semester's central question with the strongest button built this course, one buttonless comparison, and a final defence.
spec: you have chosen the strongest button you built or logged this semester and can say which week it came from
you have built one buttonless alternative to the same action, solely to test what the button itself was contributing

course.title: Applied Anomalology
course.description: An applied research methods course in observing, classifying and containing anomalous phenomena. Students run supervised on-campus fieldwork, undertake a comparative desk study of documented cases beyond campus, and apply cross-cultural warding traditions as practical countermeasures.

nodes.title: Orientation: observational method basics
nodes.description: The course's baseline method — log what you see, corroborate before you classify, never intervene — introduced before any fieldwork begins.
spec: you can state the course's three-part observation protocol (log, corroborate, classify) without reference to notes
you can explain, in your own words, why intervening during an observation voids it
you have set up an observation log using the course's supplied template

nodes.title: Historical taxonomies of anomalous phenomena
nodes.description: How the course's classification scheme took its present shape, and why three earlier taxonomies were retired rather than patched.
spec: you can name the course's current top-level classification categories and place a described phenomenon into one
you can give one retired taxonomy and the observation it failed to accommodate
you can explain why the current scheme lets a case sit in more than one category at once, rather than forcing a single fit

nodes.title: Comparative warding: nine traditions, read as applied research
nodes.description: Nine independently-developed protective traditions, from three continents and no shared contact between them, named explicitly as themselves and read as countermeasure research rather than folklore.
spec: you can state the procedure, sequence, and documented failure or limit of at least three of this week's nine traditions, in your own words
you can identify where at least two traditions converge on the same countermeasure principle despite no documented contact between them
you can explain why this course names each tradition explicitly rather than substituting a dry in-universe term for it

nodes.title: Fieldwork method & safety protocol
nodes.description: The rules that make on-campus observation safe to run at all — informed consent, the buddy system, and the disengagement rule that ends an observation before it costs anyone anything.
spec: you can state the disengagement rule and the single condition that triggers it
you can explain, in terms of what a lone observer cannot corroborate, why fieldwork is never run solo
you have signed the course's consent and buddy-pairing paperwork before next week's first case clinic

nodes.title: Case clinic 1: the seminar room past the bricked-over fire door
nodes.description: The first supervised on-campus observation — a disused Arts Annex seminar room, marked "do not reassign" on the facilities floor plan, that reads as larger on the inside than the corridor outside allows.
spec: you can produce a log of the case that a second observer, given only your notes, could use to navigate the room as you found it
you can state which of the course's four behaviour categories (persistent, recurring, responsive, dormant) currently fits this case, and why
you followed the buddy system and disengagement rule for the full observation, without exception
you ran the diagnose-then-respond structure and the nazar-amulet comparison as two separate, independently logged checks — not one blurred judgment call

nodes.title: Case clinic 2: the 13-step stairwell
nodes.description: The second supervised on-campus observation, and the week the Field Case File is due — a stairwell that returns you to the floor you started on after exactly thirteen steps, sometimes.
spec: you can produce a log of the stairwell case that distinguishes what you counted from what you inferred
you have submitted the Field Case File covering both campus cases, meeting its documentation, safety-protocol and analytical criteria
you can say, for each case, which of the course's classification categories it currently sits in and what would have to change to move it
you can state the fourteen-step edge case and what it implies about treating "thirteen steps" as a rule rather than a coincidence

nodes.title: Regional case survey: comparative method
nodes.description: Moving from the course's own two campus cases to a survey of documented regional cases, and the comparative method that makes cases from different sources comparable at all.
spec: you can state the comparative method's three requirements for treating an external case as usable data (sourcing, behaviour description, corroboration)
you can apply the course's four-category classification scheme to a case you did not personally observe
you can identify one way a documented case's write-up under-specifies what this course would need to classify it confidently

nodes.title: Global case survey: the international corpus as primary source data
nodes.description: Widening the same comparative method to a global corpus of documented cases, treated as primary source material rather than folklore to be filtered out.
spec: you can name two cases from different countries that this course's scheme classifies the same way despite no evident contact between their sources
you can explain why this course treats a widely-circulated account as data rather than discounting it for being widely circulated
you can apply last week's three sourcing requirements to at least one case from this week's corpus and say whether it passes

nodes.title: Comparative analysis: convergence across cases
nodes.description: Pooling the regional and global surveys to ask what the cross-case convergence actually supports — and where the Comparative Literature Review, due this week, has to stop short of a verdict.
spec: you can state what the pooled cases converge on, and, separately, what they do not
you have submitted the Comparative Literature Review, meeting its breadth-of-comparison and quality-of-evaluation criteria
you can name at least one competing explanation for the convergence that the review does not have enough evidence to rule out

nodes.title: Competing frameworks: cosmic prisoner theory, shadow domain theory, and others
nodes.description: A survey of the theoretical frameworks currently offered to explain the convergence identified in week 9 — read as competing, evidence-bearing claims, not a menu to choose from.
spec: you can state the core claim of at least two competing frameworks in your own words
you can name one observation each framework would need to explain but currently doesn't
you can explain why this course presents these as competing rather than complementary

nodes.title: The unifying fourth-dimensional hypothesis
nodes.description: The framework most cases in the corpus are currently read against — presented as leading, not settled, and held to the same falsifiability standard as every framework in week 10.
spec: you can state the fourth-dimensional hypothesis's core claim without overstating it as settled
you can name the strongest single piece of convergent evidence for it, and the strongest case that doesn't fit it
you can explain why this course presents it as contested despite it being the leading framework

nodes.title: Final debrief and practical wrap-up
nodes.description: The closing practical — reviewing the semester's cases and frameworks together, in the week the Final Capstone is due.
spec: you have submitted the Final Capstone — a containment/warding protocol for a novel case, grounded in the course's classification and countermeasure material
you can trace your protocol's design back to at least one specific piece of material from phases 1–3 (a classification category, a warding-tradition mechanism, or a safety-protocol rule)
you can state, without being asked to defend it, whether and how a position on the fourth-dimensional hypothesis shaped your protocol's design

nodes.title: Field Case File
nodes.description: A write-up of the two on-campus cases from weeks 5–6, marked on documentation rigor, safety-protocol adherence and analytical quality.
spec: submitted by the deadline, covering both the seminar-room case and the 13-step stairwell case
each case's log is timestamped, corroborated between buddy pairs, and free of any observation gained by intervening in the case
each case is classified against the course's four-category scheme, with the classification defended against the log rather than merely stated

nodes.title: Final Capstone
nodes.description: A containment/warding protocol for a novel case, grounded in the course's classification and countermeasure material and judged holistically.
spec: submitted by the deadline, proposing a containment/warding protocol for a novel case not covered elsewhere in the course
the protocol's design is traceable to at least one specific piece of course material — a classification category, a warding-tradition mechanism from week 3, or a safety-protocol rule from week 4
the protocol does not depend on settling the fourth-dimensional hypothesis or any other contested framework to be usable

marking.description: The capstone is judged as a whole, on whether the proposed protocol is grounded in specific classification and countermeasure material from across the semester rather than general plausibility, whether it is safe to run under the course's fieldwork rules, and whether it stands on its own as something a field team could actually follow.

nodes.title: Comparative Literature Review
nodes.description: A review of the regional and global case corpus from weeks 7–9, marked on breadth of comparison and quality of evaluation of competing accounts.
spec: submitted by the deadline, drawing on cases from both the regional and global surveys (weeks 7–8)
every case cited passes the comparative method's sourcing test from week 7 (named source, behaviour description, corroboration), or is explicitly flagged as not passing and weighted accordingly
the review states what the cited cases converge on and, separately, what they do not — it does not resolve the gap into a single cause

nodes.title: Observation as Evidence

meta.subtitle: How to observe something that should not be there.

meta.subtitle: When an anomaly repeats, but never quite the same way.

course.title: League Studies
course.description: League Studies teaches students to read a League of Legends match: how resources, information, space, tempo and composition turn individual decisions into wins and losses. The recurring question: why did this team win?

nodes.title: Getting started
nodes.description: The first session of the semester — bring a match you already know the result of, and leave with this course's first written answer to why.
spec: you have a complete match of your own (played or watched) that you can describe from memory
you have written down, in your own words, why the winning team won that match
you can point to one specific moment in that match, not just a general impression of it

nodes.title: First review
nodes.description: The second session, where the match you picked in Week 1 gets a second pair of eyes before you commit to analysing it for real.
spec: you can describe your Week 1 match's game state at one specific moment in under two minutes
you can name the one part of your "why did they win" answer you are least sure about

nodes.title: Draft to Game Plan
nodes.description: Given a completed 5v5 draft, identify each composition's strengths, likely win conditions and preferred game plan before watching the match, then compare the prediction with what happened.
spec: names each side's strengths and constraints, and a specific likely win condition, before watching the match
states a specific preferred game plan per side, not a generic strength list
identifies where the two teams' plans conflict, before watching the match
compares the prediction with what actually happened and explains any gap, rather than only noting one exists
a defensible pre-game prediction that the match outcome contradicts is not penalised for the contradiction itself

criteria.name: Post-match comparison and explanation of gaps

nodes.title: The Invisible Jungler
nodes.description: Analyse partially hidden game states and infer where the enemy jungler is likely to be, using evidence rather than guesswork.
spec: infers a plausible jungler location from a partially hidden game state, citing concrete evidence rather than intuition
names at least one plausible alternative location the same evidence does not rule out
states what additional information would change the conclusion
recommends an action for the player or team that follows from the inference and its uncertainty, not from assuming the guess is correct
a well-supported inference that turns out wrong is marked on its reasoning, not penalised for missing the hidden ground truth

nodes.title: Match Autopsy
nodes.description: The final assessment. Explain why one team won a complete match, using concepts from across the semester.
spec: identifies a limited number of pivotal transitions rather than a full timestamped recap
for each transition, states the prior game state, what changed it, the resulting advantage, how it was converted, and what it opened up or closed off
draws evidence from multiple course areas (resources, waves, information, tempo, objectives, composition, teamfighting) where relevant, without forcing every concept in
rewards a coherent causal explanation over vocabulary density
ties each claim to a specific, identifiable moment in the match

nodes.title: Solo Queue Autopsy
nodes.description: Analyse one of your own losses. Explain three decisions that materially changed the game, reasoned through the concepts from the first third of the semester.
spec: identifies three decisions that materially changed the outcome of the game
explains each using resources, the wave, or trading rather than restating what happened
another player's mistake is discussed only in terms of how it changed the decisions available to you
each decision is tied to a specific, identifiable moment, not a general impression of the game
distinguishes a good decision with a bad outcome from a bad decision

nodes.title: What Wins a Game?
nodes.description: The course's foundational question — what "winning" actually consists of, moment to moment, given that the Nexus is only ever destroyed once. Sets up the recurring principle every later week returns to.

meta.question: If destroying the Nexus is the only objective, why do players spend most of the game doing something else?

nodes.title: Gold, Experience and Power
nodes.description: Gold and experience translate into item and level advantages, but an advantage is only worth what it lets a champion do that they couldn't before. Builds on Week 1's account of what winning actually requires.

meta.question: What is an advantage actually worth?

nodes.title: The Minion Wave
nodes.description: The minion wave is the resource that gates almost every other decision on the map — where a champion can safely stand, what a gank threatens, what a lane can afford to give up. Extends Week 2's account of power into the mechanism that produces or denies it, lane by lane.

meta.question: Why do six minions determine what ten champions are allowed to do?

nodes.title: Trading
nodes.description: A trade exchanges health, resources and position, not just damage numbers — and the same exchange can be a win or a loss depending on what each side can convert it into. Builds on the wave and power concepts from Weeks 2–3 to ask what is actually staked in a fight.

meta.question: What are you really trading when you fight another champion?

nodes.title: The Jungle
nodes.description: The jungler is the one player routinely making decisions about parts of the map nobody can see, so jungling is a study in acting on incomplete information. Builds on the trading and power concepts from earlier weeks and applies them to a player whose state your opponent must infer.

meta.question: How do you make decisions about a player you cannot see?

nodes.title: Tempo
nodes.description: Tempo asks what a player does with the time an action frees up — recalling, resetting, redirecting attention — rather than only what the action itself gains. Builds on power (Week 2) and jungle decision-making (Week 5) to treat time itself as a resource to be converted.

meta.question: Why can recalling be more valuable than getting another kill?

nodes.title: Vision and Information
nodes.description: Most of the map is invisible at any moment, so vision converts gold into knowledge, and knowledge into safer tempo. Builds directly on the jungle (Week 5) and tempo (Week 6) weeks, since both depend on what a team can and can't see.

meta.question: What can you know when most of the map is invisible?

nodes.title: Objectives
nodes.description: Dragons, Heralds and towers are only good decisions when the team can convert what they grant — so the question is never whether to take an objective, but what happens next if you do. Builds on tempo (Week 6) and vision (Week 7) to treat objective calls as an extension of both.

meta.question: When is taking Dragon the wrong decision?

nodes.title: Draft and Win Conditions
nodes.description: A draft is a bet on a win condition placed before the game starts, and every earlier concept — power, trades, tempo, objectives — is a lens for reading what a composition needs in order to win. Builds on Week 1's account of winning and Week 4's account of trading.

meta.question: What does your team need to happen in order to win?

nodes.title: Teamfighting
nodes.description: A teamfight is five overlapping individual jobs, not one collective event, and reading it means asking what each champion is actually trying to accomplish inside it. Builds on trading (Week 4) and objectives (Week 8), since most teamfights exist to contest one.

meta.question: Ten champions enter a fight. What is each one actually trying to accomplish?

nodes.title: The Meta
nodes.description: The rules of the game barely change patch to patch, yet the correct way to play changes constantly — because what converts best shifts with the draft, jungle and objective landscape around it. Builds on draft and win conditions (Week 9) and teamfighting (Week 10).

meta.question: If the rules barely change, why does the correct way to play change constantly?

nodes.title: Reading a Game
nodes.description: The semester's closing question, answered with the semester's own tools — given a complete match, explain why one team won using resources, tempo, vision, objectives, draft and teamfighting together. Synthesises Weeks 1, 6, 8 and 10 rather than introducing a new concept.

meta.question: Why did they win?

course.title: Fail States
course.description: A semester spent studying how games design losing: checkpoints, permadeath, lives, difficulty curves, and the meaning players make from failure. For anyone who has ever wondered why dying in a game can feel worth doing again.

course.title: Turning Every Course You Take Into a Game
course.description: Putting 130 hours into a game is easy. Putting 130 hours into a course is not, and it is the same hours and the same person. The difference is how fast the reward arrives. Learn to build that reward, and finish a course the way you finish a game.

nodes.title: Lab 1 — Eight matches
nodes.description: Three hours of ranked play with a thirty-second note between games. The point is the notes; the matches are how you get them
spec: you play at least eight matches where the result mattered to you
you write the three notes between every pair of games, not afterwards from memory
you leave able to say how long your longest goalless stretch was

nodes.title: Lab 2 — One boss, twenty deaths
nodes.description: Three hours on a single fight you cannot yet beat, with one written line per death. If you win in six attempts you have picked the wrong boss
spec: you make at least twenty attempts on one boss and log every one
every line names something about the fight, not something about you
you can point at the attempt where the fight stopped feeling random

nodes.title: Assessment 1: a short-loop mechanism
nodes.description: Build something that gives a thirty-minute sitting the structure a ranked match has, run it for a fortnight, and demonstrate it live
spec: a sitting run under your mechanism has a win condition written before it started
you have at least ten real sittings logged, including losses
you can state one thing you decided against building, and why

marking.description: Marked live from the demonstration, on whether the mechanism actually changed a sitting and whether it would survive a bad week. A running paper system beats an elegant unfinished program. Ambition is not scored; use is.

nodes.title: Assessment 2: getting a grip on something hard
nodes.description: Attack a real subject before you understand it, take one lesson per attempt, and let the list of what you are fighting grow out of those attempts. Run it for a fortnight and demonstrate it live
spec: you attacked something before you had a plan for it, and the log shows it
your attempt log carries one testable lesson per line, not one verdict about yourself
at least one fight on your list is one you could not have named before you started

marking.description: Marked live from the demonstration, on whether the bosses are genuinely defeatable and the attempt lines genuinely testable. A tree that survived a boss splitting into three marks better than a tidy one that never met reality.

nodes.title: Assessment 3: the run
nodes.description: Thirty hours on the course you stalled on and still need, driven by the mechanism you built, ending in an exam set on the quarter you cut
spec: your target is something you have stalled on, evidenced by a specific dated failure
you can say why you still need it, in terms of something outside this course
the quarter you cut is coherent, and you can say what you left out and why
roughly thirty hours are logged inside the mechanism, with the gaps visible rather than deleted
you sit the exam

criteria.name: Evidence the mechanism drove the run
The cut, and the honesty of the account

nodes.title: Reward structures in games, and which ones a course can use
nodes.description: Six reward structures that games actually use, and an honest argument about which two of them could survive being pointed at a 130-hour course
spec: you can state the asymmetry this course starts from in one sentence, without using the word "motivation"
you can name six reward structures and say what each one needs in order to work
you can explain why four of them cannot be built by one student for one course
you can state the length of your own feedback loop in your current degree, in hours

nodes.title: Laning, roaming, objectives and the ranked ladder
nodes.description: The first three are clocks running at once inside a single match, which is why a MOBA never gives you a minute where the right move is nothing. The ladder is the separate thing that makes a hundred matches add up
spec: you can name the three clocks a MOBA runs and the decision each one forces
you can explain the difference between the match layer and the ladder layer
you can describe how hidden rating and displayed rank differ, and why that gap is deliberate

nodes.title: Playing League of Legends, and taking notes while you do
nodes.description: How to get usable notes out of a game you are also trying to win, and the three observations you have to come back from the Lab with
spec: you can play a match and afterwards name the longest stretch you had no goal
you can distinguish an observation about the game from an opinion about your performance
you arrive at week 4 with notes from at least eight matches

nodes.title: Building the mechanism on paper
nodes.description: Giving every minute of a study block a job, using nothing but a sheet of paper. If filling it in takes longer than eight seconds you will stop doing it, so eight seconds is the design constraint
spec: your sitting has a win condition you wrote before starting and can check afterwards
your sitting contains a recurring short interval that forces a decision
you can run the whole protocol, start to finish, without any application open

nodes.title: Building the same mechanism as software
nodes.description: Why a timer app has never changed anyone's semester, what code can do that paper cannot, and which tempting features you have to leave out to keep a ladder worth living with
spec: you can say what a rating curve shows you that a stack of paper sheets cannot
your implementation stores verdicts, not derived scores, and recomputes the rest
you can name at least one feature you deliberately refused, and defend the refusal

nodes.title: Why the hardest game is the one people finish
nodes.description: Because a Souls boss is hard, you die in two minutes, so you find out you were wrong in two minutes. Being hard is what makes the feedback fast
spec: you can explain how being hard is what makes a Souls loop short, rather than something it overcomes
you can measure the failure loop of any game or task in two numbers
you can explain why a legible tell is worth more than a forgiving hitbox

nodes.title: Playing a Souls game, and writing down every death
nodes.description: One written line per death, and the point in a run where the boss stops feeling random. That point is when you can finally say what you are learning
spec: you keep a one-line-per-attempt log for a single boss, with a lesson on each line
you can point at the attempt where the fight stopped feeling random
you can tell an unfalsifiable lesson from a testable one in your own log

nodes.title: Treating a subject as a set of bosses, on paper
nodes.description: The paper version of the Souls loop. You attack, you take the one lesson, you go again. The list of what you are fighting grows out of those attempts, instead of being written before you have made any
spec: you attacked something before you had a plan for it, and logged what happened
your attempt log carries one testable lesson per line, not one verdict about yourself
the things you are fighting have names you could only have written after attacking

nodes.title: Breaking a large subject into small tasks, and building it as software
nodes.description: The ladder gives you the inside of thirty minutes and nothing beyond it. Long-term planning is the other half of the job, and the way a Souls game does it is to let a large subject come apart into small tasks one attempt at a time, rather than all at once on day one
spec: you can state, in two sentences, what each of the two mechanisms is for and what it cannot do
your boss tree survives a boss turning out to be three bosses
no unit of planning in your system has a length you fixed in advance

nodes.title: Choosing the course you got stuck on
nodes.description: The course you stopped, restarted and stopped again. You still need it, and that is exactly what makes it the right thing to point this at
spec: your target is something you have actually stalled on, and you can evidence the stall
you can say why you still need it, in terms of something outside this course
you have cut a quarter of it that is coherent rather than merely the first quarter
you have a baseline the final assessment could detect movement against

nodes.title: Running both mechanisms at once
nodes.description: Attempts find the work and study blocks get it done. What reliably goes wrong in the second week of a run, and why your own records will make you look better than you actually were
spec: every sitting in your run sits inside exactly one named boss
you can name the specific way your own log overstates what you did, using your own data
you have changed at least one rule mid-run and recorded why

nodes.title: The exam, and what it cannot tell you
nodes.description: You sit an exam on what you covered, and then answer the harder question the exam cannot. Did your mechanism cause that result, and what would you cut from it now
spec: you sit the exam on your own target subject
you can argue for or against your own mechanism using your own logs as evidence
you can name what you would remove from it, and why removal is the harder judgement

course.title: League of Legends Champion Mastery
course.description: A twelve-week practice studio where League of Legends players turn one champion into a complete competitive system: every lane matchup tested, every counter explained, and every lead carried into the whole map.

nodes.title: Calibration and champion contract
nodes.description: Lock one champion and role, record a baseline, and define the first evidence-backed training queue.
spec: one champion and primary role are named, with a fallback practice mode
a replay baseline includes three timestamped decision points
the next test queue contains one mechanics, matchup, and global goal

nodes.title: Mechanics loop
nodes.description: Build and repeat two champion-specific drills until execution is stable enough to test in a live lane.
spec: each drill has a setup, action, success threshold, and reset condition
at least twenty deliberate attempts are logged
one failure pattern becomes the next drill revision

nodes.title: Wave and trade lab
nodes.description: Rehearse the first four waves against contrasting opponents and connect every trade to the next lane state.
spec: three opening-wave plans are diagrammed
every planned trade names the minion and cooldown advantage
one recall timing is tested from both winning and losing states

nodes.title: Matchup hypothesis lab
nodes.description: Turn a suspected counter into a controlled one-versus-one protocol and a falsifiable lane rule.
spec: the opponent threat is stated as a conditional interaction
side selection, wave state, level, and item state are controlled
the result produces a retained, revised, or rejected rule

nodes.title: Evidence-first VOD review
nodes.description: Review decisions from information available in the moment and convert findings into a precise re-test.
spec: three clips pause before the outcome is known
visible facts and viable options are separated from hindsight
every review note ends in a retained rule, revision, or new test

nodes.title: Adaptive setup lab
nodes.description: Compare two rune, item, or skill-order plans against the same matchup problem without confusing correlation for cause.
spec: the setup change answers one named threat or win condition
the opportunity cost of the change is documented
replay markers define what success looks like

nodes.title: Counter sprint
nodes.description: Rotate through ranged, sustain, disengage, and all-in opponents while keeping one champion plan under scrutiny.
spec: at least four opponent patterns are tested
each reset changes only one major condition
the two hardest interactions enter the priority queue

nodes.title: Portfolio review
nodes.description: Audit matchup coverage, evidence quality, and whether lane learning changes later map decisions.
spec: every claim links to a clip, log, or controlled test
uncertain entries are labelled and queued rather than hidden
at least one lane rule is connected to a mid-game decision

nodes.title: Global decision map
nodes.description: Rehearse side-lane, objective, teleport, and grouping decisions from ahead, even, and behind states.
spec: three map states are solved with a stated priority
the next two waves and next objective timer are considered
the champion's teamfight or split-push job is declared

nodes.title: Teamfight scenario lab
nodes.description: Test champion interactions outside lane through target access, peel, flank, zone, and retreat scenarios.
spec: each scenario declares the champion's job before combat begins
one interaction is recorded for every opposing role
the full-roster atlas gains at least ten verified global entries

nodes.title: Hard-counter re-test gauntlet
nodes.description: Stress-test the ten hardest matchups across three cycles and defend the resulting rules to peers.
spec: ten high-risk interactions are ranked from evidence
each receives three cycles with a changed condition
every mastered claim includes a future re-test trigger

nodes.title: Champion mastery exhibition
nodes.description: Demonstrate one complete improvement loop and hand over a living playbook with a credible next-test queue.
spec: the demonstration connects mechanics, matchup, and global decisions
evidence shows at least one failed hypothesis and useful revision
the maintenance plan explains how patch changes will be revalidated

nodes.title: Baseline Matchup Protocol
nodes.description: Design and run a controlled lane test that turns one suspected counter interaction into an evidence-backed rule.
spec: one champion, role, and opponent interaction are named
the method controls level, items, wave state, side, and success condition
the conclusion includes uncertainty and a scheduled re-test

nodes.title: Champion Mastery Capstone
nodes.description: Defend a complete mechanics, matchup, and global playbook through re-tests of the hardest interactions and a live transfer challenge.
spec: ten hardest interactions have three documented re-test cycles each
the playbook covers the full roster at lane or global-interaction resolution
the demonstration responds to an unseen condition without hiding uncertainty

nodes.title: Counter Lab Portfolio
nodes.description: Build a tested matchup library for one champion and show how repeated lane evidence changes setup and map decisions.
spec: at least twelve common lane opponents have direct test records
every claim links to a clip, log, or controlled exercise
the portfolio contains a ranked unresolved queue and re-test dates

criteria.name: Adaptation across setups and game states

nodes.title: Build a mastery loop
nodes.description: Establish a champion baseline, define observable goals, and turn every match into the next training decision.

nodes.title: Champion identity and mechanics
nodes.description: Convert a champion kit into repeatable drills for spacing, combos, cooldowns, resource use, and escape routes.

nodes.title: Trade through the wave
nodes.description: Read minion states, level timings, health budgets, and recall windows before deciding whether a trade is actually good.

nodes.title: Model every lane opponent
nodes.description: Classify range, sustain, all-in, disengage, scaling, and jungle pressure to create testable matchup hypotheses.

nodes.title: Review without hindsight bias
nodes.description: Use timestamped replay evidence to distinguish a poor decision from a reasonable decision with a bad result.

nodes.title: Adapt runes, items, and skill order
nodes.description: Treat setups as responses to threats and win conditions, then document when a default should be replaced.

nodes.title: Survive pressure and track the jungler
nodes.description: Combine wave position, pathing clues, vision timing, and weak-side objectives into a plan that preserves agency.

nodes.title: Turn lane knowledge into mid-game tempo
nodes.description: Decide when to hold side lane, move first, trade objectives, or group by comparing the next two waves and map timers.

nodes.title: Enter teamfights with a job
nodes.description: Define target access, peel, flank, zone, and retreat triggers before the fight removes time to think.

nodes.title: Build the full-roster interaction map
nodes.description: Extend lane mastery into a searchable map of threats, interrupts, mobility, range, and teamfight interactions across the roster.

nodes.title: Pressure-test the hardest counters
nodes.description: Re-run the ten most difficult interactions across three cycles and audit whether revised rules still hold under pressure.

nodes.title: Maintain mastery across patches
nodes.description: Synthesize mechanics, matchup, and global evidence into a living playbook that can be revalidated after change.

course.title: How to Never Pay Full Price
course.description: A semester about looking past the sticker price. Twelve weeks follow one purchase — $249 headphones — through discounts, unit prices, coupons, price history, changing prices and subscriptions, ending with one rule: the lowest number is not always the best choice.

nodes.title: Week 1 — What Is a Price?
nodes.description: Does a product have one true price? An introduction to sticker, reference, sale and market price, and to the $249 headphones this semester keeps returning to.
spec: names at least four different things "price" can mean for the same product
states the semester's running scenario and its opening price
does not treat the sticker price as self-evidently the whole answer
gives one concrete before-class task and one in-class activity tied to the week's topic

nodes.title: Week 2 — The Unit Price
nodes.description: Is the larger pack actually the better buy? Unit price, usable quantity, and why "cheaper per kilo" can still be a worse purchase.
spec: defines unit price as total price divided by quantity
distinguishes quantity purchased from quantity actually used
includes a worked calculator comparing two packs on both measures
gives one concrete before-class task and one in-class activity tied to the week's topic

nodes.title: Week 3 — 50% Off What?
nodes.description: A discount is a comparison, not a fact. This week asks what a reference price is measuring, who set it, and why it can be measured against itself.
spec: defines reference price and distinguishes it from market price
explains how anchoring works with reference prices, not just by name
states that discount percentage and money saved are not interchangeable
gives one concrete before-class task and one in-class activity tied to the week's topic

nodes.title: Week 4 — Coupons Are Algorithms
nodes.description: Thresholds, exclusions, stacking and bundles turn a shopping cart into a set of rules to work through, not a place to guess.
spec: writes a discount rule as a clear if-this-then-that rule, not a trick
names at least one way combining discounts can produce a worse outcome than using one alone
distinguishes a threshold discount from an exclusion and from a stacking rule
gives one concrete before-class task and one in-class activity tied to the week's topic

nodes.title: Week 5 — The Price Has a History
nodes.description: A single price is easier to judge when you know what it has been before. This week uses price history to tell ordinary prices from unusual ones.
spec: represents price as a function of time, not a single fixed value
distinguishes a median baseline from a single historical reference price
explains why a hypothetical price series must be labelled as hypothetical
gives one concrete before-class task and one in-class activity tied to the week's topic

nodes.title: Week 6 — The Price Is Watching You
nodes.description: Some prices change by time, place, demand or shopper. The price on your screen may not be the price on someone else's.
spec: distinguishes demand-sensitive pricing from personalised pricing
discusses dynamic pricing without attributing specific practices to a named real company
explains price discrimination as a pricing concept, not as a legal accusation
gives one concrete before-class task and one in-class activity tied to the week's topic

nodes.title: Week 7 — The Price That Never Stops
nodes.description: Small monthly charges are easy to underestimate. This week covers subscriptions, cheap first-month offers, forgetting to cancel, cancellation friction, and cost per actual use.
spec: turns a recurring charge into a yearly cost, not just the monthly or weekly figure
explains forgetting to cancel and hard-to-cancel services as separate problems
reuses the usable-quantity idea from Week 2 to find cost per actual use
gives one concrete before-class task and one in-class activity tied to the week's topic

nodes.title: Week 8 — Points Are Weird Money
nodes.description: Loyalty points can look like cash, but they come with expiry dates, limits, and rules that can make them worth less than they first appear.
spec: distinguishes advertised value from realistic usable value for a points scheme
names at least two rules that can make points worth less in practice
applies the same combine-the-rules thinking from Week 4 to a loyalty scheme
gives one concrete before-class task and one in-class activity tied to the week's topic

nodes.title: Week 9 — New, Used, Repair or Rent?
nodes.description: Sometimes the cheaper option is not the same item at another store. It may be buying used, repairing, renting, or borrowing instead.
spec: compares at least three ways to meet the same need, not only prices at different stores
defines lifecycle cost as more than the upfront purchase price
relates depreciation and resale value to the net cost of ownership
gives one concrete before-class task and one in-class activity tied to the week's topic

nodes.title: Week 10 — Should You Wait?
nodes.description: Waiting for a better price is a bet, not a guarantee. This week introduces expected value: a simple way to combine the chance of a discount with the size of that discount.
spec: defines expected value in terms of probability and size of a future discount
names stock-out risk and urgency as costs of waiting, not just as inconveniences
explicitly avoids claiming that future prices can be predicted with certainty
gives one concrete before-class task and one in-class activity tied to the week's topic

nodes.title: Week 11 — Your Time Has a Price
nodes.description: Search, travel and waiting all take time. This week builds a calculator that weighs time spent against possible savings.
spec: defines the cost of time using a clear value-per-hour figure
treats hours already spent searching as gone, so they do not affect the next decision
includes a working buy-or-wait tool whose recommendation is explained, not just stated
gives one concrete before-class task and one in-class activity tied to the week's topic

nodes.title: Week 12 — Sometimes Pay Full Price
nodes.description: The final week brings everything together. Price, time, risk, waste, alternatives and personal priorities all matter, so the lowest number does not automatically win.
spec: combines at least five prior weeks' concepts into a single decision framework
explicitly rejects "always find the lowest price" as the course's conclusion
states the actual conclusion in terms of information, limits and values
gives one concrete before-class task and one in-class activity tied to the week's topic

nodes.title: Assessment 2 — Beat the Shopping Cart
nodes.description: A constrained shopping scenario with thresholds, coupons, exclusions and bundles. Find the best plan without buying extra things just to chase a discount.
spec: submitted by the deadline, in the format named below
models every discount rule in the scenario explicitly, including exclusions
compares at least three plausible strategies using the same true-cost method
identifies at least one combination that appears to save money but doesn't
the final strategy is justified against the true cost, not the advertised discount

criteria.name: Correct modelling of every rule in the scenario
criteria.description: Writes each coupon, exclusion, bundle, shipping rule and loyalty rule as a clear if-this-then-that rule, including the order the rules apply.

criteria.name: How well the chosen strategy is justified
criteria.description: Compares at least three possible carts using the same true-cost method, then recommends the cart with the best total result, not the biggest advertised discount.

criteria.name: Clarity of the written or coded reasoning
criteria.description: Shows the working clearly enough that another student could repeat it, using readable tables or code and a short explanation of why the other options lose.

nodes.title: Assessment 3 — Build a Buying Engine
nodes.description: The final project. Build a small buying tool that explains its advice instead of just outputting a number.
spec: submitted by the deadline, in the format named below
accepts at least five distinct input categories from the semester's material
produces one of the named recommendation categories, not a bare price
shows the reasoning behind the recommendation, not only the recommendation itself
includes example runs that demonstrate at least three different recommendation categories
does not claim to produce a universally correct answer

criteria.name: Scope and input design
criteria.description: Chooses at least five useful input types from the course and defines them clearly, including units, assumptions and limits.

criteria.name: Recommendation logic and consistency
criteria.description: Gives one of the named recommendations using rules that stay consistent when price, urgency, uncertainty, time cost or alternatives change.

criteria.name: Explanation and example runs
criteria.description: Shows the steps behind the answer, includes example runs for at least three recommendation categories, and names what would change each answer.

criteria.name: Assumptions, limitations and responsible caveats
criteria.description: Labels invented inputs, avoids claiming the tool is right for everyone, and names important factors the tool does not handle.

nodes.title: Assessment 1 — Deal Autopsy
nodes.description: Pick one real promotion and show, with evidence, whether it is actually a good deal.
spec: submitted by the deadline, in the format named below
names the advertised claim, the reference price, and any restrictions separately
computes an actual effective saving, not just restates the advertised percentage
includes evidence for the promotion and clearly labels any assumption used to fill a gap
reaches a judgement the calculation actually supports

criteria.name: Identification of claim, reference price and restrictions
criteria.description: Clearly names the headline claim, the "was" price or other comparison number, the source you used, and any visible conditions or limits.

criteria.name: Calculation of actual effective saving
criteria.description: Shows the dollar calculation, labels any guessed number as an assumption, and includes costs or limits such as shipping, minimum spend, expiry or membership rules.

criteria.name: Evidence-based final judgement
criteria.description: Gives a final answer that follows from the evidence. If the promotion does not give enough information, says that plainly instead of pretending to know more than you do.

course.title: Linux Ricing: The Customised Desktop
course.description: An elective on ricing the Linux desktop: the compositors, window managers, dotfiles, palettes, type and status bars behind the screenshot. You build one complete, reproducible, original setup, then account honestly for the hours it cost you.

nodes.title: Getting started
nodes.description: Week 1 lab, a machine you can break, the course toolchain running, and something rough to show
spec: you have a machine, real or virtual, you are willing to reinstall
the course site builds and previews on your machine
you can show the class one screenshot you admire and say why

nodes.title: Reading the stack
nodes.description: Week 2 lab, name every layer of your desktop, and choose the stack you will build on
spec: you can name every program in your desktop stack and what it does
you have chosen X11 or Wayland and can say why
you have installed a bare compositor and reached a usable session

nodes.title: Choosing a manager
nodes.description: Week 3 lab, commit to a window manager and write the first configuration you will have to defend
spec: you have a window manager running with a config under git
you can move, resize, and switch windows without the mouse
you can state the layout policy you chose and the one you rejected

nodes.title: The dotfiles repository
nodes.description: Week 4 lab, turn a pile of config into a repository someone else could read and rebuild
spec: your config lives in one git repository with a readable history
the repository has a README that explains its structure
a partner can find where any given setting lives without asking you

nodes.title: Settling a palette
nodes.description: Week 5 lab, choose a colour system and make it hold across unrelated programs
spec: your terminal and at least two other programs share one palette
your foreground and background meet a contrast standard you can name
you can justify your palette against the obvious off-the-shelf choice

nodes.title: Type in the terminal
nodes.description: Week 6 lab, choose a typeface for the place you actually read, and know why
spec: your terminal and editor render a font you chose deliberately
icons in your bar and prompt come from a patched font that renders cleanly
you can say whether you optimised for legibility or for feel

nodes.title: Building the bar
nodes.description: Week 7 lab, build a status bar, then earn back every module by proving you read it
spec: you have a working status bar wired to real system state
every module left in the bar is one you glanced at within a day
you can defend each surviving module against being moved on demand

nodes.title: The screenshot workshop
nodes.description: Week 8 lab, compose the photograph the setup exists for, and start drafting its defence
spec: you have a composed screenshot and an honest one, side by side
you can name every deliberate choice visible in the composed frame
you have a first draft of the Defence covering those choices

nodes.title: Two churches
nodes.description: Week 9 lab, push your setup to one aesthetic pole, then defend where it landed
spec: you have pushed your setup hard toward minimalism or maximalism
you can distinguish your choice from its failure mode
you can argue your position against a partner holding the other

nodes.title: Rebuild from bare metal
nodes.description: Week 10 lab, prove the setup is reproducible by building it again on a clean machine
spec: your setup bootstraps onto a fresh machine from your repository
you have timed the rebuild and logged every manual fix it needed
you can say where on the reproducibility spectrum your setup sits

nodes.title: The reckoning
nodes.description: Week 11 lab, put a real number on the hours, and decide honestly what they bought
spec: you have a defensible estimate of the hours this setup has cost
you have separated hours that saved time from hours that bought pleasure
you have an outline of the Time Audit essay

nodes.title: The gallery
nodes.description: Week 12 lab, the final gallery, where each setup goes up and its owner defends it to the room
spec: your finished rice is presented to the room with its screenshot and defence
you can answer questions the screenshot cannot answer on its own
you can name what your desktop reveals about you, before the room does

nodes.title: The Dotfiles Repository
nodes.description: The setup as engineering, a repository graded on whether a stranger can rebuild your desktop, not on how it looks
spec: submitted as a public git repository with a README that explains how to use it
it bootstraps a bare machine to your desktop with the fewest manual steps
forked, borrowed, and AI-assisted parts are credited in a form a marker can follow

nodes.title: Lab Participation
nodes.description: The mark for the work done in the room, bringing progress to the weekly labs, giving honest feedback in the crits, and being able to defend your choices out loud rather than only in a screenshot.
spec: attend the weekly labs and arrive with something to show, however rough
give specific, useful feedback in the crits rather than polite noise
defend your own choices when the room asks, and revise them when the room is right

marking.description: Participation is judged across the whole semester, not on a single day. The marker looks at whether you brought work to the labs to be seen while it was still unfinished, engaged with your peers' crits with something more useful than politeness, and could talk about your decisions and theirs when the room asked. Consistency over the twelve weeks counts for more than one strong showing at the gallery.

nodes.title: The Rice
nodes.description: The major practical, build and document one complete, original, reproducible desktop setup
spec: submitted by the deadline as a running setup and a repository a marker can rebuild
every layer is present and working, from compositor and window manager to bar, palette, and type
the work is original and yours, with all borrowed and AI-assisted parts declared
accompanied by a short written report that argues for the setup and credits its sources

marking.description: The rice is judged as a whole, on whether the setup is complete and genuinely yours, whether its choices cohere into a point of view rather than a pile of borrowed parts, and whether it stands as a finished piece of work rather than a screenshot with nothing behind it.

nodes.title: The Screenshot
nodes.description: The composed screenshot of your desktop, marked as an act of visual craft and paired with an honest shot of the same machine as it actually looks in use.
spec: submitted as a composed hero screenshot at full resolution, staged as if for r/unixporn
paired with a second, unstaged shot of the same desktop as it actually looks on an ordinary day
clean of visual artefacts, with framing, wallpaper, and open windows all chosen deliberately

nodes.title: The Time Audit
nodes.description: A reflective essay setting the honest hours the setup cost against the honest benefit it returned
spec: submitted as a short reflective essay with a defensible estimate of hours
it separates hours that will pay themselves back from hours that will not
it reaches an honest conclusion rather than a comfortable one

marking.description: The essay is judged on the honesty and clarity of its accounting, meaning whether it puts a real number on the hours, distinguishes time that saved time from time that bought only pleasure, and reaches a conclusion it is willing to stand behind rather than a tidy moral.
