course.title: The Art of Noble Death: Design Philosophy of the Souls-like
course.description: Real difficulty doesn't kill the player — it makes them certain, the instant after they die, that the next attempt can win. Twelve design workshops dissect how a Souls-like builds that belief, through geography, combat and boss staging, each producing an artefact rather than an argument about one.

nodes.title: The frustration-curve log
nodes.description: Playing a punishing case and a cheating case back to back, and logging where each one earns or loses the player's trust
spec: you can point to the exact moment a "punishing" case earned back the player's trust after a death
you can point to the exact moment a "cheating" case lost it, and say what information was missing

nodes.title: The unreliable-narrator workshop
nodes.description: Writing three item descriptions for an original boss, each one testimony from a narrator the death mechanic has already made unreliable
spec: each of the three descriptions is written in a voice, not a stat summary, and the voice is unreliable for a reason your world explains
none of the three confirms outright what actually happened

nodes.title: The map-and-guidance workshop
nodes.description: Hand-drawing a micro-dungeon with real shortcut loops, then redesigning a cluttered map screenshot using visual guidance instead of icons
spec: your micro-dungeon has at least two shortcut loops, each one a real connection a player would have to earn by walking the long way first
your map redesign adds no new icon, arrow or label — only lighting, colour or composition changes to the existing screenshot

nodes.title: The combat drill
nodes.description: Frame-by-frame reading of one boss attack, footage in hand, to separate a learnable telegraph from an unreadable one
spec: you can point to the specific frame or cue a telegraph reveals its outcome on
you can name one attack, in any Souls-like, that fails the legibility test and say why

nodes.title: The two-phase boss workshop
nodes.description: Building the boss from Week 2's item-description exercise into a two-phase encounter with an earned transition
spec: your transition trigger has a one-sentence narrative justification that is specific to this boss, not a generic "gets angrier"
phase two introduces at least one new, telegraphed attack rather than just faster or harder versions of phase one's attacks

nodes.title: Midpoint review and Final Project launch
nodes.description: No new subsystem — a recap of the map, combat and narrative triangle so far, peer review of Boss Blueprints, and the Final Project brief released
spec: your peer-review notes on another student's Boss Blueprint name a specific fairness or narrative concern, not general praise

nodes.title: The alternative-build workshop
nodes.description: Allocating 50 attribute points to a deliberately unconventional build and drafting the pitch copy that sells it
spec: your allocation names a specific stat most players would call a dead point, and builds the persona around spending heavily on it
your draft pitch names the cost the build accepts, not just its payoff

nodes.title: The death-currency workshop
nodes.description: Designing a corpse-run-style currency mechanic and calculating how much risk it actually asks a player to carry
spec: your mechanic states exactly what is lost on death, what triggers permanent loss, and how a player recovers it
you calculate a concrete number (a percentage, a distance, a time cost) for the risk your mechanic asks the player to carry

nodes.title: The message-template workshop
nodes.description: Writing deceptive and helpful message templates for five dangerous locations, using only a fixed, templated vocabulary
spec: your five locations each get one message that reads as helpful and one that reads as deceptive, using the same restricted vocabulary
a reader who hasn't seen the location can't tell which of your two messages is honest, only what each one claims

nodes.title: The HUD-subtraction workshop
nodes.description: Redesigning a cluttered HUD screenshot Souls-style, by removing elements rather than adding better ones
spec: your redesign removes at least three HUD elements from the original screenshot and names what the player now has to remember instead of each one
you keep, at most, what a Souls-like's own HUD keeps: health, stamina, equipped items, nothing tracking objectives

nodes.title: The three-endings workshop
nodes.description: Writing three 50-word endings — good, bad and true — for your original boss's world, in item-description style
spec: none of your three endings states outright whether it is the good, bad or true one — that has to be inferable, not labelled
your "true" ending is not simply a compromise between the other two

nodes.title: The final showcase
nodes.description: Presenting the Final Project one-pager for peer review, submitting Death Notes, and the semester's closing address
spec: your peer-review notes on another student's one-pager name whether its four parts argue the same thing about the level, not just whether each part individually works

nodes.title: Boss Blueprint
nodes.description: A two-phase boss encounter — its transition trigger, its narrative justification, and the new attack phase two introduces
spec: names a phase-transition trigger and states, in one sentence, why this specific boss would change that way
phase two's new attack has a stated, learnable telegraph, not just a faster or harder version of a phase-one attack
describes one staging change to the arena that signals the transition alongside the rule change

bands.descriptor: The telegraph is readable on a first encounter — a player who has never seen this boss can react to the wind-up in time, no prior knowledge required.
The telegraph is readable, but only for a player already watching for the specific tell named; the wind-up needs one more clarifying beat before a first-timer catches it.
A telegraph is named, but it reads as a reskin of a phase-one attack — same tell, faster or harder — rather than a distinct, learnable pattern.
No learnable telegraph is described, or the "new attack" is a phase-one attack with a bigger number attached to it.
The justification is specific to this boss's fiction and could not be copy-pasted onto a different boss without rewriting it.
The justification is specific, but stated rather than staged — it would land harder with one concrete arena or animation detail carrying it, not just the sentence explaining it.
The justification is present but generic — a variant of "the boss gets angrier at half health" that would fit almost any boss in the brief.
No justification is given, or it contradicts something already established about the boss.

reflection.prompt: Name the moment while drafting or workshopping this blueprint where you were not sure the phase-two telegraph was actually learnable, and what you changed about it once you noticed.

nodes.title: Death Notes
nodes.description: Eleven weekly reflections, each naming one concrete moment from that week's material, submitted the week it covers — not held back and bundled at the end
spec: eleven entries, one per teaching week (weeks 1–11 — week 12 is the showcase, not a new content week), each naming one specific moment rather than a genre generality
no entry merely restates that week's lecture or topic essay in different words
submitted the week it covers; the best ten of eleven count, so one missed or weak week doesn't need its own extension request

bands.descriptor: Names one specific moment from that week's material — not a genre generality — and it's visibly getting more specific as the semester goes on, not repeating the same kind of observation under a new title.
Names a real moment, but restates that week's lecture or topic essay in different words rather than adding an observation the lecture didn't already make.
Late past the standard five-day extension described on the Policies page, missing, or reads as a genre generality a non-player could have written.

nodes.title: Final Project
nodes.description: A complete opening-level one-pager — map sketch, two item descriptions, a boss move summary, and an opening weak-guidance script
spec: all four required parts are present and reference the same original level, boss and setting
the map sketch includes at least two shortcut loops, per Week 3's standard
the boss move summary includes a phase transition with its narrative justification, per Week 5's standard
the opening script guides the player using diegetic cues only — no on-screen objective text or quest arrow

marking.description: Judged as a single design document, not four separate pieces. The four parts have to argue the same thing about your level — a map sketch that contradicts its own item descriptions, or a boss with no relationship to the opening script, reads as four assignments stapled together rather than one opening level.

bands.descriptor: Pull any one part out and it still names a detail — a setting, the boss's identity, a specific hazard — that at least one other part also depends on. The four parts couldn't be reshuffled onto a different level without rewriting them.
The four parts agree, but only at the level of genre convention — nothing beyond "this is a Souls-like level" ties them together; no shared proper noun or concrete detail does the connecting work.
Three of the four parts cohere; one reads as written for a different level — a boss with no relationship to the opening script, or an item description that doesn't fit the sketched space.
Four disconnected pieces that each satisfy their own spec line in isolation but do not describe the same level.

reflection.prompt: Name the one part of the one-pager you rewrote after noticing it didn't actually match the other three, and what the mismatch was.

nodes.title: Loadout Pitch
nodes.description: Pitch copy for a deliberately unconventional build — proof that a stat allocation can be a persona, not just a spreadsheet
spec: allocates a stated 50-point attribute budget to a build that is not the default balanced or meta allocation
the pitch copy sells a persona the numbers support, not a spreadsheet justification of the numbers themselves
names the specific cost the build accepts in exchange for its identity

criteria.name: Coherence of the build as a persona

bands.descriptor: Every stat choice is load-bearing for the persona — the allocation, how the build actually plays, and the pitch copy all point at the same identity.
The persona is coherent, but one point is a residual optimisation rather than a commitment to the bit — a spare point dumped into a "safe" stat the persona doesn't call for.
The persona is named, but nothing about this specific allocation is load-bearing for it — a different 50-point split could support the same persona equally well.
The allocation is the default balanced or meta build with a persona description bolted on after the fact.
Sells the specific weakness as the whole point — a skeptical reader finishes the pitch understanding why the cost is the appeal, not despite it.
Persuasive and specific, but the cost is stated rather than sold — a sentence naming the weakness, not one that makes accepting it sound worth it.
Reads as marketing copy for the genre generally ("challenge yourself!") rather than for this specific, costed build.
No stated cost, or the copy could be pasted onto a min-maxed build without changing a word.

reflection.prompt: Name the moment while designing this build where the persona and the statistically stronger allocation pulled in different directions, and which one you let win.

nodes.title: Policies and support
nodes.description: The course-wide rules for late work, extensions, academic integrity and getting help.

course.title: Professional Identity Performance
course.description: Fluency in a role you do not yet hold. Every professional identity is performed before it is inhabited; this course teaches you to do it deliberately, name what you are doing, and get hired anyway.

nodes.title: Self-Audit Clinic
nodes.description: The floor-setting tutorial: bring three real job ads and whatever materials you have, and audit every claim against evidence you could produce today.

meta.termGloss: The lowest claim you could make about yourself and still defend it in a room containing someone able to check. Most CVs are written a full storey above their author's truthfloor, which is survivable right up until the follow-up question.

streams.name: Technical Practice
streams.focus: Audit a CV plus one repo; every claim must point at something that runs.

streams.name: Creative and Communications Practice
streams.focus: Audit a portfolio; mark which pieces are finished and which are in progress.

streams.name: Commercial and Public Practice
streams.focus: Audit a LinkedIn and a cover letter; mark which claims survive a single show me.

nodes.title: Live Teardown
nodes.description: One advertisement, taken apart live into four columns, until the fourth one — the accidental confession — is visible.

meta.termGloss: The dialect job advertisements are written in. Every ad is four documents stapled together: legal boilerplate, a wishlist nobody expects met, the work you would actually do, and an accidental confession about the last person who held the job.

streams.name: Technical Practice
streams.focus: Graduate engineering ad, each bullet mapped to a verifiable artefact.

streams.name: Creative and Communications Practice
streams.focus: Studio or agency brief, identifying what is actually being bought.

streams.name: Commercial and Public Practice
streams.focus: A selection-criteria document, mapped to the answer shapes it is fishing for.

nodes.title: Blind Review
nodes.description: Teardowns are anonymised and swapped inside your stream; you write someone else's gap map before you see what they wrote about yours.

meta.termGloss: Not how large the distance between you and the role is, but what shape it has — which parts close in a fortnight, which take a year, and which you will simply have to say out loud. The specific version is the one you can plan against.

streams.name: Technical Practice
streams.focus: Technical-depth gaps.

streams.name: Creative and Communications Practice
streams.focus: Taste-and-range gaps.

streams.name: Commercial and Public Practice
streams.focus: Judgement-and-context gaps.

nodes.title: Claims Tribunal
nodes.description: You read your claims aloud, peers demand a receipt for each, and anything unevidenced is struck from the record on the spot.

meta.termGloss: The accumulated distance between the claims on your materials and the evidence you could produce for them inside ninety seconds. Invisible until somebody says show me, at which point it is charged in full.

streams.name: Technical Practice
streams.focus: A receipt is a commit, a running thing, or a measurement.

streams.name: Creative and Communications Practice
streams.focus: A receipt is a piece someone other than you has seen or used.

streams.name: Commercial and Public Practice
streams.focus: A receipt is a number, a decision, or a named stakeholder.

nodes.title: Anecdote Roleplay
nodes.description: Paired question-and-answer, rotating, with an observer scoring whether the story answered the question that was actually asked.

meta.termGloss: The one story you have told well enough that it holds up under four different questions without buckling. You need three, not twelve. Preparing is not dishonest; improvising badly is not more authentic.

streams.name: Technical Practice
streams.focus: A failure or debugging story showing reasoning under uncertainty.

streams.name: Creative and Communications Practice
streams.focus: A piece that did not work, and what the revision cost.

streams.name: Commercial and Public Practice
streams.focus: A decision made with insufficient information, and who it affected.

nodes.title: Gallery Walk
nodes.description: Work goes on the walls, critique goes on the sheets beside it, and nobody defends their own piece until the final cross-stream lap.

meta.termGloss: The layer of finish sitting between your work and the person assessing it. Thin varnish makes real work legible. Thick varnish conceals that there is not much underneath, and anyone who hires for a living can tell the difference by touch.

streams.name: Technical Practice
streams.focus: Repo front page and README.

streams.name: Creative and Communications Practice
streams.focus: Portfolio sequencing and case-study structure.

streams.name: Commercial and Public Practice
streams.focus: One-page capability brief.

nodes.title: Outreach Sprint
nodes.description: Three messages drafted in the room and scored by peers on one test: could a stranger answer this in a single line. Sending them is your call.

meta.termGloss: Somebody you have never met who nevertheless has a specific reason to reply, because you did the reading first. Warm one stranger properly rather than mailing forty, and expect silence, which is the standard reply and not a verdict.

streams.name: Technical Practice
streams.focus: Maintainers, engineering-blog authors, meetup organisers.

streams.name: Creative and Communications Practice
streams.focus: Practitioners whose specific piece you can speak about.

streams.name: Commercial and Public Practice
streams.focus: Alumni, industry-body contacts, graduate-program liaisons.

nodes.title: Red Team
nodes.description: Peers attack your materials for the weakest claim and put a stopwatch on it. You leave with a diff note and four days until Assessment 2.

meta.termGloss: The finite quantity of unevidenced claim a single document or conversation can carry before none of it is believed. The budget is shared, which is why one indefensible buzzword discredits the true sentence beside it.

streams.name: Technical Practice
streams.focus: Probe for depth behind vocabulary.

streams.name: Creative and Communications Practice
streams.focus: Probe for whose work it actually was.

streams.name: Commercial and Public Practice
streams.focus: Probe for the numbers behind the stated outcome.

nodes.title: Mock Panel
nodes.description: A mock panel run to your field's actual convention, then everyone declares an interview route — real or pool, graded identically.

meta.termGloss: The conditions of the room you did not create and cannot change. You prepare the parts you control: structure, examples, the questions you ask, and recovery from one bad answer. Everything else is weather, and weather is not a verdict on your worth.

streams.name: Technical Practice
streams.focus: Mixed live-technical and behavioural, with someone watching you think out loud.

streams.name: Creative and Communications Practice
streams.focus: Portfolio walkthrough, deliberately interrupted, so you practise resuming.

streams.name: Commercial and Public Practice
streams.focus: Competency panel answered against the written selection criteria in front of you.

nodes.title: Negotiation Simulation
nodes.description: Scripted rounds against a staff member playing the other side, with one hard rule: every student says the number out loud, in the room, at least once.

meta.termGloss: The half-second in which your face answers the salary question before you do. Entry-level negotiation is narrower than the internet claims but it is never zero, and the flinch is what costs you the parts that were available.

streams.name: Technical Practice
streams.focus: Scope, level, team allocation, and what a take-home is allowed to cost you.

streams.name: Creative and Communications Practice
streams.focus: Rates, usage rights, and declining an unpaid test brief without losing the contact.

streams.name: Commercial and Public Practice
streams.focus: Start date, rotation preference, grad-stream choice, and what is fixed by policy.

nodes.title: Artefact Swap
nodes.description: Your Dossier goes to somebody else and you present theirs to a visiting practitioner, who critiques the case in front of them rather than the person holding it.

meta.termGloss: The interval between being hired for a role and being able to perform it: normal, universal, and almost never mentioned at the offer stage. Pretending you have no lag is the fastest way to lengthen it.

streams.name: Technical Practice
streams.focus: A practitioner from the field hears a swapped Dossier and names the ramp they would expect.

streams.name: Creative and Communications Practice
streams.focus: A working practitioner responds to a swapped case, including what they would cut.

streams.name: Commercial and Public Practice
streams.focus: A practitioner from the sector reads a swapped case against how their panels actually read.

nodes.title: Closing Viva
nodes.description: Eight minutes each, examined by your own stream on a single question: which part of your performance became true, and how do you know.

meta.termGloss: The join between the version of you that was performed and the version that quietly became true, and the labour of deciding what to do about it. Seamwork is the audit: keep what is honest scaffolding, and go and learn the rest.

streams.name: Technical Practice
streams.focus: Examined by your own convenor and two peers; evidence means something that runs.

streams.name: Creative and Communications Practice
streams.focus: Examined on the body of work as it now stands, and on what you would cut today.

streams.name: Commercial and Public Practice
streams.focus: Examined against your own week-1 criteria response, read back to you.

nodes.title: Role Teardown and Gap Map
nodes.description: Dossier sections one to four: an evidenced baseline inventory, three real target ads, one four-column annotated teardown, and a gap map tiered by closeability.
spec: every claim in the baseline inventory points at evidence you could produce in ninety seconds
the teardown separates boilerplate, wishlist, actual work and accidental confession
each gap is tiered, specific, and stated without apology or bluff

criteria.name: Accuracy of the teardown — does the four-column split hold up against the ad
Specificity of gap articulation — planned against, not apologised for

course.title: Coincidence, Fate and Other Suspicious Patterns
course.description: Humans are extraordinarily good at finding patterns — in dreams, cards, stars and data. This course studies the territory between coincidence and meaning, and what happens when a pattern starts to feel like it was meant to happen.

nodes.title: The pattern-seeking animal
nodes.description: Why a brain built to spot predators in leaves now sees faces in toast, streaks in coin flips, and messages in static.

meta.question: Why does a brain built to survive keep finding meaning in noise?

activities.prompt: One of these three was flipped from a real coin, ten times in a row. The other two were typed by people asked to fake a random sequence. Which one do you think is the real coin?
options: A: H T H H H T H H H T
B: H T T H T H T H T H
C: H H H H H T T T T T
activities.reveal: It's B. People faking randomness avoid long streaks, because a run of five heads in a row doesn't feel random even though a fair coin produces one about 3% of the time. Real coin sequences look clumpier than anyone expects — the clumps are what your pattern-detector flags as suspicious.

activities.prompt: For the next real day, keep a running note of every 'that's too weird to be a coincidence' moment you catch yourself noticing — a song, a name, a number. Predict here, before you start, roughly how many you expect to catch.

nodes.title: Probability feels wrong
nodes.description: Why intuitions about chance are reliably, predictably bad — and what that means for anything you're tempted to call a coincidence.

meta.question: If two people in this room share a birthday, is that a coincidence worth investigating?

activities.prompt: How many people need to be in a room before there's a better-than-even chance that two of them share a birthday?
options: About 180 (half of 365)
About 50
About 23
activities.reveal: 23. With 23 people there are 253 possible pairs, and it only takes one matching pair to win. Most people estimate close to 180 because they imagine checking their own birthday against everyone else's, instead of every pair against every other pair — the same reasoning error that makes a coincidence in your own life feel far rarer than it statistically is.

activities.prompt: Don't take the 23 on trust — run the room yourself. Each click simulates 200 rooms of 23 random birthdays and reports how many of those rooms had a shared birthday.
activities.mechanism: Each click draws 23 uniformly random days (1–365, leap years ignored) per simulated room, 200 rooms per click, and counts how many rooms had at least one repeated day — plain Math.random() in your browser, run fresh each time, not a lookup of the theoretical 50.7% answer.

nodes.title: Omens
nodes.description: What turns an ordinary event into a sign, across cultures and centuries — and what an omen is actually doing for the person who reads one.

meta.question: What turns an ordinary event — a broken mirror, a crow at the window — into an omen?

activities.prompt: A black cat crosses your path on the morning of an exam you're already anxious about. How do you make sense of that?

choices.label: It's a bad omen — you should be careful today.
choices.response: This is the oldest reading available, and it isn't stupid: societies have used shared omens for millennia as a common language for anxiety. Believing it can even change your behaviour for the better — if you walk into the exam more careful and alert, the omen 'worked,' just not by predicting anything.

choices.label: It's confirmation bias — you'll only remember it if the day goes badly.
choices.response: Also true, and it's the mechanism, not just a competing theory. If the exam goes fine, the cat is forgotten by lunchtime. If it goes badly, the cat becomes the story you tell afterwards. The omen isn't predicting the outcome; the outcome is selecting which mornings get remembered as ominous.

choices.label: It's just a cat — there's nothing here to explain.
choices.response: Also defensible, and also incomplete on its own: 'nothing to explain' doesn't account for why you noticed it, felt a small jolt, and are still thinking about it now. Something happened at the level of attention even if nothing happened at the level of the world.

activities.prompt: Walk through a small decision, one step at a time, and see where each reading of the same omen leads.
activities.mechanism: Every node and every ending below was written in advance — there is no hidden logic beyond 'which button did you press,' and no path is scored as the winning one.

start.text: A black cat crosses your path on the way to the exam. You have twenty minutes left to get there.

choices.label: Take it as a warning and leave immediately, rattled.
Notice it, shrug, and keep walking at the same pace.

warned.text: You arrive twelve minutes early, slightly out of breath but calm by the time the exam starts.

choices.label: See how the exam goes.

ignored.text: You arrive with two minutes to spare, a little more rushed.

choices.label: See how the exam goes.

end-well.text: However it goes, notice which version of events you'll be tempted to file under 'the cat was right about something' — and which one you'll forget by next week regardless.

nodes.title: Dreams
nodes.description: Does a dream mean something on its own terms, or does the meaning get added afterward, by the waking mind that retells it?

meta.question: Does a dream mean something, or does the meaning get added afterward, awake?

activities.prompt: You dream of losing your teeth the night before a big presentation. What is the dream doing?

choices.label: Freudian: a disguised anxiety about castration or loss of power.
choices.response: Freud's specific symbolic vocabulary (teeth as a stand-in for power or virility) is one of the least testable parts of his theory, and most contemporary psychology doesn't use it. But his broader claim — that dream content connects to emotional material the waking mind is managing — remains a live and reasonable hypothesis.

choices.label: Jungian: a symbol drawn from a shared, deeper layer of meaning.
choices.response: Jung would resist reducing the tooth to one fixed meaning at all — he'd want to know what teeth mean to *you*, read against recurring symbolic patterns he called archetypes. Week 5 is entirely about this move, and about the harder question of whether 'shared symbolic layer' is a real structure or a beautiful metaphor for something else.

choices.label: Neuroscience: your brain doing overnight memory consolidation, no message intended.
choices.response: Contemporary sleep research treats dreams largely as a side effect of memory consolidation and threat-simulation processes running without narrative intent. On this account the anxiety is real and the tooth is arbitrary — your brain rehearsing 'something bad happening' using whatever imagery was lying around.

activities.prompt: Open two or three of these readings of the same tooth-loss dream side by side, rather than picking one. Notice which pairs sit comfortably together and which don't.
activities.mechanism: These three panels are fixed text, shown or hidden by your own clicks — nothing here decides which reading is correct, or blends them into a single verdict.

lenses.label: Freudian lens
lenses.text: A disguised expression of an anxiety the conscious mind won't name directly — the presentation is the real threat, the teeth are the costume it wears in sleep.

lenses.label: Jungian lens
lenses.text: A symbol worth sitting with rather than decoding — what do teeth personally represent to you, and does that meaning recur elsewhere in your own life, not just in a shared archetype list?

lenses.label: Neuroscience lens
lenses.text: No message at all: overnight memory consolidation and threat simulation running on whatever imagery happened to be active, arbitrary content wrapped around a real, ordinary anxiety.

nodes.title: Jung and synchronicity
nodes.description: Carl Jung's "meaningful coincidence" — an event linked to your inner state by meaning rather than cause — and whether that's a real category or a good name for a feeling.

meta.question: Is synchronicity a real category of event, or a name for a coincidence we refuse to let go of?

activities.prompt: You are thinking, for the first time in years, about an old friend you lost touch with. Ten minutes later, they call. What kind of event is this?

choices.label: Synchronicity — meaningfully connected, without one causing the other.
choices.response: This is Jung's own proposed category: not causal, but not coincidental either — connected by significance to the person experiencing it. It's a genuinely different claim from either of the other two readings, which is exactly why it's controversial: it asks you to accept a kind of connection that isn't causation.

choices.label: A coincidence, full stop — memorable because it's rare, not because it's connected.
choices.response: The base-rate argument from week 2 applies directly: across a lifetime of half-remembered old friends, some of them are going to call in the ten minutes after you happen to think of them, purely by chance. You don't remember the thousands of times you thought of someone and nothing happened.

choices.label: Not coincidence at all — something cued the thought (a shared memory, a mutual friend's post).
choices.response: This is the reading Jung's critics reach for most often: look for the ordinary causal link before reaching for an extraordinary one. A shared anniversary, a photo that surfaced online, a mutual contact mentioning them — any of these would make the 'coincidence' fully explicable, just not yet noticed.

activities.prompt: Hold the friend-calls-back case up against a short checklist before reading the discussion below.

criteria.label: High base rate
criteria.description: Across a whole life, how many old friends exist to think about, and how many ten-minute windows are there to catch a call in?

criteria.label: Selective memory
criteria.description: Would you remember the times you thought of someone and nothing happened, as clearly as you remember this one?

criteria.label: Findable ordinary cause
criteria.description: Is there a mutual contact, anniversary, or online trace that could have cued both of you at once, entirely without coincidence?

activities.discussion: All three boxes usually apply at once, which is the actual argument of this week: 'synchronicity' isn't a rival explanation competing with base rates and selective memory, it's a name for how the event feels once those two have already done their work. Whether that feeling deserves its own category, on top of the mechanism, is the real question Jung is asking — not whether the mechanism is real.

nodes.title: Astrology
nodes.description: Why a horoscope written for a twelfth of the planet can feel like it was written about you specifically — and what that says about reading, not about the stars.

meta.question: Why does a horoscope written for 1/12th of the planet feel like it was written about you?

activities.prompt: Read this personality sketch, supposedly written just for you: 'You have a strong need for other people to like you, yet you tend to be critical of yourself. You have a great deal of unused capacity which you have not turned to your advantage.' How personal does that feel?

choices.label: Surprisingly personal — that really does sound like me.
choices.response: In Bertram Forer's 1948 classroom study, this exact paragraph was given to every student, described as a personalised result from a personality test. Average rating of accuracy: 4.26 out of 5. The statements are written to be true of almost everyone, at a level of generality that lets each reader supply their own specific evidence.

choices.label: Somewhat — but I can see it's written vaguely on purpose.
choices.response: This is the more clear-eyed reading, and it's worth sitting with why it still felt somewhat personal even so: vague-but-flattering statements about ambivalence and untapped potential are close to universally true, because most people privately feel both confident and self-critical, both capable and underused.

choices.label: Not personal at all — this could describe anyone.
choices.response: Correct — and that's the entire mechanism, not an exception to it. This is the exact wording used in Forer's original study, and it is still the standard demonstration of what's now called the Barnum (or Forer) effect: high perceived accuracy from statements built to be true of nearly everyone.

activities.prompt: Sort each statement below as a Barnum statement (vague enough to fit almost anyone) or a specific claim (concrete enough that it could actually be wrong about you).

items.text: You sometimes doubt whether you made the right decision.
items.explanation: Almost everyone has doubted a decision at some point — there's no way for this to feel false, which is exactly the Barnum signature.

items.text: You were born in the third week of March.
items.explanation: This is either true or false, checkable against a real fact, and wrong for roughly eleven-twelfths of any audience — a specific claim in the sense this activity means.

items.text: You have ambitions that sometimes feel unrealistic to others.
items.explanation: Vague, flattering, and true of nearly anyone who has ever wanted something — no falsifying case is offered.

items.text: You have visited four countries outside your home country.
items.explanation: A concrete, checkable number. Most readers will find it simply wrong for them, which is what makes it specific rather than Barnum.

activities.mechanism: Each item's category was fixed when this activity was written, based on whether the claim is checkable and likely false for a large share of readers. Clicking doesn't analyse the sentence — it checks your guess against that fixed answer.

nodes.title: Tarot
nodes.description: If a reading only ever tells you something you already suspected, is it still doing something useful — and what, exactly?

meta.question: If a tarot reading only ever tells you something you already suspected, is it still doing something useful?

activities.prompt: You draw The Tower, reversed, while asking about a decision you've been putting off. The card traditionally means sudden, disruptive upheaval — reversed, some readers say it means upheaval you're avoiding rather than upheaval that's already happened. What is the reading doing?

choices.label: Prophecy — the cards are telling you what will happen.
choices.response: This is the strongest possible claim, and the one this course does not endorse: there is no established mechanism by which shuffling a deck could encode information about a specific future event, and no controlled study has shown reading accuracy above chance. Treating it as literal forecasting is the one framing the course asks you to set aside.

choices.label: A projective tool — a structured prompt that lets you say what you already half-know.
choices.response: This is the strongest defensible reading. A tarot deck's 78 cards each carry rich, ambiguous imagery, deliberately open enough that almost any drawn card can be made to fit almost any question. The skill isn't supernatural; it's the same skill a good therapist or coach uses — structured, open-ended prompting that helps someone articulate what they were already circling.

choices.label: A cold read — the reader is picking up on your reaction and adjusting.
choices.response: This applies more to a reading done by another person than a solo draw, but it's real: a professional reader watches your face, your pauses, which interpretation you nod along to, and follows the thread you're giving them, refined live rather than fixed at the shuffle.

activities.prompt: Three invented exhibits from a fictional reading. Open each one and see if you can name the technique before reading the tag underneath.

entries.title: 'You've been carrying something you haven't said out loud.'
entries.content: Said early, before any card is drawn, to almost any client who booked a reading in the first place — most people seeking a reading are carrying something unsaid.
entries.technique: Barnum opener — true of nearly anyone who walks in.

entries.title: 'I sense hesitation... you're not fully sure about this, are you?'
entries.content: Said just after the client's face flickers at a card. The reader adjusts the next sentence to match whether the client nods or frowns.
entries.technique: Cold reading — reacting live to the client's own signals.

entries.title: 'This card asks what you're avoiding, not what will happen.'
entries.content: Said about The Tower reversed, deliberately reframing a dramatic card as an open question rather than a forecast.
entries.technique: Projective framing — the ambiguity is handed back to the client.

activities.mechanism: These three exhibits are invented for teaching, not transcripts of a real session. Opening one always shows the same content and the same named technique.

nodes.title: The I Ching
nodes.description: A 3,000-year-old divination system built on genuinely random coin tosses — and the case that structured randomness can produce advice worth taking.

meta.question: Can a genuinely random process still produce advice worth taking?

activities.prompt: Ask a real question you're currently unsure about, then consult a small demonstration oracle built the same way: a random draw from a fixed pool of readings.
outputs: Something finished is still being carried. Put it down before picking up what's next.
The obstacle is smaller than the story you've built around it. Test it directly.
You already know which way this goes. The delay is about comfort, not information.
Wait one turn. What looks urgent today will look different once someone else moves first.
The advice you'd give a friend in this position is the advice to take.
activities.mechanism: This picks uniformly at random from five fixed lines using the same coin-flip logic the I Ching itself uses to select one of 64 hexagrams (traditionally by tossing three coins six times). Nothing about your question changes which line you get — the fit you feel afterward is you doing the work, the same interpretive move as weeks 6 and 7.

activities.prompt: See the coin-toss method itself, run at scale. Each click simulates 300 line-casts using the traditional three-coins-per-line method and reports the resulting split across the four line types.
activities.mechanism: Three virtual coins are tossed per line (heads worth 3, tails worth 2); the total (6, 7, 8 or 9) sorts the line into old yin, young yang, young yin or old yang. Doing this six times per casting is how a traditional I Ching hexagram is built — this just runs the single-line version hundreds of times to show the four outcomes aren't equally likely (1/8, 3/8, 3/8, 1/8), a real fact about the method, independent of what it's being asked.

nodes.title: Numerology
nodes.description: What a number is doing when it stops being an arithmetic fact and starts feeling like a message meant for you.

meta.question: What is a number doing when it starts to feel like a message?

activities.prompt: Numerology often reduces a birth date to a single 'life path number' by repeatedly summing its digits (for example, 15/08/1995 becomes 1+5+0+8+1+9+9+5 = 38, then 3+8 = 11, then 1+1 = 2). Draw a life path reading and see how it lands.
outputs: Life path 1: you start things other people are still deciding whether to start.
Life path 2: you notice what a room needs before anyone says it out loud.
Life path 3: you make things — the making is the point, not always the finishing.
Life path 7: you trust a conclusion more once you've taken it apart yourself.
Life path 9: you're already thinking about who this affects, not just you.
activities.mechanism: The digit-sum reduction really is deterministic arithmetic — every birth date maps to exactly one of nine numbers, with no randomness involved. This demo skips the arithmetic and just draws one of the five results above at random, so you can test how the *reading itself* feels independent of whether your real birth date produced it.

activities.prompt: Pick one number — 11, 111, or your own age — and predict, in writing, how many times you think you'll notice it in the next real week. Then actually count, off the page, and see how the prediction held up.
activities.placeholder: I predict I'll notice it about... times, mostly in these places...
activities.mechanism: This is a plain text box. Nothing you type is saved, sent anywhere, or scored — reloading the page clears it completely. The exercise only works if you genuinely tally afterward, on paper or in your head.

nodes.title: Cognitive biases
nodes.description: Confirmation bias and illusory correlation, named properly — the two mechanisms that have been running underneath every week so far.

meta.question: Which came first, the pattern or your reason for believing in it?

activities.prompt: Below are two datasets from an (imaginary) trial: 20 coin tosses each, labelled Dataset A and Dataset B. One shows a real streaky pattern; the other is genuinely random. Which one looks more patterned to you?
options: Dataset A looks patterned
Dataset B looks patterned
Neither — they both look random to me
activities.reveal: Trick question: both datasets were generated the same way, by an unweighted random number generator. Neither is more 'patterned' than the other in any measurable sense. If you picked A or B, you experienced illusory correlation firsthand — the tendency to find structure in truly random data, especially once told to go looking for it.

activities.prompt: This week names six biases. Sort each one by what it actually distorts: the evidence you notice and remember, or the outcome you expect and predict.

items.text: Confirmation bias — noticing hits, forgetting misses.
items.explanation: This changes which evidence gets registered and recalled in the first place — it operates before any prediction is even made.

items.text: Survivorship bias — judging by the data that made it into view, ignoring what didn't.
items.explanation: This is about which evidence can even reach you — the bullet holes on the planes that came back, not the ones that didn't.

items.text: Hindsight bias — 'I knew it all along' once the outcome is known.
items.explanation: This reshapes your sense of how predictable an outcome was, after the fact — a distortion of expectation, not of the original evidence.

items.text: Self-fulfilling prophecy — a belief that changes the outcome it predicted.
items.explanation: This is squarely about outcomes: the prediction itself alters what happens next, independent of any evidence about what was likely.

activities.mechanism: Each item's category was assigned when this activity was written, based on whether the bias operates on which evidence you notice (evidence-side) or on your sense of what was going to happen (outcome-side). Clicking checks your guess against that fixed classification, not a live analysis of the sentence.

nodes.title: Algorithms as modern oracles
nodes.description: When a recommendation algorithm "gets you," is it reading you personally, or reading everyone who looks statistically like you?

meta.question: When a recommendation algorithm "gets you," is it reading you, or reading everyone like you?

activities.prompt: Pick the mood you're in right now, and see what this miniature 'recommendation engine' suggests. Then read how it actually works.
outputs: Something you already own, that you haven't opened in a while.
The thing your friend mentioned once and you dismissed too quickly.
Nothing new — a repeat of whatever worked last time you felt this way.
The unfamiliar option. Growth is comfortable enough after a good day.
Whatever takes the least deciding. Some days aren't for judgment calls.
activities.mechanism: This picks uniformly at random from five stock lines, with no model of you at all. A real recommendation system instead scores thousands of items against patterns learned from millions of other users' past behaviour, and returns whichever score highest for people who behaved like you so far. The 'personal' feeling comes from scale, not from being known — the same way a horoscope's 'personal' feeling comes from breadth, not precision.

activities.prompt: Four systems this course has covered, filed side by side. Open each exhibit and guess where it falls on two axes — fixed pool vs. learned model, mechanism disclosed vs. opaque — before checking the tag.

entries.title: Exhibit A — the I Ching (week 8)
entries.content: A fixed pool of 64 hexagram texts, selected by a real, physically disclosed coin toss anyone can watch and repeat.

entries.title: Exhibit B — the horoscope column (week 6)
entries.content: A fixed pool of Barnum statements, matched to a birth-date bucket, with the mechanism typically left unstated to the reader.

entries.title: Exhibit C — the recommendation algorithm
entries.content: A model learned from millions of other users' behaviour, scoring items for you specifically; the scoring process itself is invisible to the person receiving it.

entries.title: Exhibit D — AI-generated interpretation
entries.content: A learned model generating fresh, individually-worded interpretive text on demand from an effectively unbounded space, rather than recycling a fixed shelf of lines.
entries.technique: Learned model, opaque unless a provider chooses to explain it

activities.mechanism: These four exhibits summarise material already covered in weeks 6 and 8 and in this week's own lecture text above — opening one displays a fixed classification written when this activity was made, not a live re-analysis of the system.

nodes.title: Synthesis
nodes.description: Bringing the three-part method — seeing, meaning, trusting — back together, and turning it on the last thing in the course that hasn't been examined yet — the course website itself.

meta.question: Now that you can name the trick, does a good coincidence feel any different?

activities.prompt: The homepage of this course website tells you the exact time you opened it, on which day of the week, and how many times this browser has visited before. It feels oddly personal for a static website. What is it doing?

choices.label: It's reading something real about you — your actual time and visit history.
choices.response: Correct, and worth being precise about what 'real' means here: your device's clock and a number stored in this browser's local storage are genuinely yours, not fabricated. What's being read is real. What it's being read as — a sign that this moment is significant — is the interpretive step you're supplying.

choices.label: It's a trick — the site is just showing me facts and letting me feel a coincidence.
choices.response: This is the more clear-eyed version of the same correct answer. Every visitor sees a sentence built from their own real timestamp and their own real visit count. Nobody sees anyone else's. The sentence is true and mundane; the feeling of being addressed personally is supplied by exactly the same machinery covered in week 1.

choices.label: It's the same move as a horoscope — vague enough to fit anyone, personal enough to feel targeted.
choices.response: Closer to precise than either reading above: a horoscope's statements are vague-but-universal (week 6); this sentence is narrow-but-universal — a template with your own real numbers slotted in. Different mechanism, same outcome: a shared structure that reads as individually meant.

activities.prompt: One last sort before the course ends. For each claim below, decide: has this course fully explained it away with a named mechanism, or does it leave a genuinely open question standing?
categoryLabels: Fully explained by a named mechanism

items.explanation: Fully accounted for by the Barnum effect (week 6) — no residue is left over once that mechanism is named.

items.text: Whether 'synchronicity' names a real kind of connection, not just a coincidence explained by base rates and selective memory.
items.explanation: Week 5 leaves this genuinely open: base rates and selective memory explain the *feeling*, but whether meaning-without-cause is its own coherent category is a debate this course reports rather than settles.

items.text: A recommendation algorithm 'knowing' you well enough to be useful.
items.explanation: Mechanically explained by collaborative filtering (week 11) — a real, working statistical process, not a mystery. What it raises isn't a mechanism question but a values one: whether accuracy alone should change how the system is treated.

items.text: Whether explaining why a belief feels true also proves the belief is false.
items.explanation: Week 10 names this explicitly as the genetic fallacy trap: explaining the psychological route to a belief is a different claim from disproving it, and this course deliberately leaves that separation standing rather than collapsing it.

activities.mechanism: Each item's category reflects the position this course's own lecture text actually takes (weeks 5, 6, 10 and 11) — sorting here checks your answer against that fixed, citable position, not a live judgment call.

course.title: The Fracturing of the Latter Day Saint Movement
course.description: When Joseph Smith was killed in 1844 with no named successor, his church didn't survive intact — it split into dozens of competing churches, from Utah's mainstream body to Strang's island kingdom to the modern FLDS. course.title: Nobody Speaks This Yet

course.title: The Devastating Note

nodes.title: A1 — Explain It Without the Explainer
nodes.description: Learn something unfamiliar, close every source, reconstruct it from memory, then test the reconstruction against the authority you closed.
spec: a source consulted while it was open, and a plain record of when it closed
a reconstruction produced with the source closed, not edited afterward
a comparison against the source that names at least one specific place the reconstruction was wrong, not just that it was "mostly right"
a short corrected explanation, written after seeing where it broke

criteria.name: Reconstruction accuracy against the closed source

nodes.title: A2 — Build a Bad Test
nodes.description: Design an instrument for something a peer claims to understand, administer it live, and report what it detected, what it missed, and what it fooled.
spec: a claim of understanding from a real peer, named and consenting
a designed instrument stating which rung(s) it targets, made before administration, not adjusted afterward
a real, administered session with a recorded outcome
a deliberately planted fake or edge case the instrument was meant to catch, and an honest report of whether it did
a written account of what the instrument cannot detect, not only what it can

criteria.name: Instrument design against the seven rungs
Live administration and fidelity to the design
Self-critique of what the instrument missed

nodes.title: A3 — Transfer
nodes.description: Take the model you built understanding of earlier in the course and apply it somewhere it was never shown to you, then defend the result.
spec: the model or skill applied is one built and tested earlier in the course
the new domain or case was never used to teach or test that model
a defence that stands without you present to explain it
a named claim about what A1 and A2's results did not, in hindsight, prove

criteria.name: Genuine transfer to an unrehearsed domain
Explicit account of what the earlier instruments didn't detect
Clarity for a reader who wasn't in the room

nodes.title: In-class activity
nodes.description: Weekly engagement with the sessions themselves — the reconstructions, reviews and instruments run in each week's teaching time.
spec: a genuine attempt at each week's in-class task, not a completed answer copied in beforehand
visible participation in the review or discussion that follows the task

marking.description: Assessed cumulatively across the semester on genuine engagement with each week's in-class activity — attempting the reconstruction, the review, or the instrument the session sets, and bringing a real result to discuss. This is not attendance marking and it is not a fourth artefact — showing up without attempting the week's task earns nothing, and a strong result produced without engaging in the room earns nothing either.

nodes.title: When information is cheap
nodes.description: Use a familiar Wi-Fi problem to distinguish a correct answer from evidence of understanding, with explanations and activities you can work through independently.

nodes.title: The feeling of understanding
nodes.description: Use a zip fastener and an adapted rate, explain and re-rate protocol to separate confidence from performance, and to see what a fluent explanation can still conceal.

nodes.title: Reconstruction
nodes.description: Study a supplied explanation of a pin tumbler lock, close it, rebuild the mechanism from memory, then restore the source and read the annotated difference as evidence.

nodes.title: Evidence changes with conditions
nodes.description: Read one fictional person's three accounts of the same lock, produced under three different conditions, and find out why intuitive judgements of understanding stop agreeing with each other.

nodes.title: Build the first instrument
nodes.description: Construct the course's seven-rung ladder from performances you have already read, find out where it cannot decide a case, and locate the assumption it quietly makes.

nodes.title: What are you allowed to use?
nodes.description: Follow a fictional cyclist across a city using turn-by-turn navigation, and test whether needing a resource ever tells us, by itself, that someone does not understand.

nodes.title: Change the form
nodes.description: Watch one fictional explanation of compound interest get produced for a new audience and a new problem, and use the transfer-of-learning literature to ask when a different form is better evidence of understanding.

nodes.title: What if you didn't know the test?
nodes.description: Watch a fictional baker's prepared explanation meet an unannounced follow-up question, and find out what surprise can reveal about a causal model that rehearsal cannot.

nodes.title: The prior state
nodes.description: Use a fictional gardener's plant diagnosis and Fischhoff's hindsight-bias study to explain why a prediction recorded before checking the answer is different evidence from a claim about what you "already knew."

nodes.title: Knowledge with a collaborator
nodes.description: Repeat the Week 2 knowledge paper-swap with a live AI collaborator this time, and test whether a careful record of who said what can settle whose understanding a performance demonstrates.

nodes.title: Administering an examination
nodes.description: Design a short instrument from the course's ladder, resources and notice decisions, then administer it to a real person and interpret what the record does and does not establish.

nodes.title: Defending the inference
nodes.description: Watch a fictional examinee pass every rung of the course's own instrument cleanly, then find out why that clean pass still cannot settle what it was built to settle.

course.title: SLOP4225: Budgeted Language Model Training
course.description: Study how modern large language models are really trained, then rebuild the pipeline at a controllable scale: pre-train a narrative model, reshape it through post-training, and specialise it for a defined task under a 32M design target and fixed compute budgets.

nodes.title: Project 1 Launch and Data Validation
nodes.description: Verify the supported environment and data checksums, and write a bounded Project 1 target before selecting an architecture
spec: the document-level split is confirmed, not a token-level split
all flagged exact or near-duplicate overlap has been resolved or reported
the target statement describes observable continuation behaviour, not "get the lowest loss"

nodes.title: Lab 1 — Spend a 32M Parameter Budget
nodes.description: Trace shapes through a causal decoder block and compare two legal architectures under the 32M/33.6M parameter boundary
spec: every target token depends only on its prefix
both models are at or below 33.6M learned parameters, with 32M still the design target
only one primary architecture allocation changed between Architecture A and B
data, steps, seed policy, and evaluation are identical across both runs
the conclusion distinguishes prediction from observed evidence

nodes.title: Project 1 Pilot Clinic
nodes.description: An evidence-led drop-in clinic for diagnosing a training pilot before committing to the principal Project 1 run
spec: a written decision to continue, revise one factor, or stop
a stated reason for that decision
a maximum additional spend attached to the decision

nodes.title: Project 1 Evaluation and Packaging
nodes.description: Run the released evaluation pipeline, verify a fresh-process load, and reconcile the report, ledger, and model package before submission
spec: the documented command loads the same weights described in the report
the report names the same revision as the submitted package
no secret appears anywhere in the package

nodes.title: Project 2 Target and Baseline Planning
nodes.description: Define a target voice in observable dimensions, freeze the unchanged baseline, and cost one viable post-training route
spec: a reader could decide whether the claimed style changed
a reader could decide whether narrative ability regressed

nodes.title: Lab 2 — Build and Inspect a Post-Training Batch
nodes.description: Render a response-only loss mask, run a bounded SFT update, and test whether an apparent behaviour survives prompt paraphrase
spec: another person could reconstruct the exact training string from the schema
prompt and padding labels are masked as declared
EOS is present and trained intentionally
the comparison uses the same starting checkpoint and data
synthetic or edited material is labelled honestly

nodes.title: Project 2 Behaviour Clinic
nodes.description: An evidence-led drop-in clinic for interpreting target-versus-retention evidence and difficult preference labels
spec: a frozen evaluation comparison
a justified decision about the next or final post-training stage

nodes.title: Project 2 Blind Evaluation and Packaging
nodes.description: Compare the unchanged and tuned checkpoints under blinded, matched conditions and package a reproducible Project 2 submission
spec: a style improvement alone does not justify selection if the output is unusable
a style improvement alone does not justify selection if the output is copied
a style improvement alone does not justify selection if it is supported only by favourable prompts

nodes.title: Project 3 Task Contract and Baseline
nodes.description: Choose a permitted track and bounded target behaviour, write a valid task contract, and establish the unchanged starting-model baseline
spec: correctness can be distinguished from formatting
the generalisation case is not a renamed training template

nodes.title: Lab 3 — Train and Verify a Specialist
nodes.description: Turn a task contract into valid training and evaluation records, build a verifier before training, and test one shifted slice and one retained capability
spec: the verifier was working before the model was trained
evaluation templates or prompts are absent from training data
a formatted but wrong answer fails correctness, and a correct but unparsable answer fails the technical gate
the comparison changed one meaningful factor
the pilot can reload without notebook state

nodes.title: Project 3 Generalisation Clinic
nodes.description: An evidence-led drop-in clinic for locating the generalisation boundary and separating supported conclusions from alternative explanations
spec: a candidate final checkpoint
a bounded claim
a short list of unresolved limitations that belong in the report

nodes.title: Project 3 Fresh-Load Audit and Submission
nodes.description: Reproduce the final specialist in a clean environment and submit one internally consistent evidence chain
spec: the report, code, model card, portal identifiers, and reproduced outputs all refer to the same frozen system

nodes.title: Project 1 — Build a Narrative Base Model
nodes.description: Train a decoder-only language model from scratch that can continue an incomplete story with recognisably narrative language.
spec: the checkpoint loads with the supplied command and is at or under 33.6M learned parameters
preprocessing, tokenization, training, evaluation, and sampling can be reproduced from the report's commands
at least one controlled comparison is tied to a stated hypothesis, with a meaningful baseline
tutor-evaluation continuation-only PPL is calculated with the published reference tokenizer and formula
representative and failed generated samples are shown with their decoding settings declared
the report distinguishes measurements from interpretation and includes the AI Assistance Statement
training and evaluation stay within 24 T4-equivalent GPU-hours and 4.0×10^17 training FLOPs
the ten tutor-evaluation prompts and their withheld continuations never influenced training or model selection

nodes.title: Project 2 — Give the Model a Voice
nodes.description: Post-train the frozen Project 1 checkpoint to produce stories with a recognisable target narrative style, and prove the change without hiding a regression.
spec: the starting checkpoint (own Project 1 submission or the course fallback) is declared and verified
the target style is defined in operational rather than purely impressionistic terms
the post-trained model is compared with its unchanged starting checkpoint on the same held-out cases
held-out target-style texts are separated from training data at story or source level
the report tests for regressions in the original Project 1 narrative capability
any instruction schema, special tokens, and response-only loss masking are documented
work without genuine human preference labels is not described as full RLHF
training and evaluation stay within 18 T4-equivalent GPU-hours and 2.5×10^17 training FLOPs

nodes.title: Project 3 — Build a Specialist
nodes.description: Choose Track A (narrative specialisation) or Track B (arithmetic reasoning), fine-tune an appropriate starting checkpoint, and demonstrate the acquired behaviour through controlled evaluation.
spec: one specialisation track is chosen and one primary target behaviour is declared with measurable success criteria
the starting checkpoint is declared, justified, and (when a personal earlier submission) verified against it
the unchanged starting model is used as a baseline and at least one controlled comparison or ablation is run
training and evaluation data are strictly held out from each other
at least one relevant pre-existing capability is checked for regression
an alternative Track A proposal, if used, was approved via proposal.md before substantial training
training and evaluation stay within 12 T4-equivalent GPU-hours and 1.5×10^17 training FLOPs
Track B always starts from the course general-language checkpoint

course.title: Retail Alcohol Economics
course.description: A rigorous quantitative analysis of alcohol-by-volume-to-price ratios, volumetric taxation loopholes, and retail spatial optimisation within the Australian supermarket landscape, treating every shelf tag as a dataset.

nodes.title: Getting started
nodes.description: The first lab of the semester — fixing the fiscal-molecule framing of alcohol and the standard-drink metric every calculation this course makes depends on
spec: you can state the standard-drink content of a product from its volume and ABV
you have picked one supermarket's online liquor catalogue as your working dataset for the semester
you can compute one ungraded ABV-to-dollar index value by hand before you leave

nodes.title: First review
nodes.description: The second lab, where each student's early standard-drink and index calculations meet a worked example for the first time
spec: work from lab 1 is running — your standard-drink conversion and one computed index value
you can name the one decision in that calculation you are least sure about

nodes.title: Decomposing a cask
nodes.description: Taking one cask and one bottle apart into packaging, freight, tax and margin, and finding out how much of each shelf price the production cost actually explains
spec: you can split a shelf price into four named terms and say which one you are least sure of
you have a packaging-and-freight estimate per litre for both bag-in-box and glass
you can state, in dollars, the part of each price your decomposition does not account for

nodes.title: Working the WET
nodes.description: Calculating the Wine Equalisation Tax on real products from your own catalogue, and finding the price point where an ad valorem structure stops behaving the way intuition says it should
spec: you can calculate WET payable on a product from its wholesale value
you can express that tax as cents per standard drink, not just dollars per unit
you have found the price point in your own catalogue where the per-standard-drink burden inverts

nodes.title: Reading a promotional cycle
nodes.description: Tracking ready-to-drink can prices across a promotional cycle and estimating elasticity from the only data a shopper can actually see
spec: you have at least three price observations of the same RTD product across different dates
you can state a rough elasticity estimate and name the assumptions it rests on
you can identify one price in your data that is promotional rather than structural

nodes.title: Tax per standard drink
nodes.description: Putting wine, beer and spirits on one axis — tax paid per standard drink — and reading off what each excise structure actually does
spec: you can compute tax per standard drink under both ad valorem and volumetric regimes
you can state the spirits premium as a number from your own catalogue, not a quoted figure
your WET Policy Brief has a comparison paragraph drafted

nodes.title: Mapping an outlet
nodes.description: Fieldwork — drawing the floor plan of one liquor outlet and measuring what shelf distance costs the shopper who walks it
spec: you have a hand-drawn floor plan of one outlet with the high-ABV stock marked on it
you can state the walking distance from entrance to the best index on the floor
you have recorded the index of whatever is stocked within three metres of the entrance

nodes.title: Auditing an endcap
nodes.description: Computing the index for everything on one promotional endcap and comparing it against the same categories shelved in the aisle behind it
spec: you have index values for every product on one endcap
you have index values for the matching categories in the aisle behind it
you can say which of the endcap's framing devices moved your own judgement before you did the arithmetic

nodes.title: First hundred rows
nodes.description: Getting a scraper running against your own catalogue, and meeting the four failure modes that quietly corrupt a retail dataset
spec: your scraper returns at least 100 rows with name, volume, ABV and price populated
you have a documented crawl delay and a check against the site's robots.txt
you can name which of your rows have an inferred rather than a stated ABV, and how many

nodes.title: Greedy against the constraint
nodes.description: Running a greedy ranking and a dynamic-programming selection over the same dataset and the same budget, and finding the case where they part
spec: you can rank your own dataset by index and name its top five
you have one budget and variety constraint under which greedy and dynamic programming disagree
you can state the size of that disagreement in standard drinks

nodes.title: The externality statement
nodes.description: Writing the part of the portfolio that says what the optimisation costs, and testing it against the two ways this argument usually fails
spec: you have a drafted externality statement for your own portfolio, at event scale
your statement survives both failure tests applied in the lab
you can state one thing your optimisation would change about the event, not about a shopper

nodes.title: Portfolio dry run
nodes.description: The last lab of the semester — pitching the event portfolio to the room and taking the questions a marker would otherwise ask first
spec: you have pitched your portfolio to the room inside ten minutes
you have taken at least two challenges to the inventory and answered them from your own data
your budget spreadsheet reconciles against the slides you presented

nodes.title: Retail Data Extraction Exercise
nodes.description: Extraction and analysis of retail inventory data to compute baseline ABV-to-dollar efficiencies across 150+ SKUs.
spec: extraction of a minimum of 150 distinct SKUs from a nominated regional liquor retailer
dataset must represent a stratified sample encompassing cask wine, ready-to-drink (RTD) premixes, and distilled clear spirits
individual rows must strictly isolate product name, raw volume (mL), stated ABV, retail price, and the computed standard-drink yield

the methodological documentation must allow for exact replication of your scraping parameters by a third party

nodes.title: The 50-Person Event Portfolio
nodes.description: The capstone synthesis: design and mathematically defend a hyper-efficient beverage inventory for a 50-person cohort, factoring in tax loopholes and physical logistics.
spec: A presentation deck of at least **10 slides**.
A linked, fully costed budget spreadsheet listing each SKU, retail price, and standard-drink yield.
A mathematical optimisation of total alcohol yield subject to a minimum financial cost.
A clear justification of inventory choices based on WET structures and observed pricing differences.
A physical logistics model accounting for vehicle payload limits and volumetric capacity.

criteria.name: Mathematical cost efficiency and portfolio optimization
Application of regulatory loopholes and spatial retail anomalies
Logistical realism, payload mathematics, and presentation clarity

nodes.title: WET Policy Brief
nodes.description: An academic policy brief deconstructing how the Wine Equalisation Tax structurally incentivizes the production of high-volume, low-cost cask wine.
spec: maximum 1,500 words, exclusive of reference list (in APA format)
brief explanation of the WET's ad valorem mechanism as established in Week 4
clear mathematical and logical reasoning of how a 29% wholesale tax incentivizes bag-in-box distribution
active citation of peer-reviewed health-economics or tax-law journals

criteria.name: Economic precision and correct application of tax mechanics
Structural coherence of the market argument
Adherence to academic formatting and tone

nodes.title: Alcohol Fermentation & Baseline Costs

nodes.title: The 10g Metric: Standard Drinks as Economic Currency

nodes.title: Cardboard Efficiencies: The Microeconomics of Bag-in-Box Wine

nodes.title: Wholesale Value Manipulation: The WET Tax Loophole

nodes.title: Price Elasticity in the Ready-to-Drink (RTD) Sector

nodes.title: Distillation Disparities and Federal Excise Penalties

nodes.title: Spatial Ergonomics of Suburban Liquor Retail

nodes.title: Visual Merchandising and Endcap Psychology
nodes.description: Quantifying cognitive biases in retail purchasing and the visual obfuscation of tax-inefficient inventory.

nodes.title: Automated Extraction of Retail Inventories (Web Scraping)

nodes.title: Algorithmic Maximization of the ABV-to-Dollar Index
nodes.description: Combinatorial optimization and algorithmic processing of large-scale retail datasets to identify structural market outliers.

nodes.title: Public Health Externalities and Bioethics
nodes.description: Bioethical dimensions, negative societal externalities, and public health economics of hyper-efficient retail alcohol distribution.

nodes.title: Macro-Event Logistics and Capstone Synthesis
nodes.description: Scaling algorithmic optimization to physical supply chains: payload mathematics, volumetric displacement, and economic synthesis.

course.title: Jet Fighter Piloting: Departure and Recovery
course.description: Twelve weeks on taking a single-seat jet off the ground and bringing it back able to fly again: departure and recovery only, with no air combat or formation flying in the syllabus.

nodes.title: Egress
nodes.description: The first period of the course teaches you to leave the aircraft, because that is the skill with the shortest deadline
spec: you can find and pull the ejection handle with your eyes closed
you can state the seat's minimum safe envelope from memory

nodes.title: Unstable by design
nodes.description: Why this aircraft cannot fly without the computer that flies it, and why that was the point
spec: you can explain relaxed static stability without using the word unstable as an insult

you can state what happens when the flight control computers disagree

nodes.title: Control authority
nodes.description: The limits the flight control system enforces, what it will refuse to let you do, and who is actually in command

you can describe a manoeuvre the aircraft will decline to perform
you can tell a limit you cannot exceed from a restriction you must not

nodes.title: Energy
nodes.description: Altitude and airspeed are one quantity in two denominations, and every manoeuvre is a transaction in it

nodes.title: Takeoff, and the point of commitment
nodes.description: The first simulator period, built around the speed after which stopping is no longer one of your options
spec: you can compute refusal speed for the day's weight, runway and temperature

nodes.title: The sidestick that barely moves
nodes.description: Flying by pressure rather than displacement, and learning to stop arguing with a system that responds faster than you do

nodes.title: The circuit
nodes.description: A rectangle flown at a fixed angle of attack, and why the airspeed indicator is the wrong instrument to fly an approach on
spec: you can fly the published circuit profile within tolerance, both directions
you can fly final on the angle-of-attack indexer without reference to airspeed
you can explain why angle of attack is the correct reference and speed is not

nodes.title: Landing and the aerobrake
nodes.description: The last simulator period, ending in the progression check that decides whether you fly in week 10

course.description: A comparative study of algorithmic management on delivery platforms: dispatch, ratings and incentive pay as they operate in practice, the workarounds riders build back, and the regulatory fight now under way in China, Australia and the EU over what an algorithm gets to decide about a worker's day.

marking.description: Judged as a whole rather than against a fixed rubric: whether the essay names a specific mechanism in at least two regimes, whether the comparison explains why the mechanisms differ rather than just listing them, and whether the mandatory self-review paragraph honestly names the weakest part of your own argument rather than restating its strongest point.
