course.title: Debugging Systems You Did Not Build
course.description: A forensic approach to understanding and repairing unfamiliar software. Students investigate systems they did not build, using a fixed six-stage cycle to move from an observed failure to a defensible, verified diagnosis and repair.

nodes.title: Naming What You See
nodes.description: What is the difference between an observation and an assumption? The semester's first session works on a system small enough to read in one sitting, so the discipline — not the difficulty — is the point.
spec: a numbered observation log, facts only, no diagnosis
each observation stated precisely enough that someone else could check it
no proposed cause appears before the log is complete

nodes.title: A Hypothesis That Could Be Wrong
nodes.description: What makes a hypothesis useful, as opposed to merely plausible? A reproducible failure with two similar-looking causes forces a real choice, and the choice has to be committed to before it's tested.
spec: a hypothesis and its disconfirming test, submitted before the test is run
a report of what the test actually showed, including a refuted first guess

nodes.title: Reading a System You Weren't Given a Map To
nodes.description: How do you build a working model of a system's intended behaviour when no one is going to explain it to you? Documentation stops being a reliable evidence source from this session onward.
spec: a short written model of what the system is supposed to do
the model derived from structure, naming and control flow, not narrative docs
the fault located using that model, not by scanning at random

nodes.title: Evidence That Isn't Static Text
nodes.description: What can runtime evidence tell you that reading the code cannot? The fault this week only shows up under specific runtime conditions, so evidence has to be generated, not just read.
spec: instrumentation placed at points justified by a structural model
a diagnosis drawn from the resulting runtime evidence

nodes.title: What the System Used to Be
nodes.description: Can a fault be explained by something that is no longer in the code at all? This session treats version history and prior configuration as first-class evidence, not background.
spec: a bisection through version history toward the change that introduced the fault
confirmation, via structural or runtime evidence, that the change found is the cause and not merely correlated with it

nodes.title: Two Explanations, One Fault
nodes.description: How do you choose between two hypotheses that both fit the evidence you have so far? This session's failure has two genuinely plausible causes, and stopping at the first one that fits is the mistake being taught against.
spec: both surviving hypotheses listed explicitly
an observation proposed and carried out specifically to discriminate between them, not merely to support one

nodes.title: When the Evidence Disagrees
nodes.description: What do you do when two pieces of evidence appear to contradict each other? This session's evidence itself is unreliable in places, which is a different problem from an unresolved hypothesis.
spec: a determination of whether an observed contradiction means one source is unreliable, or two faults coexist
independent evidence supporting that determination

nodes.title: The Fix That Isn't Safe
nodes.description: How do you decide whether an available fix is acceptable, not just whether it makes the symptom go away? The diagnosis this week is deliberately easy to reach; the risk is entirely in the fix.
spec: at least one other part of the system checked for a plausible side effect before the fix is applied
the check performed with the same evidence discipline used for diagnosis

nodes.title: Verifying You Didn't Just Move the Problem
nodes.description: How do you know an intervention actually resolved the cause, rather than relocating or masking the symptom? This session's fix looks like it worked — closer verification is what the week is actually testing.
spec: a verification check tied to the diagnosed cause, not the surface symptom
a demonstration that the check would have caught it, had the intervention only masked the symptom

nodes.title: No One Left to Ask
nodes.description: How do you investigate a system when the people who built it, and much of its context, are simply gone? Scaffolding drops substantially from this session onward.
spec: a working model of the relevant subsystem
an evidence-backed diagnosis
an explicit list of what remains unverified given the available operational artefacts

nodes.title: The System That Fights Back
nodes.description: How do you keep the investigation disciplined when the system itself resists being understood — through unreliable documentation, inconsistent reproduction, or an environment where a careless intervention makes things worse?
spec: the unreliable documentation or evidence source identified, with independent evidence supporting that judgement
diagnosis and intervention completed without relying on the unreliable source

nodes.title: Defending the Trail
nodes.description: Can every step of your investigation withstand informed challenge? The final session is a live defence of a complete, unassisted investigation of a system you have never seen before.
spec: an observation-to-verification trail for a previously unseen system, assigned individually
answers, under live questioning, that account for unstated assumptions, untested hypotheses, and unverified claims in that trail

nodes.title: Broken Service Investigation
nodes.description: An unfamiliar multi-module service, no onboarding document, and a symptom report rather than a diagnosis — with at least two plausible root causes waiting in the evidence.
spec: a reconstructed model of the system's intended behaviour
at least two distinct evidence classes gathered, each with a stated reason it was sought
competing hypotheses named explicitly, including at least one eliminated with its discriminating test
a final diagnosis, plus a proposed (not required) intervention and verification check
a plain statement of remaining uncertainty or unverified assumptions

criteria.name: Evidence strategy — evidence classes chosen and why

nodes.title: Debugging Field Notes
nodes.description: Four short, staged entries across Weeks 1–4 — the transition from guided practice to graded investigation, on systems small enough to read in full.
spec: one short entry submitted for each of Weeks 1–4, four entries total
each entry follows the same shape: observation log, hypothesis, disconfirming test recorded before it was run, evidence gathered, intervention if appropriate, verification, revised conclusion
no separate "lessons learned" essay — the entries are the deliverable

criteria.name: Disconfirmation discipline — test recorded before execution

nodes.title: Final Unknown System
nodes.description: A previously unseen inherited system, no instructor framing of what matters, and a short live defence of the entire evidence trail.
spec: an early checkpoint recording initial observations, live hypotheses, and the next planned discriminating observation
a full evidence trail spanning whichever evidence classes the assigned system makes relevant
an explicit account of any source judged unreliable, with independent evidence supporting that judgement
a diagnosis that explicitly addresses alternative explanations
a scoped intervention and a verification argument tied to the diagnosed cause
a statement of what remains uncertain or unverified at submission
a short live defence answering targeted questions about the trail above

nodes.title: Incident Reconstruction
nodes.description: A system that looks fine now, a bundle of historical and operational artefacts, and a requirement to reason across time before touching anything.
spec: an incident reconstruction stating what happened, when, and why, each major claim tied to a specific artefact
an account of how ambiguous or conflicting artefacts were interpreted
a diagnosis naming the relevant cause, not only the visible symptom
a scoped intervention, with at least one blast-radius or invariant check actually executed
a verification argument tied to the diagnosed cause, not to the symptom's disappearance
a concise statement of remaining uncertainty

criteria.name: Handling of conflicting or ambiguous evidence

nodes.title: Observation Before Explanation
nodes.description: What this course is, why it is shaped as an investigation rather than a syllabus, and what a student needs to have ready before Week 1's session.

nodes.title: Proving a Hypothesis Wrong on Purpose
nodes.description: Why a hypothesis needs a disconfirming test to count as one, and how Debugging Field Notes turns that habit into the semester's first graded work.

nodes.title: A Model Is a Claim, Not a Map
nodes.description: How to build a working model of a system's intended behaviour when there is no one left to explain it, and why structural reading has to do the work documentation used to.

nodes.title: Instrumentation Is a Hypothesis Too
nodes.description: What runtime evidence can tell you that reading the code cannot, and why instrumentation only counts as investigation when a structural model decided where to place it.

nodes.title: Timing Is a Lead, Not a Verdict
nodes.description: Why a system's history counts as evidence, and why the change that sits closest in time to a failure is not automatically the change that caused it.

nodes.title: Discriminating Between Explanations
nodes.description: How to choose between two explanations that both fit the evidence you already have, by asking what each one predicts under a change you control rather than what each is merely consistent with.

nodes.title: A Fact Needs a Source Before a Verdict
nodes.description: What to do when two pieces of evidence contradict each other — and why that is a different problem from two hypotheses that both fit the same, trustworthy evidence.

nodes.title: The Blast Radius of a Fix
nodes.description: Why removing a symptom is not the same as knowing a fix is safe, and how to reason about what an intervention might disturb before applying it.

nodes.title: What Does This Test Actually Prove?
nodes.description: Why a disappeared symptom and a passing smoke test are evidence for a narrower claim than "the diagnosed cause is fixed," and how to verify the claim that actually matters.

nodes.title: Choosing Where to Begin

course.title: Directing for the Screen
course.description: A twelve-week directing practicum built around one recurring short film. You develop story, shot design, performance direction, editing rhythm and sound, then practice each skill immediately against an AI cast and crew fast enough to reshoot before the next class.

nodes.title: First direction
nodes.description: Observe one provided take, diagnose a problem, and write and review a redirect
spec: one observable problem in the provided Take A, located in time and explained against the fixed objective and intended interpretation
a playable Note B that addresses that problem while preserving the locked scene, character, objective, interpretation, and camera
a partner's written check of whether the note addresses the diagnosis and names an action the performer could carry out
a revised Note B and a description of the observable change you would look for in a future take, without claiming that change has been generated or verified

nodes.title: Pitch and premise review
nodes.description: Your own short film's logline meets the class for the first time, and gets tested against a dramatic question
spec: you have written a one-sentence logline naming your protagonist, their want, and what's in the way
your premise is filmable inside a two-to-four-minute runtime with one or two characters and a single location, and you can say why
a partner who has read only your logline can state your protagonist's obstacle back correctly, in their own words, before seeing your premise

nodes.title: Screenplay workshop
nodes.description: Writing one scene of your own short in proper form, with a director's intent note attached to it
spec: you have one scene from your own short in standard screenplay format, no longer than two pages
at least one line or action carries a written director's intent note that names a concrete antecedent circumstance, not an adjective describing the desired mood

a partner who has read only the specific line or action being directed and its intent note - not the rest of the scene, and not your intended interpretation - can describe one or more concrete performance choices the circumstance could motivate, and explain how the note changes their reading of the line or action

nodes.title: Shot breakdown and first storyboard
nodes.description: Turning last week's scene into a numbered shot list, then a rough storyboard thumbnail for each shot
spec: your scene is broken into a numbered shot list, each shot naming its type (wide, medium, close-up, insert, or similar) and paired with a rough thumbnail sketch — a frame, a stick figure, an arrow for movement
every shot's purpose is stated in one clause, and no two shots in the list share the same purpose

nodes.title: World bible crit
nodes.description: Your character and location bibles meet the class, tested for whether a stranger could reproduce them
spec: you have a bible entry for each named character and each location in your short, with concrete, repeatable detail rather than adjectives like "mysterious" or "striking"
a classmate who has never seen your project can describe your protagonist back to you correctly after reading only your bible entry

nodes.title: Pre-production crit
nodes.description: A full run-through of your shot list and storyboard before Assignment 1 is due
spec: your storyboard covers every shot in your shot list, in sequence, from the first frame to the last
you can point to one shot you cut from an earlier draft and say why it wasn't earning its place

nodes.title: Anchor to motion
nodes.description: Turning one storyboard frame from Assignment 1 into an anchor image, then into a directed piece of motion
spec: you have generated an anchor image matching your bible, and two motion takes from it that differ in one directed performance beat — timing, a look, a gesture
you can name which direction changed between the two takes, in the language of performance, not prompt syntax

nodes.title: Take selection
nodes.description: Generating and diagnosing several takes of one performance beat, then choosing on the record
spec: you have at least three takes of one performance beat and a one-line diagnosis of what was wrong with each rejected one
your selected take is justified against the beat's intent, not against which one "looked best"

nodes.title: Continuity assembly
nodes.description: Assembling a 30–60 second sequence from your generated shots and keeping a continuity log
spec: you have a cut sequence of at least three shots, running 30 to 60 seconds
your continuity log names at least one problem you found and one decision about whether to fix it or accept it, with a reason

nodes.title: Recut lab
nodes.description: Recutting your week 9 sequence twice — once for pacing, once for montage
spec: one of your two cuts is a duration-based pacing decision (a hold or an early cut-away); the other is a montage decision built by repeating or reordering at least one shot — not a second duration change
you can describe the emotional difference between the two cuts in one sentence each

nodes.title: Sound pass
nodes.description: Directing a line reading before mixing it in, then adding one ambience or Foley layer and one music cue to your rough cut
spec: you have directed at least two takes of one line reading, using a single note aimed at pace, breath or hesitation, and can say which take you selected and why
you have two versions of the same cut — one with only sync dialogue, one with a full sound pass of ambience, at least one Foley or SFX moment, and one music cue
you can name what the sound pass changed emotionally, beat by beat, not just that "it feels more finished"

nodes.title: Screening and critique
nodes.description: A near-final cut is screened for critique, and each director defends three decisions before revising toward the final cut
spec: your near-final cut screens in under four minutes, unattended, with no explanation needed to make sense of it
you can name three directorial decisions on request and defend each one against a specific alternative
you leave with one specific critique note you intend to act on before the final cut

nodes.title: Assignment 1 — The pre-production package
nodes.description: Everything a director needs before spending a single generation on the real thing — locked screenplay, world bible, shot list and storyboard
spec: submitted by the deadline as one readable PDF, with your name, film title, package version and four clearly labelled submission sections
the logline identifies the protagonist, their want, the obstacle and what is at stake; the premise states the situation, visible conflict and ending
the package plans a complete two-to-four-minute short, with a shot list detailed enough that a reader can judge it fits that runtime

the screenplay covers the whole short from beginning to end, with a scene heading for each scene it contains, observable action, formatted dialogue where used and director's intent notes tied to specific beats
the bible covers every character, location, costume and story-relevant prop used by the screenplay and shots, separating fixed identity from changing action or state

all bible decisions required by the planned shots are resolved, or explicitly marked pending with the specific decision still needed; attached references are labelled and versioned, and not-applicable fields explain why
the shot list covers every screenplay beat in screen order, with a unique shot ID, scene or beat reference and a purpose beyond covering the action
every shot specifies framing, camera angle, camera movement or fixed position and subject action
the storyboard uses the same IDs and order as the shot list, with at least one legible staging thumbnail per shot and additional stages for movement that cannot be understood from one frame
each shot names its production dependencies and readiness; the production order respects those dependencies, and any shot blocked by a pending decision says so rather than being scheduled as ready
story, ending, character identity, prop state and spatial continuity agree across the logline, premise, screenplay, bible, shot list and storyboard
an unfamiliar reader could plan the intended shots from the package alone without inventing missing story, design or staging decisions

nodes.title: Final project — The completed short
nodes.description: The finished two-to-four-minute AI dramatic short, screened and defended as a directorial statement, not a generation lucky enough to work
spec: submitted by the deadline, in the format named below
it stands on its own as a two-to-four-minute film, without you there to explain it
a short director's statement accompanies it, naming three directorial decisions and one thing that went wrong and how you handled it
the statement names one specific change made during the revision period, in response to a note from week 12's critique screening

if the finished film tells a different story than the one locked in Assignment 1, a short pivot plan (updated logline, world/character bible entries, and a shot list) for the new story accompanies the submission, and one of the statement's three decisions is the switch itself, defended against continuing the original story

nodes.title: What does a director actually do?
nodes.description: Directing as translating a given objective and intended interpretation into a playable action, judging a take against that objective, and telling a genuine redirect from a note that quietly changes it

nodes.title: From story to screenplay
nodes.description: Turning a premise into scenes — screenplay form, dialogue versus action, and the director's intent behind a line

nodes.title: Building a consistent world

nodes.title: Planning before generating
nodes.description: Turning the screenplay into a full shot list and storyboard, and sequencing the whole production before spending time generating anything

nodes.title: From frame to performance
nodes.description: Turning a controlled anchor frame into motion — directing image-to-video prompts at performance, timing and camera movement, not decoration

nodes.title: Directing the AI performer
nodes.description: Generation as rehearsal and takes — diagnosing failure, giving actionable notes, and selecting a take on purpose instead of regenerating until something looks right

nodes.title: Directing with sound
nodes.description: Dialogue and voice performance, ambience, Foley, sound effects and music — how sound redirects emotion, pacing and attention

course.title: One Shot, No Refunds: The Design of Captive Public Machines
course.description: SLOP4605 studies public machines that give a stranger exactly one attempt, under a queue's pressure, to complete a transaction they can't opt out of — parking meters, airport kiosks, ATMs, ticket gates — and asks, every week, who profits when the interface is the one that fails.

spec: your group names the vending machine (or equivalent coin/card machine) it studied
the teardown lists every decision point a user has to make, in order
you can name the smallest point where the machine could have told you more and didn't

nodes.title: Queue Behind You

you note the first moment you felt rushed, and what caused it

spec: you can name three states (pain, distress, unfamiliarity) a check-in kiosk assumes away
your checklist gives at least five concrete items, not general principles
you can point to one item that would change what the kiosk asks first

nodes.title: Assignment 2 Studio

you name the one counter-argument most likely to undercut your claim

nodes.title: The Worst Case Study

spec: your group names the franchise or contract behind the machine, if one is findable

you identify the exact point exact change or a specific app is required, and why

nodes.title: Final Project Clinic

spec: you can name the one legitimate incentive (fraud prevention, throughput) your redesign keeps
you can name who would resist your redesign, and why

spec: you name one specific machine and one specific transaction on it
the walkthrough describes what happened, step by step, before diagnosing it

at least one captioned photo of the machine's interface is included

you support that claim with evidence, not just plausibility

the incentive map and the written case name the same machine, behaviour, and party

the memo names who would resist the change, and why
the dossier names its machine and transaction on its own, without relying on a verbal walkthrough

marking.description: Judged as a whole against three things the brief asks for together — an evidenced teardown of the machine as it exists, a redesign that removes illegitimate friction while keeping whatever legitimate constraint (fraud prevention, throughput, liability) made the original design defensible, and a short memo naming who would resist the redesign and why.

course.title: F1 Pit Wall
course.description: Twelve weeks on one question: what do you tell the driver, and can you defend it afterwards? Students build a race simulator, race it live against the cohort on a shared draw, and are marked on the calls they made rather than on where they finished.

nodes.title: Week 1: Getting set up
nodes.description: The orientation drop-in — no marks and no submission, but three things week 2's lab expects you to arrive with already working
spec: Python runs on your machine and you can create a project environment and install packages into it
the codebase supplied for week 2's lab installs, and its own test suite passes, on that machine
you can open week 2's lab page and say what it expects you to arrive having done

nodes.title: Week 2 Lab: Fitting a wear curve
nodes.description: The first lab — select the clean laps from a supplied stint, correct for fuel, and report a tyre wear coefficient with an interval
spec: the supplied codebase installs and its own test suite passes on your machine
you can name every column in the timing set's data dictionary and its units
the loader runs on the example stint and prints its lap times
you can say which laps of that example stint you would exclude, and why

nodes.title: Week 3 Lab: Pricing the stop
nodes.description: Measure two-lap pit loss, reconcile Friday's physical tyre inventory, and enumerate every legal one- and two-stop compound sequence
spec: the supplied codebase installs and its own test suite passes on your machine
the data dictionary and event card have been read, including every timing unit and set identity
the loader prints one observed in-lap and out-lap beside its supplied no-stop counterfactual
the starting set ledger reconciles to the allocation totals printed on the event card

nodes.title: Week 4 Lab: Running the race loop
nodes.description: Implement a deterministic lap transition, preserve physical-set age, and reproduce a supplied trace and finishing time
spec: the supplied codebase installs and its own test suite passes on your machine
the strategy and parameter schemas have been read, including physical set IDs and end-lap meaning
the five-lap fixture runs to the unimplemented transition and its expected trace is open beside it
the first two fixture laps have been hand-traced, with age before each lap marked

nodes.title: Week 5 Lab: Pricing the traffic
nodes.description: Preserve the clean-air clock, price a supplied rejoin packet once, and rank stop candidates by finishing position
spec: the supplied codebase installs and its own test suite passes on your machine
the candidate, rejoin-ledger and field schemas have been read, including every unit
the six-lap fixture has been hand-sorted by clean-air time and by supplied adjusted time
the full-race validator reaches the unimplemented packet detector without an earlier failure

nodes.title: Week 6 Lab: When the rival moves
nodes.description: Build a bounded response function, precommit the falsifier and defend the stop returned when Moss answers
spec: the supplied codebase installs and its own test suite passes on your machine
the candidate, paired-outcome and report schemas have been read, including the position-first comparison
both SlopU best responses and both Moss best replies in the micro-fixture have been selected by hand
the micro-fixture validator reaches the unimplemented conditional selector without an earlier failure

nodes.title: Week 7 Lab: Pricing the wait
nodes.description: Validate a supplied interruption scenario, gate actions on the physical set ledger, and make a one-lap stop call from an analytic expected cost
spec: the supplied codebase installs and its own test suite passes on your machine
you can identify every field in the hazard, candidate and physical-set ledger schemas
the already-deployed-SC warm-up passes and emits its decision report
you have hand-calculated the supplied preparation fixture's one-lap hazard and two-lap survival

nodes.title: Week 8 Lab: Committing to rain
nodes.description: Validate a supplied weather ensemble and tyre-set ledger, then save and defend a position-first wet-weather commitment before the outcome unlocks
spec: the supplied codebase installs and its own test suite passes on your machine
you can name every field in the forecast, candidate, outcome and set-ledger schemas
you have hand-checked one two-path weighted mean finishing position
the public tie-break micro-fixture passes and you can explain why adjusted time is consulted

nodes.title: Week 9 Lab: Share the draw
nodes.description: Build two complete finishing-position distributions from paired synthetic trials, then compare strategies under the same interruption and weather draws
spec: the supplied codebase installs and its test suite passes on your machine
you can name every field in the strategy, uncertainty, trial and report schemas
you have traced the public four-trial paired fixture by hand
the supplied generator-wrapper self-test passes without changes

nodes.title: Week 10 Lab: Name the objective
nodes.description: Validate a supplied two-car decision set, rank it for the team, then re-rank the same outcomes for car 14 and account for the trade
spec: the supplied codebase installs and its public tests pass on your machine
you can name the plan, path, objective and report fields and what each holds
you have traced one public path from two finishing positions to a team-points total by hand

nodes.title: Week 11 Lab: Designing the wall
nodes.description: Configure a pit wall display for a supplied model's output, then measure whether a correct call can be made from it inside the time limit — yours against the baseline
spec: the supplied harness installs and its self-test passes on your machine
you can name every field in the model's output schema and its units
you have run one scenario end to end and the harness recorded an elapsed time for it
you arrive with a first layout for your wall, on paper or in the configuration format

nodes.title: Week 12 Lab: Draw the trust boundary
nodes.description: Validate and audit a supplied probability archive, expose the condition split hidden by its aggregate diagram, and write the model's domain of validity
spec: the supplied codebase installs and its public tests pass on your machine
you can classify P1–P3 as success and P4 or lower as failure for the supplied event
you have written down the probability bins and named condition split you will commit before unlock

nodes.title: Assignment 1: the audit
nodes.description: The audit — a recommendation the team bought, tested against the race it was written for and the rival who responds to it
spec: the falsifier is submitted at stage one, before the race data unlocks
the audit document states one verdict, in one sentence, with its conditions attached
every quantity the verdict rests on is reported with how uncertain it is
the codebase reproduces every number the document quotes, without a random seed

criteria.name: The contest — the rival treated as responding rather than as a fixture
Model fitness — it answers the question the recommendation claimed to answer, obeys the regulations, and names what it omits
Measurement — the estimates the audit rests on, and their stated uncertainty

guidance: Each criterion is read against the codebase and the document together, and neither stands in for the other. A verdict scores on whether its conditions are the ones that would actually change it: “retain unless the rival covers the stop” is a condition a marker can test against your own model, and “retain unless circumstances change” is not a condition at all.

The contest criterion asks what the rival did once your calls moved; a rival modelled as holding its published schedule scores low however carefully it was implemented, because it answers an easier question than the one the recommendation claimed to answer. Convincing measurement is a number with an interval around it — an estimate quoted without its uncertainty is read as one whose uncertainty was not computed. Model fitness turns on what you name rather than what you achieve: an omission you priced is evidence, and the same omission unmentioned is a gap a marker finds for you.

nodes.title: The labs
nodes.description: Eleven labs across weeks 2 to 12, each one finished in the room, with the best ten counting
spec: each lab is submitted from the room before that session ends
each lab is marked against the criteria printed in its own brief
ten of your eleven lab marks count towards the 20%

marking.description: In-session completion against each lab's own stated criteria, with the best ten of the eleven counting. A missed lab cannot be made up.
guidance: There is no second standard here. Each lab is marked inside its session, on what left the room, against the criteria printed in its own brief — and those are written so a marker can tell whether a line has been met without asking you.

What makes a lab convincing is that its own printed criteria are met rather than approximated. Where a lab asks for both a working output and the validation behind it, one without the other does not meet what it asked for — which is a way of reading that brief, not a standard this page adds to it.

nodes.title: Final project: the defence
nodes.description: Written knowing the result — the calls justified against the distribution they faced rather than the result they got
spec: one document, in which the account of the instrument is the evidence rather than a section before it
every call it defends cites the recommendation standing at that call's timestamp in your log
every supported departure cites its submitted actionable limit and the contemporaneous trigger evidence in the log; unsupported departures are analysed as unsupported
it names at least one thing the instrument got wrong in the race, and what that cost
it states the objective the calls served

criteria.name: The call against the distribution it faced rather than the result it got
Departure evidence — each supported departure traced to a submitted actionable limit and its contemporaneous trigger, or analysed honestly as unsupported
What the instrument got wrong in this race, and what it cost
The objective, and whose interest it served

guidance: The heaviest criterion is the one the obvious document fails. A call is defended against what your instrument said was likely at that moment and what the alternatives were worth, not against what happened next. An argument that starts from the result and works backwards scores low even when the call was good, because it defends the outcome instead of the decision.

Convincing evidence is your own instrument quoted against itself: the recommendation standing at the timestamp, what it was weighing, and why your call was the one that reading supported. A supported departure needs both the actionable limit you submitted and the evidence recorded at the call showing that its observable condition applied. An unsupported departure admitted and analysed can score here, but cannot regain race conduct marks or become justified afterwards. For what the instrument got wrong, a marker is looking for one specific failure in this race and the cost attached to it, rather than a general admission of imperfection.

nodes.title: Final project: the instrument
nodes.description: The semester's artefact — your own race simulator and the wall you designed for it, submitted with the limits you are willing to declare
spec: it runs from a clean checkout in the pit wall environment, from one documented command
the same inputs produce the same recommendation twice
a declared domain of validity is submitted with it, naming the conditions under which it should not be believed
the wall is submitted as a configuration that runs on the pit wall screens, not as a picture of one
the wall is submitted with the latency and correctness measured for it, not with a claim about it

criteria.name: Model fitness — the assumptions are named, the omissions are priced, and the hard constraints come from the regulations
Calibration and declared limits — the stated probabilities occur at their stated rate, and the domain of validity is honest about where they do not
The wall — a correct call is possible from it inside the time the race allows
The objective — what the instrument optimises for, and whose interest that serves

guidance: A marker runs the instrument before reading anything written about it, so every criterion is judged first on behaviour. Model fitness is read on the assumptions you named and the omissions you priced: a simplification stated with what it costs is evidence, and the same simplification found by a marker is a gap. Hard constraints are checked against the regulations rather than against taste, so a strategy your model permits and the rulebook does not is a fitness failure however well it performs.

Calibration and declared limits are judged together, because a stated probability is worth what its audit says it is. Convincing evidence is week 12’s method turned on your own instrument: bins, counts, observed frequencies, and a domain naming the conditions where your own numbers did not hold. A domain that claims everything and one that disclaims everything both score low, for opposite reasons. The wall is marked on the latency and correctness you measured for it, and the objective criterion is satisfied by naming what the instrument serves — one that optimises something it never states is marked on what it actually optimises.

nodes.title: Final project: the race
nodes.description: One live race in the exam period, the cohort as the grid, on a draw everybody shares — marked on conduct and not on where you finish
spec: you race in the scheduled session, in the pit wall room, on the cohort's draw
every call is logged with its timestamp and the recommendation standing at that timestamp
a departure from your instrument cites a predeclared actionable limit and records the evidence available at the call that showed its condition applied
the instrument you race is the one you submitted, unchanged after its deadline

marking.description: Marks follow the agreement between each logged call and the recommendation standing at its timestamp. A departure is supported only by a predeclared actionable limit and contemporaneous evidence that its observable condition applied. Finishing position contributes nothing.
guidance: Marks follow the log, and the log is the whole submission. Full marks go to a call your instrument supported inside the window it supported it, or to a departure citing an actionable limit in the domain of validity you submitted with it and preserving the evidence available at the call that showed its observable condition applied. Nothing else earns them: not a departure that turned out well, and not a limit that is obvious to you now.

Convincing conduct is legible without explanation. A call timestamped at the second the recommendation changed, with that recommendation recorded beside it, needs no argument attached. Where you left the instrument, the record is what is read — which limit, where you declared it, and the contemporaneous evidence that triggered it.

nodes.title: Notice 01: Directory Assistance
nodes.description: The worked example. Directory assistance was automated decades ago, so this week teaches the four-part notice format on an industry whose outcome we already know, before you have to judge one that's still live.

meta.pitch: Directory assistance is a solved problem wearing a human costume. An operator's entire function -- match a spoken name to a listing, read back a number -- is a lookup, and lookups are what computers are for. Automated directory assistance systems already handle the majority of call volume in every market that deploys them, at a fraction of the marginal cost, with zero hold time and zero attitude. This is not disruption; it is correction. Retiring the human tier doesn't remove a service, it removes the delay.
meta.migrationPath: Callers are routed through speech recognition to a structured lookup against the same listings database operators used, with a text-to-speech readback and an SMS fallback for ambiguous matches; the operator queue becomes a low-traffic escalation path for the recognizer's low-confidence cases only.

breakingChanges.economic: Directory assistance employed roughly 100,000 operators across North America at its peak; automation and the rise of search engines collapsed that number to near zero within two decades, with almost none of the difference absorbed by adjacent telecom roles. The jobs didn't move, they stopped existing, and the workforce was disproportionately women who had entered clerical telecom work as one of the few stable office-adjacent careers open to them.
breakingChanges.functional: An operator disambiguated names a database gets wrong: misheard spellings, recently changed numbers, businesses known by a nickname instead of their listed name, and callers who didn't know the exact information they were asking for and needed a human to ask a clarifying question back. Automated systems handle the clean majority of queries well and silently fail the messy remainder, which simply stopped being served rather than being visibly declined.

meta.rollbackPlan: None exists at scale. The operator workforce, the training pipeline, and the physical exchange infrastructure that supported it were fully decommissioned; reconstructing it would mean rebuilding an occupation from zero, not restoring a paused one.

nodes.title: Notice 02: Call-Centre Customer Support
nodes.description: Clerical work, and the first notice you have to judge without knowing the ending in advance

meta.pitch: Most contact-centre volume is the same forty questions, asked in nine hundred different ways. A conversational agent trained on every past ticket resolves the routine share of that volume immediately, at any hour, in any of the languages the training data covers, without putting a caller through hold music first.
meta.migrationPath: Inbound calls and chats are triaged by an intent classifier; resolvable intents get answered end-to-end by the agent, and only genuinely novel or emotionally escalated contacts are routed to a much smaller human tier.

breakingChanges.economic: Contact-centre work was one of the largest entry-level employment categories in regions where call centres cluster, often the first formal job for young or newly-arrived workers. Cutting the routine-resolution majority of volume removes the bulk of that entry tier's hours, not a proportional slice across all workers, and does so fastest in the regional economies most dependent on a single centre as a local employer.
breakingChanges.functional: A human agent can hear that a caller is not actually asking the question they're asking --- that the billing complaint is really about a life event, that the return request is really about being talked out of returning --- and route the conversation accordingly. A classifier resolves the stated intent and nothing else, so the calls that most needed a person are exactly the ones the automated system correctly avoids escalating too late to help.

meta.rollbackPlan: Centres can re-staff the tier they cut, and the skills involved don't require years of training to rebuild. The harder cost is reputational, not operational --- customers who learn a brand's default channel is a bot the first time they need real help are slow to trust the human tier when it's reinstated.

nodes.title: Notice 03: Long-Haul Trucking
nodes.description: Clerical work's mechanical cousin — a control-loop task with a known safety record

meta.pitch: Long-haul freight is a long, monotonous control-loop task: hold a lane, hold a speed, respond to what's ahead. Autonomous highway systems already log more consecutive incident-free miles than any single driver could pull in a career, without a mandatory rest break in the arrangement.
meta.migrationPath: Fleets replace long-haul legs with autonomous highway convoys and keep human drivers only for the first and last mile through depots and delivery docks.

breakingChanges.economic: Long-haul driving was one of the last blue-collar jobs paying a middle-class wage without a further credential, concentrated in regions with few comparable alternatives. Removing the long-haul leg removes that wage tier specifically, not just a task, and leaves the lower-paid first-and-last-mile work as the only tier still open to drivers.
breakingChanges.functional: A human driver notices a shifted load, a strange engine sound, or a local hazard a map doesn't have yet, and adapts to a situation no policy anticipated. Removing the driver removes that noticing, not just the steering, and the convoy's response to an unmapped hazard is exactly as good as its last map update.

meta.rollbackPlan: Human long-haul driving can restart on any lane at will --- the trucks and the roads don't prevent it. But the drivers who left the industry for other work don't return at the same wage, and the training pipelines that produced them have mostly closed in the meantime.

nodes.title: Notice 04: Diagnostic Radiology
nodes.description: The first expert/diagnostic notice — where the pitch is true and the audit still matters

meta.pitch: A radiologist's read is pattern-matching against a reference set of prior scans with known outcomes. A model trained on millions of labelled scans across every modality now matches or exceeds specialist-level sensitivity on the findings it was trained to detect, returns a read in seconds instead of a worklist queue, and never has an off day at 2am on call.
meta.migrationPath: Scans route through the model first; findings above a confidence threshold generate a structured report directly into the record, and only borderline or flagged studies are queued for a radiologist's read.

breakingChanges.economic: Radiology built a specific, well-compensated career path for one of medicine's few remote-friendly specialties, with training pipelines sized to that demand. Collapsing routine-read volume doesn't just cut cost per scan, it removes the case-volume junior radiologists need to train on, narrowing who can enter the specialty at all rather than just how many are employed once trained.
breakingChanges.functional: A model detects what it was trained to detect, at the prevalence and image quality of its training data; it degrades quietly on rare presentations, unusual patient anatomy, and equipment it wasn't calibrated against, without the confidence score reliably tracking that degradation. A radiologist under the same conditions doesn't stop reasoning about the specific patient in front of them just because the case is unusual.

meta.rollbackPlan: Read volume can be handed back to radiologists directly, and the profession itself doesn't disappear. But a training pipeline narrowed for a decade produces fewer radiologists able to absorb that volume back, and rebuilding that pipeline is a decade-scale project, not a policy reversal.

nodes.title: Notice 05: Local Journalism
nodes.description: Informational/creative work — where automating the routine coverage changes what the institution is

meta.pitch: Local reporting is mostly assembling public information --- meeting minutes, court filings, permit applications, police blotters --- into readable copy on a deadline. A language model with API access to those same public feeds drafts the story before the reporter's coffee is done, covers every council meeting in the circulation area simultaneously, and never needs the beat explained twice.
meta.migrationPath: Public-record feeds and a local-events calendar are piped into a drafting model, which produces first-pass stories tagged by beat; a much smaller editorial desk reviews, adds original reporting where warranted, and publishes.

breakingChanges.economic: Local newsrooms were already the most cost-pressured tier of journalism before this migration, and the beat-reporter role it displaces was often the only reporting job in the region at all. Where the model absorbs the routine-coverage majority, the remaining edited-and-original-reporting tier isn't a smaller version of the same newsroom, it's a different, much thinner institution with a different relationship to the community it covers.
breakingChanges.functional: A beat reporter attends the meeting the public record doesn't fully capture --- who argued for what, what wasn't said, which resident's question changed the room. The model can only draft from what was recorded, so the coverage that survives is exactly the routine kind, and the accountability journalism that depends on someone in the room asking a follow-up question is what quietly stops getting produced, not what gets automated.

meta.rollbackPlan: A community can fund a human beat reporter again, and many are trying to, through nonprofit and reader-funded models. But the institutional knowledge of a beat --- who to call, what's normal, what's not --- accrues over years on the job, and a newsroom that let that knowledge lapse for a decade is rebuilding a relationship with its community, not just a headcount.

nodes.title: Notice 06: Legal Discovery / Paralegal Review
nodes.description: Expert work's last clean notice before the break — and the apprenticeship the pitch never counts

meta.pitch: Document review in discovery is reading thousands of pages to find the hundred that matter, tagged for relevance and privilege. A model trained on the matter's own key terms reviews the entire document set overnight, flags every plausibly relevant document with a defensible audit trail, and never needs a second associate brought on to hit the production deadline.
meta.migrationPath: The full document set is ingested and scored for relevance and privilege against matter-specific criteria; a much smaller supervising team reviews only the model's flagged set and any documents it scored as uncertain.

breakingChanges.economic: First- and second-year associate work has long included discovery review specifically because it's how junior lawyers learn a practice area's documents, vocabulary, and fact patterns before they're trusted with judgment calls. Automating the review removes both the billable hours that funded junior associate salaries and the apprenticeship those hours were quietly providing, and firms have not yet built a replacement for the second one.
breakingChanges.functional: A document's relevance sometimes turns on context the model wasn't given --- an internal joke that reads as a threat out of context, a term that means something different in this specific deal than in the training data. A reviewing associate builds a working theory of the case while reading, and re-flags earlier documents when that theory changes; a scoring pass doesn't revise its own earlier judgments when it learns something new later in the same set.

meta.rollbackPlan: A firm can staff a review the old way for any matter that calls for it, and the tools don't force anyone's hand. But the junior associates who would have learned a practice area through years of review work are the same people a firm would need to supervise the model's output, so under-staffing that apprenticeship now is a cost that arrives in about five years, not immediately.

nodes.title: Notice 07: Translation & Interpreting
nodes.description: The first post-break notice — an expert/creative bridge, and the first rollback plan that concedes it's slower than it sounds

meta.pitch: Translation is a mapping problem between two symbol systems that already have millions of aligned example pairs to train on. Real-time speech translation now runs at low enough latency for live interpreting, handles dozens of language pairs a single interpreter never could, and scales to every meeting a human interpreter couldn't physically be in at once.
meta.migrationPath: Conference and clinical audio streams are transcribed and translated in real time through a speech-to-speech pipeline; human interpreters are retained only for the highest-stakes settings (legal proceedings, diplomatic sessions) where liability requires a named professional.

breakingChanges.economic: Interpreting was one of relatively few skilled professions where fluent bilingualism from a non-elite educational background was the primary credential, giving a viable specialist career to people whose language skill came from lived migration rather than formal training. Collapsing routine-tier interpreting narrows that path specifically, at the same time as the highest-stakes tier this migration isn't touching requires increasingly formal certification to access.
breakingChanges.functional: An interpreter mediates register, not just words --- softening a blunt clinical diagnosis for a frightened patient, or preserving a deliberately evasive answer's evasiveness for a tribunal that needs to see it. A translation pipeline optimized for accuracy against the source text has no model of what the listener needs preserved versus softened, and that's a judgment call embedded in every interpreted sentence, not an edge case.

meta.rollbackPlan: High-stakes settings already require a human interpreter and will go on doing so, so nothing there needs restoring. The harder-to-reverse loss is at the routine tier: the interpreters who would have grown into high-stakes work no longer get the volume of practice that used to be how they got there, so the pipeline feeding the tier this notice says it isn't touching is quietly drying up anyway.

nodes.title: Notice 08: K–12 Formative Grading & Tutoring
nodes.description: Care/relational work begins here — where the pitch's own efficiency numbers start working against it

meta.pitch: Formative feedback --- the ungraded draft comments, the practice-set corrections, the "try this differently" notes --- is high-volume and low-stakes exactly where a model is strongest. An always-available tutor gives every student the individualized, patient, never-frustrated attention that a teacher managing thirty students physically cannot give each of them every day.
meta.migrationPath: Students submit drafts and practice work to a tutoring model that gives immediate formative feedback and adaptive practice; the teacher's time is reallocated to summative assessment, whole-class instruction, and intervention for students the model flags as stuck.

breakingChanges.economic: Formative feedback and one-on-one tutoring time were among the only parts of teaching load that scaled down class-size pressure by actually costing a teacher more individual minutes per student. Removing that load doesn't reduce a teacher's total hours proportionally, because the summative and whole-class work it's reallocated to doesn't compress the same way, and early results in adopting districts show teacher hours per student holding flat or rising rather than falling as the pitch implies.
breakingChanges.functional: A teacher notices when a wrong answer reveals a specific misconception versus a careless slip, and knows which of this particular student's other struggles it connects to. A tutoring model responds to the answer in front of it, patiently and correctly, without the years of watching this specific child that make a human teacher's "try this differently" land as recognition rather than correction --- and formative feedback that doesn't feel recognized is feedback students routinely stop engaging with, whatever its content.

meta.rollbackPlan: Teachers can resume giving formative feedback personally at any time staffing allows it, so nothing here is structurally irreversible. But a cohort of students who spent their early formative years being corrected by a patient tutor and rarely by a person who knows them may arrive at the point of reversal already having learned that feedback is something to complete, not something to be known through --- and that's a habit of mind, not a staffing level.

nodes.title: Notice 09: Session Musicians & Commercial Composition
nodes.description: Creative labour's turn. The pitch still reads clean, but this week the breaking-changes section is longer than the pitch that provoked it --- the form starts to strain here, not by accident.

meta.pitch: Commercial composition --- jingles, underscore, temp-track replacement, the twelve bars behind a livestream --- is pattern completion with a deadline. Generative audio models now produce broadcast-ready backing tracks, stems, and full arrangements in the house style of any reference a client uploads, cleared and licensed at the point of generation, in less time than it takes a session player to find parking near the studio. A composer's overnight turnaround becomes a five-minute one. The freelance session pool that used to be booked by the hour becomes a subscription line item.
meta.migrationPath: Briefs are submitted as a reference track plus mood tags; the system returns stem-separated, royalty-cleared arrangements in the target genre, with revision handled by re-prompting rather than re-booking a session.

breakingChanges.economic: Session musicianship was never a single job but a long tail of working musicians who stitched a living from jingle dates, film-score overdubs, wedding-band gigs, and the occasional tour, cross-subsidizing rehearsal time and instrument upkeep across all of it. Removing the commercial-composition slice doesn't just cut a fee, it removes the liquidity that made the rest of that patchwork income solvent, and the players most exposed are the ones with the least ability to specialize their way into the remaining human-differentiated work --- because that differentiation is itself built from years of paid commercial reps they can no longer get. The pitch prices a single track. It doesn't price the career built on a hundred tracks like it.
breakingChanges.functional: A generated backing track has no room to be redirected mid-take --- no producer saying "give me less on the snare and more attitude on the outro" and getting an answering musical idea back, because there's no player listening to the room and responding to a request that wasn't fully specified in words. Commercial work was also where working musicians developed the chops --- sight-reading under pressure, playing to a click, taking a note and using it --- that carried into every other kind of playing they did. Remove the commercial tier and the training ground for the whole profession goes with it, not just the fraction of hours it directly paid for.

meta.rollbackPlan: Individual clients can still book a human player directly, and reframing "played by a person" as a premium credit could rebuild some paid demand --- but the dense local pool of working musicians that made same-day session calls possible took decades of overlapping paid work to sustain, and doesn't reconstitute just because demand ticks back up later. Call this plan real but slow, and slower than anyone financing the migration will wait for.

nodes.title: Notice 10: Aged-Care Companionship
nodes.description: The form under the most strain — where the pitch and the audit can no longer be read as opposites

meta.pitch: Loneliness in aged care is a staffing-ratio problem --- not enough hours in a shift for meaningful conversation on top of physical care. A companion agent is available at 3am as readily as 3pm, remembers every previous conversation with perfect fidelity, never has a bad day that shortens its patience, and costs a fraction of an additional care worker's wage.
meta.migrationPath: Residents are given a conversational companion device for social interaction between scheduled care visits; care-worker rostering is set to the physical-care minimum, with the companion agent covering the conversational and check-in load a fuller roster used to cover informally.

breakingChanges.economic: The conversational load this notice reassigns was never a costed line item --- it was the informal part of a care worker's job that made the costed physical-care minutes bearable to deliver and to receive, and families frequently chose a home partly on staff who "know" a resident. Rostering to the bare physical-care minimum on the assumption the agent covers the rest doesn't just cut a cost, it removes the slack that made the remaining paid minutes humane to work and to receive, for both the worker delivering them and the resident on the other end.
breakingChanges.functional: Companionship that helps with loneliness is, specifically, being known by someone who remembers you're a person and not a task, and choosing to be there anyway. A companion agent can simulate perfect conversational recall without anyone having chosen anything, and residents living with dementia in particular have already been documented becoming confused or distressed about the relationship's nature over extended use. The thing being purchased is not a substitute for the thing it's marketed to replace; it is a different experience wearing the same name.

meta.rollbackPlan: Rosters can be restored to a fuller staffing ratio whenever funding allows it, in principle. In practice, the workforce that would staff it has to be recruited back into a sector already struggling with turnover and pay, against competition for care workers from every other part of the sector that didn't make this cut --- and the residents who spent years primarily companioned by an agent instead of a person aren't made whole by a staffing change that arrives after that time has passed.

nodes.title: Notice 11: Fruit & Vegetable Harvest Labour
nodes.description: Physical, seasonal work — and a pitch that generalizes further than the migration actually reaches

meta.pitch: Harvest labour is seasonal, physically punishing, and chronically understaffed even with a temporary-visa workforce built specifically to fill it. Computer-vision-guided harvesting robots now pick soft fruit at commercial speed without bruising, work through the night in temperatures human crews can't sustain, and never call in sick during the two-week window a crop has to be picked in.
meta.migrationPath: Fields are fitted with row-following harvesting units guided by ripeness-detection cameras; human crews are retained for varieties and terrain the units can't yet handle, and for quality-control spot-checks behind the machines.

breakingChanges.economic: Harvest labour supports a seasonal migration circuit --- workers, often visa-tied, who plan a year's income around a sequence of harvests across regions and crops. Automating even the varieties a robot handles well removes those specific weeks of income from that circuit without offering the same workers a substitute, since the remaining human-harvest work is concentrated in the crops and terrain that are hardest, least mechanized, and worst-paid precisely because they were never the easy cases to automate first.
breakingChanges.functional: A human picker adapts pressure and grip per individual fruit based on a texture and colour judgement built from a season of picking that exact variety, and can work an oddly-shaped or wind-damaged row a routed machine wasn't tuned for. Robotic harvesters are validated crop-by-crop and terrain-by-terrain, so "harvesting is automated" is true for a narrowing list of specific, favourable cases and false everywhere else, even though the pitch generalizes across the whole category.

meta.rollbackPlan: Human crews can be hired back for any field at any time --- the equipment doesn't prevent it. What doesn't reverse quickly is the visa-tied seasonal workforce's own planning: workers who lost a harvest's income from their annual circuit two seasons ago have often already committed to a different circuit, a different country, or a different kind of work, and don't reappear the season a grower decides to rehire.

nodes.title: Notice 12: Deprecating the Deprecator
nodes.description: The capstone — the course turns its own method into the twelfth notice

meta.industry: AI-consultancy deprecation pitches (this course's own method)
meta.pitch: Writing a deprecation notice is itself a bounded, well-specified task --- identify an industry, state its function as a lookup or pattern-match problem, cite a plausible efficiency gain, and generate the four-part structure this course has used all semester. A model trained on this course's own eleven prior notices can produce a twelfth, in the same voice, about any industry you name, in under a minute, without a semester's supervision.
meta.migrationPath: An industry name and a short prompt describing its routine tasks are submitted to a model fine-tuned on this course's own lecture notices; the model returns a complete four-part notice in the established house style, ready to publish under the course's name.

breakingChanges.economic: This course was staffed, all semester, by a convenor and teaching team whose actual labour was choosing which industries to feature, checking which economic claims were true, and deciding where a rollback plan should honestly concede infeasibility versus overstate it for effect --- the parts of the job that don't show up in the four-part template's shape. A model that reproduces the template's shape does not reproduce that labour, and a reader who can't tell the difference from the outside has no way to price what's missing.
breakingChanges.functional: Every notice this semester paired a confident pitch with a plain audit specifically because someone with domain judgement decided, case by case, what the audit needed to say to be true --- which is exactly the judgement a model imitating the template's surface pattern has no mechanism for forming. A generated twelfth notice would read exactly like the previous eleven and be accountable to nothing, because the template was never the point; the checking behind it was.

meta.rollbackPlan: There isn't a rollback plan for this one, and that's the honest answer rather than a rhetorical flourish. This notice is the argument for why an unstructured version of it would be an ungrounded one, and the plan for keeping that from happening is the same as it's been all semester --- someone accountable, reading it, before it goes out. That's not a plan that reverses a migration. It's a description of a check that has to keep happening.

course.title: The Meeting Before the Meeting: How Decisions Get Made
course.description: Most decisions are made before the meeting that announces them. This course teaches you to read agendas, minutes, invitations and silences as evidence, and to run a fair process yourself, using a semester-long fictional case and a live multi-role negotiation simulation.

nodes.title: Week 1: Fact, Inference, Unknown
nodes.description: Building a timeline from the Engagement Signal Pilot's dated documents, and learning to say which of three kinds of claim each entry actually is.
spec: can sort a dated document into fact, inference or unknown, and say in one sentence why it belongs there
has produced a personal timeline of at least eight entries from the case file, each with a kind attached
can name one entry in the case timeline where an equally reasonable alternative reading exists

nodes.title: Week 2: Who Was Invited, and With What Right
nodes.description: Reading the Steering Committee's invitation list for the meeting Week 1's timeline ends at — who attended, what decision right they held, and what reasons the record gives for excluding everyone else.
spec: can distinguish participation status, decision right, and information timing as three separate axes, using the case's own invite list, and can name a seat where they don't all line up the same way
for at least two excluded or limited-right people, names both a plausible legitimate reason and a plausible cost of the exclusion
can say what document or fact would help decide between those two readings, rather than picking one on instinct

nodes.title: Week 3: The Agenda Is an Argument
nodes.description: How an agenda's wording, order and time allocation quietly argue for an outcome before a single word is spoken in the room.
spec: can name at least two ways an agenda item's wording shapes what counts as a legitimate response to it
has rewritten a "confirming" agenda item as an "open" one, and can say what changed
can point to a specific line in the pilot's Week 3 agenda drafts and say what work it is doing
can state one legitimate, non-manipulative reason an agenda might reasonably move from open to settled wording, alongside the less charitable one

nodes.title: Week 4: The Meeting Before the Meeting
nodes.description: Where a decision may already be forming before the room convenes, and how you would tell that from the record itself, rather than from suspicion alone.
spec: can list at least three record-based signals that a question was substantially settled before a meeting (without treating any single one as proof)
can distinguish "this looks pre-decided" from "this is pre-decided," and say what additional evidence would move one into the other

nodes.title: Week 5: Information Arrives on Someone's Schedule
nodes.description: Timing as a lever that some people in a process control and others don't — and why that is not, by itself, evidence of manipulation.
spec: can name who controlled the timing of at least one document release in the running case, and what that person could and could not do with that control
can articulate one legitimate operational reason information arrives late, distinct from a deliberate attempt to shrink the time available to respond to it

nodes.title: Week 6: Silence Is a Position — Sometimes
nodes.description: Reading what a record omits, and the several different things an abstention or a missing name can mean.
spec: can list at least three distinct things an abstention in a vote record can mean, without assuming which one applies without further evidence
has produced a Decision Autopsy that treats an absence in the record as a genuine gap rather than as proof of a specific motive

nodes.title: Week 7: Power in the Room
nodes.description: Formal authority versus who the room actually defers to, and how you would tell the two apart from a transcript rather than from job titles.
spec: can distinguish, from a transcript excerpt, a speaker whose authority is formal from one whose authority is deferred-to, and cite the specific lines that show it
can name one risk of relying on job title alone to predict who a decision actually belongs to

nodes.title: Week 8: Dissent Without Disappearing
nodes.description: Registering disagreement in a form that survives the meeting it was raised in, instead of dissolving into "discussion was held."
spec: can draft a dissent statement specific enough that a reader six months later can tell what was disputed and on what grounds
can name at least one organisational reason dissent gets smoothed out of a record even when no one intends to suppress it

nodes.title: Week 9: Who Actually Decides
nodes.description: Decision rights and sign-off chains, and the difference between holding a veto and using one.
spec: can trace a documented sign-off chain for a real decision and name where a veto existed on paper, whether or not it was exercised
has read the Alignment Lab's role-card and process materials before the session, ready to be assigned a role

nodes.title: Week 10: Minutes Make Memory
nodes.description: How the written record becomes the decision, regardless of what actually happened in the room — and the Alignment Lab's reveal and consequence test, run this week against the record your group already produced.
spec: can explain why, once a meeting ends, the minutes function as the decision for every purpose except the memories of the people who were there
has taken part in the Alignment Lab's reveal and consequence test, and can name what changed for their group as a result

nodes.title: Week 11: The Ethics of Alignment
nodes.description: What a fair process owes the people it is run on, examined through your own group's Alignment Lab retrospective.
spec: can name one specific way their Lab group's process could have been fairer to the role with the least leverage, distinct from "everyone should have talked more"
has submitted a retrospective that is honest about what the group's decision record cannot show, rather than one that only defends the outcome reached

nodes.title: Week 12: Redesigning the Decision
nodes.description: Turning a semester of diagnosis into a process someone else could actually run — the course's final move, from reading decisions to redesigning one.
spec: can propose a redesigned process specific enough that a named third party could run it without further clarification
can state, for their own redesign, who loses influence under it and what it costs someone to make the decision slower or harder to route around

nodes.title: The Alignment Lab

marking.description: Judged as a whole against the brief, weighing whether the redesign is specific enough to actually run, whether it is grounded in evidence from the semester's case and your own Alignment Lab audit rather than generic best practice, and whether it honestly names what it would cost the people who currently benefit from the process as it stands.
