course.title: Dating for Engineers
course.description: Applies financial and game-theoretic models to romantic relationships: attraction as price discovery, dependency as a balance sheet, and commitment as a priced option, for students who trust models more than feelings.

nodes.title: Orientation
nodes.description: The first case review — naming a real situation in the model's terms before the model has given you any terms to name it with
spec: you can describe a specific situation (yours, a friend's, or a plausible composite) in two sentences without naming anyone
you can state what "success" would look like for that situation in terms a stranger could check

nodes.title: First price check
nodes.description: Applying the front-end/back-end split to last week's cases — what did the first signal actually price?
spec: you can name the front-end signal in your case from week 1
you can state one piece of information that signal did not actually carry, however strongly it felt like it did

nodes.title: The reliability audit
nodes.description: Turning "they're flaky" or "they're solid" into an actual rate, computed from your case's last five to ten interactions
spec: you can list your case's last five to ten planned interactions and mark each kept, rescheduled, or dropped
you can state the resulting rate as a fraction, not an adjective

nodes.title: Balance sheet workshop
nodes.description: Pricing your case's dependency across all five line items separately, instead of as one number called "how attached I am"
spec: you can score your case low/medium/high on each of the five dependency line items independently
you can name which line item, if withdrawn tomorrow, would cost the most to rebuild

nodes.title: The specificity test
nodes.description: Checking whether your case has crossed the line from fungible to specific provision, before you write it up for the position paper
spec: you can list what your case provides that a plausible substitute could not replace at the same cost
you can say whether that list is growing, shrinking, or steady

nodes.title: Trust test design
nodes.description: Auditing who initiates the small reversible tests in your case, and who only ever responds to one
spec: you can list the last three small trust tests in your case and name who proposed each one
you can state whether the proposing is symmetric or concentrated in one party

nodes.title: The commitment memo
nodes.description: Writing down which of the three stalled-gate diagnoses fits your case, and what evidence supports it
spec: you can state which of the three stalled-gate diagnoses (pricing delay, pricing mismatch, unilateral de facto exercise) fits your case
you can name the specific evidence that rules out the other two

nodes.title: Situationship clinic
nodes.description: Classifying stalled cases in the room against the three named failure modes, and proposing the specific fix each one implies
spec: you can classify a stalled case (yours or a classmate's, with consent) as asymmetric-cost, sunk-specificity, or silent-substitute
you can state the specific fix the classification implies, not a general one

nodes.title: Contract drafting
nodes.description: Naming which of the four contract types each case is actually operating under, versus which one each party might assume it is
spec: you can name the contract type (Date, Exclusive, Official, Investment) each party in your case appears to believe is in force
you can point to the specific evidence for a mismatch, if one exists

nodes.title: Signal versus self-report
nodes.description: Scoring your case on all seven behavioural signals over the last month, instead of asking how things are going
spec: you can estimate all seven signals for your case over the last month, from memory or a message log
you can say whether each signal is trending, and in which direction
you can name the one signal that would be most expensive for either party to fake

nodes.title: Stress test
nodes.description: Naming a stop-loss condition for your case before you need one, and drafting the standing procedure your Black Swan Protocol falls back on
spec: you can state a specific, checkable stop-loss condition for your case
you can name one person or step your Black Swan Protocol falls back on if an unanticipated event occurs

nodes.title: Portfolio close-out
nodes.description: A last full read of your case against every variable from the semester, before writing the final audit
spec: you can walk your case through all ten variables from the semester in order, without skipping one
you can name the single variable that best explains your case's current state, and why

nodes.title: Case Study Portfolio
nodes.description: A portfolio of three cases, each classified against the situationship failure modes and the four contract types, using the full model's terminology throughout
spec: submitted by the deadline, as a PDF, three cases of 500-700 words each
each case is classified against reciprocity, commitment, situationship failure mode (or "gate closed cleanly," where that's the finding), and contract type
at least one of the three cases is a stalled or situationship case, classified against one of the three named failure modes

nodes.title: Final Audit: Full Model Application
nodes.description: A capstone audit applying all ten variables from the semester to one case, judged as a whole rather than criterion by criterion
spec: submitted by the deadline, as a PDF, 2000-2800 words
applies all ten variables from the semester (framing, attraction, reliability, dependency, specificity, reciprocity, commitment, contract type, monitoring, risk) to one case, in order
states a specific stop-loss condition and a Black Swan Protocol fallback step for the case, or explains why neither applies

marking.description: The final audit is judged as a whole against the brief — whether every variable from the semester is applied, correctly and specifically, whether the reading composes into one coherent account of the case rather than ten disconnected observations, and whether the result stands on its own without the writer present to explain it. A stop-loss condition and a Black Swan Protocol step are both expected; their absence, without a stated reason, is treated as a gap.

nodes.title: Position Paper: Classify a Relationship
nodes.description: Classify one relationship (yours, a friend's, or a plausible composite) against the model's first five variables and defend the classification
spec: submitted by the deadline, as a PDF, 1200-1800 words
names a specific case (with any third-party details de-identified or composited) and classifies it against framing, attraction, reliability, dependency, and specificity
every classification is backed by a specific, checkable piece of evidence, not by a general impression

nodes.title: Course Overview: Relationships as a Two-Party System
nodes.description: What the model is and isn't, why a two-party framing beats a first-person one, and what a case review actually asks of you

nodes.title: Price Discovery: Attraction and the Front-End
nodes.description: Attraction as the market's front-end — the signal a party broadcasts before any real information changes hands

nodes.title: Recurring Contracts: Interaction Frequency and Reliability
nodes.description: Why a relationship is better modelled as a recurring contract than a single transaction, and what reliability adds that attraction can't

nodes.title: Dependency Formation: The Real Balance Sheet
nodes.description: The five things a relationship actually puts on a party's balance sheet, and why counting only one of them causes most misreadings of "attachment"

nodes.title: Object Specificity: Why Substitutes Stop Working
nodes.description: What it means for a relationship to become specific to one counterparty, and why that's the point past which "just meet someone else" stops helping

nodes.title: Reciprocal Investment: Small-Scale Trust Tests
nodes.description: Why trust is built from small, reversible tests rather than declared, and what it means when one party keeps proposing tests the other declines

nodes.title: The Commitment Gate: Pricing Exclusivity
nodes.description: Exclusivity as a priced option — what each party gives up by taking it, and why the gate is where most cases stall

nodes.title: Situationship Case Studies: Three Failure Modes
nodes.description: Three named ways a commitment gate fails to close, and how to tell them apart from a case that's simply progressing slowly

nodes.title: Contract Design: Date / Exclusive / Official / Investment
nodes.description: Four named contract types past the commitment gate, what each one commits each party to, and why picking the wrong one is a design error, not a feelings error

nodes.title: Portfolio Monitoring: Behavioral Signals Over Self-Report
nodes.description: Why an ongoing position is monitored on behaviour, not on periodic self-report, and which signals are cheap to fake versus costly to fake

nodes.title: Risk Disclosure: Stop-Losses and the Black Swan Protocol
nodes.description: Setting a stop-loss before you need one, and what a black swan event does to a position that never set one

nodes.title: Course Retrospective: Applying the Full Model
nodes.description: Assembling framing, attraction, reliability, dependency, specificity, reciprocity, commitment, protocol, monitoring, and risk into one reading of a single case

course.title: The Science of Waiting
course.description: A twelve-week investigation into why waiting feels different from the time that passes, and how people, systems and designers shape the difference.

nodes.title: Starting the wait-observation log
nodes.description: Setting up the personal log you'll keep and reinterpret all semester, and making your first entries against it.
spec: you have logged at least three ordinary waits since the session, each with a clock duration and a judged duration
at least one entry is marked prospective and at least one is marked retrospective, honestly (not assigned to make the set look balanced)
each entry names what you were attending to during or after the wait, and what information, if any, was available to you about how long it would be
none of your entries record anything identifying about another person

nodes.title: Rereading the log for attention
nodes.description: Going back over your Week 1 entries to ask what occupied your attention, then adding one more entry from a wait that naturally differs from them.
spec: you have reread at least three of your own existing log entries and noted, for each, what occupied your attention
you have logged one new entry, in the existing log format, from an ordinary wait that naturally differs in what occupied your attention from at least one of the entries you reread
for at least one pair of entries, you can state whether attention plausibly explains the difference in judged duration, whether it doesn't, or whether the log can't tell
none of your notes present a pair of log entries as proof that attention caused a duration difference

nodes.title: Rereading the log for expectation
nodes.description: Sorting your existing entries by whether the wait ran shorter, about the same, or longer than you expected, and adding one more entry where your expectation was already on record before the wait began.
spec: you have reread at least three of your own existing log entries and classified each as shorter than expected, close to expected, or longer than expected, using the "Expected wait" field you already recorded

for at least one pair of entries with a similar clock duration, you have compared their expectation classifications and their Outcome/notes and stated what, if anything, expectation plausibly explains about the difference
you have logged one new entry, in the existing log format, from an ordinary wait where you already had a genuine expectation on record before the wait began, not one assigned after the fact
none of your notes present an expectation gap as proof that the gap caused a particular judged duration or outcome

nodes.title: Rereading the log for information
nodes.description: Sorting your existing entries by whether they carried explicit waiting information, comparing entries that are otherwise similar, and adding one entry from a wait where real information arrived partway through.
spec: you have reread at least three existing log entries and classified each as carrying explicit waiting information (a countdown, queue position, progress update, or someone stating how long or how far through the wait you were) or no explicit waiting information (nothing explicitly communicated remaining time, position, or progress)

for at least one pair of entries with a similar clock duration and a similar judged duration, you have compared their information classification against Outcome/notes, and written your comparison in three explicit parts — the pattern you noticed, your plausible interpretation of it, and at least one alternative explanation or limitation
you have logged one new entry, in the existing log format, from an ordinary wait where explicit waiting information genuinely arrived after the wait had already started

none of your notes present a difference in Available information as proof that it caused a particular outcome, and none conflate this week's information classification with Week 3's expectation classification of the same entry

nodes.title: Logging the interface
nodes.description: Extending the wait-observation log with a Week 5 field that records what a digital wait's progress or status representation actually did, not just whether one was present.
spec: you have found and logged one ordinary digital wait that displayed a progress or status representation of some kind (a percentage bar, a stepped indicator, a countdown, or an indeterminate spinner), using the log's existing fields plus a new "Interface representation" field

your "Interface representation" field describes the representation's behaviour over the course of the wait (steady, paused, accelerating, jumping, resetting, or indeterminate) rather than only noting that one was present
you have written a two-part comparison — what the representation's behaviour communicated partway through the wait, and whether the wait's ending matched or contradicted that

your comparison names at least one specific finding from the Week 5 lecture (Harrison et al. on pauses or acceleration in a controlled, fixed-duration comparison, or Myers on preference for having an indicator present) and says whether your entry is consistent with it or departs from it, without claiming your one entry confirms or refutes the finding itself
none of your notes reclassify this entry using Week 3's expectation or Week 4's information labels as if the interface-representation question were the same as either

you have not built, delayed, or otherwise interfered with an interface to manufacture a more interesting entry — this stays observational, with no manipulation and no deliberately induced stalls; that kind of intervention is Week 10's territory, not this week's

nodes.title: Logging the room
nodes.description: Extending the wait-observation log with a Week 6 field for a concrete feature of a wait's physical environment, and checking whether it relates to Outcome/notes independently of Judged duration.
spec: you have logged one ordinary physical waiting environment you can safely and accessibly observe (a lobby, a campus space, a transport stop, a shop or retail queue, or another physical waiting environment you genuinely experience), in the existing log format, adding a new "Environment noticed" field that names at least one specific, concrete feature of the space (seating, lighting, noise, what was on the walls, temperature, crowding, or similar) rather than a general impression like "nice" or "bad"

you have compared this entry's Outcome/notes against its Judged duration and stated explicitly whether the space seemed to affect how you felt about the wait without any corresponding sign that it changed how long the wait felt

your write-up names the specific Pruyn & Smidts (1998) finding this connects to (the affect/mood route for waiting-room attractiveness, separate from the cognitive route for objective time) and says whether your entry is consistent with it or departs from it, without treating your one entry as confirmation of the finding

if your existing log entries contain an environmental feature that was intended or assumed to be distracting, examine whether it appeared to change your evaluation of that wait, and discuss what you find if it did not; if your log contains no suitable case, state that limitation directly rather than inventing or manufacturing one
none of your notes reclassify this entry using Week 4's information or Week 5's interface-representation labels as if they were the same question as this week's

you have not rearranged, altered, or otherwise interfered with a real waiting environment, and you have not visited or reported on any medical facility, emergency service, or other sensitive setting for this exercise; this stays observational, on ordinary, accessible waits you genuinely experience

nodes.title: Reading the queue
nodes.description: Naming a real queue's apparent rule, watching what actually happens, and being honest about what you could and couldn't verify.
spec: you have identified one real, ordinary queue you can safely and accessibly observe (a shop or retail queue, a transport stop, a campus service point, or similar) — not a medical facility, emergency service, or other sensitive setting
you have stated whether the queue's rule was stated outright (a sign, a ticket system, a "please form one line" instruction) or had to be inferred from behaviour, and what you believed the rule to be

you have recorded at least three consecutive instances of who was served or moved forward next, and stated plainly whether that sequence was consistent with the rule, inconsistent with it, or too ambiguous to judge from where you stood

if you found a genuine inconsistency, you have discussed it as a legibility question — could you actually verify the rule from your vantage point? — rather than treating it as proof the rule was broken; if you found no inconsistency, or no way to check, you've said so directly instead of inventing one

you have connected your entry to Rafaeli et al.'s finding that a queue's structure, not just an actual broken rule, can lower reported perceived justice, and said whether your case fits that pattern or doesn't, without treating one entry as proof either way
any statement about whether the queue felt "fair" is framed as your own reading ("I read this as..."), not as an objective property of the queue
you have not intervened in the queue, changed your position in it, or identified any stranger in it

nodes.title: Mapping a priority rule
nodes.description: Reading one real, published priority policy for its class, its criterion, and what it actually changes — without calculating whether it's fair.
spec: you have identified one real, publicly published priority policy (for example a supermarket express-lane sign, an airline's boarding-priority tiers, a retailer's loyalty checkout tier, a call centre's stated priority category, or a government service's priority-processing category) — not a medical, emergency, clinical, or triage setting
you have named the priority class using the policy's own published wording wherever possible
you have stated the exact, checkable criterion that creates that class
you have described the mechanical change the rule makes to who moves first, not a guess at the organisation's motive for making it
you have stated plainly what governs everyone who remains under the ordinary rule

you have named specific missing information (such as each class's typical service time, class sizes, or arrival rates) that would be needed to evaluate the resulting redistribution, without estimating or inventing values for it
you have closed with two clearly separated statements — "what this policy tells us" and "what we'd need more information to establish" — and kept them from bleeding into each other
you have not calculated a fairness score, applied RAQFM, or rendered a verdict on whether the policy is mathematically fair
you have not proposed a redesign of the policy or a moral judgement of it

nodes.title: Value-for-wait map
nodes.description: Reading one real system to tell apart an explicit value trade from a priority mechanism, using only what it actually publishes.
spec: you have identified one real, publicly published system offering at least two options that differ in wait time
you have stated the options exactly as published, including any stated time, cost, or other terms
you have stated precisely what changes between the options — time only, or also money, flexibility, certainty, or the outcome/service itself
you have stated whether the options share a queue or order position, or are entirely separate, using only what the system publishes

you have classified the system as one of value/attribute exchange, priority redistribution, both, or cannot determine from published information, and justified the choice using only the published policy or source
you have named the specific information that would be needed to judge whether the trade is actually worthwhile, without estimating or inventing it
you have not offered a fairness verdict, a pricing recommendation, a willingness-to-pay estimate, or a redesign

nodes.title: Designing a control experiment
nodes.description: Drafting one experiment protocol and pressure-testing it against five fixed questions, before the Waiting Experiment asks you to run it.
spec: you have written a full protocol before collecting any data, stating your starting point (Week 10's control mechanism by default, or a named gap from your Queue Case Study, or a specific limitation of a named course source), the manipulation, what you hold constant, the measure, and your prediction
you have named exactly one manipulated variable and stated what your design holds constant across its conditions

if you are testing control, your manipulation varies the availability of a genuine, no-penalty choice to continue or leave the waiting situation, not the information disclosed about it; you have named what wait-time and status information is held constant, and you have acknowledged that the choice instruction itself is a piece of information about which options exist

you have named a measure your design can actually observe — a bounded self-report of perceived control, a recorded continuation-or-leave decision, or another measure that matches what you are manipulating — rather than defaulting to judged duration
you have checked your design against the experiment-ethics policy and confirmed it is self-observation, a simulation, or a controlled prototype, with no live intervention on non-consenting people
if your justified starting point concerns a mechanism other than control, you have named the exact Case Study gap or source limitation that licenses it
you have not proposed a design that could equally be read as testing a different mechanism without you noticing

nodes.title: Calibrating the evidence
nodes.description: Building a nine-mechanism table from your Queue Case Study system — re-tiering the five mechanisms you already classified, and classifying four more from outside for the first time.
spec: you have produced a nine-row table covering interface, environment, queue structure, priority, value, time, attention, expectation, and information, each with a mechanism status (present, absent, ambiguous, or cannot determine) and a separately justified evidence tier (directly evidenced, plausible interpretation, or undetermined)
for the five mechanisms carried forward from your Queue Case Study, you have added only the evidence tier, without changing or redoing the original status finding
for time, attention, expectation, and information, you have produced both a status and an evidence tier from your own observation of the same system
you have not collapsed the two axes into one combined judgement anywhere in the table, and you can state, for any row, which specific claim the evidence tier is attached to

you have used only your existing Case Study evidence and, where safely and accessibly possible, additional non-intrusive public documentation — no interviews, no surveys of visitors, no identifying, naming, or photographing any individual, and no medical, emergency, clinical, or triage system
you have stated separately that your Week 10 experiment result covers control alone and have not added it as a tenth row to this table
you have not treated "cannot determine" or "undetermined" as a weaker or failed result anywhere the evidence genuinely doesn't support more

nodes.title: The tenth row and the relationships between them
nodes.description: Classifying your audited system's own control mechanism, and logging only the mechanism relationships your evidence actually supports — the last working material the Waiting Audit asks you to submit in full.
spec: you have classified control in your audited system from that system's own accessible evidence — present, absent, ambiguous, or cannot determine — with a separately justified evidence tier of directly evidenced, plausible interpretation, or undetermined

you have not treated your Week 10 experiment result as establishing, by itself, that your audited system contains a control mechanism; where the experiment is genuinely relevant to this system you have cited it as additional evidence and said so, and where it isn't relevant you have said that directly

you have produced a selective relationship log covering only mechanism pairs for which you have a plausible, evidence-grounded reason to consider a connection, not every possible pair, and an empty or short log is an acceptable result where your system doesn't support one

for each entered pair, you have classified the relationship as interacting, independent, or cannot determine, using the course's exact definitions, and have not treated mere coexistence as evidence of independence

each relationship claim carries its own evidence tier, separate from the tiers already assigned to the two mechanisms individually, and you have stated the claim's scope as about this one system, not about whether the two mechanisms interact generally

you have used only your existing Case Study and Week 11 evidence and, where safely and accessibly possible, additional non-intrusive public documentation — no interviews, no surveys of visitors, no identifying, naming, or photographing any individual, no intrusive observation, and no medical, emergency, clinical, or triage system
you have not offered a redesign, a recommendation, a fairness or efficiency verdict, or any claim about feelings, satisfaction, willingness to pay, or organisational motive without evidence for it

nodes.title: Queue Case Study
nodes.description: Decompose one real waiting system into the mechanisms actually shaping it — interface, environment, queue structure, priority, and value — instead of describing the experience of using it as one undifferentiated whole.
spec: you have chosen one real-world waiting system with sufficient publicly observable or documentable features to analyse its waiting mechanisms, and it is not a medical, emergency, clinical, or triage setting

you have not identified, named, or photographed any real person, and all observation is non-interfering and drawn only from publicly observable or documentable features, not from interviewing staff or customers
you have given a finding — present, absent, ambiguous, or cannot determine — for each of interface, environment, queue structure, priority redistribution, and value/attribute exchange
for every mechanism you find present, you have described specifically what it does using that mechanism's own course vocabulary, not a generic description of the experience

you have not treated implicit value as an observed mechanism or an empirical finding about users; any discussion of perceived value is marked as interpretation, not as something the case study established

for the priority finding, you have identified the actual ordering relationship between classes (or its absence) before applying the label, rather than treating any separate faster tier as automatically priority

you have classified the system as one of value/attribute exchange, priority redistribution, both, or cannot determine from published information or evidence, and justified the choice from what you found
you have closed with a synthesis stating which mechanisms interacted, which were independent, where the evidence was insufficient, and how you kept the classifications distinct rather than blended

you have included a limitations section covering observation and documentation limits, the time window you observed, the impossibility of inferring anyone's psychology, the absence of a controlled comparison, and the inability to generalise from one system
you have not claimed what anyone felt, satisfaction, fairness, efficiency, willingness to pay, the organisation's motive, causality, or general customer or user behaviour without evidence for it
the submission is approximately 1,200 to 1,800 words, or an equivalent combination of text and evidence — images or screenshots don't count toward that limit

criteria.name: Quality of the distinctions drawn between mechanisms
Honesty and specificity of limitations and uncertainty
Clarity and use of the course's own vocabulary

nodes.title: Waiting Audit
nodes.description: Revisit your Case Study system with the course's complete ten-mechanism toolkit, separating what you can classify from how strongly your evidence actually supports it.
spec: you have revisited the same system you analysed in the Queue Case Study; if you used a different system, you have briefly explained why the original became inaccessible, unsafe, or no longer observable

you have classified each of the ten mechanisms — time, attention, expectation, information, interface, environment, queue structure, priority, value, control — as present, absent, ambiguous, or cannot determine
for the five mechanisms your Case Study already covered, you have carried forward and re-tiered that evidence rather than re-deriving it from scratch

for every claim you make about a mechanism, you have separately stated an evidence tier — directly evidenced, plausible interpretation, or undetermined — and you have not treated "directly evidenced" as equivalent to "caused"

you have stated whether your Week 10 experiment is relevant to this system; if relevant, you have named the exact mechanism it tested and the conditions, and tiered that claim according to how strong your own experimental design actually was; if not relevant, you have said so directly
you have not extended your experiment's result to any mechanism it didn't test
you have included a whole-system synthesis and a limitations section addressing the wider scope of a ten-mechanism, single-system audit
you have not offered a redesign, a recommendation, a fairness or efficiency verdict, or any claim about feelings, satisfaction, willingness to pay, or organisational motive without evidence for it

criteria.name: Correct separation of classification and evidence tier
Honest, appropriately limited use of the Week 10 experiment

nodes.title: Waiting Experiment
nodes.description: A small, ethical, deliberate manipulation of one named waiting mechanism — usually control, this course's Week 10 mechanism — tied to a gap your Case Study or a cited source actually left open.
spec: you have named, before collecting any data, the single mechanism you are testing and why — Week 10's control mechanism by default, an ambiguous or cannot-determine finding from your own Queue Case Study, or a specific, statable limitation of a named course source
you have written a protocol before running the experiment, stating the manipulation, what changes between conditions, the measure, and your prediction
you have tested the manipulation by self-observation, a simulation, or a controlled prototype; any live intervention on a real system meets every condition in the existing experiment-ethics policy
you have reported what actually happened, including a null, mixed, or contrary-to-prediction result, without revising the prediction after the fact
you have stated plainly what your result does and does not establish, and named the confounds and limitations of a small, largely uncontrolled exercise
you have not claimed strong causal proof, generalised beyond the tested context, or treated a personal null result as evidence against a cited study
you have tested exactly one named mechanism, not several at once

criteria.name: Precision of the experimental design and stated prediction
Grounding in Week 10's mechanism or an identified gap
Honest reporting of results, including null or mixed outcomes

nodes.title: Waiting Field Notes
nodes.description: Your own wait-observation log from Weeks 1 to 4, read through the duration, attention, expectation, and information lenses those weeks built it to answer.
spec: you have submitted your wait-observation log covering Weeks 1 to 4, each entry recording clock duration, judged duration, whether that judgement was prospective or retrospective, expected wait, available information, and outcome/notes
you have separated clock duration from judged duration, and prospective from retrospective judgements, in your interpretation, per Week 1
you have checked whether attention or occupation is consistent with differences between entries, without claiming it proves anything, per Week 2
you have checked the expected wait field against outcome, per Week 3, and kept expectation separate from information
you have checked the available information field against outcome, per Week 4
you have named entries that don't fit any lens cleanly, rather than forcing them into one
you have not claimed that your log proves any mechanism, or generalised your own log to other people or to waiting in general
you have attributed every claim drawn from Block & Zakay, Block, Hancock & Zakay, Hui & Tse, Pruyn & Smidts, or Maister to that source
you have analysed your own personal record of naturally occurring waits, not an external system's design

criteria.name: Completeness and fidelity of the four-week record
Correct use of each week's distinction
Clarity and use of the course's own vocabulary

nodes.title: Five Minutes
nodes.description: Why the same five minutes on a clock can feel like nothing or like forever — and the two different ways people end up judging how long a wait took.

nodes.title: Watching the Clock
nodes.description: Why paying attention to a wait can make it feel shorter for one person and longer for another — and why the direction depends on the same forewarning distinction Week 1 introduced.

nodes.title: How Long Did You Expect?
nodes.description: Why a wait that runs six minutes late isn't the same thing as a six-minute wait — and what your log's "Expected wait" field has been quietly recording since Week 1.

nodes.title: Tell Me Where I Stand
nodes.description: Why telling someone how long they have left, or where they stand in a queue, can change how a wait is evaluated without changing how long it's judged to have taken.

nodes.title: The Progress Bar
nodes.description: What a progress bar's own behaviour communicates about an unfolding wait, and what Harrison et al.'s controlled comparison actually measured when they varied that behaviour under a fixed duration.

nodes.title: The Room
nodes.description: How a waiting environment can affect the evaluation of a wait through affect and mood, without necessarily changing how long the wait is perceived to have taken.

nodes.title: Who Goes Next?
nodes.description: Why the way a queue is arranged can lower how fair it feels to wait in it — even when nobody was actually served out of turn.

nodes.title: Who Doesn't Have to Wait?
nodes.description: Priority doesn't remove waiting from a system — it reallocates it between classes of people, and what that reallocation does depends on facts a published policy rarely tells you.

nodes.title: What's It Worth?
nodes.description: Why a wait is judged against what it buys you — sometimes the service itself, sometimes an explicit trade a system builds on purpose — and why neither of those is the same thing as who gets served first.

nodes.title: What You Can Do About It
nodes.description: Why a wait can keep the same clock duration, the same disclosed information, and the same structure while one thing still changes — whether the person waiting has any meaningful choice over whether, when, or how they remain in it — and what one service-encounter study on perceived control does, and doesn't, tell us about that.

nodes.title: Looking Without Asking
nodes.description: Why the four mechanisms your own log could report on directly turn into open, sometimes unanswerable questions once you're standing outside someone else's wait — and the two separate questions, kept apart, that let you say "cannot determine" or "undetermined" honestly instead of guessing.

nodes.title: What You Can Actually Say
nodes.description: A hypothetical café charges $2 to skip the queue. That's two mechanisms, not one undifferentiated feeling — and whether they're connected to each other is a separate claim from whether either is present at all. This week closes the toolkit — the audited system's own control mechanism, classified for the first time, and the relationships between mechanisms, read only where the evidence actually supports reading them.

course.title: Side Channels: What Machines Say Without Meaning To
course.description: A semester on what computers reveal about themselves without meaning to: the sound, current, heat, timing and light a machine leaks while it works, and what a defender does once they've noticed. No electronics or cryptography background assumed; the course builds what it needs as it goes.

nodes.title: Noticing a leak
nodes.description: The first Bench — treating a machine as something that emits, not just something that computes
spec: you can name three physical channels a running device emits besides its intended output
you can state, in one sentence, what "side channel" means without using the word "hack"
you have picked the device you will track across the semester's readings

nodes.title: Listening for keys
nodes.description: Recording a keyboard, and finding out how much of what was typed survives in the sound alone
spec: you have a recording of at least sixty keystrokes on one keyboard
you can point to two keys in your recording whose waveforms are visibly different from each other
you can state what would have to be true of a second keyboard for the same recording technique to fail

nodes.title: Tracing by hand
nodes.description: Reading a captured power trace against the code that produced it, one operation at a time
spec: you can mark, on a supplied power trace, where a loop begins and how many times it repeats
you can point to a visible difference in the trace between two branches of an if-statement
you can say, for the traced code, which single line the difference comes from

nodes.title: Timing a comparison
nodes.description: Measuring how long a string comparison takes, and watching the measurement get more honest as the sample size grows
spec: you can report the mean and spread of at least 10,000 timed comparisons
you can show a measurable difference between an early-exit comparison and a constant-time one, on the same input
you can say why a single timed run would not have been convincing

nodes.title: Shielding a room
nodes.description: Pricing out what it would take to stop a monitor's electromagnetic emissions from leaving the room they are generated in
spec: you can name the frequency band a typical display's emissions fall in
you can produce a rough bill of materials for shielding one room to a stated attenuation target
you can say what part of the cost is the room and what part is the device

nodes.title: Mapping a shared cache
nodes.description: Timing memory accesses to work out, without any special privilege, which cache lines a second process touched
spec: you can distinguish a cache hit from a cache miss in your own timing data
you can identify which of several supplied memory addresses a second, concurrently-running process accessed
you can say what privilege level this technique required and what it did not

nodes.title: Measuring a reflection
nodes.description: Recovering readable text from a photograph of light bounced off something that was never meant to be a display
spec: you can recover at least one line of known text from a supplied reflected photograph
you can state what property of the reflecting surface made recovery possible or difficult
you can identify the smallest change to the room that would have stopped it

nodes.title: Timing a decay
nodes.description: Measuring how fast a keypad forgets what was pressed on it, and finding the two different moments at which recovery stops working
spec: you can plot per-key residual intensity against time from the supplied thermal sequence, and fit a decay to it
your plot identifies two windows, not one — the interval in which the set of pressed keys is recoverable, and the shorter interval in which their order still is
you can state, from your own fitted curve, what a keypad would have to change materially to make the shorter window close before an attacker could arrive

nodes.title: Sharing a tenant
nodes.description: Working out, from the outside, whether two processes are colocated on the same physical machine
spec: you can list at least two observable signals that suggest colocation on shared cloud hardware
you can distinguish, in supplied data, a colocation signal from ordinary network noise
you can state what a cloud provider changed to make the technique you used harder, historically

nodes.title: Scoring a leak
nodes.description: Attaching a number to how much a channel reveals, then using the numbers to build two rankings that disagree
spec: you can compute a mutual-information estimate between a supplied secret and a supplied trace of measurements, and say how many samples your estimate needed before it stopped moving
you can place all seven channels from weeks 2 to 8 on the deck's six axes, using your own Bench measurements wherever you have them
you have produced two rankings — by attacker cost and by defender cost — and can name at least one channel whose position differs sharply between them, and why

nodes.title: Rewriting for constant time
nodes.description: Taking a function that leaks through its running time and rewriting it so the leak is gone, not just smaller
spec: your rewritten function's timing no longer correlates with the secret input, measured the same way week 4 measured the original
you can point to the specific branch or early return you removed
you can name one thing your rewrite made worse (code clarity, average-case speed, or similar)

nodes.title: Defending a design
nodes.description: A dry run of the capstone review, done as peer critique before it counts
spec: you have presented a device, an adversary, and a channel ranking to at least one other student before submission
you can name one objection a peer raised that changed your ranking
you can state your capstone's scope in one sentence a stranger to the course would understand

nodes.title: Capstone Design Review
nodes.description: The semester's method, applied once in full — a device, an adversary, and a ranked, quantified list of which channels apply
spec: submitted by the deadline, as a written design review
the device and adversary are stated precisely enough that a reader can tell which channels from the course apply and which plainly do not
at least one channel's leakage is estimated quantitatively, not only described qualitatively

marking.description: Judged as a whole against week 12's design method — device, adversary, applicable channels, and a defensible ranking of what to close first — rather than against a checklist of channels covered. A narrow scope, argued well and quantified honestly, outperforms a broad one gestured at.

nodes.title: Channel Report
nodes.description: A full treatment of one of the seven channels the course argues, written to the same standard the lectures introducing them were written to
spec: submitted by the deadline, as a written report of 1,500-2,500 words
the report cites the original disclosure (or an equivalent primary source) for its chosen channel
the report states a defensive cost for closing the channel, not only the mechanism that produces it

criteria.name: Technical accuracy of the channel description

nodes.title: Trace Analysis Lab
nodes.description: Reading an unannotated power trace against the program that produced it, without a lecture walking you through it first
spec: submitted by the deadline, as a short written report plus your annotated trace image
the report correctly identifies where in the trace the secret-dependent operation occurs
the report states how you would confirm the finding on a second, independent trace

meta.claim: A computation's unintended physical effects are not noise around the answer; they are a second output, and this course reads them as one.

course.title: Lost Capability: Studies in Institutional Forgetting
course.description: A capability is not stored in its documentation: institutions lose the ability to do things while retaining complete records of how those things were done, and discover the loss only when they try to do them again. Twelve cases, one method, no technical prerequisite.

nodes.title: What would it mean to lose a capability
nodes.description: Losing a capability is not the same as losing its records, and the distinction is the whole course.

nodes.title: The knowledge that isn't written
nodes.description: Polanyi, and Collins' TEA laser: nobody built one from the published papers, it took contact with a lab where one already worked.

nodes.title: Records without capability
nodes.description: Documentation is a description of a practice, not a substitute for it. Completeness is not sufficiency.

nodes.title: FOGBANK
nodes.description: A production line stopped, the paperwork survived, and the material could not be remade. An impurity nobody had recorded turned out to be doing work.

nodes.title: The F-1 engine
nodes.description: NASA held the drawings and still reverse-engineered its own engines from museum hardware. What was missing had never been on paper.

nodes.title: Loss by design
nodes.description: Braverman and Zuboff: deskilling is often a decision, not an accident. Some capabilities are given away on purpose.

nodes.title: Skill decay under automation
nodes.description: Bainbridge's ironies: the more reliable the automation, the more the operator's skill decays, exactly where it is needed.

nodes.title: Buying it back
nodes.description: Reinstatement has a price, and the US Naval Academy's return to celestial navigation is a rare chance to read the invoice.

nodes.title: Contested losses
nodes.description: Damascus steel and Stradivari varnish are claims, not facts. How to assess an assertion that something was lost at all.

nodes.title: Detection
nodes.description: Every case so far was diagnosed in retrospect. What would evidence of a loss in progress look like?

nodes.title: The live case
nodes.description: Generative models and knowledge work, read through weeks 1–10. The framework is the argument; the course does not supply the verdict.

nodes.title: Seminar
nodes.description: Student cases, and revision.

nodes.title: Case dossier
nodes.description: Pick one documented capability loss from outside the syllabus and diagnose it using the course's own vocabulary.
spec: The case is real, documented outside this course, and not one already used as a case in the syllabus.
Every factual claim carries a citation to a source a marker can find and check.
The dossier states explicitly whether the case is a records problem, a capability problem, or a contested claim in week 9's sense — and argues for that classification rather than asserting it.
No fabricated or unverifiable sources. An invented citation is graded as the most serious failure the dossier can have, worse than a weak argument built on real sources.

marking.description: Judged on whether the diagnosis actually uses the record-track / capability-track distinction to say something the source material didn't already say, and on whether every factual claim in the dossier is traceable to a real, checkable source.

nodes.title: Reproduction attempt
nodes.description: Take a small, safe, well-documented practice and try to reproduce it from the record alone, then report what the record didn't tell you.
spec: The chosen practice is small enough to attempt in the time available and involves no hazard, restricted material, or specialised equipment.
The attempt is made using only a written or recorded source, with no live help from someone who already knows the practice, until the attempt is complete.
The report names, specifically, what the record supplied and what it didn't — not just whether the attempt worked.
The report connects its gap, if there was one, to a specific case from weeks 1–10.

marking.description: Judged on the honesty and specificity of the gap report, not on whether the reproduction succeeds. A clearly reported failure, with the exact missing piece named, outscores a vague success.

nodes.title: Seminar paper
nodes.description: A full argument, in your own voice, using the course's framework on a case of your choosing — including, if you want, the live case from week 11.
spec: Takes an explicit position rather than only describing the framework.
Uses at least three cases from the syllabus, cited to the actual readings, not just to week pages.
If the case is week 11's live case, argues one side while stating the strongest form of the other, rather than dismissing it.
No fabricated or unverifiable sources, in the syllabus's cases or in any outside material brought in.

marking.description: Judged as an argument, not a survey — a paper that applies the framework to reach a specific, defensible position outscores one that summarises the syllabus. Verified sourcing throughout is a precondition, not a bonus.

course.title: Spreadsheets at War: Designing Player-Run Economies
course.description: A systems-design course in building and balancing virtual economies: currency sinks and faucets, market microstructure, and the numerical and mechanism-design tools behind EVE Online, World of Warcraft, and RuneScape's player-run markets.

nodes.title: Market Data Lab
nodes.description: A hands-on session with a real, anonymised slice of trade data — find where price and guide-price diverge, and be ready to explain why.
spec: you can locate at least one point in the provided data where traded price and guide/listing price diverge by more than a token amount
you can state a plausible cause for that divergence, not just its existence

nodes.title: Balance Sheet Clinic
nodes.description: Build a real cost-effectiveness ratio from provided cost and performance data, then argue for a rebalance using it — not a vibe.
spec: you construct a cost-effectiveness ratio from the provided data, shown as a formula, not just a final number
your rebalance argument names the specific ratio value that changed and by how much

nodes.title: Trade Route Planning Workshop
nodes.description: Plan a cargo run across a simplified risk/reward map, then price it the way an insurance market would have to.
spec: your planned route states an explicit risk estimate for at least one leg of the journey, not just a distance
you calculate what an insurance premium would need to be for the run to break even against that risk

nodes.title: Comparative Market Teardown
nodes.description: Pick two of the course's three case-study markets and find one design choice in each that the other explicitly avoided.
spec: names one specific, correctly-described design choice in each of two case-study games (matching mechanism, sink strategy, or manipulation safeguard)
explains a plausible reason the other game avoided that same choice

nodes.title: Capstone Pitch Rehearsal
nodes.description: A last rehearsal of your Economic Intervention Report's pitch, in front of peers, before it's due.
spec: you deliver a timed pitch (under three minutes) covering the real economy, the specific problem, and your proposed intervention
you receive and can restate at least one piece of peer feedback on the pitch

nodes.title: Balance Patch Notes
nodes.description: Given cost and performance data for a small set of competing in-game options, build a real cost-effectiveness ratio and write the patch notes for the numeric change it justifies.
spec: constructs at least one cost-effectiveness ratio from the provided data, shown as a formula with the substituted numbers, not just a final value
proposes one specific numeric change (a price, a stat, or a gate) and recalculates the ratio to show the effect of that exact change
is written in the form of real patch notes --- a changed number and a one-sentence reason, not a general essay

nodes.title: Capstone: Economic Intervention Report
nodes.description: Pick one real, documented virtual economy, identify one real problem in it, and propose a scoped, justified intervention using the numerical and mechanism-design tools built across the semester.
spec: names a specific real, documented virtual economy and a specific, verifiable problem within it, each with a citation
the proposed intervention is scoped to that named problem, not a ground-up redesign of the economy
includes at least one worked numerical model (a ratio, a projection, or a before/after estimate) supporting the intervention's expected effect
is presented as a timed pitch, delivered in the Week 12 session, in addition to the written report

nodes.title: Market Data Report
nodes.description: Take a slice of real, published market data from a virtual economy and produce a short report identifying its faucets, its sinks, and one place the two are out of balance.
spec: identifies at least two currency faucets and two currency sinks present in the data, each named specifically rather than generically
states one specific point where a faucet and sink are out of balance, with a number or trend supporting the claim
is legible to a reader who has not seen the source data themselves

nodes.title: Scandal Case Study Essay
nodes.description: Pick one documented market-manipulation incident from a real virtual economy and explain the mechanism it exploited well enough that a reader could see how to design against it.
spec: names a real, documented market-manipulation or exploit incident from a virtual economy, with a citation to a source describing it
explains the specific economic mechanism the incident exploited, not just a narrative summary of events
proposes one plausible design change that would have prevented or limited the exploit

marking.description: Judged as a whole on whether the essay identifies a real, specific incident, correctly explains the economic mechanism it exploited (not just what happened, but why the system allowed it), and proposes a plausible design change that would have closed the gap --- with enough specificity that a reader unfamiliar with the incident could follow the argument end to end.

nodes.title: Week 1: Economies as Designed Systems
nodes.description: Why a virtual economy is not a metaphor for a real one --- it's a system someone wrote code for, with all the same failure modes a bad API has.
spec: identifies at least three concrete design levers a game economy designer controls that a real-world central bank does not
distinguishes a currency sink from a currency faucet with an example of each from a named game

nodes.title: Week 2: Faucets and Sinks
nodes.description: The two pipes every game economy runs on — where currency comes from, and where it has to go, or inflation eats everything else you designed.
spec: names at least three distinct faucets and three distinct sinks from at least two different games, not restatements of the lecture's own examples
explains why a sink that only wealthy players can afford doesn't control inflation for anyone else

nodes.title: Week 3: Market Design and Price Discovery
nodes.description: Order books, guide prices, and why Old School RuneScape's Grand Exchange and a stock exchange are closer cousins than either fandom would like.
spec: correctly distinguishes a matched-order market (Grand Exchange style) from a direct player-to-player listing market (auction-house style)
identifies one deliberate anti-manipulation safeguard in a named game's market and explains what exploit it was built to close

nodes.title: Week 4: Case Study — The EVE Online Economy
nodes.description: A decade of Monthly Economic Reports, read as what they are — one of the largest publicly available datasets on a virtual economy anywhere.
spec: the linked deck is reachable and covers the same MER-derived case study the lecture describes
explains at least two real interventions CCP has made in response to trends visible in the published MER data

nodes.title: Week 5: Numerical Balancing — The Ship-Fitting Problem
nodes.description: Why "make it better" is not a balance patch, and how DPS-per-ISK and effective-hitpoints-per-ISK turn a vibe into a number you can compare.
spec: constructs a cost-effectiveness ratio (a "per-currency-unit" metric) for at least two competing in-game options and uses it to make a concrete recommendation
identifies at least one case where the numerically "better" option is still the wrong recommendation, and explains why

nodes.title: Week 6: Skill- and Time-Gating as Economic Design
nodes.description: Why "you have to wait" and "you have to grind" are pricing mechanisms, not just pacing decisions — and what happens when a real-money option lets players buy their way past them.
spec: explains time-gating and skill-gating as two distinct pricing mechanisms, not synonyms for "grind"
discusses at least one real example of a paid time-skip or the general pattern it belongs to, without assuming the class has purchased one

nodes.title: Week 7: Logistics and Frontier Economics
nodes.description: Why the most valuable resources in a game are often the ones furthest from safety, and why moving goods there is itself part of the economy.
spec: explains why risk (not just distance) is a real cost in a frontier supply chain, with a specific mechanism that imposes that risk
identifies at least one way a game deliberately makes frontier resources more valuable than safe ones, beyond "there's more of it there"
explains why a named material's in-game location is a deliberate scarcity lever rather than an incidental map detail

nodes.title: Week 8: Market Manipulation and Real Scandals
nodes.description: The Guiding Hand Social Club heist, and what a decades-old player scandal still teaches about the difference between a bug and a working system.
spec: accurately describes the mechanics of at least one real documented market or social-engineering exploit, not just its outcome
argues, with reasons, whether a named exploit was a design failure or the system working as specified against an unanticipated strategy
distinguishes an illicit, bot-driven faucet from manipulation of a legitimate one, and explains why enforcement rather than a new sink is the fix for the former

nodes.title: Week 9: Cross-Game Comparative Economics
nodes.description: Putting EVE Online, World of Warcraft and RuneScape's markets side by side — same underlying problem, three genuinely different mechanical answers.
spec: compares at least two of the three case-study games on a named, specific design axis (matching mechanism, sink strategy, or manipulation safeguard), not just "they're different"
explains one design choice each game made that the other two didn't, and a plausible reason for the difference

nodes.title: Week 10: Agent-Based Economic Modeling
nodes.description: Guest lecture — thousands of simple trading agents, none of them smart, still manage to reproduce the bubbles and crashes a real market produces.
spec: describes what a trading agent in an agent-based model actually needs (a strategy, a budget, a way to observe price) without overstating it as "AI"
identifies one emergent behaviour the lecture claims arises from agent interaction rather than from any single agent's design

nodes.title: Week 11: Mechanism Design and Game Theory Crossover
nodes.description: Auction theory shows up in every market this course has studied — this is the week we name it properly and ask what it would mean to design one on purpose.
spec: explains, correctly, why a second-price (Vickrey-style) auction gives bidders an incentive to bid their true value, and where a first-price auction does not
proposes one concrete way a studied game's market could adopt a mechanism-design idea, and names the tradeoff it would introduce

nodes.title: Week 12: Capstone Studio — The Intervention Clinic
nodes.description: The last lecture is a clinic, not new material — bring your in-progress Economic Intervention Report and get it stress-tested before it's due.
spec: the lecture introduces no new economic concept the semester hasn't already covered, and is explicitly framed as review-and-critique
names the specific real economy, problem, and semester concept each of at least two worked examples uses

nodes.title: Dr. Lior Tanaka-Bramwell
nodes.description: A guest lecturer for Week 10, on loan from Slop University's computational social science group to teach agent-based economic modeling.

meta.affiliation: Slop University Computational Social Science Group
meta.contact: Available by email during the fortnight around Week 10 only.

nodes.title: Marcus Whitfield-Reyes
nodes.description: Studio lead for the weekly practicals, and the person who turns a lecture's claim into a spreadsheet you can actually break.

meta.affiliation: Slop University School of Invented Disciplines

nodes.title: Dr. Sana Okafor-Lindqvist
nodes.description: The founding convenor, an economist who spent six years balancing a massively multiplayer game's live currency before she brought the job into a lecture theatre.

meta.affiliation: Slop University School of Invented Disciplines
