nodes.title: Policies and support
nodes.description: The course-wide rules for late work, extensions, academic integrity and getting help.

nodes.title: Glossary
nodes.description: Plain-language definitions for the EVE Online, World of Warcraft and Old School RuneScape terms used across the course's lectures, sessions and assessments.

course.title: Dunkelflaute: Designing for the week the weather stops
course.description: Twelve weeks on one failure condition: the period when wind and solar output are simultaneously low for long enough that normal planning assumptions stop holding. A renewable grid is not designed by its average — it is designed by the event it must survive.

nodes.title: The Average Is Lying to You
nodes.description: Two descriptions of one system — an annual share and an hourly trace — and what each is fit for.
spec: you can read a time-series chart and say what it hides
you arrive with a view on what "reliable" should mean

meta.claim: Three reporting conventions can each describe one system as healthy while none of them has a term for its worst sixty-one hours.
meta.how: One synthetic system, measured three ways, none of which can see the event.
meta.activity: Compute three reporting conventions on the course trace; find which can see the event.

nodes.title: When Does Bad Weather Become a Drought?
nodes.description: Building an operative definition: threshold, span, recovery allowance, scope, season.
spec: you can state what you looked for in week 1's trace, in numbers
you have read the course's operative definition

meta.claim: You cannot design against an event until you define it, and changing the definition changes what counts as failure.
meta.how: The same fortnight, classified four ways.
meta.activity: Vary threshold, duration, area and source mix, and watch which periods survive classification.

nodes.title: The Weather Does Not Fail Independently
nodes.description: Correlated output, and why independent-generator arithmetic overstates a fleet's reliability.
spec: you can describe the event you chose to work with, in your own parameters
you are willing to be wrong about how much diversification buys

meta.claim: Treating renewable generators as independent sources overstates reliability.
meta.how: The course trace has no independent version; its wind is one shared signal.
meta.activity: Rebuild week 2's six rejected low periods under independent draws and compare.

nodes.title: How Big Is the Weather?
nodes.description: The size of a weather system set against the size of the grid underneath it.
spec: you can explain why correlated output defeats naive reliability arithmetic
you bring a rough sense of the geography your portfolio will occupy

meta.claim: Geographic diversification helps only when the grid is larger than the weather pattern shutting it down.
meta.how: A high-pressure system drawn over a transmission map.
meta.activity: One farm, then several nearby, then widely separated, then interconnected regions.

nodes.title: Below Cut-In
nodes.description: Power curves, cut-in speed, and what a fleet does when the wind is merely weak.
spec: you can describe a threshold response in words, without a formula
you have a portfolio sketch from week 4 to test

meta.claim: In weak wind a fleet is not producing less; parts of it are absent from supply.
meta.how: The event floor sits at 0.9% of capacity; the threshold sits at 12%.
meta.activity: Derive why the course's threshold is a threshold rather than a proportion.

nodes.title: Solar Helps, Until Wind and Sun Fail Together
nodes.description: Wind and solar through a winter anticyclone, tested hour by hour rather than on annual averages.
spec: you can state the depth problem from week 5 in your own words
you accept that a portfolio may be worse than the sum of its parts

meta.claim: Wind and solar complement each other on average, and reliability is decided by the hours when the complement fails.
meta.how: A winter anticyclone — calm, cold, and overcast at noon.
meta.activity: Run wind-only, solar-only and mixed portfolios through the event. Does the mix remove the failure, shorten it, or move it?

nodes.title: Storage Is Two Problems Wearing One Name
nodes.description: Power and energy as separate specifications, and which one a multi-day event actually tests.
spec: you can say what your portfolio's shortfall looks like hour by hour
you can distinguish a megawatt from a megawatt-hour without hesitating

meta.claim: Power capacity and energy capacity solve different problems, and confusing them is how a system is under-built.
meta.how: An illustrative 1 GW / 1 GWh battery brought to a multi-day event.
meta.activity: Manipulate power, energy, state of charge and round-trip efficiency against a fixed deficit.

nodes.title: The Generator You Hope Never Runs
nodes.description: The economics of reserve plant: paying for capacity whose value is in not being needed.
spec: you can describe what happens in your system after storage is exhausted
you are prepared to defend a number you cannot fully justify

meta.claim: Reliability is bought with assets whose success is measured by how rarely they are needed.
meta.how: A fictional reserve plant that ran 41 hours last year.
meta.activity: Price reliability. What would you pay, per household per year, for an asset you hope stays idle?

nodes.title: Who Gets Turned Off?
nodes.description: Load shedding as an allocation problem, once the technical options have run out.
spec: you can state what your system does when supply is genuinely insufficient
you accept that this session has no technically optimal answer

meta.claim: When supply is short, load shedding stops being a control problem and becomes an allocation decision.
meta.activity: Fixed available generation, competing loads. Choose. The record keeps what you sacrificed.

nodes.title: A Forecast Is Only Useful While You Can Still Act
nodes.description: Forecast skill set against the lead time each available action needs.
spec: you can list the actions your system can take, and how long each needs
you can describe your allocation ordering from week 9

meta.claim: Forecast accuracy has no operational value beyond the point where the system can no longer respond.
meta.how: Three forecasts of the same event, at seven days, twenty-four hours and two hours.
meta.activity: Match each action's lead time against each forecast's skill.

nodes.title: Every Failure Gets a Story Afterwards
nodes.description: Post-mortems as documents with authors, and the system boundaries they assume.
spec: you have a dispatch record, including what went wrong in it
you are willing to read your own account as a document with an author

meta.claim: A post-mortem reports the system boundary of whoever wrote it, so the cause of a failure is partly an institutional choice.
meta.activity: Locate each report's implied system boundary. Then write the sixth.

nodes.title: The System You Are Willing to Defend
nodes.description: Studio critique of the systems you have built, and the failure boundaries you declare for them.
spec: you bring a system specified well enough for someone else to operate
you bring the event that defeats it, stated in your own parameters

meta.claim: A defensible design names the event it survives and the event that beats it.
meta.how: The configuration you nominated in week 1, brought back for critique.
meta.activity: Studio critique. There is deliberately no correct system.

nodes.title: Define the Drought
nodes.description: The first rung of the ladder — choose a threshold, a duration and a scope, then defend the periods your definition admits and the ones it discards.
spec: every parameter of your definition is stated in units a reader can apply
you name at least one period your definition discards, and say why that is acceptable
your defence argues from consequences, not from convention

meta.produces: an operative definition of the event

nodes.title: Site Against Failure
nodes.description: The second rung — place a renewable portfolio to reduce correlated low output rather than to maximise the capacity factor on a brochure.
spec: your siting decisions are justified against your A1 event, not against annual output
you show at least one case where the highest-yield choice is not the most reliable one
you state what weather pattern would defeat your portfolio

meta.takesInput: an operative definition of the event
meta.produces: a portfolio with a correlation profile

criteria.name: Reasoning from correlation rather than average yield
Use of your own event definition
Treatment of the complementarity that fails

nodes.title: The 72-Hour Dispatch
nodes.description: The third rung — run the system hour by hour through the event, spend the storage, start the reserve, shed what you must, and record the cost.
spec: every dispatch decision is recorded with the information available at that hour
your counterfactual changes exactly one thing, and you say what it shows
the log states what was shed, when, and to whom

meta.takesInput: a portfolio with a correlation profile
meta.produces: a dispatch log and a counterfactual

criteria.name: The counterfactual, and what it isolates
Honesty of the log about what was sacrificed

nodes.title: Design for the Worst Week
nodes.description: The final rung — build a system you are willing to defend, and state the event that still defeats it.
spec: the system is specified well enough for someone else to operate it
the event it survives is stated in the parameters of your own definition
the event that defeats it is named, bounded, and not dismissed

meta.takesInput: a dispatch log and a counterfactual
meta.produces: a defended system, and the declared event that beats it

marking.description: Judged as one argument. A submission is strong when the system, the event it survives and the event that defeats it are all stated precisely enough to be checked against each other, and when the declared failure boundary is a real limit rather than a token concession.

nodes.title: One System, Two Stories
nodes.description: The opening lecture — the same synthetic system described by an annual figure and by its hourly trace, and why only one of them is a design input.

nodes.title: Drawing the Line
nodes.description: The second lecture — how an operative definition is built, and how each of its parameters changes what counts as an event.

nodes.title: Power, Energy, and the Week That Tells Them Apart
nodes.description: The week 7 lecture — why "how much storage do we need" is two questions, and why a multi-day event is what forces the distinction into the open.

nodes.title: Declaring the Boundary
nodes.description: The closing lecture — what it means to state the event that defeats your design, and why that statement is the course's primary output.

nodes.title: Policies and support
nodes.description: How this course handles late work, extensions, academic integrity and the use of generative tools.

course.title: How to Keep One Cat Happy for Twenty Years
course.description: Follow one cat from her first night home into old age, learning to observe her, interpret change, make safe care decisions, and know when to seek professional help.

nodes.title: A Quiet Change at Breakfast
nodes.description: An adult cat leaves part of breakfast for four mornings; the household needs a method, not a guess.
spec: record the change against Pepper's stated baseline before selecting an explanation
compare all three responses and identify the assumption each one makes
leave with a monitoring endpoint and a clear professional-escalation boundary

nodes.title: Care Consultation: From Pattern to Safe Action
nodes.description: Work through an unfamiliar household case, compare plausible explanations, and recommend a safe owner-level next step.
spec: the opening brief separates what the household observed from what it assumes
at least two plausible responses are compared rather than dismissed
claims are connected to the registered course evidence with limitations preserved
the final recommendation distinguishes home action, monitoring and professional escalation

meta.stage: End of Part III · Keep Her Well
meta.deliverable: A structured case consultation containing an observation brief, evidence map, option comparison, and owner-facing care recommendation.

criteria.name: Safety and usefulness of the response

nodes.title: Field Notebook: Seeing Before Explaining
nodes.description: Build a reliable baseline from precise observations, then show where description ends and interpretation begins.
spec: six dated entries use concrete behaviour, context, frequency or duration rather than personality labels
the baseline names what is typical while acknowledging gaps or uncertainty in the record
one revised interpretation explains what changed after comparison with course evidence
no diagnosis or treatment claim is made from household observation alone

meta.stage: End of Part I · A New Life
meta.deliverable: A six-entry observation notebook, a one-page baseline portrait, and a short commentary revising one early interpretation.

nodes.title: Lifelong Care Dossier: Change With Her
nodes.description: Revisit one cat across a major life-stage change and build a care plan that can adapt without losing its evidence or humanity.
spec: the dossier compares at least two life stages without treating age itself as a diagnosis
an earlier household decision is revisited in light of changed mobility, health, behaviour or capacity
the care plan includes observable measures, feasible adaptations and explicit escalation boundaries
caregiver time, financial, emotional or physical capacity is addressed honestly
the ending supports shared decision-making and does not prescribe an unverified clinical outcome

meta.deliverable: A longitudinal case dossier with a baseline, change record, revised household decision, adaptive care plan, and professional-conversation brief.

nodes.title: How to Read a Capture
nodes.description: A short field guide to the recurring observation, evidence, judgement and care-plan rhythm used across all twelve chapters.

nodes.title: Mara Bell
nodes.description: A fictional Slop University convenor who helps learners turn everyday cat-care concerns into careful observations and proportionate decisions.

meta.affiliation: Slop University School of Everyday Animal Relationships (fictional)
meta.contact: Use the course discussion space for shared questions and a private course message for personal circumstances.

nodes.title: Policies and support
nodes.description: Where course learning ends, where professional care begins, and how to ask for assessment or access support.

course.title: The Unpaid Shift
course.description: Wikipedia, every subreddit and half of open source are maintained by volunteers doing unpaid janitorial work under rules nobody wrote down. Twelve weeks doing that work for real: editing, moderating, arbitrating, and handing the mop on to whoever comes next.

nodes.title: Induction
nodes.description: Accounts, project choice, and the undertaking you sign before this course lets you near anybody else's community
spec: you hold a named account on your chosen project, created for this course
your project is one of the four supported, and you can say why you chose it
you have signed the contributor undertaking on the policies page
you can find the public record of removals or reverts on your project

meta.produces: A signed contributor undertaking and a declared home project

nodes.title: Reading the room
nodes.description: Thirty days of your project's public record, read closely, turned into a map of the rules nobody wrote down
spec: your norm map cites at least fifteen specific removals, reverts or closures
every enforced rule you list is evidenced by a decision, not by the sidebar
you identify at least three rules that are enforced but not written down
you name one case where the enforcement was inconsistent, without concluding that the moderators were wrong

meta.produces: A norm map — written rules, enforced rules, and the delta between them

nodes.title: First edit
nodes.description: You make a real contribution to a real project, in the room, with people who can tell you what will happen to it
spec: you have made at least one contribution visible in your project's public history
the contribution is small, uncontested and useful — a fix, not a rewrite
your edit summary states what you changed and why, in one line
your log entry records what you predicted would happen to it

meta.produces: At least one real contribution, logged with its diff and a prediction

nodes.title: Talk page
nodes.description: Your prediction meets reality, and you write the reply that either opens a conversation or ends one
spec: your prediction from week 3 is marked against what actually happened
you have posted on a talk page, issue thread or changeset discussion
your post states the change, the reason and the source, and asks one real question
you have not reverted anyone

meta.produces: A talk-page post responding to a revert, review or removal

nodes.title: The sourcing bench
nodes.description: A worked comparison of two standards of evidence, run over the same claim, until you can tell which project you are in by what it refuses
spec: you have taken one claim and assembled the evidence each project would require for it
your dossier identifies at least one source that is reliable under one standard and inadmissible under the other
you have checked every cited link resolves, and archived the ones that do
you can state, in one sentence, the failure mode each standard accepts

meta.produces: A sourcing dossier for one contested claim, argued under both standards

nodes.title: Deletion debate
nodes.description: A live deletion discussion, run properly, on a real borderline subject, with one of you closing it and having to justify the close
spec: the discussion ran to the project's actual procedure, not a debate format
every participant's argument rests on sources or policy, not on worth
the closer read for consensus and can say which arguments they discounted and why
the cohort identified which way the systemic bias ran in this case

meta.produces: A closing rationale for a contested deletion discussion

nodes.title: Writing the rules
nodes.description: The cohort writes the rules for the course sandbox, encodes some of them in AutoModerator, and then has to live under both until week 12
spec: the ruleset is short enough that a newcomer will read all of it
every rule names what it prohibits and what happens on a first breach
at least one rule is deliberately left to human judgement, and the ruleset says which and why
the AutoModerator config is version-controlled, with a stated rationale per rule

meta.produces: The sandbox ruleset, and the AutoModerator config that enforces part of it

nodes.title: The queue
nodes.description: Rostered enforcement on the course sandbox — you remove things, you write the reason, and somebody appeals it to a person who is not you
spec: every decision you made is in the log with the rule it applied
every removal carries a written reason naming the rule, the evidence and whether the door is open
you handled at least one appeal against a decision you did not make
no decision of yours was reversed on appeal for being unexplainable

meta.produces: A shift of logged enforcement decisions, each with a written reason

nodes.title: The rota
nodes.description: You design the roster that will carry the sandbox through to handover, and argue about what the work is worth
spec: the rota caps individual shift length and rotates people off the worst queue
decisions above a stated severity require a second signature
the rota names who covers a no-show, before one happens
you have costed the sandbox's moderation at a real hourly rate and stated who you think should pay it

meta.produces: A rota with caps, rotation and escalation rules, and a costing of the work

nodes.title: Fork drill
nodes.description: The scenario that asks what your leverage actually is, run as a decision under time pressure with people who will be harmed either way
spec: the decision states its aim and the condition under which it would end
you identified who bears the cost, separately from who you are bargaining with
a fork was costed against the data, the tooling and the people it would need
the dissenting position is recorded in full, by its holders

meta.produces: A cohort decision on a withdrawal-of-labour scenario, with the dissent recorded

nodes.title: Bot audit
nodes.description: You audit ShiftBot against four weeks of its own decisions and find out what the rules you wrote in week 7 have actually been doing
spec: every ShiftBot rule is checked against its actual decisions since week 7
you have found at least one false positive and traced it to the rule's text
each rule is kept, amended or retired, with a reason recorded in the register
your Governance Redesign states a position on machine contribution

meta.produces: An audit of automated decisions, with a list of rules to amend or retire

nodes.title: Handover
nodes.description: You write the document that outlives you, hand the sandbox to next year's cohort, and leave your home project properly
spec: the handover note records what exists, what was decided, and what was decided against
every live rule has a rationale a stranger can read without asking anyone
you have posted a closing note on your home project, or stated that you are staying
the succession is named — who holds what, from when

meta.produces: A handover note for the sandbox, and a closing note on your home project

nodes.title: Conflict Autopsy
nodes.description: Reconstruct a real dispute in a volunteer community from its public record, and explain what each party could see at the time

criteria.name: Reconstruction — is the sequence right, and is it evidenced
Reading each party charitably on the evidence available to them
Identifying the structural cause rather than the villain

nodes.title: Contribution Log
nodes.description: Ten weeks of real contributions to a real project, logged with their diffs, their outcomes and an honest account of what happened to each one

criteria.name: Quality of the annotation: prediction, outcome, and what you misread
Conduct, as visible in the public record

nodes.title: Governance Redesign
nodes.description: Take a real community, rewrite how it governs itself, and defend the rewrite against the evidence of what your own rules did for four weeks

criteria.name: Diagnosis — is the problem the real one, and is it evidenced
The redesign itself — enforceable, appealable, staffable
Argued against your own sandbox evidence, including what failed

nodes.title: Shift participation
nodes.description: The rostered work itself — queue shifts, appeals, and turning up for a community that depends on you having turned up

course.title: Cryptotaxonomy: A Linnaean System for the Shanhaijing
course.description: Build a classification system for any material, on a book that resists. The 山海经 (Shanhaijing, the Classic of Mountains and Seas) files hundreds of creatures by where you would meet them and never says what any of them is a kind of. Twelve weeks: build it, strain it, rebuild it.

nodes.title: What a classification system is
nodes.description: What the Classic of Mountains and Seas is, what Linnaeus did that we are going to copy, Borges' fake Chinese encyclopedia as the counter-example, and what the book already sorts by.
spec: you can say what the Classic of Mountains and Seas is, and what one of its records contains
you can name Linnaeus' three moves and say which one a given attempt is missing
you can state what the Classic of Mountains and Seas sorts by, and point at its table of contents to show it

meta.rule: The text is already a classification: it files every creature by where you would meet it, which is a claim about the world and not the absence of one.

nodes.title: Reading the source text
nodes.description: Where our characters come from. Candidates come from repetition, they have to survive three tests, and the first one the Classic of Mountains and Seas offers is incomplete in more than half the records we cite.
spec: you can find three candidate characters in unfamiliar material and say where each one came from
you can disqualify a candidate and name which of the three tests it failed
you can rule a record into slots and leave an unsupplied slot visibly blank

meta.rule: 其状如X，Y首，见则Z is a template the text reaches for and often leaves incomplete, so the first character a taxonomy has to handle is an absent one.

nodes.title: Morphological classification
nodes.description: Four composite bodies taken apart into parts and counts. Two of them differ only in where a number sits, one disagrees with itself between its two records, and one is assembled out of no animal at all.
spec: you can write a composite body as parts and integers, with nothing left in prose
you can name two creatures whose inventories differ only in where a number sits, and say how the text files each of them
you can say what your inventory does with 帝江, in one sentence that does not excuse itself

meta.rule: A composite body is assembled from a small closed set of parts, so the parts and not the whole are what a taxonomy can count.

nodes.title: Geography and habitat
nodes.description: Three records fill the habitat field the same way and mean three different things by it — a mountain at a derivable position on a route, an unspecified sea, and a country placed relative to the entry before it.
spec: you have drawn one 山經 route from the stated bearings and distances, without consulting a modern map
you can name the sentence at which your drawing of a 海經 chapter stopped, and say what was missing from it
you can state your position on splitting the habitat field, ready to defend in the week 7 proposal

meta.rule: The 山经 routes can be mapped and the 海经 cannot, so a habitat field that accepts both is recording two different kinds of fact under one name.

nodes.title: Omens and uses
nodes.description: 見則天下大旱 stands word for word on six creatures that share no part and no chapter. The omens do fill a closed grid of scope against event, and the cell a creature lands in follows from nothing else on its card.
spec: you have counted the occurrences of 見則天下大旱 in the five 山經 chapters yourself, from the edition
you can fill the scope-by-event grid with at least one creature in every cell you claim exists
you can argue either side of keeping the omen column, and say which side you are on

meta.rule: Neither an omen nor a use is a character of the creature: 见则天下大旱 attaches word for word to at least six unrelated creatures, and a use states what a person gets rather than what the creature is.

nodes.title: The 神 and the 獸
nodes.description: 陆吾 and 开明兽 guard one mountain with nearly one body and are filed in different kingdoms. The difference between them in the record is a job rather than a limb, and several records name no kind at all.
spec: you can say which part of the body differs between 陆吾 and 开明兽, and which does not
your classification design names what its kind field does when the record supplies no kind-word
you can cite one record that is called a 神 without being given an office

meta.rule: The text's own words 神, 獸, 鳥 and 人 do not sort by body: 陆吾 and 开明兽 guard one mountain with nearly one body and are filed apart, and several records name no kind at all.

nodes.title: Drift
nodes.description: The 青丘之山 record names no beast. 九尾狐 is a handle attached later, so everything the name now carries was added after the record closed — and the same process runs inside the edition, on 狌狌 and on 讙头.
spec: you have found the 青丘之山 passage yourself and confirmed the name is not in it
you can list three properties 九尾狐 now has that no record in the edition supplies
you can name the two spellings under which 狌狌 appears, and where each one stands

meta.rule: A name outlives its record: 九尾狐 is never named in the text, so everything the name now carries was added after the record closed.

nodes.title: Where classification fails
nodes.description: 肥遗 names two incompatible snakes and a bird across two chapters, 窫窳 has two records that cannot describe one body, and the entry form has a single name field that cannot hold either fact.
spec: you can state the two failures separately, and say which of your own fields each one attacks
you have located all three 肥遗 records and can say which chapter each sits in
you can say why adding a synonyms field does not solve the second failure

meta.rule: One name takes many creatures and one creature takes many names, and no field in the entry can hold either fact.

nodes.title: Comparative systems
nodes.description: Two bestiaries that never needed a species concept, read for their organising principle rather than ranked against ours. Both sort by what a creature is for the reader, and then the same test is turned back on 其状如.
spec: you can name the organising principle of the medieval bestiary in one sentence, without using the word "religious"
you can point at one slot in our own entry form that encodes a reader rather than a creature
your essay names the creature you are reclassifying and the system you are reclassifying it into

meta.rule: Other bestiaries sort by what a creature is for the reader, so their top division is a fact about the reader rather than about the creatures.

nodes.title: Cross-system comparison
nodes.description: Four creatures filed twice, once under our own system and once under one of last week's two. 夔's two filings drop opposite halves of one line, 帝江 has a clause none of the three can hold, and 驺吾 is the one our system alone fails.
spec: you can file one creature in two systems and list what each filing dropped
you can say which of two systems is better at a stated job, and name the job
you can name one feature that neither system has anywhere to put

meta.rule: Putting one creature through two systems shows which of its features each system had to ignore, and the ignored features are where the two systems actually disagree.

nodes.title: Modern reconstruction
nodes.description: The first material this course meets that the edition did not produce. 夫诸's three clauses leave six decisions a model has to make anyway, 帝江 forces a renderer to draw an absence, and on 九尾狐 the audit stops working.
spec: you can list six decisions a designer must make about 夫诸 that its record does not make
you can say what 渾敦無面目 requires a renderer to draw
you can name one creature whose reconstructions have become the source for later reconstructions

meta.rule: A system transfers only as far as its characters do, so the test of one is naming which of its characters the next material will not supply.

nodes.title: The taxonomic congress
nodes.description: Entries are tabled and challenged on one ground only, an undeclared field. 猼訑 shows what the rule does to a shared trait, 窫窳 forces a pick nothing justifies, and the course answers its own question.
spec: your entry cites at least one line and names the chapter it sits in
your entry has a declarations section listing every field the cited line does not supply
each of your two peer reviews names one undeclared field, or states that it found none and why

meta.rule: A new entry is admissible only if it cites a line and declares which of its own fields that line does not supply.

nodes.title: Bestiary entry
nodes.description: What the congress tables. One new entry for a creature outside the course's twenty-five, admissible under the week 12 rule, with its gaps declared.
spec: the creature is not one of the twenty-five the course already carries
at least one citation, giving the 卷 and, for the five 山經 (Shānjīng, the Mountains chapters) chapters, the 次 section and locus
every quoted line matches the edition character for character, in traditional forms
the entry names which of its own fields the cited line does not supply

criteria.name: Admissibility — a real cited line, and the fields it does not supply declared
The entry form — every field filled to the standard the course's entries meet
The binomial, and the diagnostic trait it was built from
What the entry costs the system, argued rather than asserted

nodes.title: Classification design
nodes.description: The capstone, in two parts. Part 1 at week 7 is the system the rest of the semester tries to break. Part 2 at the end is the transfer test — run it on material this course never gave you, and declare what does not survive.
spec: names every field, with a one-sentence rule for what goes in it and what does not
states the sort order the system imposes, and what that order is a claim about
states at least two questions the system refuses to decide, and why refusing is better than guessing
works through at least three creatures from weeks 1 to 6, including one the system handles badly
Part 2 applies the same system to a body of material this course did not supply, with its records cited the way the Classic of Mountains and Seas ones are
Part 2 names every character of your own system that the new material does not supply, and says what you did about each

criteria.name: Part 1 — the field set, defined so two readers would fill it the same way
Part 1 — what the system sorts by, and why that and not something else
Part 1 — declared refusals, stated as rules rather than as apologies
Part 1 — tested against at least three creatures from weeks 1 to 6
Part 2 — the system run on material this course did not supply
Part 2 — the characters that material does not supply, named rather than regretted

nodes.title: Peer review
nodes.description: At the week 12 congress, review two other bestiary entries against the admissibility rule and against the systems their authors proposed.
spec: two reviews, of two different entries, neither of them your own
each review states whether the entry is admissible under the week 12 rule, and on what grounds
each review reports whether the cited line was found in the edition, and where it was looked for
each review names one change that would improve the entry, specific enough to act on

criteria.name: The admissibility rule applied to the entry as written
The citation checked against the edition, not against plausibility
What the entry costs its own system, named rather than only its errors

nodes.title: Reclassification essay
nodes.description: Take one creature whose records disagree, argue for a single reading, and state what that reading costs the system you proposed at the midterm.
spec: names one creature whose records disagree, and quotes both records from the edition
argues for one reading rather than presenting the disagreement as a balance
states what the reading costs — which record is set aside, and what is lost with it
says what evidence would change the reading

marking.description: Judged as one argument rather than against separate criteria, because the parts cannot be marked apart. A reading, the evidence for it, and the declared cost of adopting it either hold together or they do not. A well-argued reading the marker disagrees with scores above an unargued reading the marker shares.

nodes.title: Specimen cards
nodes.description: One card a week, on one creature from that week's list, applying that week's rule. Twelve cards, written as the semester runs and submitted together.
spec: twelve cards, one per teaching week, each naming a creature from that week's list
every card cites a 卷, and for the five 山經 (Shānjīng, the Mountains chapters) chapters a 次 section and a locus
every card names at least one field the cited line does not supply
a card that could not find its line is marked unverified rather than filled in

criteria.name: Coverage — a card for every week, on a creature from that week's list
Fit between the card and the week's rule
Citation, and accuracy about what the record supplies
Declared gaps — what the record withholds

nodes.title: Idris Fenn
nodes.description: Philologist and tutor. Runs the close reading, and asks which edition a line came from before it is allowed into anybody's entry.

meta.affiliation: Slop University Institute for Textual Criticism
meta.contact: In the session, or by email between sessions. Bring the line and the edition you found it in, not a translation of it.

nodes.title: Marisol Quaye
nodes.description: Systematist and convenor. Supplies the Linnaean machinery the course tries to fit to a text that has no specimens, and rules on what a character is.

meta.affiliation: Slop University Department of Systematics and Nomenclature
meta.contact: Consultation after the Monday session, in the seminar room. Email for anything about the course as a whole, or about a mark.

course.title: Underground Diplomacy: Trade, Espionage and Betrayal in the Mycorrhizal Network
course.description: A postgraduate seminar treating forest fungal networks as a diplomatic system: trade agreements, espionage, sanctions and betrayal beneath the soil.

nodes.title: Credentials
nodes.description: The opening Briefing — what has to be true before anything under the soil counts as "a network," and the ground rules for keeping this course's central metaphor honest.
spec: you can state, from memory, the difference between an arbuscular and an ectomycorrhizal association
you can name one claim about fungal networks you have heard outside this course, and say what evidence would move you to believe or doubt it
your development environment runs the course's toolchain and you can preview the site locally

meta.metaphor: Credentials — what it takes to be recognised as a network at all
meta.phenomenon: Mycorrhizal symbiosis basics: hyphae, the arbuscular/ectomycorrhizal split, and what counts as evidence of connection rather than mere proximity

nodes.title: Trade agreements
nodes.description: Reading the plant-fungus carbon-for-nutrient exchange as a negotiated rate rather than a fixed act of generosity.
spec: you can state what each partner in an AM or ECM association gives and gets, in the form "X for Y"
you can describe one experimental method used to measure that exchange

meta.metaphor: Trade agreements — negotiated exchange with terms both sides can enforce
meta.phenomenon: Carbon-for-nutrient exchange in mycorrhizal mutualism, and biological market theory's account of how the exchange rate is set

nodes.title: Foreign aid
nodes.description: Separating what the mother-tree carbon-sharing experiments measured from what the popular retelling added to it.
spec: you can name the two tree species most associated with the mother-tree carbon-sharing story
you can state, separately, what the original experiments showed and what the popular retelling adds to it

meta.metaphor: Foreign aid — resources moved to a needy party without an immediate return
meta.phenomenon: Carbon transfer between connected plants through a shared mycorrhizal network, and the popular 'mother tree' account of that transfer

nodes.title: Espionage
nodes.description: Plants that draw carbon from a mycorrhizal network without ever paying into it, and whether the network has any way to notice.
spec: you can name one fully mycoheterotrophic plant genus and one plant group with only initial (seedling-stage) mycoheterotrophy
you can state what the fungus involved gets out of the relationship, if anything

meta.metaphor: Espionage — extracting value from a network while paying nothing into it
meta.phenomenon: Mycoheterotrophy: plants such as Monotropa uniflora and many orchid species that draw carbon from mycorrhizal fungi without photosynthesising any back

nodes.title: Sanctions and chemical warfare
nodes.description: Chemical suppression of rivals — allelopathy and antifungal defence — read against the negotiated exchanges of week 2.
spec: you can name one plant that produces a well-documented allelopathic compound, and one thing it suppresses
you can state what "mycorrhizosphere" refers to

meta.metaphor: Sanctions and chemical warfare — suppressing a rival rather than negotiating with it
meta.phenomenon: Allelopathy and antifungal secondary metabolites produced by ectomycorrhizal fungi, suppressing competing fungi and pathogens in the surrounding mycorrhizosphere

nodes.title: Double agents
nodes.description: The Field Dispatch Briefing — the same fungal partner as mutualist to one host and exploiter of another, and the mechanisms that keep this in check.
spec: you can name one factor that shifts a given fungal-plant pairing along the mutualism-parasitism continuum
you can bring a specific, citable case for your Field Dispatch draft, not a general claim about fungi "sometimes" behaving this way

meta.metaphor: Double agents — the same actor mutualist on one front, exploitative on another
meta.phenomenon: Context- and partner-dependent shifts along the mutualism-parasitism continuum in mycorrhizal fungi, and the partner-sanctioning mechanisms that keep this in check

nodes.title: Border disputes
nodes.description: Contested soil between fungal individuals, and the recognition systems that decide where one genet's growth stops and another's begins.
spec: you can define "genet" as distinct from "the fungal individual you can see above ground"
you can state one consequence of self/non-self recognition succeeding or failing at a contact zone

meta.metaphor: Border disputes — contested territory and the recognition of who holds it
meta.phenomenon: Root and mycelial territoriality: competition for substrate between fungal genets, and self/non-self recognition at contact zones

nodes.title: Refugee crises
nodes.description: Disturbance, displacement and resource reallocation in mycorrhizal communities after fire, drought or logging.
spec: you can name one specific disturbance type studied for its effect on mycorrhizal communities
you can state one difference in how the reading's example communities respond to that disturbance

meta.metaphor: Refugee crises — displacement and reallocation after a shock
meta.phenomenon: Shifts in mycorrhizal community composition and resource reallocation after fire, drought or logging disturbance

nodes.title: Arms races
nodes.description: Whether the sanctioning and cheating-detection mechanisms from weeks 2–6 can honestly be called an arms race on the evidence a semester can show.
spec: you can connect one week-4 or week-6 example to a plausible selective pressure it places on the fungal partner
you can state why "arms race" implies a timescale this course's evidence cannot directly show

meta.metaphor: Arms races — escalating measures and countermeasures between opposed interests
meta.phenomenon: Coevolution between exploitative strategies and the partner-choice and sanctioning mechanisms that oppose them

nodes.title: Cold war and détente
nodes.description: Hyphal fusion between compatible fungal individuals against rejection between incompatible ones — the closest this course's vocabulary gets to literal.
spec: you can state what a het locus does in one sentence
you can distinguish anastomosis from the contact-zone antagonism discussed in week 7

meta.metaphor: Cold war and détente — sustained non-aggression punctuated by rare, careful cooperation
meta.phenomenon: Vegetative incompatibility (het-locus recognition) preventing hyphal fusion between incompatible fungal genets, versus fusion between compatible ones

nodes.title: Treaties broken
nodes.description: The garlic mustard case — an invasive plant degrading a native mycorrhizal mutualism as a side effect of establishing itself.
spec: you can state what garlic mustard produces that is implicated in suppressing native AM fungi
you can name one downstream consequence for native plants that depend on those fungi

meta.metaphor: Treaties broken — an established arrangement destroyed by an outside actor
meta.phenomenon: Invasive plants disrupting native mycorrhizal mutualisms via allelochemicals — the case of garlic mustard (Alliaria petiolata) and native arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi

nodes.title: The peace conference
nodes.description: The closing Briefing — auditing every week's diplomatic label against the credentials test set in week 1, before the capstone is due.
spec: you can list, from memory, at least four of the eleven phenomena covered by week and pair each with its diplomatic label
you can state, for one label, the specific sentence where using it would have overclaimed something the biology does not support

meta.metaphor: The peace conference — the closing session where every side's account of the negotiation gets checked
meta.phenomenon: Synthesis of the semester's phenomena, and an explicit accounting of where the diplomatic frame sharpened observation versus where it substituted for one

nodes.title: Field Dispatch
nodes.description: A short, individual case study — take one documented fungal partner whose role shifts by host or context, and argue whether "double agent" survives contact with the evidence.
spec: submitted by the deadline, as a single markdown or PDF dispatch
names one specific, citable fungal-plant case, not a general claim about fungi "sometimes" switching role
states plainly which claims are measured and which are your own inference

nodes.title: The Peace Conference
nodes.description: The capstone — run the semester's own credentials-and-overclaiming audit against a mycorrhizal phenomenon of your choosing, in writing, alone.
spec: submitted by the deadline, in the format named below
names a real, citable mycorrhizal phenomenon and a diplomatic label for it
explicitly states where the label sharpens the biology and where it overclaims, using the week 1 credentials test as the standard

marking.description: The Peace Conference is judged as a whole against the brief, with particular weight on whether the biology is accurately represented, whether the diplomatic framing is defended rather than merely repeated, and whether the self-critique is genuine rather than a token closing paragraph.

course.title: Unfinished Thinking
course.description: Thinking that never gets to finish starts again. That is what a spiral is. This course builds the conditions under which one can close, outdoors, in silence, ten minutes at a time. Then it aims the same unreasonable rigour at what could go right.

course.title: Implementing SNOBOL4
course.description: A twelve-week compiler-construction studio built around a single 1962 language, SNOBOL4, and the backtracking pattern-matching engine that made it strange. You write the whole thing yourself, in OCaml, one incremental submission at a time.

nodes.title: Getting started
nodes.description: Toolchain setup, and a skeleton hand-rolled lexer that recognises integer literals — the smallest thing the course can call a running compiler
spec: your OCaml toolchain (an opam switch and dune) builds and runs
your lexer turns a string of digits into an integer-literal token
you can name, in one sentence, why SNOBOL4 needed a portable implementation strategy

nodes.title: Arithmetic expressions
nodes.description: Extending week 1's lexer to arithmetic, and parsing it with a small Pratt parser
spec: your lexer tokenizes +, -, *, / alongside integer literals, respecting the blank-sensitivity rule from this week's lecture
your parser builds an expression tree respecting precedence (* and / bind tighter than + and -) and left-associativity
you can parse and evaluate a small arithmetic expression such as 2 + 3 * 4 to the correct result

nodes.title: Assignment and a symbol table
nodes.description: Implementing assignment statements over a single flat symbol table — variables as SNOBOL4 actually has them, not as most languages have them
spec: your evaluator has a symbol table mapping names to values, built once, consulted at run time, with no lexical scoping

assignment statements (`subject = object`) update the symbol table — this course's subset keeps the classic `=` surface form rather than real SNOBOL4's blank-only notation, a deliberate simplification documented in `interpreter/README.md`
looking up a name that has never been assigned returns the null string rather than an error

nodes.title: Strings, concatenation, and a working evaluator
nodes.description: String literals and concatenation by juxtaposition, wiring weeks 1–4 into one evaluator that runs real toy SNOBOL-subset programs
spec: your lexer recognizes quoted string literals
your evaluator concatenates two blank-separated string-valued operands with no operator token, at lower precedence than arithmetic
a handful of small SNOBOL-subset programs (literals, arithmetic, assignment, concatenation) run end to end and produce the expected values

nodes.title: The goto field
nodes.description: Turning Movement I's evaluator into a statement executor — the goto field, failure propagation, and a couple of predicates to branch on
spec: a program is a sequence of labeled statements, executed by a program counter, not a single expression evaluated once
every statement produces success or failure, and a goto field (:S(label), :F(label), :S(label)F(label), or :(label)) determines the next statement to execute based on which
at least LT, LE, GT, GE, EQ, and NE exist as predicate primitives that succeed (producing the null string) or fail, with no value worth storing either way
a toy program using only assignment, predicates, and the goto field implements a counting loop with no if/while/for construct anywhere in its source

nodes.title: DEFINE, call frames, and RETURN/FRETURN/NRETURN
nodes.description: User-defined functions on top of last week's statement executor — call frames, save/restore, and recursion that needs no special case
spec: DEFINE(prototype, entry) registers a function's name, formal arguments, locals, and entry-point label in a function table
calling a defined function saves the function-name variable, all formals, and all locals, binds formals to argument values, and jumps to the entry label
reaching RETURN or NRETURN in a function body restores the saved values and produces success with the function-name variable's value; reaching FRETURN restores the saved values and produces failure
a recursive function (at least two levels deep) produces the correct result with no special-casing for the recursive call

nodes.title: Building the backtracking search
nodes.description: Literal, concatenation, and alternation as pattern values, matched against a subject with an explicit backtracking stack — or OCaml's own call stack, your choice
spec: your pattern type represents at least literal strings, concatenation, and alternation, and a pattern value can be built once, stored, and matched against more than one subject
your matcher advances a cursor over a subject string without ever mutating the subject, and restores the cursor exactly to where it was found whenever a match attempt fails

alternation retries — when one branch of a `|` fails, or something later in the pattern fails and forces backtracking into it, the matcher tries the untried branch rather than having committed to the first one that matched

you can point at the exact place in your code where a backtracking alternative is recorded and the exact place where it is resumed on failure, whether that is a push and pop on an explicit stack or a recursive call and its return

nodes.title: The primitives, not the search
nodes.description: Extending last week's matcher with ANY, NOTANY, SPAN, BREAK, ARB, ARBNO, and BAL — no change to how backtracking itself works
spec: LEN, ANY, NOTANY, SPAN, and BREAK match against a target character set or fixed length, correctly handling the null-match case for BREAK
ARB and ARBNO retry by growing one unit at a time on backtrack, reusing the same alternative-retry machinery week 7 built for `|`
BAL is implemented as a composition of NOTANY and ARBNO, not as a hand-written paren-counting special case
all seven primitives satisfy the same three-condition cursor contract from week 7 with no primitive-specific exception

nodes.title: Getting something back from a match
nodes.description: Wiring conditional and immediate assignment, @X, and the enumerate-all-matches idiom into last week's matcher
spec: a matched fragment can be captured into a variable with conditional assignment, and that capture is genuinely undone if backtracking later revises what the subpattern matched
immediate assignment sets a variable the instant its subpattern matches, and that assignment is not undone even if the overall match later fails
the cursor-position operator binds a variable to a position, not a substring, and does so immediately
a small program built on the enumerate-all-matches idiom (a repeated statement, a capture, and a trailing FAIL) finds every match of a pattern in a subject, not just the first

nodes.title: The exhaustiveness checker earns its keep
nodes.description: Widening the interpreter's value type to cover ARRAY and TABLE, and turning on the compiler warning that catches an unhandled case
spec: the value type has a constructor for arrays and a constructor for tables, alongside everything Movements I–III already needed
array indexing and out-of-bounds table/array lookups fail rather than raising an OCaml exception, consistent with every other failure this interpreter already produces
a table grows correctly when assigned an unseen key, and returns the same mutable object on every subsequent reference to that key
the project builds with exhaustiveness warnings promoted to errors, and every existing match over the value type still compiles clean

nodes.title: Making CSNOBOL4 disagree with you
nodes.description: Attaching source positions to every value your parser produces, and building a small differential-testing harness against CSNOBOL4
spec: every AST node your parser produces carries the source line (and, where practical, column) it came from
a syntax error names the specific token or position where parsing failed, not just "syntax error" with no location
at least one error case names a second, earlier location relevant to the mistake, not only the point of detection
a small script runs a set of programs through both your interpreter and CSNOBOL4 and reports any output the two disagree on

nodes.title: Finishing, not adding
nodes.description: The last studio before the final project is due — cutting scope, proving the extension actually works, and drafting the retrospective
spec: the chosen extension has at least one concrete test case that passes, not just a partial implementation in progress
any scope that won't be finished in time is named explicitly and cut, rather than left half-working and undocumented
the differential-testing harness from week 11 has been run against the extended interpreter at least once
a rough draft of the retrospective exists, naming what the extension cost and what it actually taught, before the session ends

nodes.description: The shortlisted painting, argued with every instrument the semester has built, the week the dossier is due.
spec: you have applied at least three distinct evidence types to the shortlisted painting and logged where they agreed and disagreed
your dossier is submitted by the end of this week

nodes.title: Model audit
nodes.description: Running Wren's stroke-level classifier against the semester's shortlist, then trying to break it.
spec: you can state what the classifier's training set actually contained, and one way that could bias its output
you have found at least one input that makes the classifier confidently wrong

nodes.title: The forger's own account
nodes.description: Reading Zhang Daqian's interviews and later scholarship on his forgeries in his own words, and in the words of the collectors he fooled.
spec: you can describe one Zhang Daqian forgery case in enough specific detail to explain what actually fooled the experts involved
you can state your own position on whether skilled forgery is a form of scholarship, with a reason

nodes.title: Reading the six as-ifs
nodes.description: A close, unhurried reading of the Diamond Sutra's closing gatha against Tang Yin's own choice of it as a name.
spec: you can explain what each of the six images in the gatha is doing, not just recite the list
you can state, in your own words, what changes about the course's central question if the gatha is taken seriously

nodes.title: Defenses
nodes.description: Ten-minute live defenses of the final project's verdict, questioned by the room, and the re-sort from week 1.
spec: you have defended your verdict live and answered at least one question that named a specific weakness in it
you have re-sorted week 1's six reproductions and can say what changed and why

nodes.title: Attribution note
nodes.description: A short, single-thread argument for or against one painting's attribution, built from materials and/or brushwork evidence alone.
spec: argues one specific, falsifiable attribution claim about one named painting
rests on materials and/or brushwork evidence only --- seals and colophons aren't taught until weeks 5--6, and using them here reads as skipping ahead rather than as extra rigour
names at least one piece of evidence that complicates its own conclusion, and says why it doesn't overturn it

nodes.title: The dossier
nodes.description: A full authentication dossier on one disputed painting, working every evidence type the semester has taught and logging where they disagree.
spec: works at least three distinct evidence types (materials, brushwork, seals, colophons, market context) against one named painting
keeps an explicit evidence log, including evidence that complicates or contradicts the eventual conclusion
reaches a stated verdict with a stated confidence level, not an open-ended "more research is needed"

nodes.title: Final project: verdict and defense
nodes.description: A full dossier on one painting of your choosing, defended live in the week-12 seminar against questions aimed at its weakest point.
spec: a full dossier, in the dossier assessment's format, on one painting -- from the semester's shortlist or your own reading
a stated verdict with a stated confidence level, and an explicit account of what evidence would change it
a ten-minute live defense in the week-12 seminar, answering at least one question that named a specific weakness in the argument

marking.description: Judged as a whole against the brief: whether the written dossier stands on its own for a reader who wasn't in the room, whether the stated verdict is proportionate to the evidence actually assembled rather than overclaimed or hedged into meaninglessness, and whether the live defense shows the verdict was actually understood rather than rehearsed. A dossier that reaches a confident, well-supported verdict and survives real questioning in the defense outperforms one that hedges everywhere to avoid ever being wrong.

course.title: The Perfect Apology
course.description: A postgraduate seminar on why apologies succeed or fail. Students diagnose real apologies for their components, motives, timing and power, then design and defend responses of their own, building toward what a perfect apology would even mean.

nodes.title: Component Teardown
nodes.description: Tag which of the four apology components are present, absent, or hollow in a real apology
spec: you bring one apology — yours, one you received, or a public one — that you have not yet marked up
you can point to where each of the four components is present, weak, or missing in it, quoting the exact words that do the work
you can name one component that looks included but isn't doing anything

quiz.question: Which four components does the lab ask you to identify in an apology?
options: Acknowledgment, responsibility, regret, remedy
Apology, excuse, promise, sorry
Cause, blame, guilt, punishment
Greeting, context, apology, farewell

quiz.question: What does it mean for a component to be 'present but hollow'?
options: It's missing entirely
It appears in the wording but isn't doing any real work
It's the strongest part of the apology
It was added after the fact

quiz.question: If a partner's apology has every component clearly present with nothing to flag as hollow, what should you do?
options: Manufacture a doubt anyway, so you have something to report
Say which component came closest to feeling redundant with another, and what would collapse them
Report that the apology is perfect and move on
Reject the apology as too good to be real

nodes.title: The Ablation Test
nodes.description: Remove one component at a time from a working apology and identify which removal actually breaks it
spec: you bring the apology you marked up in Session 1 (or a new one, marked up the same way)
you can show which component's removal breaks your apology, and which removal barely changes it
you can explain why a component that broke your apology might not break someone else's

quiz.question: What does the ablation test involve?
options: Removing one component at a time and rereading what's left
Adding new components to strengthen an apology
Comparing two completely unrelated apologies
Timing how long an apology takes to deliver

quiz.question: If removing every component damages the apology by roughly the same amount, what should you do?
options: Force a single 'winner' component anyway
Report that the apology has no single load-bearing part — a real, reportable finding
Discard the apology as invalid
Assume you made a mistake and redo the test

quiz.question: If two pairs' apologies disagree about which component is load-bearing, what's the right response?
options: Ignore the disagreement
Pick whichever pair argued more confidently
Write down what was different about the two situations that made a different component critical
Average the two results

nodes.title: Spot the Non-Apology
nodes.description: Sort a set of real "apologies" into genuine vs. non-apology and name the specific deflection each one uses
spec: you bring, or are assigned, three non-apologies that fail for different structural reasons
for each, you can name the exact function that's hollow or missing and show the ablation test that proves it
you can produce a minimal repair of one non-apology that fixes only the broken function and changes nothing else

quiz.question: What is the goal of the minimal repair exercise?
options: Rewrite the whole apology into a polished version
Fix only the one broken function with the smallest possible edit
Add a remedy no matter what was actually broken
Replace vague words with different vague words

quiz.question: If your minimal repair still doesn't read as a working apology, what should you check first?
options: Whether you actually diagnosed the right function
Whether the sentence is long enough
Whether the recipient will accept it
Whether it sounds more polite now

quiz.question: Which of these counts as a specific, checkable finding from running the ablation test on a non-apology?
options: The 'if,' the missing agent, or the redirected object — naming the exact word or clause doing the damage
A general feeling that it sounds fake
The length of the apology
Whether it was said out loud or in writing

nodes.title: Who Does This Serve?
nodes.description: Diagnose which of four functions — repair, self-protection, reputation management, closure — a real apology's wording actually serves
spec: you analyse two apologies responding to comparable incidents — your own examples or ones brought to the session
for each, you can name which function or functions the apology's structure serves, using evidence in the wording, timing, or context — not a guess about private feeling
for at least one, you can state what would have to be true of the wording for repair to be its primary function, and whether that is actually present

quiz.question: Which four functions can an apology's actual wording serve, per the lecture?
options: Repair, self-protection, reputation management, closure
Truth, justice, mercy, peace
Speed, cost, length, tone
Apology, excuse, denial, silence

quiz.question: What counts as valid evidence for which function an apology serves?
options: A guess about the speaker's private feelings
A specific phrase, a publication timing relative to other events, or a concession that cost the speaker something
How sincere it sounds when read aloud
Whether the speaker appeared to cry

quiz.question: If an apology seems to serve two or three functions about equally, what should you do?
options: Pick whichever function your evidence best supports
Say so directly, rather than forcing a single dominant function
Assume it must be a non-apology
Ignore the ambiguous case

nodes.title: One Apology, Two Audiences
nodes.description: Draft a private and a public version of the same apology and identify exactly what has to change between them
spec: you bring a real public apology statement, or use one provided
line by line, you can say whether each line functions for the harmed party, for observers, or both, with evidence for the call
you produce a rewritten version that prioritises the harmed party over observers, and can name what it costs in public accountability

quiz.question: In the line-by-line analysis, who might a given line be built to serve?
options: The harmed party specifically, observers who weren't harmed, or genuinely both
Only the speaker's lawyer
Only search engines
Only future employees

quiz.question: When you rewrite the apology to prioritise the harmed party, what should you explicitly say afterward?
options: How much shorter the new version is
What the rewrite gives up — what an observer can no longer judge or be reassured about
Whether the new version rhymes
Nothing — the rewrite needs no further comment

quiz.question: If a line seems to serve the harmed party and observers equally well, what should you check?
options: Assume it's a coincidence and move on
Whether it satisfies both by genuine specificity, or is simply vague enough for each audience to read in what they need
Whether the line is grammatically correct
Whether the audience noticed at all

nodes.title: Same Words, Different Clock
nodes.description: Test how delaying delivery or switching medium changes what an otherwise-identical apology means
spec: you produce two versions of one apology that differ only in timing or medium, holding the wording mostly constant
for each pair, you can name what the recipient gains and loses under each version — the ability to reread, ask a follow-up, respond on their own schedule, or read tone in the moment
you can say whether one version reads as more effective in your case, and show that the difference comes from timing or medium, not wording

quiz.question: In the timing-pair exercise, how many extra sentences are you allowed to add to the delayed version?
options: None
Exactly one, showing what the delay was actually used for
As many as needed to explain the delay
A full paragraph

quiz.question: What should you check before concluding a difference between two versions came from timing or medium?
options: That the wording actually held constant between the two versions
That both versions are the same length
That the recipient liked one version better
Nothing further is needed

quiz.question: In the medium-pair exercise, what might a face-to-face version show that a text message can't?
options: A pause, a raised voice, or a straight face — stage directions
The exact time it was sent
A spelling correction
Whether it was proofread

nodes.title: Who's Expected to Go First
nodes.description: Map a scenario's power relationships to work out who is obligated to apologise and who is excused
spec: you construct, or are given, two structurally similar incidents that differ mainly in the relative power of the person who caused the harm
for each pair, you can say whether the obligation to apologise actually changes with power, or only the likelihood or form of the apology changes, and defend which
you can point to a concrete signal — timing, channel, whether a personal response happens at all — that shows power at work, without claiming the more powerful person could never have apologised

quiz.question: What should stay held constant between the two incidents you construct?
options: The identities of both people involved
The kind of mistake — only the direction of the power relationship should change
The public platform used to respond
The apology's length

quiz.question: What evidence does the lab ask you to use for whether power changes the obligation to apologise?
options: Whether a personal response happens at all, how quickly, and through what channel
How famous the person is
How much money is involved
Public opinion polls

quiz.question: What does the lab say about a senior person who never personally responds?
options: They have definitely lost the obligation to apologise
They may simply have avoided the obligation at low cost to themselves, not lost it
They can no longer be held responsible at all
It proves power has no effect on obligation

nodes.title: Forgiveness on Whose Terms
nodes.description: Analyse a case where accepting an apology is coerced, withheld, or used as leverage
spec: you are given (or construct) several different recipient responses to one identical apology

for each, you can classify it among hearing, acknowledgment, acceptance, forgiveness, reconciliation, repair, and closure, and defend at least one classification against a partner's alternative reading
you can identify whether any response amounts to a demand no apology could satisfy, and say what you think is actually being asked for instead

quiz.question: Which seven terms does the lab ask you to sort recipient responses against?
options: Hearing, acknowledgment, acceptance, forgiveness, reconciliation, repair, closure
Sorry, guilty, angry, sad, relieved, calm, done
First, second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh
Legal, moral, social, personal, public, private, professional

quiz.question: Can more than one of the seven terms apply to the same recipient response?
options: No, each response gets exactly one term
Yes — that's expected, not a sign you've done it wrong
Only for responses given in public
Only if the whole group agrees unanimously

quiz.question: For a recipient response that keeps shifting its objection no matter how the apology is revised, what should you consider?
options: That it's always a legitimate standard not yet met
That it may be a demand no apology could satisfy — and asking what's actually being requested instead
That the apology must be poorly worded
That the recipient is lying

nodes.title: Words vs. Actions
nodes.description: Design a concrete repair action for a harm that no apology alone would fix
spec: you are given (or bring) an apology that is linguistically adequate by every earlier week's standard, attached to a harm that was never actually repaired
you design at least three distinct repair actions and can say exactly which of restitution, behaviour change, structural repair, or prevention of recurrence each one targets
you can say what the apology's own wording already promised, and which of your proposed actions were owed by that wording versus additional to it

quiz.question: What four outcomes can a proposed repair action target?
options: Restitution, behaviour change, structural repair, prevention of recurrence
Apology, excuse, promise, silence
Speed, cost, visibility, sincerity
Guilt, shame, regret, relief

quiz.question: In this lab, are you allowed to rewrite the apology's wording again?
options: Yes, rewriting the wording is the main task
No — the wording is already adequate; the task is designing repair actions
Only if the wording is grammatically incorrect
Only the closing line may be changed

quiz.question: If an apology's own wording already promised an action (e.g. 'we'll make sure of it'), how should that action be classified?
options: As something extra you're generously adding
As something already owed and unpaid, not a new addition
As irrelevant to the repair plan
As proof the apology was insincere

nodes.title: Should You Even Apologise?
nodes.description: Argue for silence or deferral as the responsible move in a scenario built to tempt a premature apology
spec: for each of three ambiguous cases, you choose one of apologise now, acknowledge harm without a full apology, investigate first, act first, or delay, and defend that choice against the other four
you can name a concrete cost of your chosen option, not only its benefit — every option gives something up
for at least one case, you can say whether the delay you're proposing would produce genuine new understanding or would just protect the responsible party while the harmed party waits

quiz.question: Which five response types does the lab ask you to choose between for each case?
options: Apologise now, acknowledge harm without a full apology, investigate first, act first, delay
Deny, minimise, blame, ignore, escalate
Cry, argue, leave, wait, forget
Sue, settle, apologise, resign, retire

quiz.question: What must every chosen response also name, per the lab?
options: A concrete cost of that option, not only its benefit
The exact time of day it should happen
A witness to confirm it happened
A law that requires it

quiz.question: What test should you apply to a proposed delay?
options: Whether it's long enough to seem sincere
Whether the delay would produce genuine new understanding, or just leave the harmed party waiting
Whether it avoids embarrassment
Whether it matches company policy

nodes.title: Apology Autopsy
nodes.description: Diagnose a real public apology using the component model, then redesign it into one that would actually work
spec: a real public apology, not one studied in class, cited with a link or a full quotation
a component-by-component diagnosis naming what is present, absent, or hollow, and which component this specific apology depends on
a redesigned version of the apology, plus a short note on exactly what each change repairs

criteria.name: Diagnostic accuracy against the component model

nodes.title: The Constrained Apology
nodes.description: Given a scenario with real constraints, decide whether, when, and how to respond — and defend every decision against the alternatives you rejected
spec: one scenario, chosen from the three below, with its constraints kept intact rather than simplified away
a decision on whether, when, and how to respond, using this course's vocabulary — apologise now, acknowledge harm without a full apology, investigate first, act first, or delay
a justification that names what your decision costs, not only what it achieves, and explicitly rules out at least two of the other options
the designed response itself, in the form it would actually take — a message, a statement, a script — matching the audience, timing, and medium you argued for

criteria.name: Quality of the justification against the stated constraints

nodes.title: Final Project: Reconsidering "Perfect"
nodes.description: A full apology-design report on a complex harm, closing with an argued answer to what "perfect" turned out to mean, against your own Week 1 definition
spec: a harm scenario of real complexity, either your Constrained Apology scenario carried into its aftermath or a new one of comparable weight
a full diagnosis using the semester's framework — components and their function, audience, timing and medium, power, and what repair the harm would actually require
an argued decision on whether, when, and how a response happens, and an explicit account of what "perfect" means for this specific case
your own Week 1 one-sentence definition of apology, quoted, alongside a direct argument for what it missed

marking.description: Judged as a whole against whether it earns its own reconsideration of "perfect" — not against a checklist of concepts mentioned. A report that cites every week's terminology but never actually revises its Week 1 definition has not done the thing this project asks for.

nodes.title: What Is an Apology, Actually?
nodes.description: Apology defined against its nearest neighbours — regret, excuse, and justification — using four ordinary "sorry" messages that are not all doing the same job
spec: you bring one real "sorry" you've received or sent — a text, an email, or something you can quote from memory — that felt off in some way
you can say which of regret, excuse, justification, or apology it actually was, and defend the call against a partner's objection
you leave with a one-sentence definition of apology you're willing to put your name to

nodes.title: Taking an Apology Apart
nodes.description: A public apology gets marked up line by line into four separable components, and the marking reveals how few of them most apologies actually contain

nodes.title: The Parts That Do the Work
nodes.description: Two apologies, two different components turn out to be doing the work — an ablation test replaces the hunt for one universal hierarchy

nodes.title: The Non-Apology
nodes.description: Four statements that sound like apologies fail for four different structural reasons — a checklist of bad phrases would miss all of them

nodes.title: Whose Apology Is It?
nodes.description: Four things an apology can accomplish for the speaker, and a test for telling them apart that doesn't require reading anyone's mind

nodes.title: Public and Private Don't Apologise the Same Way
nodes.description: The same incident, two apologies — one specific and private, one vague and public — and neither wording choice is simply better

nodes.title: Timing and Medium Change the Words
nodes.description: The same sentence, sent two minutes after an argument and again three weeks later — identical wording, and only one of them is doing anything

nodes.title: Who Has to Apologise?
nodes.description: Two colleagues, two mistakes, and only one of them produces a fast, personal apology — the difference is who can afford to let it sit

nodes.title: Who Gets to Accept It?
nodes.description: A friend says "I hear you, thanks for saying that" and keeps their distance for months — which of seven different things just happened?

nodes.title: Saying Sorry Is Not Repairing Harm
nodes.description: A courier apologises well, refunds the loss, and does nothing about the depot process that caused it — three months later, the same thing happens again

nodes.title: When Not to Apologise
nodes.description: A team lead says "sorry if anyone was affected by my decision" within the hour — before anyone knows what decision, or whether it was theirs

nodes.title: Can a Perfect Apology Exist?
nodes.description: One sentence, evaluated eight different ways as a single variable changes each time — audience, timing, power, and what happens after
spec: you return to the message you brought in Week 1 and the one-sentence definition of apology your pair wrote that week

you produce a full analysis of that same message using the semester's tools — components and their function, whether it's a non-apology, what function it likely serves, how audience, timing, medium, and power shape it, and what repair it would actually require
you write a specific comparison of what your Week 1 definition and verdict missed or got wrong, quoting your own Week 1 words against your Week 12 analysis

nodes.title: Idris Fenn
nodes.description: A tutor teaching the weeks that stress-test an apology once it exists — its components, its audience, its power, and what happens after it.

nodes.title: Policies and support
