course.title: Advanced Involution
course.description: A doctoral seminar on involution: the discipline of increasing effort for decreasing returns, from Geertz's rice paddies to hustle-culture LinkedIn posts — taught by a syllabus that keeps escalating.

nodes.title: Seminar: Naming Your Own Involution
nodes.description: The opening session — find one place in your own life where effort has been rising while the result hasn't, and bring it
spec: you can describe one real instance of your own effort rising without a matching result
you can say, roughly, since when
you have Geertz's definition well enough to tell involution apart from ordinary hard work

nodes.title: Crit: First Review
nodes.description: The second session — the instance you named in week 1 meets a skeptical room for the first time
spec: the instance named in week 1 demonstrates continued validity under adversarial questioning, not just author confidence
you can situate one pre-2020 precedent within the same analytic frame

nodes.title: Crit: Spot the Involution
nodes.description: Bring one system you're part of and argue, to a skeptical room, whether it's involuted or just competitive
spec: you can distinguish involution from ordinary competition using Geertz's test, not just a feeling
you can name what a win would look like in the system you picked, and whether anyone is getting closer to it

nodes.title: Crit: Your Resume, Annotated
nodes.description: Bring a resume — yours, a friend's, or a fictional one — and annotate every line that exists to compete rather than to inform
spec: every annotated line identifies the specific competitive signal it is optimised to send, not merely its stated content
you can identify at least one "value-add" line that would disappear entirely if competitive pressure were removed

nodes.title: Seminar: Confess Your Overtime
nodes.description: A closed-room session benchmarking self-reported hours against verifiable output — separating activity from impact
spec: you can decompose one week of your own hours into impact hours versus visibility hours
you can forecast the delta in your own workload under a zero-visibility counterfactual

nodes.title: Crit: Auto-Ethnographies
nodes.description: Assignment 1 is due this week — a short session to present the instance you've been tracking since week 1, before it's marked
spec: you can present your instance and its mechanism in under two minutes
you can name the one piece of evidence you're least sure holds up

nodes.title: Crit: Engagement Farming
nodes.description: Take one account, feed, or creator and run a growth-loop audit to diagnose whether their posting behaviour is involuted, and by whose metric
spec: you can name the specific north-star metric your subject's growth loop appears to be optimising for
you can specify the falsification criteria that would overturn your diagnosis

nodes.title: Crit: Grade Your Own Syllabus
nodes.description: A continuous-improvement review of the course's own KPIs — does this syllabus show evidence of impact commensurate with its workload, or merely evidence of activity?
spec: you apply Geertz's test as an internal audit instrument against this course's own deliverables, not solely against an external case study
you can produce a defensible retention/discontinuation recommendation naming one component with evidence of impact and one without

nodes.title: Crit: Lying Flat, Discussed
nodes.description: Three ways of opting out, weighed against what each one actually costs
spec: name one real cost of the exit you're defending
say what happens if everyone does it at once

nodes.title: Crit: Three Case Studies
nodes.description: Compare involution across three unrelated domains and test, carefully, whether they share one mechanism or only a resemblance
spec: you compare at least two of K-pop trainee systems, standardised-test admissions, or housing markets against one named mechanism, applied consistently
you can say what would falsify "these are the same thing"

nodes.title: Studio: Design an Intervention
nodes.description: Workshop a real or speculative fix to one zero-sum system from the semester, ahead of committing to it for the final project
spec: your intervention targets the mechanism, not just one symptom of it
you can say who loses if your intervention works, and whether that's acceptable

nodes.title: Final Crit
nodes.description: Present your intervention to the room and face the same test the course opened with
spec: you present the mechanism your intervention targets, not just its surface fix
you answer the room's hardest question live, not by pointing back at the write-up

nodes.title: Auto-Ethnography of Your Own Involution
nodes.description: Document and analyse one real instance of your own effort rising while your progress didn't, using the semester's own vocabulary to name why
spec: submitted by the deadline, in the format named below
the instance is something you actually did, with dates or evidence a reader could check
the analysis names which weeks 1-5 mechanism is operating, not just that "it felt like a lot of effort for nothing"
the work is yours, with any assistance declared

criteria.name: The instance is real and specific, not hypothetical
The analysis names the mechanism, not just the feeling

nodes.title: Intervention Design: Breaking the Loop
nodes.description: Design a real or speculative intervention into a zero-sum system from the semester, and defend that it changes the mechanism rather than the paint
spec: submitted by the deadline, in the format named below
it stands on its own, without you there to explain it
it names the mechanism it targets and the system it's drawn from
it says who loses if the intervention works, and whether that's acceptable

marking.description: The final project is judged as a whole against the brief, with particular attention to whether the intervention targets the mechanism identified in weeks 1-10 rather than one of its symptoms, and whether it honestly names who bears any cost of it working.

nodes.title: Involution 101: Geertz's Rice Paddies
nodes.description: Where the term comes from — agricultural intensification that adds labour without adding yield — and why it outlived the paddies

nodes.title: Diminishing Returns Before It Was Cool
nodes.description: Involution had a life before the internet — in peasant economies, guild ladders, and the slow inflation of "entry level"

course.title: Chain of Custody: Content Forensics for the Synthetic Age
course.description: A graduate methods course in detecting, verifying and tracing AI-generated text, images, video and audio. Every claim online is treated as a case that deserves a chain of custody, not a hunch.

nodes.title: Scene of the crime
nodes.description: The first casework session — establishing the difference between a hunch and evidence, before you're given any tools to tell them apart
spec: you have brought one piece of content you suspect is synthetic, with no proof required yet
you can state, out loud, the difference between your hunch about it and actual evidence for it

nodes.title: Your first SIFT
nodes.description: Running the four SIFT moves on a real, currently-circulating claim, in order, without skipping ahead
spec: you have run the four SIFT moves, in order, on a claim you did not already know the answer to
you can point to the original source the claim traces back to, or explain precisely why you couldn't find one

nodes.title: The text workup
nodes.description: Applying independent textual checks to the same passage, and reconciling it when they disagree
spec: your Assignment 1 submission is in, applying at least two independent textual checks to the same passage
you can defend your verdict to a classmate who was assigned to disagree with it

nodes.title: The image workup
nodes.description: Running a reverse image search and an automated detector on the same image, and taking their disagreement seriously
spec: you have run a reverse image search and one automated detector on the same image
you can state, specifically, where the two methods agreed and where they didn't

nodes.title: The video workup
nodes.description: Working out which of this week's checks you can actually apply to a short clip, and which you can't
spec: you have reviewed a short clip and listed which checks from this week you could actually apply to it, and which you couldn't

nodes.title: Watermark hunting
nodes.description: Embedding a watermark, then trying to destroy it through nothing more hostile than ordinary handling
spec: you have embedded a watermark in a sample file and attempted to destroy it through screenshotting, recompression and cropping
you can state in one sentence what a watermark surviving that process would and wouldn't prove

nodes.title: The full workup
nodes.description: Combining independent methods from weeks 3 to 7 into one report on a mixed-media case, with a confidence level the evidence actually earns
spec: your Assignment 2 report combines at least three independent methods from weeks 3–7 on a mixed-media case
your stated confidence level matches the strength of the evidence you actually gathered, not the strength of your suspicion

nodes.title: Breaking a detector
nodes.description: Trying to make your own content evade a detector, and taking your success or failure seriously as evidence
spec: you have attempted to make a piece of content evade at least one detector, and documented what worked
you can explain what your result implies about that detector's real-world reliability, not just about your own cleverness

nodes.title: The office file
nodes.description: Reviewing a sample workplace document for workslop indicators without assuming bad faith on the part of whoever wrote it
spec: you have reviewed a sample workplace document for workslop indicators without assuming bad faith on the part of its author
you can separate "this document doesn't do the job" from "this person is lazy or dishonest"

nodes.title: Drafting a policy
nodes.description: Writing one clause of a synthetic-media disclosure policy that handles a case the real-world example didn't
spec: you have written one clause of a synthetic-media disclosure policy that handles a case this week's real-world example policy did not

nodes.title: Cross-examination

spec: your Assignment 3 submission argues both sides of the assigned provenance dispute before reaching a verdict
your final verdict states explicitly what evidence would have changed it

nodes.title: The Slop Report
nodes.description: Final case presentations, and the submission of a full independent investigation
spec: you can present your investigation to the class in under five minutes
your final report would be legible to someone who was not in this course

nodes.title: Assignment 3: Cross-Examination
nodes.description: Arguing both sides of a real provenance dispute before you're allowed to reach a verdict
spec: submitted by the deadline as a paired dossier plus a verdict
argues both assigned sides of the dispute before reaching a verdict
states explicitly what evidence would have changed the verdict

nodes.title: Assignment 1: First Forensics
nodes.description: A single passage of text, two independent checks, and a verdict you can defend to someone assigned to disagree with you
spec: submitted by the deadline as a short written workup
applies at least two independent textual checks to the same passage
states a confidence level that matches the evidence actually presented

marking.description: Marked as one piece of work rather than a checklist — whether at least two genuinely independent checks were applied rather than two versions of the same check, whether the write-up would let a stranger retrace the reasoning, and whether the stated confidence matches the evidence actually gathered rather than the strength of the initial hunch.

nodes.title: Assignment 2: The Full Workup

nodes.title: Assignment 4: The Slop Report

course.title: Wrong in Public
course.description: A mistranslation is not a failure to be corrected. It is the only visible seam in a system that is otherwise invisible. Twelve weeks reconstructing the machines that made the errors we read in public.

nodes.title: First specimen
nodes.description: The opening bench — everyone puts one artefact on the table and learns what a provenance record has to contain before anyone argues about meaning
spec: you have one artefact, photographed or transcribed, that you can show in under a minute
you can say where it was and when you recorded it
you can say which verification level it sits at, and why it is not the level above

meta.leaves: a provenance record in the shared corpus

nodes.title: Reconstruct the entry
nodes.description: Three outputs, one dictionary — working backwards from what a lookup table printed to what it must have contained
spec: you have written a dictionary entry that would produce the output you were given
you can name one output your reconstructed entry does not explain
you have said which of your evidence is the artefact and which is your inference

meta.leaves: a dictionary entry someone else can break

nodes.title: Trace it back
nodes.description: The field's most repeated anecdote, chased through its citations until they stop — and a written record of where they stopped
spec: you have a written citation chain for the story, in order, with dates
you have marked the point where the chain stops resolving
you can name what would count as a primary source, whether or not one exists

meta.leaves: a written record of where the chain stopped

nodes.title: Find the seam
nodes.description: Locating the phrase boundary inside an error that reads fluently for six words and then does not
spec: you have marked where in the output the source stopped being followed
you have a dated estimate of when the artefact was produced, with your reasoning
you have said what a lookup-table explanation cannot account for here

meta.leaves: a dated estimate and the reasoning behind it

nodes.title: Starve it
nodes.description: Feeding a neural system input it has nothing for, and recording what it produces instead of nothing
spec: you have a log of inputs and outputs with the system, direction and date recorded
you can point at an output that is fluent and has no relationship to its input
you have said what your log does not establish

meta.leaves: a dated log of what a system invents

nodes.title: Field week
nodes.description: No lecture — the collection protocol, and then the room empties and everyone goes out and uses it
spec: you can state the protocol from memory before you leave the room
you have five candidate locations and know which one you will not photograph
your notebook has a place for the date and it is filled in before you get home

meta.leaves: four specimens and a notebook filled in at the scene

nodes.title: Read the standard against the sign
nodes.description: A national signage standard on one side of the table, a sign that ignores it on the other, and the question of who is answerable
spec: you have the clause and the sign side by side and can quote both
you can say who was obliged by the clause and who actually made the sign
you can name the workflow step where the two came apart

meta.leaves: the workflow step where the two parted

nodes.title: Annotate, then remove
nodes.description: Subtitling a clip with everything a fansub would keep, then stripping it back to what a commercial release would allow
spec: you have two versions of the same forty seconds, annotated and clean
you can name one thing the clean version cannot recover
you have said who each version is for

meta.leaves: two subtitle tracks and an account of what the clean one lost

nodes.title: What stays out of the exhibit
nodes.description: The bench where the course decides, out loud, which specimens it is not willing to display and why
spec: you have named one specimen in the shared corpus you think should not be exhibited
you have given a reason that is not "it is offensive"
you have heard the counter-argument and said whether it moved you

meta.leaves: a list of what stays out, with reasons

nodes.title: Round trip
nodes.description: Making errors on purpose under controlled conditions, and finding the point where a chain of translations stops changing
spec: you have a numbered log of every hop, with the system and date at each one
you can identify the iteration at which the text stopped moving
you can say what the fixed point tells you and what it does not

meta.leaves: a numbered log and the iteration it settled at

nodes.title: Try the method on something fluent
nodes.description: The last working bench — running the semester's reconstruction on output that no longer looks wrong, and recording how far it gets
spec: you have attempted a reconstruction from fluent output and written down where it failed
you can say what evidence you would have needed
you can say whether that evidence exists anywhere you could reach

meta.leaves: the exact sentence where the method stops working

nodes.title: The exhibit
nodes.description: No lecture — the room becomes the display, and every card on the wall carries the provenance the semester has been arguing about
spec: every card on your wall carries source, date and verification level
your wall text says what you left out and why
you can walk a stranger through it in four minutes without defending it

meta.leaves: a wall a stranger can read without me

nodes.title: Bench contribution
nodes.description: The mark for the room — arriving with something on the table, and taking somebody else's record apart in a way they can use
spec: you arrive with an artefact at benches where the brief asks for one
you have challenged at least one other person's verification level, on the record
you have revised one of your own after being challenged

marking.description: Marked across the twelve benches as a whole rather than week by week. The question is whether the room worked better because you were in it: did you arrive with an artefact, did you challenge a verification level that deserved challenging, and did you change your own record when somebody challenged yours.

nodes.title: Specimen log
nodes.description: One artefact a week, recorded to a standard someone else could re-check, and a mechanism you are willing to be wrong about in writing
spec: eleven entries, one per teaching week, each with source, date and verification level
every mechanism attribution is marked as an inference and not as an observation
at least one entry revises an earlier entry, and says what changed

marking.description: The log is marked on the quality of its records rather than the interest of its finds. A dull specimen recorded so that a stranger could verify it beats a spectacular one that cannot be traced, and a log that revises an earlier verification level upward or downward is doing the thing this course is for.

nodes.title: The exhibit
nodes.description: The corpus curated for someone who was not in the room, with the exclusions documented alongside what made it onto the wall

the exhibit documents what was excluded and why

course.title: HEX ARAM: The Hand You're Dealt
course.description: Playing well with a hand you did not choose. Twelve weeks on decision-making, adaptation and design inside HEX ARAM, where you cannot pick your champion, cannot retreat, and cannot avoid the fight. Offered as SLOP4223 and SLOP8223.
learningOutcomes: Evaluate a randomly assigned champion against the needs of a specific game rather than a fixed build identity
Assess rerolls, augments and items as contextual trade-offs rather than isolated rankings
Identify the functional strengths, weaknesses and win conditions of a composition nobody drafted
Analyse positioning, engagement timing, death timing and tempo inside a single-lane environment
Revise a plan when enemy builds, augments, threats or game state invalidate its assumptions
Distinguish optimisation within the mode from the design decisions that shaped the mode

nodes.title: Assignment 1: One roll, explained
nodes.description: A champion, a reroll state, three augment tiers and an opening item, none of them chosen by you — account for what you did with them
spec: a decision is recorded for the roll, the reroll, each augment tier and the opening item
every decision names the alternative it beat and what it gave up
the account still stands if the game was lost

criteria.name: Use of evidence (game state, patch, data)

nodes.title: Assignment 2: Read the Game
nodes.description: Both team compositions and one frozen mid-game state — name the win condition, the threat, and what you would change about how you are playing
spec: our win condition and their primary threat are each named in one sentence
positioning, item adaptation and death timing are argued from the state given, not from general principle
at least one claim is tested against match or patch data

criteria.name: Use of evidence (game state, patch, data)

nodes.title: Final: One Game, Twelve Decisions
nodes.description: One game from champion roll to nexus, stopped twelve times — decide at each stop, then write the post-game analysis
spec: a decision is recorded at each of the twelve stops
the post-game analysis names the single decision that most moved the win probability, and argues why
the account keeps decision quality and outcome apart

criteria.name: Use of evidence (game state, patch, data)

nodes.title: Mapping the hotspots
nodes.description: Turning raw collision counts into a defensible hotspot ranking — and watching that ranking change once traffic and road length are accounted for.
spec: you can count recorded collisions by road and produce a first ranking
you can join a road dataset and calculate counts per kilometre and rates per million vehicle-kilometres
you can state an explicit hotspot definition and apply it consistently
you can challenge another pair's hotspot definition using traffic exposure and reporting coverage
you can explain which conclusion changed between your first and revised ranking, and why

nodes.title: Modelling impact
nodes.description: A short introductory recap of the physics, then a calculator-only session turning speed, mass and two constant assumptions into numbers you can plot.
spec: you can convert the scenario speeds to metres per second and calculate kinetic energy
you can calculate reaction distance, braking distance and total stopping distance for each speed
you can produce a graph of speed against energy and against stopping distance
you can explain how changing one assumption changes the result

nodes.title: The Visibility Budget
nodes.description: Calculating distance margins for four invented scenarios, then testing what a written scene description can and can't tell you about detection.
spec: you can calculate stopping distance and distance margin for a stated scenario
you can isolate the effect of a single changed input by comparing two scenarios that differ in only that input
you can name a factor that could make an animal harder to detect, from a described roadside scene
you can state one limitation of a distance-margin calculation built on an assumed detection distance

nodes.title: The Vendor Demo Tribunal
nodes.description: Cross-examining three fictional wildlife-safety specification cards — classifying their real function, calculating their real performance, and deciding what evidence would actually justify a recommendation.
spec: you can classify a described safety technology as detection, warning, automatic braking or impact protection
you can calculate a detection rate, false negative rate and false positive rate from a stated trial table, with the correct denominator for each
you can propose a fair test for a technology claim, or state that the evidence supplied is insufficient

nodes.title: Designing the road
nodes.description: Matching three real road profiles from this unit's dataset to an engineering measure, then defending that choice against a complication.
spec: you can match a candidate hotspot to an appropriate intervention type and state why, using the evidence and cost tables from the lecture
you can name a case where engineering alone can't close the gap, and what changed your recommendation when it was raised

nodes.title: Who pays
nodes.description: Working through three fictional strike scenarios to determine who plausibly pays, and on what basis.
spec: you can state how fault is typically assessed in a wildlife-strike claim, citing the specific clause or standard that applies
you can explain why a rental agreement treats a strike differently from an owned-vehicle policy

nodes.title: After the collision
nodes.description: A desk-based tabletop exercise working through three roadside scenarios — no animal contact, no real roadside activity.
spec: you can list what an untrained bystander should and shouldn't attempt at a strike scene, and why the boundary sits where it does
you can state what information a driver should give when contacting a rescue service, and to whom

nodes.title: Briefing a tourist
nodes.description: Drafting a one-page risk briefing, then watching someone unfamiliar with it read it cold and revising on the spot.
spec: your briefing survives being read by someone with no prior context
you can name one common warning pattern that overstates the risk, and what a calibrated version of it would say instead

nodes.title: Learning from elsewhere
nodes.description: A debate exercise arguing whether specific overseas findings can be imported, adapted, or set aside for lack of local evidence.
spec: you can apply the five transfer questions to a specific claim and reach a defensible verdict, even if your group disagrees with another group's verdict on the same claim
you can state what additional evidence would change your verdict

nodes.title: Presenting the intervention
nodes.description: A proposal defence clinic — talk through your draft with peers and a fictional review panel before the real submission deadline.
spec: you can state your proposal's single primary intervention, at least three evidence strands, and its evaluation plan in about three minutes
you can identify at least one gap in a peer's proposal using the feedback prompt questions

nodes.title: Literature review and hotspot analysis
nodes.description: A critical review of the wildlife-vehicle collision literature, paired with your own hotspot analysis of a dataset from weeks 1 through 6.
spec: submitted by the deadline, as a single document with the analysis code or workbook attached
the literature review does more than summarise — it identifies where sources disagree, and says why
the hotspot analysis states its exposure adjustment and defends the threshold it uses for "hotspot"
the work is yours, with any assistance declared

nodes.title: Research proposal: a safety intervention
nodes.description: A capstone research proposal for a single wildlife-vehicle safety intervention, defensible on ecological, physical, human-factors and policy grounds at once.
spec: submitted by the deadline, as a single proposal document
it recommends one specific intervention, for one specific stretch of road or class of road, not a general survey of options
it argues from at least three of the unit's strands (ecology, data, physics, human factors, engineering, policy) rather than one
it states a realistic cost and approval pathway for the jurisdiction it targets
it stands on its own, without you there to explain it

marking.description: The proposal is judged as a whole against the brief, with particular attention to whether it argues from evidence covered across the semester rather than from a single strand of it, whether its scope and costing are realistic for the jurisdiction it targets, and whether it stands on its own for a reader who wasn't in the room.

nodes.title: Welcome to the Road. Please Remain a Student, Not a Statistic.
nodes.description: The unit's opening lecture — what risk, exposure, outcome measures, and uncertainty mean, worked through a single fictional collision, from a professor whose own qualifications now include "an unusually comprehensive incident report."
spec: you can explain the difference between a single incident and a rate, using risk and exposure correctly
you can name an outcome measure in a road-safety claim, and say what it does and doesn't capture
you can identify at least one source of uncertainty in a given incident account
you can restate a blame-laden verdict as a research question
you can explain why a research question is investigated while only a hypothesis derived from it can be shown wrong

nodes.title: Macropod behaviour and circadian activity
nodes.description: Why kangaroo–vehicle collisions cluster at particular times of day — and why the graph that seems to show this is not yet the explanation for it.
spec: you can explain what "crepuscular" means without treating it as a complete explanation
you can create and interpret a basic time-of-day distribution
you can distinguish an observed pattern from an explanation for that pattern
you can identify a recording artefact in a dataset
you can explain how animal activity, driver visibility, traffic exposure and reporting practices can produce the same apparent pattern
you can revise a conclusion after discovering a data-quality problem

nodes.title: Spatial and temporal patterns of vehicle strikes
nodes.description: Why a map of recorded strikes looks like a finding before anyone has checked what the dots represent — and what survives once you check.
spec: you can count recorded collisions by road from the dataset
you can distinguish a raw collision count from an exposure-adjusted rate
you can state a simple, explicit hotspot definition and apply it consistently
you can identify a reporting-coverage limitation that a map alone can't show
you can revise a hotspot claim after comparing it against an alternative measure

nodes.title: The physics of a kangaroo strike
nodes.description: Why a modest change in speed produces a disproportionate change in stopping distance and available kinetic energy — and what a simplified model can and can't tell you about that.
spec: you can convert a speed in kilometres per hour to metres per second
you can calculate kinetic energy for a stated vehicle mass and speed
you can distinguish reaction distance from braking distance
you can compare stopping distance and kinetic energy across several speed scenarios
you can explain what a simplified collision-physics model leaves out

nodes.title: Human perception and reaction time at dusk
nodes.description: Why "the driver should have seen it" assumes a detection distance nobody measured — and how far a stopping-distance model can travel once you give it one.
spec: you can distinguish detection from the response that follows detection
you can explain how contrast, glare, vegetation and attention may affect detection
you can use a stated detection distance with the week 4 stopping model to calculate a distance margin
you can recognise why a classroom exercise cannot establish an individual's driving safety

nodes.title: Roo bars, AEB, and their blind spots
nodes.description: What a safety technology actually does, under what conditions it's been shown to work, and what evidence would justify recommending one.
spec: you can distinguish detection, warning, automatic braking and impact protection as four separate functions
you can interpret a technology's stated operating limits rather than its marketing headline
you can explain why a high detection rate is not the same claim as a high collision-prevention rate
you can identify a false positive and a false negative in a stated trial result, given the denominator
you can propose a fair comparison test for a safety-technology claim

nodes.title: Fencing, signage and wildlife crossings
nodes.description: Why the interventions with the best headline results are also the ones hardest to fund, and what that means for recommending one.

nodes.title: Law, liability and insurance after a strike
nodes.description: Why "no one is at fault" doesn't mean "no one pays" — and why the payer depends on which document you read, not on fault in the everyday sense.

nodes.title: First aid, reporting, and wildlife rescue
nodes.description: What an untrained bystander should actually do in the minutes after a strike — and the hard line between that and treating the animal yourself.

nodes.title: Communicating risk to visitors and new drivers
nodes.description: Why a dense, legalistic warning fails the exact reader who needs it most — and what a plain-English brief has to do instead.

nodes.title: Does the evidence travel?
nodes.description: Two real overseas case studies, and the five questions to ask before importing anything they found into a different road, country, or species.

nodes.title: From evidence to a proposal
nodes.description: How to structure a scoped, evaluable intervention proposal — and what separates a proposal a marker can act on from one they can only admire.

course.title: Generation Loss
course.description: Copies leave clues. In this course, you will investigate what changes when recordings, images and texts are copied, reconstruct possible histories from incomplete evidence, and decide what is worth preserving.
learningOutcomes: Characterise changes caused by a copying process using reproducible measurements and controls.
Construct and compare plausible copying histories, marking unresolved relationships.
Evaluate whether a feature supports a provenance claim or has another explanation.
Evaluate a restoration or preservation claim against the available evidence.
Defend a preservation decision with explicit costs, assumptions and tradeoffs.

nodes.title: The office that ate itself
nodes.description: How can we measure a copy becoming harder to read?
spec: you can apply the counting rule twice to the same transcription and get the same number
your table separates a misread character from an illegible one
you can say what your numbers do not establish

meta.heroImageAlt: Week 01 banner: The office that ate itself
meta.learningTarget: Define a repeatable measurement and explain why two readers of the same copy disagree.
meta.archiveDeposit: Character-error table for the supplied print generations, with the exact-copy control recorded beside them.
meta.accessibleRoute: Every copy is supplied as two readers' transcriptions, already aligned character by character against the card. The task is comparison and counting, not reading damaged print, and nothing here grades eyesight.

nodes.title: Hiss as a signature
nodes.description: Which shared features are useful evidence of a common intermediate copy?
spec: every relationship you propose names the specific feature that supports it
you state the assumption under which that feature is good evidence
you test one alternative explanation and say why you rejected it

meta.heroImageAlt: Week 02 banner: Hiss as a signature
meta.learningTarget: Distinguish a feature two copies inherited from one they both descend from, from one they share for some other reason.
meta.archiveDeposit: Feature-to-relationship evidence table naming one supported pair, the feature that supports it, and the alternative explanation tested against it.
meta.accessibleRoute: The evidence is a feature table: what each feature is, where it sits, and which recordings carry it. No recordings are supplied and nothing here requires listening, because the inference runs on the table.

nodes.title: What the ear cannot hear
nodes.description: How would we test whether repeated re-encoding caused a measured change?
spec: your protocol names one independent variable and lists what you held fixed
your prediction is written before you look at the matching results
your conclusion is limited to the source, settings and measure you actually used

meta.heroImageAlt: Week 03 banner: What the ear cannot hear
meta.learningTarget: Design a comparison that isolates one variable, and report a result the comparison cannot see as a result.
meta.archiveDeposit: One-page protocol and results table for a comparison that holds the bitrate fixed, with a conclusion limited to the source, settings and score used.
meta.accessibleRoute: The evidence is a table of numbers with a stated arithmetic rule. Nothing requires listening, and the score is eight additions.

nodes.title: The poor image
nodes.description: Can different histories fit the same available image evidence?
spec: you state the tolerance under which two histories count as indistinguishable
your request for further evidence says in advance what result would separate the routes
your report records what remains unresolved rather than choosing to look decisive

meta.heroImageAlt: Week 04 banner: The poor image
meta.learningTarget: Show that a defined evidence set cannot separate two histories, then specify evidence that could — and accept when the answer stays open.
meta.archiveDeposit: Ambiguity report: two route diagrams, an observation table, the stated scope of indistinguishability, and a justified request for further evidence.
meta.accessibleRoute: The evidence is an observation table, two written route cards and an evidence menu, all in plain text. The task is inference from stated measurements, and no image needs to be looked at.

nodes.title: The scriptorium
nodes.description: Which copying mistakes can become useful evidence?
spec: your error table classifies each disagreement as an omission, a repetition or a substitution
you can say why a shared normalisation is weaker evidence than a shared omission or repetition
your witness labels are anonymised before you hand the table to another group

meta.heroImageAlt: Week 05 banner: The scriptorium
meta.learningTarget: Classify omissions, repetitions and substitutions, and say which are weak evidence.
meta.archiveDeposit: Anonymised text witnesses and a classified error table, with the true parent log withheld.
meta.accessibleRoute: Editable text with line identifiers; no unfamiliar-script skill is assessed.

nodes.title: Reading the damage backwards
nodes.description: Which family tree does the evidence support, and what remains unknown?
spec: every edge in your tree names the specific shared error it rests on
you name the strongest alternative tree the same evidence table would also support
your correction note says whether your reasoning was defensible where it did not match the log

meta.heroImageAlt: Week 06 banner: Reading the damage backwards
meta.learningTarget: Justify proposed edges and compare at least one competing history.
meta.archiveDeposit: Proposed tree, competing explanation and a post-reveal correction note.
meta.accessibleRoute: Textual edge list and evidence table alongside every diagram.

nodes.title: When ancestry becomes hard to read
nodes.description: What happens to ancestry inference as copying errors increase?
spec: your rate-by-rate reading records the seed-to-seed spread, not only the mean
you name one conclusion the model's assumptions do not support
your trend prediction is written before you open results.csv or plot.svg

meta.heroImageAlt: Week 07 banner: When ancestry becomes hard to read
meta.learningTarget: Describe how a simulation's assumptions limit its conclusion.
meta.archiveDeposit: Parameter-labelled ancestry-agreement plot and a limitations note naming what the model omits.
meta.accessibleRoute: Plot data as a table plus a prose description of the trend.

nodes.title: Copying without loss
nodes.description: What resources can protect a message from a specified error pattern?
spec: your overhead table records payload bits, transmitted bits and errors corrected per triplet
you can state the exact error pattern the repetition code does not protect against
your costing line states what the redundancy buys, not that it removes the risk entirely

meta.heroImageAlt: Week 08 banner: Copying without loss
meta.learningTarget: Calculate redundancy overhead and state the protection's limit.
meta.archiveDeposit: Overhead table recording payload, transmitted bits, errors corrected and the failure case.
meta.accessibleRoute: Labelled text blocks worked by hand; no implementation required.

nodes.title: The curse of recursion
nodes.description: Under what conditions can recursive sampling lose rare cases?
spec: your conclusion is scoped to the stated condition and seeds, not a general claim
your retention table records whether a run that reached zero ever recovered
you name one property of a real trained model this six-category toy has no analogue for

meta.heroImageAlt: Week 09 banner: The curse of recursion
meta.learningTarget: Compare stated conditions rather than infer training history from style.
meta.archiveDeposit: Rare-category retention comparison across three sampling conditions, labelled a simplified model.
meta.accessibleRoute: Count tables and an annotated chart description.

nodes.title: Enhance
nodes.description: Does a convincing restoration match the original?
spec: your feature table separates a verified match from a merely plausible one
you classify a feature as uncertain when its block had no internal variation to recover from
you state which of your judgements you could still have made without the retained source

meta.heroImageAlt: Week 10 banner: Enhance
meta.learningTarget: Distinguish plausible detail, verified agreement and remaining ambiguity.
meta.archiveDeposit: Supported, unsupported and uncertain feature table for one restoration claim.
meta.accessibleRoute: Enlarged labelled details with equivalent written feature descriptions.

nodes.title: Chain of custody
nodes.description: What does a provenance record establish, and what can it omit?
spec: you classify every field as retained, a documented removal, an undocumented change or never captured
you distinguish a field absent from both manifests from one the log describes changing
you name one proportionate logging improvement and say what it would still not catch

meta.heroImageAlt: Week 11 banner: Chain of custody
meta.learningTarget: Distinguish recorded history, missing history and the truth of a claim.
meta.archiveDeposit: Provenance audit comparing manifests before and after a documented stripping operation.
meta.accessibleRoute: Plain-text manifests and the corresponding processing log.

nodes.title: The original that never was
nodes.description: What should this archive preserve, given a limited budget?
spec: your memo names the specific loss you accept by not choosing the other allocation
you check whether your chosen proposal still fits budget under the revised rate
you write your own answer to the objection before reading the supplied one

meta.heroImageAlt: Week 12 banner: The original that never was
meta.learningTarget: Defend a preservation choice while acknowledging a worthwhile alternative.
meta.archiveDeposit: Preservation memo allocating a stated budget across families, plus a response to one objection.
meta.accessibleRoute: Budget table and a written participation alternative to the debate.

nodes.title: Generation Checks
nodes.description: Twelve five-minute evidence responses, one at the start of each workshop, marked on your reasoning rather than on getting the answer right.
spec: you cite the specific evidence you reasoned from, not the conclusion alone
you name one limitation or alternative your answer does not settle
a wrong final choice with sound reasoning still earns most of the marks

marking.description: Each check earns 0–4 raw points — 2 for relevant evidence, 1 for a defensible interpretation, 1 for a material limitation or alternative. The best ten of twelve count, and your course contribution is the sum of those ten divided by 40 and scaled to 10 percentage points.

nodes.title: The Chain
nodes.description: Investigate one artefact through ten documented copying steps, and report what each step changed in measurements someone else could reproduce.
spec: another person could repeat your comparison from the files and settings you submit
your control isolates at least one competing explanation
your recorded prediction is compared with the result, not rewritten to match it

nodes.title: The Lossless Argument
nodes.description: Propose a preservation decision for one bounded object or collection, price it, and show what changes when your largest assumption is wrong.
spec: you state which property counts as preserved, in terms someone could test
your costing states its units, horizon and assumptions
you engage a serious objection rather than the weakest available one

nodes.title: The Stemma
nodes.description: Reconstruct a family tree from a curated set of undocumented text witnesses, then argue the strongest case against your own tree.
spec: every proposed edge names the specific shared feature that supports it
portions you cannot resolve are marked as unresolved rather than guessed
you present the strongest competing tree the same evidence allows

nodes.description: How work is submitted, how sources and tools are declared, what accessible participation means here, and how to get an extension.

course.title: The Political Economy of the Refrigerator
course.description: The refrigerator promises to stop time, and the bill arrives as waste.

nodes.title: Blind tasting: is freshness real?
nodes.description: Fresh, three days refrigerated, and freeze-dried — taste all three without knowing which is which, then argue about what "fresh" means
spec: you have tasted all three samples without knowing which was which
you have written a description of each before the reveal, in your own words
you can state a position on whether freshness is a physical state or a cultural construct

nodes.title: Decoding the advertisement
nodes.description: A visual semiotics workshop on refrigerator advertising, 1950–1980 — who is operating the fridge, and what is the white enamel saying?
spec: your group has analysed at least three advertisements across at least two decades
you have identified who is depicted operating the appliance, and who is depicted enjoying it
you can name one thing the advertisement promises that is not about food

nodes.title: The food mileage map
nodes.description: Photograph the three most off-season things in your fridge, then reverse-track where they came from and what it cost to bring them
spec: you have photographed three off-season or exotic items from your own fridge, before the session
you have traced each to a country of origin and a plausible transport route
you can state an estimated ecological cost and say honestly how rough the estimate is

nodes.title: Fridge archaeology
nodes.description: Bring the interior of your own fridge and we will draw the power map together — authority zones, marginal zones, and the tragedy of the commons
spec: you have a photograph or hand-drawn map of a real fridge interior
the class power map marks your authority zone, marginal zone and commons zone
you can name one rule your household follows that nobody ever agreed to out loud

nodes.title: The debate: who owns the food in a shared fridge?
nodes.description: A structured ethical debate on a share-house dispute — ownership, hygiene boundaries, and the contract nobody wrote down
spec: you have argued a position you were assigned, not the one you already held
you can state the strongest argument on the side you opposed
you can apply Douglas's matter-out-of-place to at least one moment in the scenario

nodes.title: Dual curation: the fridge door and the feed
nodes.description: Compare the two surfaces you curate for other people — one physical and semi-private, one digital and public. They are not saying the same thing.
spec: you have brought both a photograph of a fridge door and a view of your own feed
you can name the audience for each, and say how they differ
you have workshopped your ethnography argument with two other people

nodes.title: Label forensics
nodes.description: Bring 5–10 confusing date labels, work out what the regulations actually require, and draft an honest label to replace each one
spec: you have brought 5–10 items or photographs with confusing date labels
your group has separated the safety baseline from the peak of flavour for each
you have drafted at least one honest label and can defend its wording

nodes.title: Personal waste audit
nodes.description: Record everything you throw out for a week, then cost it in money and calories. The illusory fortress, itemised.
spec: you have a week of records covering every item discarded from your fridge
you have calculated its monetary value and its caloric value
you can say which single category cost you most, and why it was that one

nodes.title: Psychological mapping: the ideal fridge and the anxious fridge
nodes.description: Draw the fridge you want and the fridge you have when things are bad, then ask what you were actually buying
spec: you have drawn both an ideal fridge and an anxious fridge
you have named the specific circumstance your anxious fridge belongs to
you can state one thing you buy for emotional value rather than use value

nodes.title: Design the dystopia
nodes.description: Build the most exploitative smart fridge you can imagine, in groups, and then take your own design apart
spec: your group has specified a Smart Fridge 2.0 with at least four exploitative features
you have identified which of your invented features already exist in some form
you can name three inferences drawable from a fridge inventory that are not about food

nodes.title: Fermentation and sharing workshop
nodes.description: Make a quick pickle with your hands, or design the rules for a community pantry — preservation that does not need a plug
spec: you have either made a ferment or drafted operating rules for a community pantry
you can explain what your chosen method preserves against, and what it does not
you can distinguish a genuine safety requirement from a hardened convention, with an example of each

nodes.title: Final pitches and the unplugged picnic
nodes.description: Present your reconstruction proposal, then eat a meal that never needed a fridge — the argument, in embodied form
spec: you have pitched your final project in five minutes and taken questions
you have named who your proposal is for and what it asks them to give up
you have brought something to the picnic that never saw the inside of a fridge

nodes.title: Final Project — the Counter-Fridge
nodes.description: A reconstruction proposal — spatial design, art installation, or behavioural experiment — that refuses the argument of this course, and defends the refusal
spec: submitted by 17:00 Friday 28 May, in any medium, with a written rationale
the rationale is 1000–1500 words
pitched in five minutes at the week 12 session
it names who it is for and what it asks them to give up

bands.P: A proposal is presented but stays close to a straightforward improvement on the existing fridge rather than a genuine alternative to it.
bands.CR: A proposal that clearly refuses at least one assumption behind refrigeration-as-usual, realised in enough detail to judge how it would actually work.
bands.D: A proposal whose form itself embodies the refusal — the medium is doing some of the argument's work, not just illustrating a decision made in the rationale.
bands.HD: A proposal specific enough to be built or run as described, that could not be swapped for a different medium without losing part of what it argues.

bands.P: The rationale explains what the proposal is, but does not say who it is for or what it costs them, or answers those questions only in general terms.
bands.CR: The rationale names who the proposal is for and what they are asked to give up, and connects the proposal to a specific claim from the course it means to refuse.
bands.D: The rationale identifies a real, unanswered objection to its own proposal and takes it seriously rather than dismissing it.
bands.HD: The rationale survives its own strongest objection, naming a trade nobody asked about and showing why the proposal is worth it anyway — not just that it exists.

bands.P: The pitch and the write-up separately make sense, but do not reinforce each other, or the pitch leans on slides rather than the artefact and argument.
bands.CR: The five-minute pitch stands on its own — proposal, argument, and the unanswered objection — without notes doing the work slides would otherwise do.
bands.D: The pitch anticipates the room's likely questions, and the write-up answers them in more depth than the five minutes allowed.
bands.HD: The pitch changes how the room understands the proposal in five minutes, and the rationale rewards a second, closer reading with detail the pitch had no time for.

note: Markers see the pitch before they read the rationale, so the five minutes in week 12 set the frame the document then has to earn. A striking artefact that cannot answer 'who is this for?' out loud loses marks on 'the argument for it' before the write-up is even opened.

'The proposal' and 'the argument for it' are not interchangeable: a beautiful artefact with a thin rationale still caps low, and a well-argued refusal with no artefact is marked on the same scale, not a lesser one. What lifts a submission is naming the trade nobody asked about and the objection it cannot answer — the two things this course's own artefacts, in weeks 6 and 10, were criticised for skipping.

nodes.title: Assessment 2 - Critical Essay
nodes.description: Apply the course's theory to one fridge-related phenomenon — and then tell me what the course gets wrong about it
spec: submitted by 17:00 Friday 30 April, as a PDF
every quantitative claim states how it was measured
it takes a position, including against this course if that is where the argument goes

bands.P: A position is stated but arrives late or stays close to the brief — asserted rather than argued, or so close to what a lecture already says that dropping the phenomenon would leave the same paragraph.
bands.CR: A specific position, stated early and defended for the length of the essay, though it stays within the course's own account rather than testing it.
bands.D: A specific position that presses on a genuine limit of the course's account rather than only applying it, with that pressure stated early enough to organise the essay.
bands.HD: An argument that identifies where the course's account of this phenomenon breaks down, presses a real objection to it, and survives that objection by the end rather than only naming it.

bands.P: Figures or examples are used, but at least one quantitative claim states no method, or states one the reader cannot judge.
bands.CR: Every claim states its method well enough to know who measured it and how, but the evidence mostly illustrates a point already made rather than testing it.
bands.D: Evidence, including at least one piece of the writer's own primary material, is specific enough that its method's weaknesses are visible and acknowledged rather than glossed over.
bands.HD: Evidence is used to genuinely test the argument rather than illustrate it, including a moment where the writer's own material complicates the position instead of confirming it.

bands.P: Douglas, Goffman or another course framework is named and correctly defined, but not applied to the phenomenon chosen.
bands.CR: A framework is applied to the specific phenomenon, though the application mostly restates the framework in the phenomenon's terms.
bands.D: A framework is used to reclassify or reinterpret the phenomenon in a way that is not obvious from the framework's usual examples.
bands.HD: A framework is extended, combined with another, or pushed against a case it does not obviously fit, doing analytical work the lectures had not already done.

note: Markers read the essay once for the position, then again for whether each quantitative claim states its method. A figure cited without a method is marked as rhetoric, not evidence, regardless of how well the surrounding paragraph reads.

'Argument' and 'evidence and method' pull in the same direction only when the position is stated early and the numbers are what defend it, not what decorate it. An essay that agrees fluently with the lectures and surveys three views without holding one caps out on 'argument' no matter how sound its method is elsewhere; one that presses a real objection to the course's own claims, well-evidenced, can outscore an essay that only restates them.

nodes.title: Assessment 1 - Fridge Ethnography
nodes.description: Observe one real refrigerator as a micro-sociological site and read it as governed space — Module 2's method, applied to a kitchen you have access to
spec: submitted by 17:00 Friday 2 April, as a PDF
2500–3000 words, plus field materials in an appendix that does not count towards the word limit
everyone identifiable has agreed to be written about, and is anonymised
it makes an argument, not only a description

bands.P: Fieldwork is present but thin: a handful of observations, mostly what was already expected going in, with little that could not have been guessed from outside the fridge.
bands.CR: Sustained observation showing a clear pattern, but the description leans on the obvious cues (labels, position) rather than the harder-to-notice behavioural traces.
bands.D: Detailed, specific observation that surfaces something not visible at a glance — a habit, a negotiation, a discrepancy between what people say and what the fridge shows.
bands.HD: Fieldwork uncovers something genuinely unexpected and follows it up rather than noting it in passing, with enough specificity that a marker could reconstruct the household from the appendix alone.

bands.P: An argument is stated, but it stays close to description — restating what was observed rather than explaining what governs it.
bands.CR: A clear claim about what governs the fridge, stated early, that mostly holds up against the evidence presented.
bands.D: A specific, defensible claim that accounts for the evidence and addresses at least one obvious counter-reading of it.
bands.HD: An argument a reader could not have predicted from the brief alone, sharpened against real counter-evidence, and stated early enough to organise the whole submission around it.

bands.P: Douglas, Goffman or the power-mapping method are named and briefly defined, but not applied to this fridge specifically.
bands.CR: At least one framework is applied to a specific observation, though the connection is asserted more than demonstrated.
bands.D: Frameworks are used as tools to reclassify or reinterpret specific evidence, not just cited alongside it.
bands.HD: Frameworks are put to work against each other, or extended to a case they do not obviously fit, doing real analytical labour rather than supplying vocabulary.

note: Markers read the PDF in one sitting: the argument first, then the appendix behind it, then a check of whether Douglas, Goffman and the power-mapping method are doing real work or only being named. A submission that reads well aloud but leaves the marker unable to say back what governs the fridge has failed on 'analytical argument' regardless of how much fieldwork sits behind it.

'Quality of observation' and 'analytical argument' are not the same axis: thin fieldwork with a sharp claim still loses marks for evidence, and rich fieldwork with no claim caps out in the same range no matter how detailed the appendix. The two move together only when the argument is stated early and the fieldwork is what proves it, not what replaces it.

course.title: Software Archaeology
course.description: Excavating intent from abandoned code. Students learn to date, read, and diagnose dead software using forensic techniques — git blame as stratigraphy, commit messages as inscriptions, dependency graphs as tool inventories — then confront the ethics of reviving someone else's abandoned work.
learningOutcomes: Date and phase an undocumented codebase from its version-control record, and state the confidence and limits of that dating
Reconstruct a development team's architecture, conventions and working practices from artefacts alone, without access to its members
Diagnose a project's cause of death against a taxonomy of failure modes, and defend that diagnosis against competing explanations of the same evidence
Conduct oral-history enquiry with former maintainers under an explicit research-ethics framework, including deciding when not to make contact
Evaluate the ethics of reviving abandoned work, distinguishing what a licence permits from what its authors intended
Execute a restoration under the principle of minimum intervention, and justify every change and every deliberate non-change
Communicate a technical excavation to a non-specialist audience as a sustained, evidenced argument

nodes.title: The dead repo
nodes.description: Survey — what makes software dead, how to tell, and how to choose a dig site you will spend the semester excavating.
spec: you have chosen a dig site — a public, abandoned repository with a visible history
you can clone it, read its log, and name its last active date
you can articulate why you chose it over the alternatives you considered

nodes.title: Stratigraphy
nodes.description: Dating techniques — reading the commit history as geological layers to identify periods of construction, maintenance, and abandonment.
spec: you can produce a commit-frequency timeline for your dig site
you have identified at least two distinct periods in its history
you can name the boundary event between the active and decay periods

nodes.title: The inscriptions
nodes.description: Reading the inscriptions — commit messages as primary sources for a team's communication norms, morale, and working patterns.
spec: you have categorised your dig site's commit messages by convention and quality
you can describe the team's communication norms without reading their code
you have identified at least one commit message that reveals something the code alone would not

nodes.title: Tool inventory
nodes.description: Dependency analysis — reading package manifests as archaeological tool kits to date the project and reconstruct the technological era it belongs to.
spec: you can list your dig site's direct dependencies and the era each belongs to
you have identified at least one dependency choice that tells you something about the team
you have checked which dependencies are themselves now abandoned

nodes.title: Architecture from ruins
nodes.description: Spatial analysis — reconstructing the mental model the original authors had from directory structure, entry points, and file naming conventions alone.
spec: you have drawn an architecture diagram of your dig site based on its directory structure
you can identify the entry point and the main data flow without reading function bodies
you can name at least one structural decision that tells you how the team thought about the problem

nodes.title: The documentation layer
nodes.description: Epigraphy — reading the writing the authors left behind, and diagnosing the project from the gap between what the docs promise and what the code does.
spec: you have catalogued every piece of documentation in your dig site
you can describe the gap between what the docs promise and what the code delivers
you have identified at least one undocumented behaviour that matters

nodes.title: Oral history
nodes.description: Interview technique — how to find former maintainers, how to approach them, and what you learn that no artefact can tell you.
spec: you have attempted to contact a former contributor to your dig site, or documented why you chose not to
if contact was made, you followed the course's oral-history ethics guidelines
you can name at least one thing you learned (or would hope to learn) that no artefact reveals

nodes.title: Cause of death
nodes.description: Forensic diagnosis — why projects die, a taxonomy of failure modes, and how to distinguish burnout from ecosystem shift from silent success.
spec: you have diagnosed your dig site's cause of death using the course taxonomy
your diagnosis is supported by evidence from at least three earlier sessions
you can distinguish your project's failure mode from at least one alternative explanation

nodes.title: Preservation
nodes.description: Conservation — the difference between preserving code and preserving the ability to run it, and the institutions that try to do both.
spec: you can explain the difference between archiving source code and preserving executability
you have tested whether your dig site can be built or run today
you can name one thing that would be lost if the repository were deleted tomorrow

nodes.title: Restoration ethics
nodes.description: Whose code is it — the ethics of forking abandoned work, the difference between licence and intent, and when revival is continuation vs appropriation.
spec: you can distinguish between what a licence permits and what the author intended
you have a position on whether your dig site should be revived, and can defend it
you can name a case where forking an abandoned project would be wrong despite the licence allowing it

nodes.title: The restoration
nodes.description: Minimum intervention — reviving one piece of your dig site the way a conservator restores a painting: stabilise, do not repaint.
spec: you have restored one specific feature or module of your dig site to working order
your restoration follows the principle of minimum intervention
you can list every change you made and justify each one

nodes.title: The exhibit
nodes.description: Presentation — your complete excavation presented as a museum exhibit, for an audience who has never seen the codebase.
spec: your exhibit tells the story of one codebase from construction to abandonment to partial restoration
an audience member who has never seen the repo can follow the narrative
you can answer questions about your methods, your evidence, and your ethical choices

nodes.title: The Dig Report
nodes.description: Survey your dig site — its stratigraphy, its tool inventory, its architecture, and your first hypothesis for how it died.
spec: covers all four methods taught in weeks 1-4 (survey, dating, inscriptions, tools)
includes a commit-frequency timeline visualisation
cause-of-death hypothesis is stated and supported by at least two pieces of evidence
all evidence cites specific commits, files, or dependency versions
1500 words, plus the timeline visualisation

nodes.title: The Forensic Analysis
nodes.description: Go deeper — the documentation layer, the oral history, and a revised cause-of-death diagnosis supported by the full weight of your evidence.
spec: covers methods from weeks 5-8 (architecture, documentation, oral history, diagnosis)
cause-of-death diagnosis is revised from the Dig Report and supported by at least four pieces of evidence
if oral history was attempted, the ethics guidelines were followed
if oral history was not possible, secondary sources are cited and the gap is acknowledged
1500 words

nodes.title: The Exhibit
nodes.description: Your complete excavation — the site, the findings, the diagnosis, the ethics, and the restoration — presented for an audience that has never seen the codebase.
spec: tells the complete story of one codebase from construction to abandonment
includes a restoration with a documented change log
the restoration follows the principle of minimum intervention
the ethical position on revival is stated and defended
presentation is 10 minutes; written companion is 2000 words

nodes.title: Reconstructing architecture

nodes.title: What the docs do not say
nodes.description: Documentation as archaeological evidence — what was written, what was maintained, and what the gap between them reveals.

nodes.title: Finding the people
nodes.description: Oral history methodology for software — finding former maintainers, the ethics of contact, and what living sources reveal that artefacts cannot.

nodes.title: Cause of death
nodes.description: A taxonomy of software failure — why projects die, how to tell the modes apart, and why the diagnosis matters.

nodes.description: Software preservation — the institutions that try, the difference between archiving code and preserving the ability to run it, and what still gets lost.
