course.title: Advanced Fréchet Inception Distance
course.description: A semester spent auditing one number. FID governs what counts as progress in generative modelling, and it is biased, sample-size dependent, and routinely compared across incompatible conditions. We rebuild it, break it, and decide what it can honestly be asked to say.

nodes.title: The number
nodes.description: The bold number in a results table is the field's account of what got better, and nothing in the table says what it was computed against. The bench is built here.
spec: you can name three things a reported FID depends on besides the model
you have a working bench, two generators and a reference set, and have scored it once
you can say what sample size the paper that introduced the score used, and what reason it gave

meta.log: the two scores, their sample size, and the implementation that produced them

nodes.title: The Fréchet distance
nodes.description: The closed form for two Gaussians, derived rather than quoted, and the assumption it smuggles in
spec: you can derive the closed form from the definition without notes
you can say which step requires the Gaussian assumption and what breaks without it
you have computed the distance on the bench by hand for a two dimensional projection and matched the library

meta.log: both estimates with their N, beside the population values you derived by hand

nodes.title: The instrument
nodes.description: Inception-v3 was trained to name a thousand ImageNet classes. The score measures distance in the space it built to do that.
spec: you can say which layer the features come from and how many dimensions it has
you can state one way the classifier's objective shapes what the score can and cannot see
you have re-scored saved bench samples through a fixed toy feature map, checked a rotation-only control and labelled the resulting distances correctly

meta.log: the identity, rotation and rotation-plus-ReLU scores on saved samples, with N, seeds and a distinction between a toy Gaussian distance and image-based FID

nodes.title: Getting it right
nodes.description: The same samples can receive different scores. Separate preprocessing from numerical arithmetic, then pin the protocol you can defend.
spec: you have compared two candidate resize settings while keeping the source images, reference features and the rest of the scoring pipeline fixed
you have compared four numerical configurations on the same saved bench moments, reporting A and B separately and checking numerical residuals
the bench is scored through a single pinned implementation from here on, and you can say what it pins

meta.log: the controlled resize comparison, four numerical configurations with two candidate scores each, and the protocol you pinned

nodes.title: The bias
nodes.description: Finite-sample FID is biased, the bias depends on the generator, and fixing N does not repair the comparison
spec: you can explain the leading bias in expectation from the expansion, and distinguish it from the error in one estimate
you have produced two models whose measured ranking is stable, repeatable, and wrong
you can say what an N-honest comparison is, and why it is not enough

meta.log: the sampling protocol, seed, N and repetitions; the lecture's finite estimate, fitted FID∞ and population baseline, with the ladder and repeated intercepts

nodes.title: Blind spots
nodes.description: A generator that memorised the reference set scores perfectly. What else the score cannot see, demonstrated on the bench.
spec: you can construct a bench candidate that scores well and is obviously wrong, and say why the score cannot tell
you can distinguish a failure of the estimator from a failure of the quantity it estimates

meta.log: the finite FID comparison and fitted FID∞ for A and your candidate D, with the shared ladder and reference protocol, and the per-sample measure chosen first

nodes.title: Dropping the Gaussian
nodes.description: An unbiased estimator need not detect every difference. Compare KID, density and coverage against the bench's known Gaussian-distance baseline.
spec: you can distinguish precision and recall from the density and coverage quantities plotted here
you can explain KID's unbiased estimator without claiming complete sensitivity or an exact answer from one finite sample
you have an N-honest comparison of A, B and C with R-again under the three plotted scores, labelled separately from the population baseline

meta.log: the KID, density and coverage strips for R-again, A, B and C at each stated d and N, separating population baselines from estimates and uncomputed FID∞

nodes.title: Video
nodes.description: FVD keeps the Gaussian distance but changes the features. Test what a temporal instrument preserves before transferring claims from images.
spec: you can say exactly what changed between FID and FVD and what did not
you have compared all three lecture instruments on the same sequence sets, with predictions, settings and observed scores recorded
you can demonstrate a toy feature invariance and design a separate test of temporal sensitivity in an actual FVD pipeline

meta.log: the lecture's three-instrument comparison and an audit plan separating measured toy results from untested FVD claims

nodes.title: Human evaluation
nodes.description: The judgement the score stands in for. How a rating study is designed, what it costs, and why it is so rarely run.
spec: you have designed a rating protocol for the bench and costed it in hours and dollars
you can say what inter-rater agreement you would require before trusting it over the score

meta.log: the rating protocol you designed, its cost in hours and dollars, and the assumptions behind both

nodes.title: Correlation
nodes.description: Put the ranking a score produces beside the ranking people produce, and ask whether they agree. That question decides whether the previous nine weeks were worth doing.
spec: you can cite a study where the score and human raters disagreed on a ranking, and say what changed the result
you can say what an N-honest correlation study would require

meta.log: the method section for an N-honest correlation study, and everything you had to specify that the papers did not

nodes.title: Why it persists
nodes.description: Nine years of results tables carry an FID column, and that continuity is the strongest argument anyone has for keeping it. What the number costs to leave out, stated honestly.
spec: you can make the strongest case for continuing to report the score, and mean it
you can name what it would cost a paper to stop

meta.log: the paragraph justifying omission, and how you expect a reviewer to read it

nodes.title: What you would report instead
nodes.description: Defend your proposal by the standard built across the semester. Bring the final bench comparison and the conditions under which you would still report FID.
spec: your replacement has been scored on the bench N-honestly against both FID and FID∞
you can say where your proposal fails, in the same terms you used for the score

meta.log: the final A, B and C comparison under finite FID, fitted FID∞, KID, density, coverage and your proposal, with protocols, baselines and a dated defence note

nodes.title: Assignment 1: Reproduce the number
nodes.description: Take a published FID from a real paper. Reproduce it. Explain the gap. Marked on the explanation, not on the size of the gap.
spec: the paper, the number and its page are cited
the reproduction can be re-run by the marker from what is submitted
every difference between your setup and the paper's is named

criteria.name: The reproduction attempt, pinned and repeatable

nodes.title: Assignment 2: Break the number
nodes.description: Construct a bench candidate that scores well and is visibly wrong, or scores badly and is visibly fine. Submit the set, the score and the mechanism.
spec: the candidate is reproducible from a seed
the score is reported N-honestly against the bench
you say which layer the failure lives in

criteria.name: The mechanism, stated in terms of the estimator or the quantity

nodes.title: Final report
nodes.description: Propose what you would report in place of the score, then evaluate your proposal by the standard this course applied to FID. Most proposals fail. Say how yours does.
spec: your metric is scored on the bench against FID and FID∞
its bias, blind spots and human correlation are each addressed, or their absence is justified
the report names the condition under which you would still report FID

criteria.name: Evaluation by the course's own standard

nodes.title: Measurement log
nodes.description: One entry a week from week 1. Every entry records a number, the sample size it was computed at, and the implementation that produced it.
spec: twelve dated entries, one per teaching week
every number is accompanied by its N and its implementation
at least one entry compares a prediction recorded before measuring with the observed result and explains the agreement or discrepancy

nodes.title: The bench, live
nodes.description: The week 1 exercise as an instrument you can run in this page. Draw your own samples, score them, and watch the estimate disagree with the truth.

nodes.title: The Fréchet distance
nodes.description: The week 2 derivation delivered as a sequence rather than a page, one step of the chain per slide, ending on the bench scored by hand

nodes.title: Question the estimate
nodes.description: Bias and noise are different problems. Return to the week 2 baseline, measure the bias on the bench, and take its price with it.

meta.activity_lead: The ladder above spent its draws across five sample sizes and fitted a line to estimate where the bias runs out. The activity below spends them differently: the distributions stay fixed, and you change only the seed, then only the number of repetitions. Watch which part of the gap moves. Repetition tightens the spread around what the estimator expects to report. It leaves that expectation where it was, above the population value, at every sample size you hold fixed.

nodes.title: Change the instrument
nodes.description: Two honest numbers from the same recordings can disagree about which candidate is worse. Put three instruments on one bench and find out why.

meta.activity_lead: The bench above shuffled frames inside each sequence, and only an instrument that reads order could tell. The activity below shuffles something else: the order of whole images in a collection, in the image lab, with real Inception features. Predict what that shuffle can change before you press it, and keep the two kinds of order apart when you bring the result back to the pooled frames and the whole sequence.

nodes.title: Defend the report
nodes.description: A number is not evidence. Declare the protocol behind a claim, run it twelve times, and find out what it will carry.

meta.activity_lead: The protocol above could be run twelve times because every number in it was synthetic and every setting was declared. The activity below has neither advantage: one image comparison, on pixels you choose, measured once. What carries over is the order of work. Write the claim and the result that would contradict it before you measure, and keep every setting beside the number when you export it.

nodes.title: The number is not the conclusion
nodes.description: A careful account of what a score supports is worth more than a confident ranking. A closing word before you finish the final report.

nodes.title: Dr Helen Sandoval
nodes.description: Convenor and lecturer. Leads the Measurement Reliability Group, studying finite-sample bias and what evidence a reported model ranking needs.

nodes.description: PhD candidate, tutor and bench maintainer. Studies reproducible evaluation pipelines and helps students separate sampling variation from implementation errors.

course.title: Seeing Through Obfuscated Code
course.description: Obfuscation, assembly, and recovering program semantics. Twelve weeks on how much of a program's meaning survives a change of representation — and on why a deobfuscated result that looks cleaner is not yet a result that is correct.

nodes.title: From C to machine code
nodes.description: One computation, four truthful descriptions of it, and the beginning of a habit — saying which description you are looking at before you say what it means.
spec: you can read a short C function and predict what it returns
you can say what a 32-bit register is, and what `+`, `^` and `-` do to one
nothing else — every representation in this course is introduced on this page or the two after it

meta.question: If the source, the IR and the machine code disagree about how complicated a program is, which one is wrong?

nodes.title: What is obfuscation?
nodes.description: Five tools, one program, and a definition strong enough to be useful — which means a definition that tells you what evidence would show whether anything happened.
spec: you have finished week 1's studio and can point at one operation in all three representations
you can state what `-O0` means to a compiler, and what it does not mean
you have skimmed the claim boundaries page and know why it exists

meta.question: An obfuscator ran and exited zero. What has it actually done, and what would show that?

nodes.title: Instruction substitution
nodes.description: The oldest trick in the book, applied to twenty-four sites, and largely undone by the compiler backend before anyone tried to analyse it.
spec: you can expand `a + b` into an identity that uses a third constant and cancels it
you can read a four-line SSA chain and say which value is stored
you have week 1's annotated XOR site written down

meta.question: If the obfuscator expanded every single addition, why can I still see additions in the machine code?

nodes.title: MBA and semantic simplification
nodes.description: Mixed Boolean-arithmetic, the tools that reduce it, and the difference between a shorter expression and a proved one. The honest scoreboard is in here.
spec: you can evaluate `~(x ^ k)` and `(~x) ^ k` and say whether they are the same
you know what SAT, UNSAT and UNKNOWN mean as answers to a question
you can say what `modulo 2³²` changes about an algebraic identity

meta.question: A simplifier returned a shorter expression. What exactly has been proved, and by what?

nodes.title: Optimization versus obfuscation
nodes.description: The compiler flag is part of the experiment. Change it and a transformation can halve, double, or vanish — while the obfuscator's own output file stays exactly the same.
spec: you can say what `-O0` stops the compiler doing, in concrete terms
you have week 3's finding written down — what survived to machine code, and what did not
you can compute a ratio and say what the denominator has to be for it to mean anything

meta.question: Is this result about the obfuscator, or about the optimisation flag that came after it?

nodes.title: Bogus control flow and opaque predicates
nodes.description: Four branches the programmer wrote, twenty-two a tool injected, and the question of how you tell them apart when you do not have the source.
spec: you can read a CFG and identify a loop, a reconverging branch and a dead edge
you can read `demo_bogus_control_flow` in the source and list its four conditions
you know why an `-O0` specimen is being used this week

meta.question: Which of these twenty-six conditional branches did the programmer actually write?

nodes.title: Symbolic execution and SMT
nodes.description: One branch, two queries, and a solver that answers one of them with a witness and the other with nothing at all. Plus the assumption that turns zero proofs into three.
spec: you can read a bit-vector SMT-LIB formula well enough to follow `bvand`, `bvsub` and `ite`
you have week 6's hand-argument written down — the one with the hole in it
you can state the difference between a satisfying model and a reachable program input

meta.question: What exactly has a solver established when it returns UNSAT for one direction of a branch?

nodes.title: From proof to a working binary
nodes.description: Six bytes, of which four differ. The audit that reconciles seventy blocks with thirty-seven. And 4,591 test triples, which is a great many inputs and not all of them.
spec: you can compute an x86-64 relative branch displacement by hand
you have week 7's two obligations written out for the gate at RVA 0x1667
you can say what an RVA is and how it differs from a virtual address

meta.question: A solver proved an edge impossible. What has to happen next, and who has to do it?

nodes.title: Control-flow flattening
nodes.description: The dispatcher, the state variable, and why the thing being hidden here is not a value but a relationship — which block runs next.
spec: you can identify a loop and a switch in a CFG with no source to hand
you can read `demo_flattening` in the source and name its three regions
you have week 8's distinction between reachable and physical blocks written down

meta.question: If every block returns to the same dispatcher, where did the program's structure go?

nodes.title: Unflattening and hidden assumptions
nodes.description: Four runs of one unmodified tool. Two working rewrites, one valid executable that returns the wrong answer, and one failure that never reached the part of the tool everybody talks about.
spec: you can read a block listing and follow fall-through from one instruction to the next
you have week 9's state table for the parity branch written down
you can say what a precision and a recall of 1.0 do and do not tell you

meta.question: The tool exited zero and the graph got smaller. How would you find out whether it worked?

nodes.title: Lifting machine code back to LLVM IR
nodes.description: One tool, one afternoon, two verdicts. Sixty-eight verifier-clean LLVM modules, one of which miscomputes 3,917 of 4,118 inputs — and the fold that did it is four operators long.
spec: you can read LLVM IR with `select`, `icmp` and bitwise operators
you can evaluate `(~A & B) | (A & C)` for small values of A, B and C
you have week 10's verdict on the incorrect rewrite written down

meta.question: The lifted IR verifies, recompiles and is smaller than the machine code. Is it right?

nodes.title: How generic can deobfuscation be?
nodes.description: The one week with no new evidence. What transferred between implementations, what did not, and the protocol for choosing a method when nobody tells you what was done to the binary.
spec: you have a draft capstone limitations section, however rough
you can name, from memory, the four outcomes this course keeps apart
you have picked the two representations your capstone will work in

meta.question: Given an unfamiliar obfuscated function, what would you do first, and what would you have to check?

nodes.title: A1 — Trace the transformation
nodes.description: Follow one operation from C to IR to x64 across a clean/obfuscated pair you have not seen, and write down what you established and what you did not.
spec: submitted as a single PDF by the deadline, with every claim citing a file and a line or address
one named operation is located in the source, the post-pass IR and the disassembly, with line numbers or addresses given for each
the comparator is a clean build of the same compiler family at the same optimisation level, and the submission says so
every count states its representation and its counting convention
the submission contains a section listing what it does not establish, and that section is not padding
the arithmetic identity claimed is checked modulo 2^32, not over the integers

criteria.name: Accurate tracing across the three representations
Correct comparator, convention and optimisation level
What the evidence does not establish

nodes.title: A2 — Recover the semantics
nodes.description: Given a flattened or gated function, a recovered graph and a set of solver results, decide what has been established — and defend the boundary you draw.
spec: submitted as a single PDF by the deadline, with every claim citing a retained file
each branch discussed has its two obligations written out, with the path prefix named
each solver status is reported as SAT, UNSAT or UNKNOWN, and UNKNOWN is never treated as equivalence
the state and memory assumptions the analysis depends on are listed explicitly
block and edge counts name their recovery convention and are not compared across conventions
the submission reaches a verdict on the supplied claim and says what evidence would change it

criteria.name: Proof obligations, stated correctly and in scope
Reasoning from the graph and the solver record
Judgement on the claim you are asked to adjudicate

nodes.title: Capstone — Seeing through an unfamiliar binary
nodes.description: One sample, withheld identity, every method you have. Choose an approach, justify it, validate whatever you conclude, and state the boundary of your own result.
spec: submitted by the deadline as a report plus the working files needed to follow it
every artefact discussed is identified by filename and SHA-256
at least two representations are used, and the report says why those two
each method used is justified against a stated assumption it depends on
every conclusion names the level it was validated at — expression, graph, lifted function, or executable
the report distinguishes analysis success, semantic proof, a produced binary, and runtime correctness, and does not conflate them
a limitations section states what was not established and what evidence would settle it
no claim of a working rewritten binary is made without a runtime record

criteria.name: Method selection, and the reasons given for it
Analysis across more than one representation
Validation — what was checked, how, and at what level

nodes.title: Same program, four stories
nodes.description: Why a compiler already makes a program harder to read before anyone tries to, and what it means to say that two very different listings are the same function.

nodes.title: Something always simplifies it for you
nodes.description: Three different things reduce obfuscated arithmetic — the algebra, the compiler backend, and your own reading — and confusing them is how people come to believe a simplifier recovered something it never touched.

nodes.title: What a proof is worth
nodes.description: A solver can show that a branch has only one reachable outcome. Turning that into a working executable takes a separate tool, and neither step is the same as knowing the program is still correct.

nodes.title: The smaller graph problem
nodes.description: Two results in this corpus look like successes and are not. Both were caught by running the program; neither would have been caught by looking at the output. That is the course's conclusion, and this is where it gets argued.

nodes.title: Course information
nodes.description: What you need before week 1, how the teaching runs, what you may and may not run in the lab, and how the evidence is made readable.

course.title: Slop Opera: Serialized AI Video Drama
course.description: A studio course in vertical serialized drama, where the machine does the shooting and only the technique you add to the rig earns a mark. Twelve weeks take you from an empty GPU to one finished pilot episode: one shot, one hook, one episode.

nodes.description: The week's first dailies — whether the rig runs at all, twice.

nodes.title: The Repeat Test

nodes.title: The Line-up

nodes.title: The Turnaround

nodes.title: One Shot Judged

nodes.title: The Continuity Pass

nodes.title: A4
nodes.description: The five-tier turnaround ladder, one prompt and one strength held constant across five inputs of rising finish.

nodes.title: A6
nodes.description: The five-tier keyframe-to-motion ladder, submitted as five clips with a note on where identity held or drifted.

nodes.title: A8
nodes.description: The four-tier reference ladder, audited item by item against one two-shot scene.

nodes.title: A9
nodes.description: The four-tier beat-sheet-and-storyboard ladder for one short sequence, including its three-second hook.

nodes.title: Dailies Participation
nodes.description: What you bring ready to screen and the notes you give on what the room brought, across all twelve Dailies, judged together rather than week by week.

marking.description: Judged across all twelve Dailies sessions together, not week by week — presence, bringing that week's exercise ready to screen, and the quality of critique given to other students' work, weighted toward consistency across the semester rather than any single strong or weak week.

nodes.title: The Pilot
nodes.description: One finished episode — sixty to ninety seconds, vertical, hooked in its first three seconds and held together end to end, submitted with a production log legible enough to rerun any shot in it.

nodes.title: The Showcase
nodes.description: A process account presented to the room — reading your own pilot's likely retention curve, and what you'd change for a second episode.

nodes.title: The Rig
nodes.description: Setting up the rig for the semester — a VRAM budget or a credit budget, where model weights and their licences come from, and the graph or the request log as the artefact that survives the render.

nodes.title: The Loop
nodes.description: The basic cycle every generator runs on — the interface against the workflow underneath it, rolling and selecting rather than prompting once, and the seed as the address of a specific result.

nodes.title: Text to Image
nodes.description: The first generator — prompt grammar for a single keyframe on anime-trained checkpoints, from one line to a full colour script.

nodes.title: Image to Image
nodes.description: The second generator — pushing an existing image toward a finished keyframe with denoising strength, ControlNet, and IP-Adapter, on the turnaround from rough input to finished frame.

nodes.title: Text to Video
nodes.description: The third generator — the four-sentence prompt that controls motion directly from words, a model's native clip length, and how to read a take that failed.

nodes.title: Image to Video
nodes.description: The fourth generator — keyframe-first control, locking a first and last frame, and the difference between directing motion and losing identity.

nodes.title: Your Own Workflow
nodes.description: Reading and rebuilding the workflow this course has been supplying — loaders, conditioning, samplers, and a fix pass — and the permission to go photoreal that comes with owning your own graph.

nodes.title: Continuity
nodes.description: Holding a character and a location steady across shots with a reference library and a model sheet — LoRA and DreamBooth against reference adapters, the scene master plate, and the audit that checks it held.

nodes.title: Script and Storyboard
nodes.description: Writing a vertical episode as a beat sheet of states rather than transitions, the three-second hook that opens it, and the storyboard as a shot list with sizes and references attached.

nodes.title: Production, Week One
nodes.description: Turning nine weeks of technique into an actual episode — the shot queue, split roles, the patch-or-reshoot decision, and the quality gate nothing skips.

nodes.title: Production, Week Two
nodes.description: Finishing an episode — assembling the queue's shots into one cut, sound and captions, loudness standards, and the delivery spec a platform actually expects.

nodes.title: After Five Minutes
nodes.description: What happens after a pilot ships — the series bible, the release calendar, reading a retention curve, and which parts of this semester's process actually scale into a season.

nodes.title: Dutch Meridian
nodes.description: Dutch Meridian directed television commercials for just over thirty years, across every format from fifteen-second spots to the handful of feature-length campaigns nobody was allowed to cut down. Three decades convinced him that only the first three seconds of anything are actually being watched, and he built a career, then a teaching practice, entirely on that conviction. He retired from commercial work the year clients started asking for content instead of advertisements, on the grounds that the job hadn't changed, only the word for it. He watches student dailies with the same stopwatch discipline he once billed by.

meta.contact: Wednesdays 17:00–18:00, after Dailies
meta.photoAlt: Portrait of Dutch Meridian, Tutor.

nodes.title: Vera Lin
nodes.description: Vera Lin spent eleven years writing for a long-running television soap opera, the last four as its head writer, before leaving broadcast for vertical drama the year the format found an audience larger than her old timeslot. She has never issued a public correction, a retraction, or an apology for a storyline, on the standing position that a season either works or it doesn't, and a statement afterward changes neither. She teaches the anime-to-live-action ramp the way she wrote for daytime television — one episode at a time, on a schedule that does not move for anyone's rewrite.

course.title: How to Run Anything in the Browser
course.description: Everything can be made to run in a browser; the question is what it costs. Twelve weeks comparing shims, compilation, POSIX surfaces, binary translation and whole kernels against a target you choose before Assignment 1 and carry to the end.

nodes.title: Four things that should not work
nodes.description: Run a PC, a kernel and two games in a browser tab, and form an opinion about what each one costs before anybody tells you
spec: you arrive with a laptop and a modern browser
you have read nothing about how any of these work

nodes.title: What does it need?
nodes.description: Take a program apart from the outside and write down what it requires, using evidence rather than assumption
spec: you bring a program you did not write and can run locally
you can read a linker or dependency listing without guessing

nodes.title: The shim that almost works
nodes.description: Run real programs against a fake runtime and find the exact line where impersonation stops paying
spec: you can run a JavaScript program in a tab with no server involved
you bring one program that works under a shim and one that does not

nodes.title: Which interface stops you first?
nodes.description: Compile several things that have no business compiling, and find the pattern in how they fail
spec: you have a working Emscripten or wasm32 toolchain before you arrive
you can read a linker error without flinching

nodes.title: What does it ask the kernel for?
nodes.description: Take the syscall inventory of a real program and decide which surface could actually host it
spec: you can run a native binary under a syscall tracer
you bring a program that does something more than compute

nodes.title: Tested in Node, broken in a tab
nodes.description: Reproduce a defect that only exists in a browser, and work out what your test environment was quietly forgiving
spec: you can serve a page with COOP and COEP headers set
you have read the previous week's syscall inventory for your program

nodes.title: What does it need from a filesystem?
nodes.description: Establish what your program actually requires of a filesystem, then break a filesystem that looks correct
spec: you can write a small conformance test against a real POSIX system first
you know whether anything other than your program reads its files

nodes.title: What does it talk to?
nodes.description: Inventory your program's network requirements, then find out which of them a browser can actually satisfy and what the rest would cost
spec: you can read a request and response in full, headers included
you bring a list of every host, port and protocol your program contacts

nodes.title: Could it run unmodified?
nodes.description: Establish what it would take to run your target as a binary rather than as source, and price the answer
spec: you can obtain or cross-compile a build of your target for another architecture
you know from week 5 what your target asks the kernel for

nodes.title: Measuring a kernel
nodes.description: Take your own numbers off a prepared machine, then work out what a whole operating system would cost your target
spec: you arrive with the cost estimates you have made for at least two other approaches

nodes.title: The rendering path
nodes.description: Trace a pixel from a program to the screen, and find out what a committed approach leaves you able to draw with
spec: you can say which approach you committed to in Assignment 2
you bring something that draws, even if it is not your target

nodes.title: Defending the commitment
nodes.description: Present the approach you committed to and have it attacked by people who committed to something else
spec: you can state your commitment in one sentence and its cost in numbers
you have re-read your own Assignment 1 and know where it was wrong

nodes.title: Assignment 1: The reduction
nodes.description: Choose a target, establish what it actually requires, and reduce the option space to the ones worth attempting — with reasons
spec: a target is named, and its requirements are established from evidence rather than assumption
every option is addressed, including the ones you discard immediately
each reduction gives a reason that is a trade-off, not a claim of impossibility
the reasoning is recorded well enough that you could disagree with it in week 12

nodes.title: Assignment 2: The commitment
nodes.description: Build enough of at least two approaches to measure them, then commit to one and show what closed the decision
spec: at least two approaches are built far enough to produce real measurements
each experiment distinguishes between stated alternatives rather than demonstrating one
measurements are reproducible, and the conditions they were taken under are stated
a commitment is made, and the evidence that closed it is identified

nodes.title: Assignment 3: The re-opening
nodes.description: Give yourself a new requirement, work out what it does to the approach you committed to, and grade your own Assignment 1 against what you now know
spec: a new requirement is chosen, stated plainly, and is one a real user could ask for
its effect on the committed approach is worked out, including what must be discarded
Assignment 1 is audited against what is now known, naming what was wrong and when it became knowable
the cost of changing approach is estimated, and the estimate is grounded in your own measurements

criteria.name: Difficulty and handling of the adjustment

nodes.title: Running code in the browser
nodes.description: Thirty years of running foreign code in a web page, almost all of it the same idea — and the option space that replaced it

nodes.title: Characterising a target
nodes.description: Everything is possible, so the interesting question is what a program actually requires — and how those requirements reduce the set worth attempting

nodes.title: Shims, polyfills and reimplementation
nodes.description: The cheapest option in the course — implement the interface instead of the machine — and the three very different things people mean by it

nodes.title: Compiling for the web
nodes.description: Pure computation compiles and always did. Everything that makes a program useful is an interface, and interfaces are what break a port

nodes.title: The web is not POSIX-compatible (i)
nodes.description: What a kernel-shaped surface has to provide, how much of it the web standards deliver, and what happens when a call is present but wrong

nodes.title: The web is not POSIX-compatible (ii)
nodes.description: A browser is not a multiprocessing operating system, and a runtime that is correct on your desktop will deadlock in a tab

nodes.title: The filesystem
nodes.description: Giving a guest a filesystem is easy. Giving two runtimes the same filesystem is where the design is, and where five good designs went to die

nodes.title: The network
nodes.description: There are no sockets, so you build one out of message passing — and then discover the wall was never TCP

nodes.title: Running "native" binaries
nodes.description: Take the source requirement away entirely — and find that most of the ways to do it are not emulation at all

nodes.title: Running a full OS kernel
nodes.description: Stop faking the kernel and bring one. Two quite different projects hide under that sentence, and only one of them is emulating a machine

nodes.title: Graphics
nodes.description: Of everything an approach quietly decides on your behalf, the rendering path is the least negotiable

nodes.title: Committing, and changing your mind
nodes.description: How to commit on evidence, and why changing your mind here is not an iteration — it is discarding an execution environment
